verdict.summary: All proto-map lookups and indexed accesses are guarded with fail-closed checks (iterator != end, value_size() == 1); attacker-controlled op names and the possibly-unset output are only consumed by code not shown, so no in-code security impact is instantiated.

assumptions: init_op_name out-param is assumed non-NULL by the caller; no assert exists in this code, but no deref of attacker data occurs either.
MetaGraphDef accessors (signature_def, collection_def, node_list, value) are assumed to be safe protobuf accessors as used.
limitations: Attacker-controlled init op name (*init_op_name from proto) is later executed by the caller's session-restore code, which is not shown; impact chain (arbitrary op execution / CWE-78-style) not instantiated in this code.

When the init-op signature is absent and neither collection key is present, the function returns OK without writing *init_op_name; a stale/uninitialized value reaching control flow would be a caller-side defect not shown here.

verdict.summary: This nfs4_file_open implementation mirrors the upstream Linux NFSv4 open path. The only attacker-influenced input, filp->f_flags (openflags), is passed through nfs_check_flags before any use, cannot underflow when decremented ((openflags & 3) == 3 -> 2), and is masked of O_CREAT|O_EXCL before being handed to the callee; it never indexes memory, sizes a copy, or forms a pointer in this code. Both failure-capable callee results are guarded in execution order (err = PTR_ERR(ctx); if (IS_ERR(ctx)) goto out; and if (IS_ERR(inode)) with a switch over err), the open_context-returned inode is identity-checked against d_inode(dentry) before nfs_fscache_open_file uses it, a NULL (non-ERR_PTR) return is caught by the same identity check, dentry/ctx reference counts are balanced on every path, and the stale path fails closed (d_drop + err = -EOPENSTALE) rather than presenting a success state. The remaining concerns (dget_parent on a possibly disconnected dentry, partially initialized struct iattr, callee-side interpretation of openflags) require states or use sites not produced or contained in this code and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: dentry/file_dentry(filp) is a connected, positive cached dentry when this callback runs; the code's comment documents 'We only get this far for a cached positive dentry.', but the connectivity invariant itself is enforced by the VFS/dcache, not by any statement in this code.

alloc_nfs_open_context encodes failure as an ERR_PTR compatible with IS_ERR/PTR_ERR; this is a callee contract, not quotable here (though the IS_ERR guard in this code is the correct handling for that encoding).

NFS_PROTO(dir)->open_context consumes only the struct iattr fields flagged in attr.ia_valid (ATTR_OPEN, optionally ATTR_SIZE with ia_size = 0); fields left uninitialized when O_TRUNC is absent are assumed unused by the callee.
nfs_check_flags validates the openflags bits this code does not strip; the callee is not shown, but this code still guards its own flow: it returns err before any further use on failure.

nfs_file_set_open_context(filp, ctx) takes ownership of a ctx reference, so the subsequent put_nfs_open_context(ctx) on the fall-through success path is a balanced transfer, not a double put; the transfer semantics live in the callee.
limitations: Candidate (speculative, guard absent): parent = dget_parent(dentry); dir = d_inode(parent); has no check that dentry has a distinct parent or that dir is a directory. If the VFS ever invoked ->open on a disconnected (IS_ROOT) dentry, dir would alias the file inode and NFS_PROTO(dir)->open_context would be dispatched with a non-directory. No statement in this code can produce or accept that state (the code documents the cached-positive-dentry precondition), and the harmful dispatch occurs inside the not-shown callee, so the trigger was not instantiable per STEP 4(a)/(d).

Candidate (impact outside given code): struct iattr attr is only partially initialized (attr.ia_valid = ATTR_OPEN; attr.ia_size set only under O_TRUNC) and is passed by address to NFS_PROTO(dir)->open_context. Any read of unset fields happens in the callee, which is not given; the impact chain breaks at an unquoted link.

Candidate (dismissed as non-defect): err = PTR_ERR(ctx) is assigned before the IS_ERR(ctx) test, but every subsequent return path reassigns err (err = PTR_ERR(inode), err = 0, err = -EOPENSTALE) before it is returned, so no uninitialized/garbage error value escapes.

verdict.summary: All string copies into the v4l2_capability fields are bounded by sizes quoted in this code: cap->card is filled via snprintf with labellen = min(sizeof(cap->card), sizeof(dev->card_label)) (guaranteeing NUL termination even for a non-terminated card_label), cap->bus_info via snprintf with sizeof(cap->bus_info) (worst-case expansion of 'platform:v4l2loopback-%03d' exceeds 31 chars only for device numbers with more than 10 digits, where snprintf safely truncates), and cap->driver via strlcpy with its own sizeof. Format strings are constant literals, so no attacker-controlled format or injection sink exists. Capability bits are computed from actual device state with no fail-open path. No guard absence or instantiated memory-safety, injection, or security-state defect remains.

assumptions: The 'cap' pointer passed to this ioctl handler is non-NULL and points to a caller-allocated struct v4l2_capability; this is a v4l2-core contract that cannot be quoted from the given code, but cap is only a destination whose fixed field sizes are used for all bounds.

dev (from v4l2loopback_getdevice(file)) is assumed to be a valid registered device, including dev->vdev being the registered video device whose driver data is the non-NULL v4l2loopback_private struct; this contract is not shown in the given code.
device_nr is assumed to be a small sane device index set at device-creation time; even for extreme values the bounded snprintf only truncates, so this assumption has no memory-safety consequence.
limitations: video_get_drvdata(dev->vdev) is dereferenced without a NULL check (lines 6-7). If drvdata were ever NULL for the device through which this handler is invoked, a kernel NULL-pointer dereference (denial of service) would result. No statement in this code can produce that NULL value, and no quotable contract establishes or excludes it, so the trigger precondition could not be instantiated; recorded as speculative, not a finding.

dev->card_label content is attacker-influenced only by whoever configures the loopback device (module parameter/configfs, a privileged operation outside this code); regardless of content, the copy is bounded by the quoted labellen computation, so no overflow arises from any label content.

verdict.summary: gitn_box_del frees ptr->entries[i].name for every i < ptr->nb_entries with no bound tying nb_entries to the number of allocated/initialized entries; attacker-controlled box content can leave nb_entries larger than the initialized entry count, so a non-NULL uninitialized or out-of-range pointer is passed to gf_free (invalid free / use of uninitialized memory reaching a free).

evidence.reason: The loop trusts attacker-parsed nb_entries verbatim; there is no check in this code bounding nb_entries to the allocated/initialized entry count, and the only guard on the freed value is a NULL test ('if (ptr->entries[i].name)'), which passes for uninitialized garbage. gf_free of such a pointer is an invalid free / use of uninitialized value reaching a free.

assumptions: The entries array and nb_entries are populated by the not-shown ISOBMFF box parser from file content; the parser's allocation and initialization loop cannot be quoted here, so the exact un-initialized-state producer is assumed.
gf_free behaves as a standard free (no quoted zeroing or validation of the pointer in this code).
limitations: The concrete parse-path state (nb_entries incremented past the last initialized entry) is in code not given; the trigger is instantiated only up to the box-parser behavior assumed from this function's role as the deletion handler for parsed box state.

verdict.summary: This function is orchestration-only: it parses bundle data via flatpak_bundle_load and forwards the results (ref, origin, collection_id, gpg_data, basename) into non-shown callees (flatpak_dir_create_origin_remote, flatpak_dir_modify_remote, flatpak_dir_get_deploy_data). No memory access, copy, indexing, size arithmetic, format string, or injection sink operates on attacker data within the given code. The checks this code does perform (metadata NULL, deploy_data NULL, gpg_data NULL in the modify branch, remote NULL, and the four out-pointer NULL guards) are present and correctly ordered on every path. Candidate defects involving unvalidated bundle-derived values (e.g., NULL ref, attacker-chosen origin/collection_id, NULL remote on success) have their harmful uses and impact links entirely inside callees not given, so their triggers cannot be instantiated with quoted statements in this code; they are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: flatpak_bundle_load is assumed to return non-NULL metadata only together with valid non-NULL ref/origin/to_checksum; no statement in this code asserts or checks this contract (only 'if (metadata == NULL) return NULL;' is present, which checks metadata, not ref).
flatpak_deploy_data_get_origin is assumed to return a non-NULL origin for a successfully found deploy_data; this code does not test the returned origin before g_strdup or the final return.
flatpak_dir_create_origin_remote is assumed to accept a NULL gpg_data (in the else branch it is passed unconditionally, unlike the modify branch which is guarded by 'if (gpg_data != NULL)').

flatpak_dir_ensure_repo, flatpak_dir_get_deploy_data, flatpak_decomposed_dup_id, flatpak_decomposed_get_ref, and g_file_get_basename are assumed to handle the passed values safely; none of their contracts are quotable from this code.
The deployment context (who can invoke this function, privilege level of the FlatpakDir) is not expressed in the given code and was not used to promote or demote any candidate.
limitations: Unvalidated bundle-derived 'origin' and 'collection_id' from flatpak_bundle_load are passed to flatpak_dir_create_origin_remote; if that callee builds remote configuration, URLs, or keyring state from them without validation, a malicious bundle could influence update sources or remote identity. The harmful use and impact chain are inside the not-shown callee, so this could not be confirmed in this code (candidate C2).

If flatpak_bundle_load can succeed with a NULL 'ref', flatpak_decomposed_dup_id(ref) and flatpak_dir_get_deploy_data(self, ref, ...) receive NULL; the dereference occurs inside non-shown callees (candidate C1).

If flatpak_deploy_data_get_origin returns NULL for an existing deployment, 'remote' becomes NULL and is returned via 'return g_steal_pointer (&remote);' on a path where out_ref/out_checksum/out_metadata were already set — a NULL return on a partially-successful path; the NULL-producing condition and the caller's reaction are both outside this code (candidate C3).

In the else branch, 'gpg_data' (possibly NULL when extra_gpg_data is NULL and the bundle contains no keyring) is passed unconditionally to flatpak_dir_create_origin_remote; NULL handling is a callee question (candidate C4).

Attacker-derived values (origin, basename, collection_id) reach remote-configuration callees from an intake point for untrusted bundle content; if a future audit of those callees shows unsafe use, this call boundary is where the unvalidated data crosses into configuration construction.

verdict.summary: GetHintFormat dereferences hmhd (hmhd->type) before the NULL check; InfoHeader is attacker-controlled parsed-file state that can be NULL, so the dereference at line 4 crashes the parsing process while the intended !hmhd guards at lines 7/9 are unreachable dead code. Attacker-triggerable denial of service via a crafted file.

evidence.reason: Use-before-check NULL pointer dereference: hmhd is assigned from trak->Media->information->InfoHeader (parsed untrusted file state with no non-NULL guarantee in this code) and immediately dereferenced at 'hmhd->type' on line 4. The NULL guard 'if (!hmhd || !hmhd->subType)' on line 7 executes only after the dereference, so it is dead code for the NULL case; the crash (NULL+offset dereference) occurs before any check. Trigger: crafted media file whose track has InfoHeader == NULL.

assumptions: The GPAC IsoMedia API is assumed to expose GetHintFormat to callers processing untrusted (file/network) media, per its signature consuming parsed GF_TrackBox state; this matches the function's own NULL-handling branches which treat InfoHeader == NULL as a reachable value.
GF_Box-derived boxes share a leading u32 'type' field, so the pre-validation read hmhd->type at a common offset does not itself constitute an out-of-bounds access.
limitations: Secondary unguarded dereference chain at line 8: 'trak->Media->information->sampleTable->SampleDescription->child_boxes' — sampleTable/SampleDescription are not NULL-checked. Same CWE-476 class, but the exact parser condition leaving them NULL is not shown in this code, so it is recorded rather than confirmed as a separate primary finding.

Type confusion via the cast of InfoHeader to GF_HintMediaHeaderBox* was examined and rejected: only the shared leading 'type' field is read before validation, and deeper fields (subType) are read only after the type check confirms the object is an HMHD box.

verdict.summary: gitn_box_del performs correctly with respect to the state it can observe: a NULL guard on line 5 covers all paths, the entries-NULL check at line 6 skips the loop and both frees safely, the inner-pointer/array/struct free order is correct, and the loop bound i<nb_entries is the only size variable this code sees. The dangerous pattern (freeing ptr->entries[i].name for i up to nb_entries when the entries array was allocated for fewer elements, yielding an out-of-bounds read and potentially an arbitrary free) requires a mismatch between nb_entries and the allocation size that no statement in this given code can produce — the allocation is performed in the not-shown box reader. That trigger is therefore speculative here and is recorded as a limitation, not a finding in this code.

assumptions: The caller passes a GroupIdToNameBox* (the downcast (GroupIdToNameBox *)s is unchecked here; the type fidelity is enforced by the caller/box-dispatch table, which is not shown).

ptr->entries and ptr->nb_entries were produced by the (not-shown) parsing routine; this code contains no statement asserting the invariant entries-allocated-size >= nb_entries, so that invariant is an assumption, not a quotable contract.
gf_free is a correct free wrapper and a single invocation of gitn_box_del is assumed (nothing here prevents a caller-invoked double free, but nothing here produces one either).
limitations: Potential out-of-bounds read of ptr->entries[i] and free of an out-of-bounds ptr->entries[i].name if ptr->nb_entries exceeds the allocated array size (CWE-125/CWE-787 pattern). The mismatch state can only be created by the not-shown reader (e.g., an allocation-size integer overflow in gitn_box_read); no statement in the given code allocates, resizes, or assigns nb_entries, so the trigger precondition could not be instantiated in this code and the defect is not attributed here.
Double-free of ptr or ptr->entries if gitn_box_del is invoked twice on the same box; the second invocation is purely caller behavior, not producible from statements in this code.
Type confusion on the (GroupIdToNameBox *)s downcast if the dispatcher ever passes a different box type; not checkable from the given code.

verdict.summary: All attacker-data sinks in this function are guarded by quoted, execution-order-verified checks: `node.input_size() > 0` protects the `node.input(0)` access, `IsTensorIdControlling(tensor_id)` rejects control-input sentinels before lookup, and the `input_node == nullptr` check precedes the only dereference `IsSwitch(*input_node)` with no intervening branch or mutation. Every error arm fails closed (`return false`), so no security-state misrepresentation or fail-open path exists. The one unvalidated value — the result of ParseTensorName — is only ever used as a lookup key whose miss is null-checked; any abort/CHECK-failure on malformed names would occur inside the not-shown callee and is recorded as a limitation, not a vulnerability in this code.

assumptions: Deployment context (whether this runs in a setuid tool, daemon, or library) is not derivable from the code and was not used in the judgment.
Semantics of IsIdentity, IsIdentityNSingleInput, and IsSwitch are not shown; they are treated as pure classification predicates that do not consume memory-unsafe values in this code.

GraphDefs are commonly deserialized from untrusted model files, so node.input(0) was treated as attacker-data throughout; this treats the data maximally as untrusted and does not demote any candidate.
limitations: ParseTensorName (callee not shown) may CHECK-fail or abort on malformed input strings (e.g., "^" alone, "a:b:c", or an empty string). Since node.input(0) is attacker-controlled serialized model content, such an abort could be a denial of service — but the defective statement lies entirely inside the not-shown callee and its existence cannot be quoted from the given code, so the trigger is speculative here.

The result of ParseTensorName is consumed without an explicit parse-success check in this code. If the callee returned a failure sentinel (e.g., empty node name), the value would reach graph.GetNode; a lookup miss is handled by the quoted `if (input_node == nullptr) return false;` guard, but behavior of GetNode on degenerate names (e.g., crash on empty string) cannot be verified because GetNode is not shown.
No race-condition window exists in this code (const reference, no mutation between null check and dereference), but thread-safety of the caller's use of MutableGraphView is not shown.

verdict.summary: GetInitOp dereferences the iterator returned by an unchecked inner map lookup: when an attacker-controlled MetaGraphDef (parsed from an untrusted saved-model file) contains a signature_def entry keyed kSavedModelInitOpSignatureKey whose outputs() map lacks that key, outputs().find() returns end() and '->second.name()' (line 7-9) dereferences the end iterator, an out-of-bounds/undefined read that crashes or reads invalid memory in the process loading the model. No check of the inner find result exists anywhere in the function, in contrast to the outer find (line 6) and the collection path (lines 23-24), which are both guarded and edge-tested safe.

evidence.reason: The outer lookup is guarded (line 6), but the inner outputs().find(kSavedModelInitOpSignatureKey) result is dereferenced with '->second.name()' without any comparison to end(). Trigger: attacker supplies a MetaGraphDef whose signature_def contains the key kSavedModelInitOpSignatureKey but whose SignatureDef outputs() map is empty or lacks that key; the inner find returns end() and the dereference at line 9 performs an out-of-bounds/undefined read (typically SIGSEGV) in the model-loading process. No fix form (end()-check, count(), HasKey, checked accessor, default arm) exists on any path to this sink in the given code.

evidence.snippet:
const auto& init_op_sig_it =
      meta_graph_def.signature_def().find(kSavedModelInitOpSignatureKey);
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted control value: meta_graph_def is a content-bearing parameter of this non-static entry point (serialized/model state), so the presence/absence of the signature key and the contents of the resulting SignatureDef (including its empty outputs() map) are attacker-controlled, which is what makes the unguarded inner find at lines 7-9 return end().

assumptions: meta_graph_def is treated as untrusted serialized/model state per the data-origin impact model (discipline 3), since it is a content-bearing parameter of a non-static function; no deployment context is assumed.

init_op_name is assumed non-NULL as the code's own output-parameter convention; the code contains no assert or documented precondition quoting this, but no path in this code dereferences it conditionally on attacker data.
limitations: If neither kSavedModelMainOpKey nor kSavedModelLegacyInitOpKey is present in collection_def (line 23 false), the function returns Status::OK() without writing *init_op_name; whether a caller relies on the value being set on OK is not shown in this code, so no finding is made here.
export_dir is concatenated into an error string (line 26) with no format-string/command/SQL sink in this code; no injection finding.

The value(0) read at line 28 is safe: the guard at line 24 ('node_list().value_size() != 1') rejects sizes 0 and >=2, including the case where the CollectionDef oneof kind is not NodeList (default empty message, size 0), and lies on the only path to the sink.

verdict.summary: IsIdentityConsumingSwitch dereferences the raw pointer returned by graph.GetNode(tensor_id.node()) without a null check. The node name comes from the attacker-controlled input string node.input(0) (parsed serialized graph/model content), and when that name does not match any node in the graph, GetNode's not-found sentinel (nullptr) is passed directly to IsSwitch(*input_node), causing a null-pointer dereference and process crash — a denial of service reachable by any party that can supply a malformed GraphDef.

evidence.snippet:
NodeDef* input_node = graph.GetNode(tensor_id.node());
    return IsSwitch(*input_node);
evidence.reason: The lookup `graph.GetNode(tensor_id.node())` can return its not-found sentinel (nullptr) because tensor_id.node() is derived from the attacker-controlled string node.input(0) and nothing in this code requires the referenced name to exist in the graph. The result is dereferenced unconditionally at `IsSwitch(*input_node)` with no intervening null check, default arm, or checked accessor — verified absent by exhaustive search of all fix forms. Trigger: an Identity node whose input(0) is "ghost_node:0" where ghost_node is absent from the graph → input_node == nullptr → *nullptr dereference → crash.

evidence.snippet:
TensorId tensor_id = ParseTensorName(node.input(0));
    if (IsTensorIdControlling(tensor_id)) {
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: node.input(0) is attacker-controlled content from the parsed node definition, and ParseTensorName produces the node-name string later used as the GetNode lookup key. The only guard, IsTensorIdControlling, filters control ('^') inputs only; it does not validate that the parsed name references an existing node, so a dangling name flows unvalidated to the dereference at line 11.

assumptions: graph.GetNode(name) returns nullptr when the name is not present in the graph (callee not shown); this is the standard failure sentinel of a name-based lookup, and the defect is this code's failure to test it before dereferencing.
IsIdentity, IsIdentityNSingleInput, IsTensorIdControlling, and IsSwitch behave per their names; none of them are claimed as guards for the not-found case.

NodeDefs / MutableGraphView originate from serialized model/graph content that can cross a trust boundary (untrusted saved models or remotely supplied graphs); no deployment context is used to reach this conclusion — the input strings themselves are attacker-data at this entry point.
limitations: No other sink (allocation sizing, copy lengths, format strings, injection, crypto, authz) exists in this six-statement function, so no further candidates were generated.

verdict.summary: GetHintFormat dereferences the parser-supplied track structure 'trak->Media->information->sampleTable->SampleDescription' (line 8) without any NULL check on sampleTable or SampleDescription. The only NULL guards in the function ('!hmhd' at lines 4, 7, 9) provably guard the wrong variable: hmhd is already known non-NULL at line 7 because lines 4-5 return early, making the line 7 and 9 checks dead. A crafted MP4 containing a hint track (hmhd present with matching type, subType == 0, but no stbl/stsd box) drives execution into the line 7 branch and dereferences a NULL sampleTable pointer at line 8, crashing the process that parsed the untrusted file — a denial-of-service vulnerability at a file-format trust boundary.

evidence.reason: Root cause: unguarded NULL-pointer dereference. Line 8 dereferences trak->Media->information->sampleTable and ->SampleDescription with no NULL check anywhere in the function; the '!hmhd' checks at lines 7 and 9 test a different variable that is already guaranteed non-NULL by the early return at lines 4-5, so they cannot protect this sink. Instantiated trigger: a hint track parsed from an attacker-supplied file with a valid hmhd (type == GF_ISOM_BOX_TYPE_HMHD so line 4 does not return), hmhd->subType == 0 (the code's own 'unset' sentinel, entering the branch at line 7), and a missing sample table (no statement in this code creates or checks sampleTable) — execution reaches line 8, reads sampleTable as NULL, and dereferences NULL->SampleDescription, terminating the process that consumed the untrusted file (denial of service).

assumptions: trak and its Media/information/InfoHeader/sampleTable/SampleDescription fields are populated by an ISO-BMFF parser that is not part of the given code; their values are treated as attacker-data per the data-origin model (serialized/model state from file content), not as trusted.

GF_HintMediaHeaderBox::subType is a field whose 0 value means 'unset'; the code's own branch at line 7 encodes this, and no other assignment to subType exists before this point except the parse (not shown).
gf_list_get(list, 0) returns NULL for an empty list (handled by the 'if (a)' guard at line 10).
limitations: The producibility of a NULL sampleTable/SampleDescription depends on the not-shown parser accepting a minf without stbl (or stbl without stsd); no statement in the given code prevents this, so per guard-anchoring the candidate stands, but this unshown link is why confidence is 0.7 rather than higher.

The unchecked dereferences of trak->Media and trak->Media->information at line 3 are the same defect class (unvalidated parser-supplied pointers) but are not separately evidenced; the primary finding at line 8 subsumes the root cause.

The type-confusion concern from casting InfoHeader to GF_HintMediaHeaderBox* is dismissed by the quoted guard at lines 4-5 ('if (!hmhd || (hmhd->type != GF_ISOM_BOX_TYPE_HMHD)) return 0;'), which lies on every path and precedes every hmhd field use.
Worst-case impact is process termination (crash/DoS) via a wild dereference of a NULL-derived pointer; no memory-corruption write primitive was identified in this function.

verdict.summary: The function's own statements are guarded: the size check `if (alloc_size <= 0) return NULL;` (line 3) rejects non-positive computed byte counts before malloc, the malloc NULL sentinel is tested at line 5 before the first dereference, and the only write, `ret->size = size;` (line 6), is within the allocation for every alloc_size this code can produce. The plausible defect — integer overflow/narrowing in the size-to-bytes computation at line 2 causing under-allocation and a misrepresenting ret->size — cannot be instantiated: the arithmetic of TfLiteIntArrayGetSizeInBytes and its return width are not shown, and the out-of-bounds use of any mis-sized array lies in consumers not given. Both trigger and impact chain break at unquoted links, so no vulnerability is confirmed in this code alone.

assumptions: The implementation and return type of TfLiteIntArrayGetSizeInBytes are not shown; whether it can overflow, wrap, or truncate for large or negative `size` cannot be quoted from the given code, so neither a safe nor an unsafe reading can be anchored.

The layout of TfLiteIntArray (size of the header, presence of a trailing flexible data[]) is assumed from context but not quotable from the given code; it affects whether the line-6 write could ever exceed a minimal allocation.
The entry point's reachability by an attacker (who can call TfLiteIntArrayCreate and with what `size` values) is a deployment property not stated in the code.
limitations: C1 (not recorded as a finding): `int alloc_size = TfLiteIntArrayGetSizeInBytes(size);` (line 2) — if the callee computes the byte count in a wider type (e.g., size_t) or overflows for size near 2^30, the narrowing assignment can yield a small positive alloc_size that passes the line-3 check, causing under-allocation at line 4; `ret->size = size;` (line 6) would then misrepresent capacity. Trigger could not be instantiated (callee arithmetic/return width unquotable), and the resulting out-of-bounds read/write of the data array occurs entirely in consumers not given.

C2 (not recorded): a negative `size` is only rejected if the unshown callee maps it to a non-positive byte count; if it did not, line 6 would stamp a negative ret->size. Producing branch not instantiable from given code; harmful use in not-shown consumers.
C3 (not recorded): the line-6 write would be out-of-bounds only for alloc_size in {1,2,3}; no statement in this code can produce such a value without assuming unshown callee behavior.

verdict.summary: BiasAndClamp validates the relationship between array_size and bias_size only with a debug-compiled-out TFLITE_DCHECK_EQ and performs no runtime check that bias_size > 0 or array_size >= 0. With attacker-controlled sizes (e.g., array_size=10, bias_size=7), the non-NEON loop writes up to bias_size-1 floats past the end of array_data (array_data[7..13] for a 10-element buffer), and the NEON loop's 'array_ptr != array_end_ptr' termination never fires, producing an unbounded out-of-bounds read/write walk. bias_size <= 0 additionally causes a non-terminating loop (and division by zero inside the DCHECK itself in debug builds). Line count verified: line 9 is the DCHECK, lines 57-61 are the non-NEON sink.

evidence.reason: The only validation of the attacker-controlled sizes is a debug-only DCHECK (a no-op in release builds), and it covers neither bias_size > 0 nor array_size >= 0. The NEON loop terminates on pointer inequality ('array_ptr != array_end_ptr') with stride bias_size: with array_size=10, bias_size=7 the pointer takes values +0, +7, +14, ... and never equals data+10, so vld1q/vst1q at lines 38-41 and the scalar store at line 52 read and write past the buffer forever; with array_size < 0 the end pointer starts behind array_ptr and the loop likewise never terminates. Missing-check site at line 9 plus the faulty loop head at line 15.

Out-of-bounds write sink (non-NEON path). The outer bound tests only array_offset < array_size; it does not bound array_offset + i. Trigger simulated with bias_size=7, array_size=10 (10-float buffer): iteration at array_offset=7 passes '7 < 10', the inner loop runs i=0..6, and the store writes array_data[7..13] — indices 10..13 lie past the end of the buffer. No check, clamp, or residual bound (min(bias_size, array_size - array_offset)) exists anywhere on any path; additionally bias_size=0 makes array_offset never advance, yielding a non-terminating loop (denial of service).

assumptions: TFLITE_DCHECK_EQ is a debug-only macro that compiles to a no-op in release (NDEBUG) builds; this is standard TFLite macro semantics, not quotable from the given code, but line 9 is the only candidate guard and it performs no control-flow rejection even when active.
array_data is assumed to hold exactly array_size floats and bias_data exactly bias_size floats, per parameter naming; no statement in this code enforces or documents this sizing contract.

The release context (production inference server loading untrusted models) is not shown; per discipline 3, judgment rests solely on the fact that these are content/size parameters of a non-static exported function, hence attacker-data.
USE_NEON is a compile-time branch; at least one of the two paths is always compiled, and both are defective.
limitations: If the divisibility precondition array_size % bias_size == 0 were treated as an interface contract documented by line 9's DCHECK, candidate C1/C2's non-divisible trigger would weaken to a caller-contract violation; however, the DCHECK is not an enforcement in release builds and covers neither bias_size <= 0 (non-terminating loop, division by zero in the DCHECK itself) nor array_size < 0 (NEON unbounded walk), so the missing-validation defect stands regardless.

The precise upstream origin of bias_size/array_size (tensor shape computation in callers) is not shown; the values are treated as attacker-data per discipline 3 rather than traced to a concrete untrusted parse in this code.
The scalar helper ActivationFunctionWithMinMax is not shown, but it only receives already-clamped floats, so its internals cannot affect the bounds analysis.

verdict.summary: In vidioc_querycap, dev->card_label is passed as the snprintf FORMAT argument at line 14 instead of as a '%s' conversion argument. No statement in this code constrains or sanitizes the label content, so any '%' directive in the configured device label is interpreted by the kernel's vsnprintf against zero supplied variadic arguments, consuming kernel stack/register values and copying them into the capability buffer returned to the unprivileged VIDIOC_QUERYCAP caller (kernel information disclosure), and can fault the kernel. The correct pattern (literal format, variable as argument) is used for bus_info two lines below, confirming the misuse.

evidence.reason: Root cause: dev->card_label is used as the format string of snprintf instead of being passed as a %s argument. The label's content is unconstrained device configuration (no check, assert, or escape anywhere in this function), so a label containing '%' makes the kernel format interpreter consume variadic arguments that were never supplied, leaking kernel stack contents into cap->card — the buffer VIDIOC_QUERYCAP returns to userspace. Line 15-16 shows the correct pattern, proving the argument misuse at line 14.

Taint origin: the device object whose card_label content (set by external configuration, unconstrained by any statement in this code) flows to the format-string sink at line 14; labellen only bounds the destination size and does not constrain the label's content.

assumptions: dev->vdev and the video_get_drvdata() result (line 9) are assumed non-NULL by the kernel V4L2 framework; this code neither checks nor documents it, but no attacker-content value reaches that dereference.
device_nr is assumed to be a small non-negative integer; it is used only as a %03d argument, never as a format, so width/truncation has no security effect.

The V4L2 core copies cap to the ioctl caller's userspace after this handler returns; the exact copy site is framework code not shown, but the buffer's role as the querycap response is the function's documented purpose.
limitations: Exploitation requires the configured card_label to contain a '%' directive; the code that sets card_label is not shown, and no statement in this code restricts its content, so the precondition is treated as within the input surface rather than speculative.

%n-based writes are refused by modern kernel vsnprintf, so the write-primitive form of this format-string bug is limited to older kernels; the disclosure (reading unsupplied arguments) persists on current kernels.

verdict.summary: MakeDataset validates the shapes of the attacker-supplied 'indices' and 'dense_shape' tensors but never validates their element type, then unconditionally interprets them as int64 via indices->matrix<int64_t>()(i, 0) and dense_shape->vec<int64_t>(). An attacker who supplies these op inputs with a different dtype (e.g. int32) reaches the typed access with no dtype check on any path, causing a process abort (denial of service) or misinterpreted reads in the process executing the graph.

evidence.reason: The loop at line 43 bounds i against indices->dim_size(0), but the typed access indices->matrix<int64_t>() at line 44 assumes the attacker-controlled tensor's dtype is DT_INT64. No OP_REQUIRES on indices->dtype() (or any equivalent range/default/error arm) exists anywhere on any path in this function; a caller supplying an int32 indices matrix passes every shape check (lines 11-31) and reaches this typed access, whose type mismatch aborts or misreads the process executing the op.

Same root cause for the second attacker-controlled input: dense_shape is consumed as dense_shape->vec<int64_t>() with no dtype check in this function (only its shape is validated at lines 17-19 and 27-31, and NumElements > 0 at line 32), so a non-int64 dense_shape tensor reaches the int64 typed access here without validation.

assumptions: The behavior of Tensor::matrix<int64_t>()/vec<int64_t>() on a tensor of a different dtype is not shown in the given code; the conservative impact modeled is a CHECK-style abort (denial of service). If the type check is DCHECK-only in the build in question, the defect escalates to type-confused reads.
sparse::SparseTensor::Create is assumed to validate full row-major ordering of indices and the non-negativity of dense_shape dims; that validation is inside a callee not shown.
The op's registered input dtypes (whether the framework constrains indices/dense_shape to int64 at registration) are not shown in the given code and cannot be used to dismiss the candidate.
limitations: Out-of-bounds read of indices(i,0) was dismissed: line 43's loop bound 'i < indices->dim_size(0)' together with the matrix check (line 11) and the size-match check forcing dim_size(1) >= 1 (lines 27-31) guard both indices on every iteration.
Negative/huge dense_shape element values are consumed inside TensorShape/SparseTensor::Create (callee not shown); no unvalidated use of those values occurs in this function's own statements.

verdict.summary: In gf_odf_av1_cfg_read_bs_size, the declared payload length 'size' (u32, attacker-controlled box size) is only tested against zero before 'size -= 4' is executed. When size is 1, 2, or 3, the subtraction wraps to ~0xFFFFFFFF, and the 'while (size)' loop then parses, allocates, copies and retains OBU data far beyond the declared config extent, since the in-loop 'size<obu_size' guard is evaluated against the wrapped value and sits after the OBU has already been stored. The parser is the intake point for this container data, so the missing size>=4 validation is the vulnerability.

evidence.snippet:
size -= 4;

	while (size) {
evidence.reason: Root cause: u32 underflow. With attacker-supplied size=3 (never rejected; the only prior checks 'if (!size) ...' and 'if (!size) return NULL;' test only zero), 'size -= 4' yields 0xFFFFFFFF. The loop bound 'while (size)' then treats ~4 billion bytes as remaining, and the guard 'if (size<obu_size)' inside the loop compares against the wrapped value, so OBUs lying beyond the declared config extent are parsed (gf_av1_parse_obu), malloc'd, copied via gf_bs_read_data, and appended to cfg->obu_array before any bound is considered. No check anywhere on any path requires size >= 4 before the subtraction.

Origin of the tainted value: 'size' is an attacker-data parameter (box payload size from the container being parsed). The only statements touching it before the underflow are these two zero-tests; neither rejects the undersized values 1..3 that trigger the wrap at 'size -= 4'.

assumptions: gf_bs_read_int/gf_bs_read_data/gf_bs_available/gf_bs_seek are assumed to be bounds-safe against their own backing buffer; their implementations are not shown, so the absolute memory ceiling of reading past the declared size cannot be quoted.

gf_av1_parse_obu's internal handling of obu_size (whether it can return GF_OK with obu_size 0 or set obu_size inconsistently with consumed bytes) is not shown; the 'assert(obu_size == gf_bs_get_position(bs) - pos)' is compiled out under NDEBUG and enforces nothing in release.
gf_odf_av1_cfg_new is assumed to return non-NULL under normal allocation; its result is not checked before 'state.config = cfg' and the first field write.
limitations: Possible non-terminating loop / unbounded list growth if gf_av1_parse_obu returns GF_OK with obu_size == 0: speculative, since it depends on callee behavior that cannot be quoted from this code.
NULL dereference of cfg if gf_odf_av1_cfg_new fails: requires an allocation failure no attacker can deterministically induce; robustness, not a security finding.

The 'Forwarding' GF_LOG call passes one argument (pos) for three format conversions (%u, LLU, LLU) — a varargs mismatch producing garbage debug output, but the format string is constant, so there is no attacker-controlled format-string injection.

The (u32) cast of gf_bs_available(bs) can itself truncate a >4GB stream to a small value (including 1..3), reproducing the same underflow; this is an alternate instantiation of the same primary defect, not a separate finding.

verdict.summary: RepeatedAttrDefEqual detects duplicate AttrDef names in a1 (lines 6-8) but only logs the error and does not return false; the subsequent map assignment at line 10 overwrites the earlier entry, silently discarding the conflicting AttrDef. As a result the function can return true (the 'equal' verdict) for repeated fields that are not equal — e.g. a1 = [{name:x, type:T1}, {name:x, type:T2}] versus a2 = [{name:x, type:T2}] returns true — a fail-open misrepresentation of the verified/equal state on an explicitly detected error path.

evidence.reason: Duplicate names in a1 are detected (find() succeeds) but the branch only emits LOG(ERROR) and falls through; no return false, exception, flag, or count check exists anywhere in the function. Line 10 then overwrites the previous map entry, so all but the last AttrDef sharing a name become unobservable, and the final 'if (!a1_set.empty()) return false;' cannot detect the collapse. Simulated trigger: a1 = [{name:x,type:T1},{name:x,type:T2}], a2 = [{name:x,type:T2}] — iteration 2 takes the LOG(ERROR) branch, line 10 stores &A2 discarding A1, the a2 loop matches A2, the map ends empty, and line 19 returns true, presenting the 'equal' verdict for unequal inputs carrying explicitly detected invalid data.

evidence.snippet:
if (!a1_set.empty()) return false;
  return true;
evidence.reason: The only post-loop verification is a name-set emptiness check; after the duplicate-name overwrite at line 10 it is satisfied even when the two repeated fields differ in size and content, so line 19 emits the equal/verified state on the error path instantiated above.

assumptions: AttrDefEqual is not shown; its correctness is assumed. The arguments passed to it in this code (a dereference of a stored pointer into the never-modified const container a1, and a loop reference into const a2) are in-domain, so no defect is attributed to this code for that call.

a1 and a2 are treated as attacker-data per the data-origin model because no documented caller contract about their content is quotable in the given code; the concrete downstream consumer of the returned bool (e.g., op-compatibility validation) is outside this code.
std::unordered_map and protobuf string handling are assumed to be memory-safe library implementations.
limitations: The concrete exploitation of the bogus 'true' verdict (what the caller accepts or registers as a consequence) is not shown in the given code; the confirmed defect is the fail-open equality misrepresentation inside this function itself.
No memory-safety defect found: all stored pointers reference elements of a const container never mutated in this code, and no raw indexing, copying, or format-string sink exists here.
No attacker-scalable amplification found: map work is proportional to input size.

verdict.summary: ReadPSDChannelPixels reads PSD channel data through the pointer p (= pixels) for exactly image->columns iterations, advancing 1, 2, or 4 bytes per iteration via *p++ / PushShortPixel / PushFloatPixel, with no bound on the source buffer: the function receives no length parameter and contains no check relating p to the end of the data. Because image->columns, image->depth (hence packet_size), and the pixel buffer content all derive from the parsed PSD file, a file declaring more columns than the supplied (decompressed) channel data contains drives out-of-bounds heap reads of attacker-scalable extent (columns * packet_size bytes), with the over-read bytes decoded into output pixels (information disclosure) or causing a crash in the decoding process.

evidence.reason: Root cause: out-of-bounds read. The loop bound is the attacker-controlled header field image->columns, not the size of the buffer pixels points to; p advances by 1, 2 (PushShortPixel, line 39), or 4 (PushFloatPixel, line 47) bytes every iteration, and no statement in the function compares p against any end/length (no length parameter exists). Trigger: a PSD with columns=1024, depth=8 (packet_size=1) and a 16-byte channel buffer makes iteration x=16 execute *p++ reading pixels[16], out of bounds, and continues to pixels[1023]; the bytes read are stored into the decoded image via SetPSDPixel (lines 52/66), leaking heap contents or crashing the decoder.

Taint origin and setup: p is initialized from the unvalidated file-derived buffer pixels (parameter, line 3, with no accompanying size), and the only guard present (q == NULL, lines 28-29) protects the destination pixel queue q, not the source pointer p. packet_size is selected from image->depth-derived state (GetPSDPacketSize) with no relation to the amount of data actually available, fixing the per-iteration over-read stride at 1, 2, or 4 bytes for image->columns iterations.

assumptions: The pointer pixels is assumed to reference the decompressed PSD channel data buffer supplied by the calling PSD reader; the buffer's allocated length is not expressed anywhere in this function's interface (no size parameter), so no caller-side bound can be quoted from the given code.

GetPSDPacketSize, PushShortPixel, PushFloatPixel, SetPSDPixel, GetAuthenticPixels, GetAuthenticIndexQueue, and SyncAuthenticPixels are callees not shown; their internal behavior (e.g., that PushShortPixel reads exactly 2 bytes and PushFloatPixel exactly 4 bytes, and that GetPSDPacketSize returns 1/2/other based on image->depth) is inferred from usage, not quoted.
limitations: row and type parameters are forwarded to GetAuthenticPixels and SetPSDPixel without local validation; any harmful use of an out-of-range row would occur inside the not-shown callee, so it could not be instantiated here (contract question, not a finding in this code).

indexes = GetAuthenticIndexQueue(image) (line 30) is not NULL-checked before use at lines 52 and 66; the callee's guarantee that a non-NULL queue exists for the image could not be quoted, and a NULL-producing path could not be simulated without the callee, so this remains speculative.

The exact disclosure impact (heap bytes rendered as decoded pixels) depends on the decoded image later being viewed/exported, which happens outside this function; the direct, fully-quoted consequence here is the out-of-bounds read itself of attacker-chosen extent.

verdict.summary: BiasAndClamp enforces its critical invariant (array_size must be a positive multiple of bias_size) only with TFLITE_DCHECK_EQ, which is compiled out in release builds and passes negative divisors that divide evenly. With model-controlled tensor dimensions (untrusted serialized state) where array_size % bias_size != 0, both code paths write past the end of the array buffer: the non-NEON path performs a bounded heap out-of-bounds write (final block writes up to bias_size-1 elements past array_size), and the NEON path uses an equality loop test (array_ptr != array_end_ptr) with stride bias_size, so the pointer skips past the end and the loop never terminates, producing an unbounded out-of-bounds read/write walk over the heap with attacker-influenced clamped bias values. Negative bias_size additionally causes an infinite loop (hang) even when the DCHECK passes.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the divisibility invariant is asserted only via TFLITE_DCHECK_EQ, a debug-only no-op in release, which also passes negative bias_size values that divide array_size evenly (e.g., 8 % -4 == 0). The NEON loop terminates on equality (array_ptr != array_end_ptr) with attacker-controlled stride bias_size: when array_size % bias_size != 0 the pointer skips past array_end_ptr and the loop never stops, so every subsequent iteration reads and writes out of bounds. No runtime check of bias_size range, divisibility, or array_size exists on any path.

Sink of the out-of-bounds write. Simulated trigger: array_size=10, bias_size=4 (model-controlled). Third outer iteration has array_ptr = array_data+8 (8 != end=10); the 4-wide loop loads vld1q_f32(array_ptr + 8) reading offsets 10-11 past the 10-element buffer and vst1q_f32(array_ptr + 8, x) writes offsets 10-11 out of bounds with attacker-influenced clamped values; array_ptr then advances to +12, never equals +10, and the loop continues corrupting heap memory indefinitely.

Non-NEON sink: the outer bound array_offset < array_size checks only the start of each bias_size-sized block, never array_offset + i. With array_size=10, bias_size=4, the final block at array_offset=8 writes array_data[8..11], a 2-float heap out-of-bounds write past the 10-element output tensor. Negative bias_size also makes array_offset += bias_size decrease indefinitely, an infinite loop (hang) on model-controlled input.

Origin of the attacker-data: bias_size and array_size are 32-bit int parameters derived from tensor shapes of a loaded model (untrusted serialized state), and the only entry guard is the zero check for bias_size — it does not reject negative bias_size nor non-divisible size pairs, allowing the OOB triggers above.

assumptions: TFLITE_DCHECK_EQ is a debug assertion that is compiled out when NDEBUG is defined (release builds); this is the standard TFLite macro semantics, not quotable from the given snippet itself.

The callers of BiasAndClamp (TFLite kernels) are not shown; per the analysis rules, the content-bearing size parameters bias_size/array_size are treated as attacker-data from untrusted model tensors, and no caller-side enforcement is assumed.

bias_data is assumed to be an allocation matching bias_size elements, as no statement in this code can verify the allocation size; reads bias_data[0..bias_size-1] are therefore in-bounds relative to that assumption.
limitations: A potential out-of-bounds read of bias_data if bias_size exceeded the actual bias tensor allocation could not be instantiated: the producing allocation is not shown and no statement in this code misuses bias_size relative to a visible buffer.

The non-NEON bounded overwrite distance is at most bias_size-1 elements per final block; exploitability (heap layout, allocator) is outside the given code, but the out-of-bounds write itself is fully instantiated and is memory corruption regardless.

verdict.summary: ReadPSDChannelPixels reads a full row of pixel data from the caller-supplied buffer 'pixels' with no bound on how many bytes it consumes: the loop is bounded only by the attacker-controlled image->columns, and p advances by packet_size (1, 2, or 4 bytes) on every iteration via *p++ / PushShortPixel / PushFloatPixel. No length parameter, end pointer, or bounds check on p exists anywhere in the function, so when the decompressed PSD channel data is shorter than columns*packet_size bytes (fully controlled by the file author), the loop reads out of bounds past the heap allocation, scaling up to attacker-chosen column counts — a heap out-of-bounds read (crash/DoS on image decoding, with out-of-bounds bytes flowing into the decoded image).

evidence.reason: Root cause: heap out-of-bounds READ. The source pointer p is initialized from the untrusted channel buffer 'pixels' (line 26) and is advanced by packet_size bytes on every iteration of a loop bounded only by the attacker-controlled image->columns (line 32). Instantiated trigger: a PSD whose decompressed channel row is shorter than columns*packet_size (e.g., columns=64, packet_size=1, 10-byte buffer) makes *p++ at line 35 (and PushShortPixel/PushFloatPixel at lines 39/47 for packet_size 2/4) read past the end of the allocation for the remaining ~54 iterations, with no length, end-pointer, or bounds check anywhere on any path (the only checks in the loop protect the destination q or clamp the bit loop, never p).

Same unguarded source-read sink on the packet_size==2 and default (float) paths: p advances 2 or 4 bytes per iteration with no bound, extending the out-of-bounds read when the caller-supplied buffer is shorter than columns*packet_size bytes.

assumptions: GetPSDPacketSize, PushShortPixel, PushFloatPixel, GetAuthenticPixels, GetAuthenticIndexQueue, SetPSDPixel, and SyncAuthenticPixels are not shown; their internal bounds/NULL behavior is not relied upon for the primary finding.

The size of the heap allocation backing 'pixels' is decided by the (not shown) caller; since this function receives no length parameter and documents no length contract, 'pixels' is treated as attacker-data per the data-origin impact model, and the code is judged as the last line of defense.
image->columns and image->depth are treated as attacker-controlled PSD file metadata; no statement in this code re-validates them.
limitations: C2: indexes=GetAuthenticIndexQueue(image) (line 30) is not NULL-checked and is passed to SetPSDPixel; the dereference, if any, occurs entirely inside the not-shown callee, so it is not a finding in this code.
C3: the (ssize_t) cast of image->columns (lines 32, 61, 69) could wrap only for columns > SSIZE_MAX; no statement in this code can produce such a value, so the trigger is speculative.

Information disclosure of OOB bytes into a saved output image depends on consumers outside this code (image write path); the confirmed impact here is the out-of-bounds read itself (crash/DoS and OOB data entering the decoded pixel row).

verdict.summary: In Compute (sparse-count op kernel), the batch index read from the attacker-controlled indices tensor is assigned to int batch (line 63) and the only bounds check is `if (batch >= num_batches)`, which enforces solely the upper bound and is entirely skipped for negative values. A negative batch (e.g. indices = [[-1]] with shape = [2, 5]) passes unvalidated to `per_batch_counts[batch][value]` (lines 75/77/79), where the row collection was sized `BatchedMap<W>(num_batches)` (line 48) — producing an out-of-bounds write (map operator[] insertion/`++` read-modify-write on memory before the container).

evidence.reason: Root cause: `batch` comes from the attacker-controlled int64 tensor element `indices_values(idx, 0)` and the only validation is the upper-bound check `if (batch >= num_batches)` wrapping `batch < num_batches` — the guard block is skipped entirely for negative batch values, so no lower bound is ever enforced. Instantiated trigger: indices = [[-1]] (1x1 matrix), values = [0], shape = [2,5] → num_batches = 2, num_values = 1, all earlier OP_REQUIRES pass, idx=0 sets batch = -1, the `if (-1 >= 2)` test is false, and the sink `per_batch_counts[batch][value]` executes with batch = -1 — an out-of-bounds row access followed by the inner `[value]` map write (operator[] insertion or `++`), i.e., an out-of-bounds write outside the num_batches-sized container.

evidence.snippet: auto per_batch_counts = BatchedMap<W>(num_batches);
evidence.reason: Origin of the bound that makes negative batch out of range: the row collection consumed at the sink is constructed with exactly num_batches entries, so valid indices are [0, num_batches); the negative index reaching `per_batch_counts[batch]` at lines 75/77/79 is outside this code's own allocation.

assumptions: BatchedMap's definition is not shown; it is assumed to be a sequence container indexed O(1) by integer row (vector-of-maps style), consistent with its construction `BatchedMap<W>(num_batches)` and two-level `per_batch_counts[batch][value]` indexing. Even without its definition, the code's own sizing statement at line 48 bounds valid indices to [0, num_batches), and no statement in this code remaps or validates a negative batch before the indexing sink.
maxlength_, minlength_, and binary_output_ are kernel construction-time attributes treated as internal-trusted; no statement in this code allows tensor input to mutate them.
GetOutputSize and OutputSparse are not shown; the corruption at lines 75/77/79 occurs before they are reached, so the finding does not depend on them.
limitations: Width truncation at line 63 (`int batch = ... indices_values(idx, 0)` from int64 to int) and at line 28 (`int num_batches = ... shape_vector(0)`) and line 29 (`int num_values = values.NumElements()`): a shape value like 2^31 would truncate num_batches to a negative int and reach `BatchedMap<W>(num_batches)` at line 48 with a negative size, but triggering this requires tensor dimensions at the 2^31 scale and the impact depends on BatchedMap's constructor, which is not in this code — recorded as speculative. The small-negative direct trigger (batch = -1) does not depend on truncation.
values.NumElements() truncating to a negative int would require a values tensor with >= 2^31 elements; not instantiated as a concrete trigger here.

verdict.summary: MapStageOp's Compute fetches the attacker-controlled 'indices' op input (line 12) and passes it to the ordered staging map's put() (line 26) with no validation of its emptiness, dtype, shape, or element-count consistency with the 'key' input (which itself receives only a NumElements()>0 check). Any op caller can supply an empty or mismatched indices tensor; the ordered StagingMap consumes per-key-element index data, so the missing validation at this trust-boundary intake point permits out-of-bounds/CHECK-fail consequences downstream. The only guard present ('key must not be empty') does not cover indices on any path.

evidence.reason: Trust-boundary intake: the public op handler pulls attacker-controlled 'key', 'indices', and 'values' tensors from the op inputs. The sole validation performed is key non-emptiness; indices_tensor is fetched and never checked for emptiness, dtype, shape, or length match with key. The ordered staging map requires index data consistent with the key's element count, and no such precondition is documented, asserted, or checked anywhere in this code.

evidence.snippet: OP_REQUIRES_OK(ctx, map->put(&key, indices_tensor, &tuple));
evidence.reason: Unguarded sink: the raw, unvalidated indices_tensor is passed to StagingMap<Ordered>::put alongside the length-checked key. Instantiated trigger: an op caller supplies key with NumElements()==3 and indices with NumElements()==0 (or 1, or non-int64 dtype) — line 12's fetch succeeds, line 14's key check passes (3>0), and line 26 hands the mismatched attacker data to the map, which consumes per-key-element index values. No OP_REQUIRES, comparison, dtype/shape check, clamp, validated copy, or checked accessor referencing indices_tensor exists on any path from line 12 to line 26.

assumptions: Compute is a TensorFlow OpKernel entry point: 'key', 'indices', and 'values' tensor contents, dtypes, shapes, and counts are controlled by the op caller (session feed), i.e., attacker-data per the trust-boundary model; the given code contains no caller contract or session-layer validation that could be quoted.

The downstream behavior of StagingMap<Ordered>::put is not part of the given code; the known upstream consequence (per-element index consumption against the key count leading to out-of-bounds access / CHECK-fail on empty or wrong-dtype indices) is asserted from domain knowledge, not from quotable statements.
limitations: The concrete out-of-bounds access or CHECK-fail occurs inside the not-shown StagingMap<Ordered>::put; this code's quotable defect is the missing validation of the 'indices' input at the intake point (the upstream fix adds indices non-emptiness and key/indices length-equality checks exactly where line 26 is reached).

Candidate on 'values_tensor' (no validation before put) was dismissed: the only use in this code is the framework-bounded push_back loop (lines 21-23) with i < values_tensor.size(); any defective use would be entirely inside the not-shown callee with no local defective statement.
Tensor copy 'Tensor key(*key_tensor)' (line 18) is a refcounting copy, not a validating one; no security effect in this code.

verdict.summary: FractionalAvgPoolGrad's Compute trusts the contents of row_seq_tensor and col_seq_tensor as index values without validating them: only element-count checks (row_seq_tensor.NumElements() > out_rows, col_seq_tensor.NumElements() > out_cols) exist. Negative sequence entries (or a out_depth/in_depth mismatch between out_backprop and orig_input_tensor_shape) produce an out-of-bounds in_index/row index that is written through in_backprop_tensor_temp_mat.coeffRef(d, in_index) into the in_backprop temp buffer, giving attacker-controlled out-of-bounds memory writes.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write: in_row_start/in_col_start come directly from the attacker-controlled row_seq_tensor/col_seq_tensor contents; only the END values are clamped (std::min against in_max_row_index/in_max_col_index), so a negative seq value yields in_r < 0 and a negative in_index, and the write at coeffRef(d, in_index)/in_backprop_ref += lands before the allocated in_backprop buffer. Trigger simulated: orig_input_tensor_shape=[1,2,2,1], out_backprop shape [1,1,1,1], row_seq=[-5,0], col_seq=[0,1] gives in_index in {-10,-8,-6,-4,-2} against a 4-double buffer.

Origin of the tainted index values: row_seq_tensor_flat(r)/col_seq_tensor_flat(c) are read from the attacker-supplied input tensors 2 and 3. The only guards on these tensors are the element-count checks row_seq_tensor.NumElements() > out_rows and col_seq_tensor.NumElements() > out_cols; there is no check that the values are non-negative, within [0, in_rows)/[0, in_cols), non-decreasing, or that row_seq_tensor_flat(0) == 0. The std::min clamps apply only to the end indices, never the start indices.

The write matrix has in_depth rows while the depth loop is bounded by out_depth (for d < out_depth), and no statement in this code asserts out_depth == in_depth. With out_backprop shape [1,1,1,3] and orig_input_tensor_shape [1,1,1,2], d=2 at in_index=0 makes in_backprop_tensor_temp_mat.coeffRef(2, 0) compute offset 2 + 0*2 = data[2] on a 2-double buffer — a one-past-the-end out-of-bounds write, second instantiated trigger for the same OOB-write sink.

assumptions: overlapping_ is kernel constructor state (fixed at graph construction) and was treated as internal-trusted; either value still yields the OOB with appropriate seq inputs.

context->input(...) tensors are attacker-controlled, per the standard TensorFlow threat model where a session client can feed arbitrary tensor contents and shapes; the code contains no statements restricting them.
Eigen Maps use column-major storage, so coeffRef(row, col) accesses data[row + col*rows]; this determines the concrete OOB offsets but the OOB holds under either layout.
limitations: Negative in_rows/in_cols/in_batch/in_depth pass the != 0 checks (in_batch != 0, in_rows != 0, in_cols != 0, in_depth != 0) because only non-zero, not positive, is enforced; however, the allocation of in_shape with a negative dim via forward_input_or_allocate_temp is not shown to succeed in this code, so this path alone was not counted as a separate primary finding (the positive-dimension triggers already fully instantiate the OOB write).
Huge positive seq start values are neutralized by the std::min clamp on the end indices (loop becomes empty); the instantiated vectors are negative start values and the depth mismatch.

verdict.summary: flatpak_dir_ensure_bundle_remote parses an untrusted bundle file with flatpak_bundle_load but never validates the out-parameter `ref` (initialized to NULL at line 11) before using it. evidence.reason: Sink: `ref` (FlatpakDecomposed*, initialized to NULL at line 11 and filled only by the parse of attacker-controlled bundle content) is consumed here without any NULL check. On the trigger path (bundle with metadata but no ref entry), deploy_data is NULL, the else branch runs, and flatpak_decomposed_dup_id(ref) / flatpak_decomposed_get_ref(ref) dereference the NULL pointer — attacker-triggered crash (DoS). No guard on `ref` exists anywhere on the path from the parse to these uses.

The only validation after the parse is `if (metadata == NULL)` — it checks the wrong variable; a bundle whose header carries metadata but no ref yields metadata != NULL while ref == NULL, and the missing `ref == NULL` check is the root cause of the NULL dereference at lines 65/72.

assumptions: flatpak_bundle_load, flatpak_dir_get_deploy_data, flatpak_decomposed_dup_id, and flatpak_decomposed_get_ref are not shown; it is assumed (from the FlatpakDecomposed accessor convention and this code initializing ref to NULL at line 11) that the accessors dereference the FlatpakDecomposed pointer and that a bundle header lacking a ref leaves ref NULL while metadata is non-NULL.

Whether this function runs in a privileged helper (e.g., the system-helper processing bundle installs) is not expressible from the given code; the DoS classification rests on the attacker-controlled file content crossing the parse boundary in this function, not on deployment privilege.
limitations: Attacker-controlled ref text, origin, and basename flow into flatpak_dir_create_origin_remote (lines 68–77); a crafted ref/origin could plausibly inject into remote names or repo config, but the harmful use and its effect are inside a callee not shown, so this impact chain is not instantiated and no finding is recorded for it.

Consequently the function returns true (the 'equal/verified' state) for inputs that are not equal (e.g., a1 with two identical-named AttrDefs vs a2 with one), a fail-open misrepresentation rooted in missing release-mode input validation.

verdict.summary: recalc_intercepts copies and merges intercept bitmaps between VMCB control areas using element-wise loops bounded by the local compile-time constant MAX_INTERCEPT. verdict.summary: FractionalAvgPoolGrad's Compute never validates that the out_backprop tensor's batch and depth dimensions match the original input shape's batch/depth dims. The destination buffer in_backprop_tensor_temp is allocated with in_shape ([in_batch, in_rows, in_cols, in_depth]) and wrapped in an Eigen map with in_depth rows and in_cols*in_rows*in_batch columns, but the distribution loop iterates b < out_batch and d < out_depth while computing in_index = (b*in_rows + in_r)*in_cols + in_c. An attacker supplying out_backprop with out_batch > in_batch (or out_depth > in_depth) drives coefficient writes past the end of the heap-allocated temporary tensor via in_backprop_tensor_temp_mat.coeffRef(d, in_index), with attacker-influenced values (out_backprop contents divided by the pooling-cell size). This is a heap out-of-bounds write reachable entirely from the four attacker-controlled input tensors.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write sink. in_index scales b by in_rows (line 126) and d ranges over out_depth (line 128), but the destination map in_backprop_tensor_temp_mat was sized with in_depth rows and in_cols*in_rows*in_batch columns. With in_batch=1, in_rows=2, in_cols=2, out_batch=2, the second batch iteration (b=1) computes in_index = (1*2+in_r)*2+in_c ∈ {4,5,6,7} against a 4-column map; coeffRef(d, in_index) at line 132 then writes attacker-influenced doubles past the 4-element heap allocation. No check anywhere relates out_batch to in_batch or out_depth to in_depth.

Size-mismatch origin. The write surface is bounded by in_depth rows and in_cols*in_rows*in_batch columns (attacker-controlled via input(0)), while the outer loop at line 96 iterates b < out_batch (attacker-controlled via input(1)'s shape). No OP_REQUIRES in the function compares out_batch/out_depth to in_batch/in_depth, so out_batch > in_batch or out_depth > in_depth flows unchecked to the coeffRef write.

assumptions: overlapping_ is a constructor-set member; its value is not part of the shown code's statements. Either value still permits the trigger (only in_row_end/in_col_end offsets shift by 1 and remain clamped).

The op's four input tensors are treated as attacker-data per the data-origin model: this Compute is the intake point for op invocation content (untrusted model/graph execution), and no caller precondition is documented in the given code.
limitations: Negative in_batch/in_rows/in_cols/in_depth pass the '!= 0' checks (lines 59-70) and reach TensorShape::AddDim (line 76) and the Eigen map construction (lines 86-88); the consequence (CHECK-failure crash or error) depends on TensorShape/allocator internals not present in the given code, so it is recorded as speculative and did not drive the verdict.

Row/col sequence values exceeding in_rows/in_cols cannot cause OOB here: in_row_end/in_col_end are clamped by std::min to in_max_row_index/in_max_col_index (lines 102, 112) and the loops (124, 125) only execute while in_r <= in_row_end / in_c <= in_col_end, so oversized starts yield zero iterations.

Reads of out_backprop_mat (line 130) stay in bounds because its map is built from out_backprop's own shape (lines 89-91) and both d < out_depth and out_index < out_cols*out_rows*out_batch by loop construction.

If a shape with num_elements() < 0 other than -1 (or an int64 product overflow producing a negative N with huge dims) is constructible, this function accepts it, stores the shape via 'shape_ = shape;', sets 'buf_ = p' (nullptr), and returns true. verdict.summary:
In ReadPCLImage, the PCL header-copy loop appends a byte with *p++=(char) c; before checking the buffer bound ((size_t) (p-command) < (MagickPathExtent-1)), and the bound is evaluated after the write and only on the continue path. Once p reaches command+MagickPathExtent-1 the condition is false, but the byte that caused the flush has already been written at index MagickPathExtent-1 — one past the last valid index MagickPathExtent-2 of the stack buffer char command[MagickPathExtent]. A crafted PCL file (untrusted blob read via ReadBlobByte) with a token longer than MagickPathExtent-2 bytes performs an out-of-bounds stack write with attacker-controlled content; the separator forced at the boundary ('/' or '
') is itself written out of bounds, and EOF (-1 -> 0xFF) is also written. The *p='\0'; termination flushes only after the overflow.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds stack write: the untrusted blob byte is written via *p++=(char) c; BEFORE the only bound check ((size_t) (p-command) < (MagickPathExtent-1)), which tests the post-increment offset with '<' against MagickPathExtent-1, permitting p-command == MagickPathExtent-1 at the next write. Trigger fully instantiated: a PCL file containing a run of MagickPathExtent-1 bytes with no '/' or '\n' makes the (p-command) < (MagickPathExtent-1) test fail at p-command == MagickPathExtent-1 while the byte stored by *p++=(char) c already sits at command[MagickPathExtent-1], one past the end of char command[MagickPathExtent] (last valid index MagickPathExtent-2). The overflow byte is attacker-controlled (any file byte, including the boundary-forced '/' or '\n', or 0xFF from EOF cast to char). No clamp, no >= check, no early flush at the boundary, and no corrected loop bound exists anywhere in the function.

assumptions: MagickPathExtent is the fixed on-stack buffer size of command (char command[MagickPathExtent]); its numeric value is not shown, but the defect is independent of the exact value.

ReadBlobByte returns the next byte (0..255) from the image blob or EOF (-1); per GUARD ANCHORING its range is not documented in this code, so it is treated as attacker-controlled including the -1 sentinel (which the code itself handles by testing 'c != EOF' but still stores (char)c).
LocaleNCompare/CastDoubleToLong/GetDelegateInfo/ExternalDelegateCommand are not shown; no claim about their behavior is relied upon for the confirmed finding.

The N-1 slack in the bound is best interpreted as intended room for the '\0' terminator of a token of MagickPathExtent-2 bytes; the defect is that the byte written at index MagickPathExtent-1 (the forced separator or any byte when the size test fails) is never covered by the guard.
limitations: Unvalidated sscanf %lf doubles from attacker file content flow into CastDoubleToLong and then page.width/height and '%.20g' formatting into the delegate command string; CastDoubleToLong's clamping is not shown and cannot be quoted, so an out-of-range write or malformed command-string argument via crafted CropBox/MediaBox values is a possible second defect but its trigger beyond the off-by-one case is not instantiated here.

FormatLocaleString(command, ..., GetDelegateCommands(delegate_info), ...) is only safe if the delegate's command template contains at least six %s conversions; the template is configuration not shown, so an argument/parameter mismatch under the delegate's control is not instantiated in this code.

page.width/height are reassigned (never reset) inside the do/while loop over the image list, so all list images receive the first image's page; robustness/behavioral issue only, no security impact instantiated.

Attacker-influenced integer underflow of page.width/page.height via negative MediaBox deltas is bounded downstream by the '%.20g' textual conversion and ParseAbsoluteGeometry fallbacks; no memory-unsafe sink for the underflowed value is present in this code.

ReadImage(read_info,exception) renders the output of the GhostPCL delegate; a malicious delegate could overwrite read_info->filename, but planting such a delegate requires system-level privileges not exercisable by the PCL file alone.

verdict.summary: TfLiteIntArrayCreate accepts an unvalidated signed 'size' at an exported entry point and passes it directly into the allocation-size computation and into the object's size field. The only guard, 'if (alloc_size <= 0) return NULL;', compares an unsigned size_t and therefore rejects only alloc_size == 0; it cannot detect a negative size that wrapped to a small positive allocation size. With size = -1, the size_t arithmetic in TfLiteIntArrayGetSizeInBytes wraps to a small positive alloc_size, malloc succeeds with an undersized buffer, and 'ret->size = size;' stores the negative attacker value, returning an inconsistent array object whose consumers will index out of bounds. No check on size's sign or magnitude exists anywhere in the code.

evidence.reason: Root cause: attacker-controlled signed 'size' (line 1, exported function, no documented/checked non-negative contract) flows unvalidated into the allocation-size computation (line 2) and the size-field write (line 6). The sole guard (line 3) tests 'alloc_size <= 0' on a size_t, so it is true only for 0 and cannot reject a negative size whose size_t computation wrapped to a small positive value. Instantiated trigger: size = -1 at the entry point → wrapped small-positive alloc_size bypasses line 3 → malloc allocates an undersized buffer (line 4) → line 6 stamps ret->size = -1, producing a malformed heap object returned at line 7; any consumer using ret->size as a count/index bound accesses memory out of bounds.

assumptions: TfLiteIntArrayGetSizeInBytes is not included in the given code; its exact wrap behavior for negative size (assumed to be header + (size_t)size * sizeof(int) style arithmetic) and the sizeof/layout of TfLiteIntArray are assumptions, which is why confidence is moderate rather than high.
sizeof(size_t) is assumed to be wider than int on the target platform; on a 32-bit size_t target, large positive sizes (e.g., near INT_MAX) would also wrap in the callee's computation.
limitations: The concrete wrapped value of alloc_size for a given negative size cannot be quoted because the callee TfLiteIntArrayGetSizeInBytes is not shown; for some wrap outcomes (0 or a huge value) the code returns NULL by accident rather than by the guard's design.

The out-of-bounds reads/writes that consumers of the returned TfLiteIntArray would perform using the corrupted ret->size occur in code not given; this code's instantiated impact is the undersized allocation plus the attacker-controlled size field written at line 6.
The flexible-array region ret->data is never initialized (CWE-908); its impact depends on consumers not shown, so it is recorded here rather than as a finding.

verdict.summary: diST_box_read reads bytes from the parsed file in a loop terminated only by a NUL byte, writing each byte to a fixed 1024-byte stack array with no check that the index i stays below 1024. A file whose diST box contains more than 1024 non-NUL bytes causes str[i] = gf_bs_read_u8(bs) to write attacker-controlled bytes past the end of str, a stack out-of-bounds write (memory corruption) with both the overflowing data and the overflow length fully attacker-controlled.

evidence.reason: The loop writes each attacker-supplied file byte to str[i] (line 10) with the only termination condition being a NUL byte in the attacker's data (line 11) — the index i is never compared to the 1024-byte capacity of str, and ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE(p, i) at line 14 runs only after the loop and cannot protect it. With i = 1024 (reached after 1024 non-NUL bytes via i++ on line 12), str[1024] = gf_bs_read_u8(bs) writes an attacker-chosen byte one past the stack array, and continues overwriting adjacent stack memory for every further non-NUL byte — an out-of-bounds stack write with fully instantiated trigger (CWE-787).

assumptions: gf_bs_read_u8 reads the next byte of the input file/box payload; its content is attacker-controlled file data, which is the trust boundary this parser code guards.
gf_bs_read_u8 returning 0 on stream exhaustion is assumed only as a loop-termination fallback; the out-of-bounds write at i==1024 occurs before any such termination matters.
limitations: gf_strdup(str) at line 16 assumes str is NUL-terminated; termination is provided either by the attacker NUL byte or bitstream exhaustion, so no independent unterminated-strdup finding is claimed.
Any size accounting defect in ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE(p, i) with an over-read i is preempted by the out-of-bounds write occurring earlier in execution order; not counted as a separate finding.

verdict.summary: mrb_ary_shift_m consumes the attacker-controlled integer n (Array#shift argument) at an untrusted entry point, but every sink is guarded by quoted, correctly ordered checks: 'if (n < 0) mrb_raise(...)' rejects all negatives before first use, 'if (n > len) n = len;' clamps the upper bound, 'if (len == 0 || n == 0) return mrb_ary_new(mrb);' handles degenerate cases, and 'else if (len == n)' prevents the copy loop's 'size = len-n' from degenerating; on the loop arm 0 < n < len holds, so the maximum read index (n + len - n - 1 = len-1) and maximum write index (len-n-1) are both in bounds, and the shared-array pointer advance 'a->as.heap.ptr+=n; a->as.heap.len-=n;' with 1 <= n <= len cannot underflow len or leave the visible window. No trigger with an in-code impact chain could be instantiated.
