Method dispatch guarantees self is an Array (function is bound as Array#shift); mrb_ary_ptr is assumed valid for that receiver.
mrb_int is treated as a fixed-width signed integer (typically 64-bit); the quoted comparisons are exact for the full declared width, so no wrap case exists within the comparisons themselves.
limitations: When n == len on a shared array, 'a->as.heap.ptr+=n' advances the pointer to one-past the visible window while len becomes 0. Whether later operations (push, resize) on such an array are handled safely occurs in mruby code not given; no dereference of that pointer exists in this function, so no impact could be instantiated here.

Behavior of the callees mrb_ary_shift, ary_make_shared, mrb_ary_new_from_values, and ary_modify_check is not shown; if any mishandles an input (e.g., an embedded array with len > ARY_SHIFT_SHARED_MIN passed to ary_make_shared), that defect would live in the callee, not in the statements given.

Concurrency: if the mruby VM were run with unsynchronized threads mutating the array between line 10 (len read) and the mutation sites, a TOCTOU could exist, but no thread-interleaving statements are present in this code.

verdict.summary: The grouped-convolution functor divides attacker-controlled tensor dimensions without any validation: `num_groups = in_depth / patch_depth` divides by zero when filter.dim_size(2) == 0, and `tensor.dim_size(3) / num_groups` (pre_shuffle/post_shuffle, executed at the TensorShape construction on line 35) divides by zero whenever num_groups truncates to 0 (in_depth < patch_depth or in_depth == 0), causing a SIGFPE that kills the process consuming the attacker-supplied model (denial of service). Additionally, on the EXPLICIT-padding path, explicit_paddings[2..5] are read via unchecked std::vector::operator[] with no size validation anywhere in this code, an out-of-bounds heap read whose values flow into the convolution output.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled filter depth reaches the division sink unguarded: with filter.dim_size(2) == 0 the statement `num_groups = in_depth / patch_depth` performs integer division by zero (SIGFPE, process termination), and when in_depth < patch_depth the truncated quotient num_groups == 0 poisons the later division at lines 20/26. No check on patch_depth, in_depth, or their divisibility exists anywhere in this function; the only check present is the debug-only DCHECK on data_format.

Second division sink: `tensor.dim_size(3) / num_groups` divides by num_groups, which is 0 whenever in_depth < patch_depth (truncated division at line 12) or in_depth == 0. The lambda executes immediately at line 35 (`Tensor input_shuffled(input.dtype(), TensorShape(post_shuffle(input)));`) on every invocation before any loop, so the zero quotient causes an unconditional SIGFPE — a denial of service triggered by attacker-supplied tensor shapes.

        functor::SpatialConvolution<CPUDevice, T>()(
            ctx->eigen_device<CPUDevice>(), output_slice, input_slice,
            filter_slice, row_stride, col_stride, row_dilation, col_dilation,
            static_cast<int>(explicit_paddings[2]),

verdict.summary: iloc_box_read's extent-parsing loop (line 52) is bounded solely by the attacker-supplied extent_count (line 50, u16 from the file). When the attacker sets offset_size and length_size to 0 (lines 7-8, both valid 4-bit values), each extent iteration consumes zero bytes of box data (line 64 decrements 0; lines 66-67 read 0 bits) while performing an unconditional heap allocation (line 53) that is retained via gf_list_add (line 56). A ~10-byte payload forces 65535 retained allocations, and a ~400 KB file (item_count up to 65535 at line 17, 6 mandatory bytes/item) drives ~4.29e9 allocations (~137 GB retained heap), an attacker-scalable memory-exhaustion / CPU denial of service in the media-file parsing process.

evidence.reason: The inner loop bound is the attacker-controlled extent_count read directly from the bitstream (line 50) with no validation against the remaining box size between the read and the loop; each iteration unconditionally allocates and retains a GF_ItemExtentEntry (lines 53, 56), giving an allocation count bounded only by the attacker's count field.

Per-iteration box-byte consumption is offset_size+length_size; when both are 0 (allowed values from lines 7-8), this statement consumes 0 bytes and the two reads consume 0 bits, so the loop at line 52 runs extent_count times (up to 65535) from essentially zero input, making the amplification link concrete: tiny input -> unbounded work and retained allocations.

verdict.summary: pjmedia_rtcp_xr_rx_rtcp_xr dereferences the packet buffer (reading rtcp_xr->common.pt and rtcp_xr->common.length, the first 4 bytes) before performing any validation of the size parameter. The only size check, 'if ((pkt_len + 1) > (size / 4)) return;', executes after these reads, so a caller-supplied size of 0-3 bytes (this function is the intake point for a received RTCP XR message) causes an out-of-bounds read of up to 4 bytes past the buffer. All subsequent report-block reads are properly guarded by the quoted per-block bounds checks against (char*)pkt + size, and the parse loop is correctly bounded.

The only size validation, 'if ((pkt_len + 1) > (size / 4))' (line 19), is a too-late sentinel: it runs after the reads. Trigger (fully simulated): caller passes pkt = {0x00, 207} with size = 2; line 14 reads pkt[1] == RTCP_XR and line 17 reads pkt[2..3] out of bounds of the 2-byte buffer. Root cause: missing minimum-size validation at the trust-boundary intake point, giving an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).

assumptions: pjmedia_rtcp_xr_pkt.common is assumed to be the 4-byte RTCP common header (pt at byte 1, 16-bit length at bytes 2-3) per pjmedia type definitions, which are not included in the given code.

The caller is assumed to pass pkt pointing to an actual buffer of at least `size` bytes; a mismatch there cannot be evaluated from this code.
Struct sizes used in the per-block guards (e.g. sizeof(*rb_stats)) are taken as the sizes of the packed on-wire structures per pjmedia definitions not shown.

The parse loop can iterate up to ~65535 times on an attacker-crafted packet, but the work is proportional to input size, so this is not attacker-scalable amplification.

All per-report-block reads (rb_rr_time, rb_dlrr, rb_stats, rb_voip_mtc) are guarded by the quoted checks 'if ((char*)rb_hdr + sizeof(...) <= (char*)pkt + size)', which are evaluated before the pointers are saved and use the correct inclusive boundary; no OOB was found there after edge-testing (rb_len = 0, 65535; pkt_len = 0/1; size exactly 4*(pkt_len+1)).

verdict.summary: In Compute (EditDistance op), the flattened output index `loc` is computed as a signed int64_t inner product of attacker-controlled sparse-tensor group coordinates (`truth_indices`/`hypothesis_indices`) with output strides. Every guard checks only `loc < output_elements` and never `loc >= 0`, so a negative index value (e.g., loc = -1) passes the one-sided check and `output_t(loc)` writes out of bounds before the output tensor buffer. The offset magnitude is attacker-scalable (large negative index -> write far before the buffer) and the written value is attacker-influenced, giving a memory-corruption primitive from unvalidated op input.

                             " which would require in writing to outside of "
                             "the buffer for the output tensor (max elements ",

        output_t(loc) =
evidence.reason: Root cause: one-sided bounds check. `loc` is a signed int64_t derived from attacker-supplied index values via g_truth (group coordinates from truth_indices). The guard `loc < output_elements` verifies only the upper bound; there is no `loc >= 0` check anywhere on any path (the identical pattern repeats in the g_truth > g_hypothesis branch, the else branch, and both trailing while loops). Instantiated trigger: attacker supplies truth_indices containing a negative index (e.g., row [-1,0] with shape [2,3]) -> g_truth = {-1}, output_strides = [1], loc = -1; guard evaluates -1 < 2 -> passes; `output_t(-1)` performs an out-of-bounds write 4 bytes before the output tensor's data buffer, with attacker-scalable negative offsets (e.g., index -100000 -> write ~400KB before the buffer) and attacker-influenced values (Levenshtein result, sequence size, 1.0, or infinity). Out-of-bounds write (CWE-787).

Origin of the tainted values: the attacker-controlled tensor truth_indices (input at `ctx->input("truth_indices", &truth_indices)`, line 11) is consumed here; its index values later flow unmodified through group() into g_truth/g_hypothesis and then into `loc` at the inner_product. No statement in the given code sanitizes or range-checks the sign of these index values before they reach the inner_product and the output_t(loc) sink.

assumptions: Bodies of ValidateShapes, TensorShapeUtils::MakeShape, sparse::SparseTensor::Create, and sparse::Group::group are not part of the given code; any index/rank validation they might perform is unquotable and was therefore not treated as a guard (per GUARD ANCHORING it may not demote the finding).
OP_REQUIRES/OP_REQUIRES_OK are assumed to abort kernel execution on failure (standard TF macros); the guards they encode were quoted where present.
normalize_ is a member flag not settable per-call in this code; treated as internal-trusted, and it does not affect the bounds defect.

Secondary (instantiable DoS): if truth_st_shape.dims() == 0 (empty shape tensor), line 46 `std::vector<int64_t> group_dims(truth_st_shape.dims() - 1);` constructs a vector with count (size_t)(-1), causing std::bad_alloc/length_error and process abort.

The OOB-write pattern is present at four additional loc sites (g_truth > g_hypothesis branch, zero-length-hypothesis branch, and both trailing while loops); only the first occurrence is shown as evidence; all share the identical missing `loc >= 0` lower-bound check.
Exact behavior on mismatched hypothesis/truth ranks depends on unshown ValidateShapes/group internals; no candidate relied on it.

verdict.summary: diST_box_read computes the allocation size as sizeof(char) * (s->size+1) with no bound on s->size (the attacker-controlled box size from the parsed media file). When s->size == 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF, s->size+1 wraps to 0, gf_malloc(0) returns a minimal non-NULL chunk that passes the NULL check, and gf_bs_read_data then copies attacker file bytes into the undersized buffer (heap buffer overflow), while the terminator write p->content_script_types[s->size] = 0 lands at ptr-1 (out-of-bounds write). No range check, clamp, or corrected bound exists anywhere in the function.

evidence.reason: Root cause: unchecked integer overflow in the allocation size. With the attacker-file-derived box size s->size = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF, 's->size+1' wraps to 0, so gf_malloc(0) returns a minimal allocation that passes the line-6 NULL-only check. gf_bs_read_data at line 7 then copies attacker-controlled stream bytes (length truncated to u32 0xFFFFFFFF, bounded only by bytes available) into the undersized chunk — a heap buffer overflow — and the line-8 write p->content_script_types[s->size] = 0 indexes at 2^64-1, which wraps to ptr-1, an out-of-bounds write below the allocation. No bounds check, clamp, or range guard on s->size exists on any path in this function.

evidence.snippet: GF_Err diST_box_read(GF_Box *s, GF_BitStream *bs)
evidence.reason: Taint origin: s->size enters through the GF_Box parameter at the function boundary; it is the box payload size parsed from attacker-supplied media-file content by the (not shown) box parser. No statement in this code bounds or validates it before it is used in arithmetic at line 5, as a copy length at line 7, and as a write index at line 8.

assumptions: GF_Box.size is an unsigned 64-bit field populated by the ISO-BMFF box parser from attacker-controlled file content (parser not shown); no quotable statement in this code bounds it.
gf_malloc wraps the C library malloc; malloc(0) is assumed to return a minimal non-NULL allocation (glibc behavior), so the line-6 NULL check does not reject the wrapped size.
gf_bs_read_data takes a u32 length and copies at most min(length, bytes remaining in the bitstream), so the overflow depth is bounded by attacker-supplied remaining file bytes.

The diST box is reachable during parsing of an attacker-supplied 3GP/DIMS file; box sizes at the 2^64-1 scale require the 64-bit largesize escape, which is part of the format's attacker-controlled header surface.
limitations: The return value of gf_bs_read_data (line 7) is discarded; on a truncated stream the buffer retains uninitialized heap bytes inside the NUL-terminated string between the read count and s->size. Potential heap disclosure, but the consumer that outputs content_script_types is not shown, so the impact link is not instantiated in this code (CWE-908-adjacent robustness defect).

The u64-to-u32 truncation of s->size at line 7 is only observable for sizes >= 2^32; on 64-bit targets such sizes independently cause a >= 4 GiB allocation that fails and is handled at line 6, except when the line-5 arithmetic wraps (already counted as the primary finding).

verdict.summary: MakeDataset validates only that the 'indices' input has 2 dimensions (IsMatrix) and, in the empty case only, that element counts match. It never validates the number of columns. An attacker-supplied indices tensor of shape [N,0] (with an empty 'values' vector) passes every check: IsMatrix accepts it, NumElements()==0 equals num_values==0, and the ordering loop is bounded by dim_size(0)=N. The loop then executes indices->matrix<int64_t>()(i, 0), which reads flat index i*0+0 == 0 from a tensor holding zero elements — an out-of-bounds read (or NULL dereference for empty-tensor storage) occurring directly in this function on every loop iteration. No guard of any form (dim_size(1) check, element-count-vs-rows check, checked accessor, or degenerate-matrix rejection) exists on any path.

evidence.snippet:
for (int64_t i = 0; i < indices->dim_size(0); ++i) {
      int64_t next_batch_index = indices->matrix<int64_t>()(i, 0);
evidence.reason: Sink: column-0 access into the indices matrix. With indices of shape [3,0] (attacker-controlled op input, dtype int64) the loop bound dim_size(0)=3 executes the loop, and the accessor resolves (i,0) to flat index i*0+0 = 0 of a tensor with zero elements — an out-of-bounds read of an 8-byte word from a zero-length (possibly NULL) buffer. Trigger: indices=[3,0] matrix, values=[0] vector, dense_shape=[1] vector; all quoted checks (IsMatrix at line 11, the 0==0 empty-case equality at lines 18-19, IsVector checks) pass for these values.

For a 0-element tensor, the allocator may return either a zero-byte non-null buffer (heap overread) or a null data pointer (NULL dereference); both are memory-safety failures but only the form, not the defect, depends on this.
The op registration (which in TensorFlow constrains input dtypes to DT_INT64) is not shown and was not treated as a guard.
limitations: Mismatched indices rows vs values length (e.g., indices [2,2] with a 1-element values vector) is not validated — the equality is enforced only in the empty case (lines 18-19). The harmful use of this mismatch (CHECK failure or OOB access) occurs inside sparse::SparseTensor::Create or the Dataset iterator, which are not shown, so it is recorded as a precursor defect rather than a confirmed vulnerability; the same missing check (indices->dim_size(0) == values->NumElements()) would cover both it and the confirmed finding.
Dtype confusion: indices->matrix<int64_t>() and dense_shape->vec<int64_t>() perform dtype checks inside the not-shown accessors; a crash there is not instantiated in this code.
Negative or invalid dense_shape entries reach TensorShape(dense_shape->vec<int64_t>()) (line 55); any CHECK/error occurs inside the not-shown TensorShape constructor.

verdict.summary: ReadPCLImage parses CropBox/MediaBox extents from the untrusted PCL file with sscanf into doubles and converts them to size_t via `(size_t) floor(bounds.x2-bounds.x1+0.5)` with no range, sign, or upper-bound validation. A negative or enormous extent (e.g. MediaBox [0 0 -1e9 -1e9) wraps to an astronomic size_t (undefined out-of-range double-to-integer conversion), which this code then formats into the GhostPCL delegate option `-g<W>x<H>` and executes via ExternalDelegateCommand (attacker-scalable resource amplification from a ~30-byte file), and stores into image->page of every returned image.

evidence.reason: Root cause: file-derived doubles bounds.x1..y2 are converted to size_t with no validation of sign or magnitude; only `if (count != 4)` (parse count) and the zero-check `if ((page.width == 0) || (page.height == 0))` exist — neither rejects out-of-range values. Trigger: a PCL file containing 'MediaBox [0 0 -1e9 -1e9' yields count=4, width=(size_t)(-1e9) → undefined conversion producing ~2^64, assigned to page.width/page.height; the huge value is re-cast at lines 192-195, formatted into '-g%.20gx%.20g' options (lines 196-197) and executed by ExternalDelegateCommand (lines 224-225), and stored via image->page=page.

count=(ssize_t) sscanf(command,"MediaBox [%lf %lf %lf %lf",

evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted values: bounds.x1..bounds.y2 are filled directly from the PCL file content accumulated in `command` from ReadBlobByte, with attacker-controlled magnitude and sign (sscanf accepts negative and huge floating-point literals), and flow unvalidated into the size_t conversions at lines 153-154.

verdict.summary: The seccomp rule-installation error check is inverted: `if (r < 0 && r == -EFAULT)` only acts on the benign 'unknown syscall' sentinel documented by the in-code comment, while every real seccomp_rule_add failure (e.g. -ENOMEM, -EINVAL, -EDOM) for a security-critical blocklisted syscall (mount, unshare, clone with CLONE_NEWUSER, ioctl TIOCSTI, ptrace) is silently ignored. verdict.summary: ComputeAsync indexes tensor shape metadata with the unvalidated attacker-controlled rank before any validation: 'const int64 n = input.dim_size(ndims - 1);' and 'const int64 nrhs = rhs.dim_size(ndims - 1);' execute before the 'ndims >= 2' and 'rhs.dims() == ndims' checks. evidence.reason: Root cause: the index ndims - 1 is computed from the attacker-controlled rank of input and used to index both input's and rhs's shape metadata before any rank validation. verdict.summary: pjmedia_rtcp_xr_rx_rtcp_xr parses attacker-supplied RTCP XR report blocks without any per-block bounds validation. The only size check, `if ((pkt_len + 1) > (size / 4))`, bounds the packet-declared length only; the parse loop's block length field (rb_len) and the fixed-size report structs (BT_STATS ~40 bytes, BT_VOIP_METRICS ~36 bytes, BT_DLRR 16 bytes, BT_RR_TIME 12 bytes) are never checked against the remaining buffer. A block whose header lies inside the packet but whose declared length is short (e.g., rb_len = 1) is still cast to a full struct pointer, and the field reads after the loop (rb_stats->lost, jitter_*, toh_*, rb_dlrr->item.lrr/dlrr, rb_voip_mtc->*, rb_rr_time->ntp_*) dereference up to ~36 bytes past the end of the `size`-byte buffer, causing an attacker-triggerable out-of-bounds heap read (values are also persisted into session statistics). Trigger fully simulated: a 12-byte packet with common.length=2 and a BT_STATS block of length 1 at offset 4 with flags 0xA0 makes line 155 read bytes 12-15 of a 12-byte buffer.

evidence.reason: Missing-check site (root cause): the only bounds validation in the function, `if ((pkt_len + 1) > (size / 4))`, bounds only the packet-declared word count. Inside the parse loop, rb_hdr is bounded by pkt_len, but the block's own length (rb_len, line 25) and the size of the struct being saved in the switch below are never validated against the remaining `size` bytes — no check exists that rb_hdr + rb_len + 1 words, or rb_hdr + sizeof(report struct), lies within pkt + size. An attacker block with bt=BT_STATS and rb_len=1 positioned near the end of the buffer is stored as a full pjmedia_rtcp_xr_rb_stats pointer and later dereferenced far past the buffer end.

Out-of-bounds read sink: attacker-controlled flag bits (rb_stats->header.specific) gate field reads whose offsets are fixed by the struct layout, not by the block's declared length. With the simulated trigger (12-byte packet, common.length=2, BT_STATS block at byte offset 4 with rb_len=1 and flags=0xA0), rb_stats->lost at struct offset 8 reads packet bytes 12-15 — past the end of the 12-byte buffer — and jitter_min/max/mean/dev (lines 163-167, packet bytes 20-31) and toh_* (lines 171-175) read further past the end. No bounds or NULL check on rb_stats protects these dereferences (line 138 `if (rb_stats)` is a presence check only).

assumptions: Struct layouts of pjmedia_rtcp_xr_rb_stats (~40 bytes: header 4, begin_seq/end_seq 2+2, lost/dup 4+4, jitter 4x4, toh 3x1+4), rb_dlrr (16 bytes), rb_rr_time (12 bytes), rb_voip_mtc (~36 bytes) are inferred from field usage in this code, not quoted from a definition; the OOB conclusion holds for any of these structs being larger than the (attacker-chosen) rb_len block extent.
sess->rtcp_session->ts_freq.u64 (used in TRACE_ at line 61) is assumed initialized non-zero elsewhere; not quotable from this code.
The precise meaning of RTCP_XR/pj_ntohs/pj_ntohl and struct field offsets are taken as standard pjproject/network byte-order semantics.
limitations: Secondary candidate (same CWE, not counted as a separate finding): `rtcp_xr->common.pt` (line 14) and `rtcp_xr->common.length` (line 17) are read before any size check, so a caller passing size < 4 causes a small OOB read; the parameter surface permits size 0-3, but the RTCP demux path that computes `size` is not shown, so its practical reachability was not instantiated from given-code statements.

`eedelay = now - lrr - dlrr;` (line 83) wraps in 32-bit before widening to pj_uint64_t, allowing a wrapped-small bogus RTT; the subsequent `if (eedelay <= 30 * 1000 * 1000UL)` and `sess->stat.rtt.n!=0` checks confine the effect to statistics pollution with no memory-safety, bypass, or amplification impact — not classified as a vulnerability.

Information disclosure impact of the OOB read (adjacent heap bytes persisted into sess->stat / logged) depends on consumers of the session statistics not shown in this code; the out-of-bounds read itself is fully instantiated in this function.

verdict.summary: The SVDF Prepare function indexes tensor dimension arrays (input->dims->data[0]/[1], weights_feature->dims->data[0]/[1], weights_time->dims->data[1]/[0], bias->dims->data[0]) without first validating that those tensors have the required dimensionality. Only the state tensor is rank-checked ('TF_LITE_ENSURE_EQ(context, NumDimensions(state), 2);'), so a malicious model containing a scalar or 1-D tensor in the input/weights/bias slots causes heap out-of-bounds reads whose garbage values then reach control flow and tensor-sizing decisions. Additionally, the full-integer path dereferences unchecked quantization params (input_params->scale->data[0]) — a model with an int8 input lacking quantization metadata crashes the process (NULL deref, DoS).

evidence.reason: Heap out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) caused by improper validation of array indices (CWE-129): the dims TfLiteIntArray of input, weights_feature and weights_time (and bias at line 37) is indexed at [0] and [1] with no NumDimensions/rank check anywhere on any path — the only rank check in the function ('TF_LITE_ENSURE_EQ(context, NumDimensions(state), 2);', line 47) covers the state tensor only. Trigger fully instantiated: an attacker-supplied model with a scalar (dims->size==0) SVDF input passes the type check at lines 19-20, then line 25 ('input->dims->data[0]') and line 31 ('input->dims->data[1]') read past the heap-allocated dims array; the garbage batch_size/num_filters values flow into TF_LITE_ENSURE_EQ control decisions and into output/scratch size arrays. The same defect applies to weights_time->dims->data[1] (line 30) for a 1-D tensor and weights_feature->dims->data[1] (line 32).

NULL-pointer dereference (CWE-476, denial of service across the model trust boundary): quantization.params and the scale arrays are attacker-supplied model metadata with no NULL or size validation anywhere on the path (the only optional-input guard in the function, 'if (bias)', line 36, does not apply). Trigger fully instantiated: an int8 SVDF input passes the type check at lines 19-20, sets is_full_integer (line 61), enters the block at line 169, and a model whose int8 tensors omit quantization metadata yields input_params == nullptr, so 'input_params->scale->data[0]' (line 194) reads through a null pointer and crashes the inference process. An empty scale array would likewise produce an OOB read of scale->data[0].

assumptions: node->builtin_data and node->user_data are populated by the interpreter/Init code, which is not shown; their non-NULL-ness is an assumption (op_data is dereferenced at line 4 without check).

GetInputSafe/GetOutputSafe/GetTemporarySafe are assumed to validate tensor-index bounds only ('Safe' naming); no quotable statement validates tensor dimensionality or quantization metadata upstream, so none of these can dismiss the confirmed findings.

IsHybridOp(input, weights_feature) semantics are not shown; for candidate 2 it is assumed to return false when both tensors are int8 — but the full-integer block executes regardless of the hybrid block, since the two ifs are independent.
Deployment context (how the model file reaches this process) is unknown; per the data-origin impact model, model-derived tensor metadata is treated as attacker-data.
limitations: Signed integer overflow at line 49-50 ('SizeOfDimension(state, 1) == memory_size * num_filters'): attacker-chosen memory_size and num_filters whose product wraps (e.g., 65536 * 65536 -> 0) let an undersized state tensor pass the consistency check, but the resulting out-of-bounds access occurs in Eval(), which is not given — impact not instantiated here.

Negative params->rank passes 'TF_LITE_ENSURE(context, rank != 0);' (rank = -1 makes num_filters % rank == 0 trivially true), producing a negative num_units fed into output/output_temp size arrays; the negative-size consumption happens inside context->ResizeTensor, which is not shown.
TfLiteIntArrayCreate results are never NULL-checked (e.g., lines 53, 74, 171), but these are fixed small allocations; failure requires unattackable OOM, not an attacker-induced condition.
Size arrays (output_size_array, scratch_size_array, etc.) leak on early error returns; this is a memory leak with no security impact in the given code.

verdict.summary: All bitstream reads in iloc_box_read are preceded, in execution order and on every path, by an ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE check whose decrement (in bytes) exactly matches the data the corresponding gf_bs_read_* call consumes (2-byte nibble header, 2/4-byte item_count/item_ID, 2-byte construction_method, 2+base_offset_size for data_reference_index+base_offset, 2-byte extent_count, index_size bytes for extent_index, offset_size+length_size bytes for extent_offset+extent_length). The 4-bit size fields (max 15) are used consistently in the same unit by both guard and read, and the extent loop's index branch short-circuits for version 0 so the never-assigned index_size is never read. Loop iterations are bounded per-iteration by these checks, so consumption stays proportional to input. No candidate's trigger plus impact chain could be fully instantiated within this code.

assumptions: ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE is a macro not shown in the given code; its semantics (reject and return an error when the requested decrement exceeds the box's remaining size, otherwise subtract it) could not be quoted and is treated as an assumption, though its decrement amounts were verified to match the subsequent reads byte-for-byte.

ptr->version and ptr->size are set/maintained by the box-parsing framework (not shown) and are treated as attacker-controlled parsed content; ptr->location_entries is assumed created by the box constructor (not shown).

gf_bs_read_int behavior for nBits > 32 (base_offset_size/offset_size/length_size up to 15 gives up to 120 bits) is inside a callee not shown; no memory-unsafe behavior could be established from the given code, and the size accounting for those bits is correct.
limitations: Candidate: base_offset/extent_offset/extent_length are read via 32-bit gf_bs_read_int with up to 8*15=120 bits; if that callee truncates or asserts beyond 32 bits, the instantiated consequence inside this code is only a misparsed/truncated offset value, and any security impact would occur in downstream consumers of these offsets, which are not given.

Candidate: version > 2 boxes are parsed with the version-2 layout (u32 item_count/item_ID, construction_method=0, no extent_index); all reads remain guarded, so this is a spec-strictness issue, not a memory-safety defect in this code.

Candidate: unchecked gf_list_new/gf_list_add returns (GF_OUT_OF_MEM-only paths) and partially initialized entries left in lists on early error returns depend on the not-shown box destructor for cleanup; no use of those values occurs in this code.

Historical GPAC iloc vulnerabilities (missing size accounting before base_offset, extent_offset/extent_length, construction_method, item_ID, or extent_count reads) are all fixed in this version by the corresponding ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE statements quoted in STEP 2.

verdict.summary: In DecodeChunk, chunk offsets from the EXR file (attacker-controlled 64-bit values) are bounds-checked only by `offsets[i] + sizeof(int)*N > size`. This addition wraps modulo 2^64: for offsets >= 2^64-8 (scanline) or 2^64-20 (tiled), the sum wraps to a small value, the check passes, and `data_ptr = head + offsets[i]` points before the buffer. The subsequent memcpy calls (line_no/data_len in the scanline path, tile_coordinates/data_len in the tiled path) then perform out-of-bounds heap reads, and the read values influence decode control flow (line_no, data_len, tile coordinates). No check on the range of offsets itself exists anywhere on any path.

evidence.reason: Unsigned integer wrap in the sole bounds guard. With offsets[0] = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF8 (attacker-written 64-bit EXR offset-table value, unbounded by any quotable check), `offsets[y_idx] + sizeof(int) * 2` wraps to 0, so `0 > size` is false and the else branch runs; `data_ptr = head + 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF8` = head - 8; `memcpy(&line_no, data_ptr, 4)` and `memcpy(&data_len, data_ptr + 4, 4)` read 8 heap bytes before the `head` buffer (out-of-bounds read). The read values are then byte-swapped and used as line_no/data_len controlling decode. Root cause: integer overflow (CWE-190) in the bounds check producing an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).

Same wrap defect in the tiled path. With offsets[tile_idx] = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF0, `offsets[tile_idx] + sizeof(int) * 5` wraps to 4, the guard `4 > size` passes, `data_ptr = head - 16`, and `memcpy(tile_coordinates, data_ptr, sizeof(int) * 4)` performs a 16-byte out-of-bounds heap read before the buffer. No range check on `offsets[tile_idx]` alone exists on any path.

assumptions: offsets, exr_header fields, and head/size are attacker-controlled EXR file content; no statement in this code (or quotable contract) bounds the 64-bit offset values below 2^64 before the additions at lines 94 and 184.
head points to a buffer of exactly `size` bytes; nothing in this code re-bounds or copies it before the memcpys.
limitations: calloc result for exr_image->tiles (lines 82-83) is not NULL-checked before `exr_image->tiles[tile_idx].images` (line 87); triggering requires an allocation failure driven by an enormous offset table, and the consequence is a crash/degradation only — not promoted to a finding.

tile_coordinates[0]/[1] (lines 141-142) and line_no/num_lines are passed to DecodeTiledPixelData/DecodePixelData, callees not shown; any further OOB impact inside those callees cannot be instantiated from the given code.
On 32-bit builds `total_data_len_overflown` is hard-coded false (line 162), disabling the size guard; exploitation of a wrapped total_data_len occurs inside AllocateImage (not shown).
The final loop `exr_header->pixel_types[c] = exr_header->requested_pixel_types[c]` trusts num_channels against array sizes established outside this code — not instantiable here.

`data_width = data_window[2] - data_window[0] + 1` can invoke signed-overflow UB, but every practically-wrapped result is caught by the `< 0` check (line 19) and the threshold check (line 32); no exploitable path was instantiated.

verdict.summary: njs_module_path computes the size bound for the stack buffer src[NJS_MAX_PATH+1] from dir->length (+ an optional trailing '/') only, discarding info->name.length via 'length = dir->length;', while the subsequent njs_cpymem copies info->name.length additional attacker-controlled bytes. The only guard 'if (njs_slow_path(length > NJS_MAX_PATH))' therefore does not bound the total copy, producing a stack out-of-bounds write with fully attacker-controlled content (the module-name string) whenever dir is non-NULL and dir->length + trail + info->name.length exceeds NJS_MAX_PATH.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds stack write: after copying dir->length bytes (plus an optional '/'), njs_cpymem at line 39 appends info->name.length attacker-controlled bytes into the fixed stack buffer src[NJS_MAX_PATH + 1] (declared at line 6) with no check bounding info->name.length on the dir != NULL path. With e.g. dir = "/x/" (length 3, trail 0) and info->name.length = NJS_MAX_PATH + 200, the line-25 guard tests length == 3 (passes) and line 39 writes NJS_MAX_PATH + 203 bytes into a NJS_MAX_PATH + 1 byte buffer.

Origin of the size miscalculation: line 9 assigns info->name.length, but inside the dir != NULL branch line 12 overwrites it with dir->length ('length = dir->length;'), so the line-25 check 'njs_slow_path(length > NJS_MAX_PATH)' bounds only dir->length + trail and never accounts for the info->name.length bytes copied later at line 39. The correct computation would add (+=) dir's length to the name length; no such fix form (bounds check on the total, clamp, larger buffer, checked copy) exists anywhere in the function.

assumptions: NJS_MAX_PATH is a positive compile-time constant (exact value, e.g. 4096, not shown); the overflow holds for any value ≥ 1.

info->name is the module-name string (e.g. the require() argument) supplied by upstream JS source and is treated as attacker-data because it is a content-bearing parameter of a non-static exported function with no quotable contract bounding its length in this code.
The struct field info->path (target of realpath) is declared elsewhere; its capacity relative to PATH_MAX could not be quoted and is not relied upon.
njs_cpymem is a memcpy-like unchecked copy helper (definition not shown); its use is treated as a raw memory copy.
limitations: TOCTOU between realpath(&src[0], &info->path[0]) and open(&info->path[0], O_RDONLY): the file resolved by realpath could be swapped before open; exploitation requires an attacker able to interleave filesystem operations on that path, which this code's own statements do not instantiate — not counted as a primary finding.
Possible insufficient capacity of info->path for realpath output cannot be evaluated because the njs_module_info_t struct is not in the given code.

verdict.summary: xml_parse_node recurses once per nested element (line 83), and tail-recurses for PI and comment constructs (lines 24 and 40), with no depth counter, limit, or iteration bound anywhere in the function. The sub-node loop at lines 80-83 is bounded only by the attacker-controlled byte count of the XML document being parsed: an input consisting of "<a>" repeated N times enters a new stack frame per 3 input bytes before any frame returns, so a document of a few hundred kilobytes exhausts the process stack and terminates the parsing process. This is an attacker-reachable, trust-boundary-crossing denial of service (uncontrolled recursion / unbounded resource consumption) in the parser of externally supplied XML.

evidence.reason: Root cause: uncontrolled recursion. The loop condition at lines 80-81 depends only on attacker-controlled document bytes, and line 83 calls xml_parse_node recursively once per nested '<' element with no depth limit anywhere in the function. Simulated trigger: input "<a>" repeated N times — line 8 sees '<', lines 12/28 are skipped (next byte 'a'), line 50 yields name "a" at '>', lines 53/68 are skipped, line 76 consumes '>', lines 80-81 evaluate true at the next '<', line 83 re-enters with the cursor advanced 3 bytes; frames never return before new ones are created, so depth grows linearly with attacker input and the stack is exhausted, crashing the process.

Origin/recursion site: after consuming a Processing Instruction construct, the function tail-recurses into itself at line 24 (and identically at line 40 for the comment construct) with no depth accounting; both feed the same unbounded recursion primitive instantiated at line 83 for nested elements.

assumptions: pj_scanner cursor/buffer contracts (NUL sentinel at scanner->end, EOF checks inside pj_scan_get_char/get_until_chr/get_until_chr/get_quotes/strcmp/advance_n, and whether get_until_chr skips leading whitespace) are not shown in this code; no statement here documents or asserts them.
on_syntax_error is assumed non-returning (longjmp/throw); its control flow is not shown, so code paths after on_syntax_error calls are analyzed on the assumption they are unreachable.
alloc_node/alloc_attr return values are never checked in this code; the allocator's non-NULL behavior is not quotable here.
PJ_CHECK_STACK() at line 6: its semantics and build-time enablement are not shown; it is not treated as a recursion depth bound.

The caller (pj_xml_parse, not shown) is assumed to pass a scanner over an externally supplied XML document buffer; per discipline 3 the parsed document content is treated as attacker-data regardless of the unshown caller.
limitations: Attribute loop (lines 53-66): if pj_scan_get_until_chr stops immediately on a delimiter such as the space separating two attributes without consuming it, *scanner->curptr never advances and the loop would iterate forever, allocating an attr per pass (unbounded memory). Whether the callee skips leading whitespace is not shown, so the trigger could not be instantiated from this code alone.

Lines 61-62 ('++attr->value.ptr; attr->value.slen -= 2;'): if pj_scan_get_quotes could ever return slen < 2 (e.g., unmatched quotes near EOF), slen would become negative and downstream consumers would read out of bounds; the callee's guarantee is not quotable here, so this is speculative.

Direct dereferences of *scanner->curptr and *(scanner->curptr+1) at lines 8, 12, 17, 53, 68, 80-81, 88, 93-94 (only line 88 has an is_eof check, guarding one use): safety against reads past the buffer end depends on the pj_scanner buffer NUL-sentinel contract, which is not shown.

CDATA block (lines 96-105): node->content.slen = scanner->curptr - node->content.ptr is safe under this code's own data flow (content.ptr is set at line 97 before any use and curptr only advances), and advance_n(…, PJ_TRUE) EOF behavior is not shown.

verdict.summary: mrb_vm_exec executes bytecode operands (register indices a/b/c, pool/syms/reps indices, jump offsets) fetched from the irep/iseq carried by its parameters without any bounds validation: no statement compares operands to irep->nregs, plen, symlen, or ilen. A crafted irep reaching this exported VM entry point makes `regs[a] = regs[b];` (OP_MOVE) write a full mrb_value at an attacker-selected offset (up to 16-bit via EXT prefixes, 32-bit for W-format operands) far past the stack allocated by `mrb_stack_extend(mrb, (irep->nregs < 4) ? 4 : irep->nregs);` — an out-of-bounds write with attacker-chosen index and attacker-influenced value. The same unvalidated indices produce out-of-bounds reads at `SET_SYM_VALUE(regs[a], syms[b]);`, `switch (pool[b].tt)`, `irep->reps[b]`, and OP_STRING's `mrb_str_new_static(mrb, pool[b].u.str, len)` with attacker-scalable len. The only existing bounds checks (`if (e && b < MRB_ENV_LEN(e))`, `if (MRB_ENV_LEN(e) <= m1+r+m2+1)`) cover env access only, confirming no analogous guard exists for pool/syms/reps/regs operand sinks.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write (primary). Operand a (uint32_t, line 11) and b (uint16_t, line 12) are decoded from the bytecode at pc with no bounds check anywhere in the function against the stack size (which is itself sized from the same attacker-controlled irep via `mrb_stack_extend(mrb, (irep->nregs < 4) ? 4 : irep->nregs);`). Instantiated trigger: crafted irep with nregs=4 and iseq {OP_MOVE, 0xC8, 0xC8} executes line 48 with a=b=200, writing a full mrb_value ~3200 bytes past a 4-slot stack; regs[b] is simultaneously an OOB read supplying the written value. Attacker-selected index (up to 16-bit via EXT1/EXT2, 32-bit for W-format) plus attacker-influenced content = memory-corruption primitive.

Out-of-bounds read confirming the same missing operand validation. syms is derived at line 6 from the parameter-carried irep; no statement compares b to irep->symlen (the only syms-related check anywhere is absent; mrb_assert statements in other opcodes check type flags, not indices). Trigger: irep with symlen=0 and iseq {OP_LOADSYM, 0, 5} executes `syms[5]` on a zero-length table, reading attacker-selected adjacent heap memory as a symbol id.

Origin of the tainted data: irep, pool, and syms are taken directly from the proc parameter (serialized program state) at the exported entry point; every subsequent operand index into these tables (pool[b] in OP_LOADL/OP_SYMBOL/OP_STRING/OP_ERR, syms[b], irep->reps[b]) is unvalidated in this function.

assumptions: The given code defines no documented precondition on proc/pc (the only assert is commented out at line 3), so per guard anchoring the irep/iseq content is treated as attacker-data at this exported entry point, not as a trusted compiler contract.
mrb_assert statements are assumed compiled out in release builds (NDEBUG); in any case none of them bounds an operand index against plen/symlen/nregs/ilen — they check type flags.

Operand fetch widths (8-bit base, 16-bit via EXT1/EXT2, 32-bit W-format) are inferred from the declared types `uint32_t a; uint16_t b; uint16_t c;` and the EXT dispatch blocks; the FETCH macros themselves are not shown.
sizeof(mrb_value) is 8 or 16 bytes depending on MRB_NAN_BOXING/MRB_WORD_BOXING and MRB_64BIT; the OOB write exists under any of these.
limitations: Real-world exploitation requires hostile bytecode/irep to reach mrb_vm_exec (e.g., an embedding application loading an untrusted compiled .mrb or generated irep); mruby's own source compiler normally emits in-range operands. Per the analysis rules this deployment dependency is unquotable and does not demote the finding, but it constrains practical reachability.

C5 (unbounded `pc += (int16_t)a;` / `pc = irep->iseq + a;` jumping outside the instruction sequence) is a real unguarded sink of the same class, but its full impact chain continues through the FETCH/dispatch macros that are not shown, so it is recorded here rather than as an independent primary finding.

C4 (`irep->reps[b]` unvalidated), C6 (OP_ARGARY lv==0 reads stack[m1+r+m2] with no length check, unlike the guarded lv>0 branch), C7 (OP_HASH `for (i=a; i<lim; i+=2)` with lim=a+b*2 unchecked), and C8 (OP_ERR `pool[a]` with 32-bit a) are additional unguarded uses of the same unvalidated operand class; they corroborate but were not individually simulated to full impact.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability instantiated in the given code. The buffer is sized, filled, and NUL-terminated consistently (startspaces + textlen + endspaces + 1 bytes exactly consumed); the alloc failure sentinel is checked before first use; the trailing-space trim loop reads only textstart[0..textlen-1] because bd->endspaces is forced to 0 by a statement gated on the same condition as the loop, and pnew can never decrement below the buffer base. All identified hazard candidates (unbounded y_idx index write, negative/overflowing bd->textlen in the alloc sum and memmove size, NULL y_current->y_array) depend on values produced exclusively by callers/callees not shown, so their triggers are not instantiable from this code's own statements.

assumptions: alloc(), mch_memmove(), vim_memset(), VIM_ISWHITE(), and (*mb_head_off)() semantics are inferred from Vim conventions; none is shown in the given code.
struct block_def field types (int startspaces/endspaces/textlen, char_u *textstart) are inferred from Vim's actual definition; the struct definition is not given.
y_current and y_current->y_array are assumed initialized by code not shown.

mb_head_off is assumed to return a non-negative offset not exceeding the byte's distance from the textstart base (head byte at or after textstart); this callee contract cannot be quoted from the given code.
limitations: Out-of-bounds write candidate: y_current->y_array[y_idx] = pnew uses an unchecked long index; no bound exists anywhere in this code, but the trigger requires a caller-supplied y_idx outside the array, and the caller (loop over y_array in code not given) is the missing precondition — not instantiable here.

Heap-overflow candidate: (size_t)bd->textlen in mch_memmove and the int sum bd->startspaces + bd->endspaces + bd->textlen + 1 in alloc are unchecked; a negative or INT_MAX-scale textlen would corrupt memory, but no statement in this code can produce such a value — it must arrive via the bd parameter from block-construction code not shown.

mb_head_off desync: if mb_head_off returned a positive offset while the byte is ASCII whitespace, pnew and s desynchronize; *pnew = NUL still lands in-bounds (stale trailing bytes remain, a correctness artifact only). If mb_head_off returned -1, s would never decrease and pnew-- would loop unboundedly (hang); both require the not-shown callee to violate its head-byte semantics.
NULL dereference candidate: y_current or y_current->y_array may be NULL; their initialization is outside the given code.

verdict.summary: Tensor::FromProto is the intake point for an untrusted TensorProto but never validates that the size of proto.tensor_content() (or the count of typed fields) is consistent with N = shape.num_elements(). Both the attacker-controlled content (line 11) and the attacker-derived element count (line 7) are passed directly to Helper<T>::Decode / FromProtoField<T> (lines 12, 15); the only checks (IsValid, DT_INVALID, N>0, non-empty content, and the post-hoc 'dtype_error || p == nullptr' test at line 18, which runs after the call) never compare content length to N. A serialized proto with a mismatched shape/content pair is accepted and handed to the decode path, enabling a trust-boundary DoS (CHECK-fail) and potential out-of-bounds copy in the decoder.

evidence.reason: N is derived solely from attacker-controlled proto.tensor_shape() (line 6) and content is the attacker-controlled tensor_content blob (line 11). No statement in this code compares content.size() with N * sizeof(T) before both are passed into Helper<T>::Decode (line 12). The non-empty check (line 10) rejects only length 0; the null-result check (line 18) executes after the decode call and cannot protect values already consumed by the callee. A proto with dtype=DT_FLOAT, shape dim [2] and a 3-byte tensor_content passes every guard and reaches line 12 with a mismatched (content.size(), N) pair — the trigger is fully instantiated at this intake/decode function.

Second, symmetric sink of the same defect: when tensor_content is empty, the whole attacker-controlled proto (whose typed repeated fields can carry any count of values) is passed together with attacker-derived N to FromProtoField<T>. No field-count-versus-N validation exists on this path either; the same mismatch trigger applies.

assumptions: The implementations of TensorShape::IsValid, TensorShape::num_elements, Helper<T>::Decode, FromProtoField, and the CASES_WITH_DEFAULT macro are not given; their internal behavior cannot be quoted and is treated as unknown.
TensorProto is treated as serialized/model state content per discipline 3; the concrete deployment (SavedModel loading, wire format) is not shown and is not relied upon.
MemoryLoggingEnabled() is assumed typically false; the guarded dereference at line 26 is safe either way.
limitations: The concrete copy/CHECK site (memcpy in Helper<T>::Decode, or size assertions in FromProtoField) is inside a callee not shown, so the exact downstream consequence (CHECK-fail DoS vs out-of-bounds read/write) cannot be quoted; the defect confirmed here is the missing length/count-versus-N validation at this trust-boundary intake.

A potential overflow of shape.num_elements() (product of large attacker dims, CWE-190) occurs inside TensorShape, whose code is not given; the multiplication cannot be quoted, so this candidate is speculative.
The N==0-with-non-empty-content path silently drops the content and returns true with buf_=nullptr; no security-state misrepresentation is quotable in this code, so it is not a finding.

verdict.summary: ConcatShapeHelper fetches the attacker-controlled constant axis tensor (c->input_tensor(dim_index)) and validates only its nullness and the input's shape rank, never its dtype. The value dispatch `if (concat_dim_t->dtype() == DT_INT32) ... else concat_dim = concat_dim_t->flat<int64_t>()(0);` is an unguarded catch-all: any axis constant whose dtype is not DT_INT32 (e.g., a DT_FLOAT scalar in a crafted model) reaches flat<int64_t>() without any check that the dtype is DT_INT64, causing the templated accessor's dtype check to abort the process (denial of service during shape inference on untrusted model content) or, absent that check, a type-confused read of the tensor buffer whose garbage value then flows into min_rank, WithRankAtLeast, Subshape and Dim.

evidence.reason: The else branch is a catch-all with no `concat_dim_t->dtype() == DT_INT64` validation anywhere in the function (verified by exhaustively searching every fix form on every path). Trigger: an attacker-supplied model wires a scalar constant of a dtype other than DT_INT32 (e.g., DT_FLOAT) to the axis input; line 4's WithRank(…, 0) passes (it constrains shape rank only), line 5 returns the non-null tensor, line 6's null check passes, and line 44 executes flat<int64_t>() on a non-int64 tensor, aborting the process (or misinterpreting the buffer if the accessor's dtype check is absent).

evidence.snippet:
const Tensor* concat_dim_t = c->input_tensor(dim_index);
  if (concat_dim_t == nullptr) {
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: the axis tensor is attacker-controlled model content (a constant node's dtype and value); the only guard applied to it anywhere in the function is this null check, which validates neither its dtype nor its contents before the flat<int64_t>() use at line 44.

assumptions: Tensor::flat<T>() is assumed (from tensor.h, not shown) to CHECK the tensor dtype against T; whether the impact at line 44 is a clean process abort or a type-confused read cannot be quoted from the given code — the root cause (missing dtype validation in this function) stands either way.

The declared input shape at c->input(dim_index) is assumed consistent with the actual constant tensor returned by c->input_tensor(dim_index); the element-count safety of flat()(0) rests on this framework invariant plus the quoted WithRank(…, 0) guard at line 4.

Deployment context (shape inference runs while loading an attacker-supplied GraphDef/SavedModel in a shared process) is inferred, not quoted; per the rules it is not used to demote or promote candidates.
limitations: OOB read via a zero-element axis tensor at flat<int32>()(0)/flat<int64_t>()(0) is blocked by the quoted line 4 guard `TF_RETURN_IF_ERROR(c->WithRank(c->input(dim_index), 0, &unused));`, which rejects any non-scalar axis before the tensor is used; only a shape/tensor inconsistency (not shown) could bypass it.

Negative axis values other than -1 (e.g., -2) reach c->Subshape(input, 0, -2, …), c->Dim(input, -2), and c->Subshape(input, concat_dim + 1, …) with negative indices; whether these callee accesses are bounds-checked or rank-relative cannot be quoted from the given code, so no memory-safety impact is instantiated here.

Second instance of the same inverted fail-open check, on the non-devel blocklist path (perf_event_open, personality, ptrace). A non--EFAULT failure of seccomp_rule_add leaves these sandbox-relevant syscalls unblocked while setup still reports success and installs the --seccomp filter, misrepresenting the sandbox's security state.

verdict.summary: In AssignOp::Compute, the destination-buffer size for the copy is validated only while the ref mutex is held (num_elements equality at lines 38-39), but when use_exclusive_lock_ is false (an attacker-settable op attribute) execution falls through past the end of the mutex scope (line 80) and performs the copy at line 86 on a tensor re-fetched via mutable_input(0, false) at line 85 with no re-validation. A concurrently scheduled second Assign on the same variable (whose replace_ref_input at lines 61/74 installs an arbitrarily shaped tensor) can interleave in the window between lock release and copy, so Copy is invoked with a destination holding fewer elements than rhs (e.g., 10 vs 1000), producing a heap out-of-bounds write of attacker-chosen scale, plus an unsynchronized data race on the shared variable buffer.

evidence.snippet:
Tensor old_unlocked_lhs = context->mutable_input(0, /* lock_held */ false);
    Copy(context, &old_unlocked_lhs, rhs);
evidence.reason: Out-of-lock copy sink. The destination tensor is re-fetched with lock_held=false after the mutex scope has already closed (line 80 '}' ends the mutex_lock l scope), and its size is never re-checked against rhs before Copy. Trigger: attacker builds two independent Assign ops on one variable; op A with use_exclusive_lock_==false validates a 1000-element rhs against the variable under the lock, then op B (via replace_ref_input at line 61/74) installs a 10-element tensor in the window between lock release and A's line 85 fetch, so A's Copy writes 1000 elements into a 10-element buffer — heap OOB write; even absent replacement, two fall-through instances race unsynchronized on the same buffer.

evidence.snippet:
if (old_lhs.IsInitialized() &&
          old_lhs.shape().num_elements() == rhs.shape().num_elements()) {
evidence.reason: Origin of the stale size invariant: the buffer-fit check that the later unlocked copy relies on is performed here, only on the tensor held under the mutex taken at line 18. This validated object is not the tensor consumed at line 85 after the lock is released, and no statement between line 80 and line 86 re-establishes num_elements equality, so the invariant does not reach the sink in execution order.

assumptions: Copy is a private helper of this kernel (not shown in the given code); it is assumed to perform an element-wise copy whose safety depends on the operand sizes supplied by this code — no bounds check inside it can be quoted.

The op registration signature constraining the ref input dtype, the value input dtype, and the kernel template T to be identical is outside the given code and cannot be quoted; per GUARD ANCHORING it is not used to dismiss candidates.

The graph executor can run two independent (no control dependency) Assign ops targeting the same variable concurrently; the attacker (untrusted model/graph author) controls use_exclusive_lock_, validate_shape_, relax_constraints_ attributes and all tensor shapes.
mutable_input(0, false) returns a Tensor by value aliasing the current ref tensor, so the buffer is kept alive by refcount; the defect is the un-re-validated size, not use-after-free.
limitations: Dtype-confusion candidate (element-count fit check ignores element byte size, so an lhs of smaller dtype than rhs would be overrun): the trigger requires a runtime dtype mismatch between the ref lhs and rhs, which no statement in this code can produce, and the harmful write would occur inside the not-shown Copy; the only enforcement is the un-quoted op-registration typing. Not counted as a finding.

validate_shape_==false allows the variable's shape to change ([2,3] -> [3,2] via CopyFrom at line 46) while the buffer is reused; within this code the copy is memory-safe (equal element counts). Any downstream static-shape confusion (e.g., XLA-compiled consumers) occurs in code not given — impact chain not instantiated here.
CHECK(reshaped_old_lhs.CopyFrom(old_lhs, rhs.shape())) at line 46 cannot fail on any reachable path (num_elements equality is guaranteed by the enclosing branch guard), so no DoS via CHECK abort.

All single-threaded paths were simulated (buffer-reuse same-shape, buffer-reuse reshaped, rhs-alias early return, allocate_temp) and each copy destination's element count equals rhs's element count; no single-threaded memory-safety defect was found.

verdict.summary: This is the upstream NFSv4 file-open path. Every attacker-influenced input (open flags from filp->f_flags) is either stripped of dangerous bits ('openflags &= ~(O_CREAT|O_EXCL);' on the sole path to the open_context call) or delegated via guarded early returns. assumptions: alloc_nfs_open_context returns an ERR_PTR (never NULL) on failure; this code's 'if (IS_ERR(ctx))' check would not catch a NULL return, but no statement in this code can produce NULL.
NFS_PROTO(dir)->open_context returns either a valid inode pointer or an ERR_PTR; this code tests IS_ERR before any use of the result.
nfs_open(inode, filp) and put_nfs_open_context/d_drop/dput have their documented kernel semantics; their bodies are not shown.
The VFS supplies a valid filp/inode pair at this ->open handler per the kernel file_operations contract; not quotable from this code.
limitations: struct iattr attr has an uninitialized ia_size field when O_TRUNC is clear; a read of it would occur only inside the not-shown open_context callee and only if that callee ignores the ia_valid gating that this code sets correctly ('attr.ia_valid = ATTR_OPEN;' and the ATTR_SIZE/ia_size pairing). The harmful use is not in this code, so the candidate is not instantiated.

verdict.summary: digest_generic_verify contains no memory-unsafe or fail-open defect within its own statements: tmp is sized exactly by 'tmp = xmalloc(len);', the digest_final failure path is checked ('if (ret) goto end;') and propagates the error, free(tmp) runs exactly once on all paths, and the comparison uses constant-time crypto_memneq with a length matching the allocation. The remaining candidates are not instantiated in this code: an over-read of md (line 13) requires the caller to pass a buffer shorter than digest_length(d) — a caller-created memory state this code cannot measure, with the dereference occurring inside the not-shown crypto_memneq; a len==0 vacuous-verify requires the unshown digest_length to return 0; an unchecked xmalloc result requires allocator failure. All are recorded as limitations/assumptions.

assumptions: xmalloc never returns NULL (barebox convention: it aborts on allocation failure) — not quotable from the given code; the NULL-dereference trigger via digest_final(d, tmp) is therefore OOM-only and not attacker-inducible.
digest_length(d) returns a sane positive digest length (e.g., 16/20/32/64) — produced by an unshown callee; this code performs no arithmetic on len, so it cannot degrade the value.

digest_final(d, tmp) writes exactly digest_length(d) bytes to tmp and returns nonzero on failure — unshown callee contract; if it returned 0 without filling tmp, uninitialized heap would reach the comparison (CWE-908 shape), but that state cannot be produced by any statement in this code.
crypto_memneq reads exactly len bytes from both md and tmp and is constant-time — unshown callee; the constant-time property is why no timing-side-channel candidate is raised.
md references at least digest_length(d) readable bytes — undocumented interface contract; no statement in this code documents, asserts, or checks it.

limitations: Out-of-bounds read candidate on md (line 13, crypto_memneq(md, tmp, len)): no guard exists in this code for md's extent (verified by exhaustive search for NULL checks, bounds/range checks, clamps, and length parameters — none present), but the trigger requires the caller to supply a buffer shorter than digest_length(d). That buffer extent is caller-created memory state, not an input value of this function, no statement in this code produces it, and the actual over-read dereference occurs inside the not-shown crypto_memneq. Per the unquoted-link rule this is a limitation, not a finding; a caller passing an undersized md has its own memory-safety bug, and a caller free to choose md's extent already controls that memory.

len == 0 fail-open: if digest_length(d) returned 0, crypto_memneq(md, tmp, 0) returns 0 and the else arm sets ret = 0, presenting 'verified' without comparing anything. No statement in this code can produce len == 0 (single assignment, line 4, from an unshown callee), so the trigger is speculative. A 'if (!len) { ret = -EINVAL; goto end; }' guard is absent.

Unchecked xmalloc result (line 7): if xmalloc could return NULL, digest_final(d, tmp) would dereference NULL inside a callee not shown. Trigger requires allocation failure only, which no attacker induces; the never-NULL property of xmalloc is an unquoted assumption.

Uninitialized-read candidate: tmp is not zeroed; if digest_final returned 0 while writing fewer than len bytes, uninitialized heap would influence the verification result (ret). Requires the unshown callee to violate its fill contract; not instantiable from this code.
Signedness: int len widened to size_t at the crypto_memneq call would wrap to a huge value if digest_length returned a negative int; no statement here produces such a value, so speculative.

verdict.summary: recalc_intercepts performs a bounds-guarded bitmap merge: it copies the host's (L0) intercepts into the effective vmcb02, clears a small set of host intercept bits for guest-domain events under quoted conditions, then ORs the nested guest's (L1) intercept bits in. The only array accesses are guarded by 'for (i = 0; i < MAX_INTERCEPT; i++)' on both loops, positioned in the loop headers so they precede every use on every path, with an unsigned index and a compile-time constant bound that no input can influence; the bit clears use constant bit positions. Guest-controlled data (nested.ctl, populated from the L1 vmcb12) can only ADD intercept bits, never remove host-required ones, and the clear-before-OR ordering of CR8/VINTR/VMMCALL means only the host's own bits are cleared while L1's legitimate requests survive. No memory-safety, injection, or bypass sink reachable by attacker data exists in this code; candidate defects (guest re-enabling cleared intercepts, SMI intercept stripping, hypothetical NULL of vmcb01.ptr) have no instantiated security impact within this code.

assumptions: The definition of struct vmcb_control_area and the value of MAX_INTERCEPT are not in the given code; it is assumed intercepts[] is declared with length MAX_INTERCEPT per the kernel's constant definitions. All three pointers c, h, g have the same struct type, so all indexing is type-symmetric, and the loop bound i < MAX_INTERCEPT is a kernel constant unaffected by any input.

svm->vmcb, svm->vmcb01.ptr, and svm->nested.ctl are assumed to be valid kernel-allocated objects; no statement in this code assigns or can NULL them, and guest data reaches the contents of nested.ctl, not these pointer values.
intercept_smi is a host-set module parameter; no statement in this code allows guest mutation of it.

The contents of svm->nested.ctl originate from the L1 guest's vmcb12 copied at nested VMRUN (code not shown); they were treated as attacker-data throughout the analysis, and their consumption here is limited to bit tests and bit-ORs with no unsafe use.
limitations: Candidate: L1 can set CR8_READ/CR8_WRITE/VINTR/VMMCALL intercept bits in nested.ctl which survive the host-bit clears because the clears run before the OR loop ('c->intercepts[i] |= g->intercepts[i]'). The consequence — L0 intercepting those L2 events and reflecting them to L1 — is implemented in nested exit-handling code not given; no L0 control bypass, memory effect, or other security impact is instantiated inside this function.

Candidate: when intercept_smi is false, the SMI clear also strips L1's requested SMI intercept; the impact is nested event-delivery semantics in code not shown, and the quoted comment shows this is deliberate host-capability-driven behavior.
Candidate: NULL dereference of svm->vmcb01.ptr if it were uninitialized — no statement in this code can produce that NULL, so the trigger is speculative.
No exploitable trigger with a security impact was instantiated; the function is a bounded bitmap merge with constant-index bit clears matching the upstream Linux KVM SVM implementation.

verdict.summary: Gather validates only that indices are non-negative but never checks them against the axis dimension of the input tensor, so attacker-supplied positive indices (or any indices when PositionsT is an unsigned type) are passed unchecked to optimized_ops::Gather, producing an out-of-bounds read of the input tensor whose contents are copied into the attacker-readable output tensor (heap memory disclosure).

evidence.reason: The validation loop checks only the lower bound (`indexes[i] < 0`); there is no comparison of any index against the input tensor's axis dimension, so positive out-of-range indices pass `TF_LITE_ENSURE` unvalidated.

evidence.snippet:
optimized_ops::Gather(op_params, GetTensorShape(input),
                        GetTensorData<InputT>(input), GetTensorShape(positions),
                        GetTensorData<PositionsT>(positions),
                        GetTensorShape(output), GetTensorData<InputT>(output));
evidence.reason: Unvalidated attacker-controlled positions data (e.g., a single index value 1000000 with input axis dimension 2, which passes the negativity check) is passed to the gather sink, which reads input data at index*scale past the input allocation and writes the out-of-bounds contents into the readable output tensor.

assumptions: optimized_ops::Gather (callee, not shown) does not itself clamp or reject indices exceeding the axis dimension; this function is the validation point for the positions trust boundary (its lower-bound check demonstrates that validation belongs here), so the missing upper-bound check is the defect in this code regardless.
limitations: num_indices derived as positions->bytes / sizeof(PositionsT) assumes byte-count divisibility by element size; a mismatch between checked count and callee-read count was not instantiated by any statement in the given code.
params.axis is not validated against the input tensor's rank in this function; any resulting defect would occur entirely inside the not-shown callee.

verdict.summary: RestoreTensor indexes context->input(1) (tensor_name, line 16) and, when restore_slice is set, context->input(2) (shape_spec, line 53) with the unvalidated int parameter restore_index, without any check that those tensors have more than restore_index elements. Only input(0) is size-checked (size == 1). An attacker supplying a Restore op call with a tensor_name tensor shorter than restore_index (e.g., 1 element with restore_index = 1) causes an out-of-bounds read of a tstring, which is then dereferenced in HasTensor and embedded in error messages, enabling a crash or disclosure of out-of-bounds process memory.

  const string& tensor_name = tensor_name_t.flat<tstring>()(restore_index);
evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read: restore_index (an unvalidated int parameter, attacker-data) indexes input(1) with no NumElements/bounds check anywhere in the function (the only size check, lines 5-11, applies to input(0) only). Trigger: tensor_name_t with 1 element and restore_index = 1 executes flat<tstring>()(1) out of bounds; the resulting OOB tstring is dereferenced at reader->HasTensor(tensor_name, ...) and printed into error messages.

Anchor showing the only input-size validation present: it guards input(0) exclusively; the analogous check (NumElements() > restore_index) for input(1) at line 16 and input(2) at line 53 is absent on every path, confirming via the counterfactual patch test that no bounds/range/clamp/checked-accessor form exists for those sinks.

assumptions: restore_index provenance (kernel instantiation loop vs. direct parameter) is not quotable from the given code; per the data-origin rules it is treated as attacker-data, since no assert, documented contract, or check bounds it in this code.
context->input(1)/input(2) contents and lengths are attacker-controlled op inputs; no decode-site constraint is quoted in this code, so no such constraint is relied upon.

verdict.summary: In DecodeChunk, the only bounds check on attacker-controlled 64-bit chunk offsets, `offsets[y_idx] + sizeof(int) * 2 > size` (scanline) and `offsets[tile_idx] + sizeof(int) * 5 > size` (tiled), performs the addition in unsigned 64-bit arithmetic that wraps. An offset near 2^64 (e.g. 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFC) makes offsets+8 wrap to a small value, the check passes, `head + offsets[i]` wraps to a pointer outside the file buffer (e.g. head-4), and the subsequent memcpy (line 195/197, and line 106 in the tiled branch) reads out of bounds, enabling a crash or limited out-of-bounds read from a crafted EXR file.

evidence.reason: The guard adds before comparing in wrapping size_t/tinyexr_uint64 arithmetic: with offsets[0]=0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFC and size=1000, offsets[0]+8 wraps to 4, 4>1000 is false, data_ptr = head+0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFC = head-4, and memcpy at line 195 reads 4 bytes before the buffer (out-of-bounds read, CWE-125 via integer overflow CWE-190). Trigger fully instantiated from file-supplied offset-table content.

Same root cause in the tiled branch: offsets[tile_idx]+20 wraps (e.g. 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF0 + 20 -> 4), the check passes, data_ptr = head-16, and the 16-byte memcpy at line 106 reads out of bounds before the file buffer.

assumptions: `offsets` carries the EXR chunk-offset-table values parsed from the attacker-supplied file (the code itself compares them against the file size at lines 94/184), and `head`/`size` describe that file buffer; no documented caller precondition exists in the given code.
size_t is 64-bit on the target platform (matching the tinyexr_uint64 offset type the code declares); the wrap analysis applies where sizeof(void*)==8.
limitations: Signed int overflow at line 209 (`line_no + num_scanline_blocks`) can wrap and defeat the end_line_no bound, passing out-of-domain values (e.g. line_no=2147483637, num_lines=16, data_height=101) to DecodePixelData; the harmful use (image-buffer indexing) occurs in the not-shown callee, so the impact chain is not instantiated in this code.

Return values of calloc (lines 82-83) and AllocateImage (lines 87, 174) are never checked for NULL; a NULL dereference requires an allocation-failure/oversized-input scenario whose instantiation depends on the not-shown offset-table parsing.

On 32-bit builds the overflow check at line 162 is explicitly disabled (`: false`), so the size_t product at lines 160-161 can wrap; the consequence depends on the not-shown AllocateImage/DecodePixelData.
Data race on `invalid_data` inside the OpenMP parallel region (line 181) is benign (all racing writes store true).
Early returns after line 87 leak per-tile allocations (robustness only).

verdict.summary: Two NULL pointer dereferences reachable from attacker-controlled ISOBMFF file content in the top-level box parser: (1) on the default (non-debug) MOOV path, `trak->Media->information->sampleTable->sampleGroups` is dereferenced without any check that the track's sample table exists — a moov containing a trak whose minf has no stbl yields sampleTable == NULL and crashes the process parsing the file; (2) on the MOOF path in GF_ISOM_OPEN_KEEP_FRAGMENTS mode, `mov->moof->mfhd->sequence_number` is dereferenced without checking that the moof contains an mfhd box — a moof without mfhd yields mfhd == NULL and crashes. Both are denial of service triggered solely by crafted file structure.

evidence.reason: NULL pointer dereference (CWE-476). The trak objects come from gf_list_get(mov->moov->trackList) where mov->moov is the box tree parsed from attacker file content (line 58, `mov->moov = (GF_MovieBox *)a;`). The chain trak->Media->information->sampleTable is dereferenced with no NULL check on any link; sampleTable is only non-NULL when the track's minf contained an stbl box, which is purely attacker-controlled file structure. The only prior MOOV-path check, `if (!mov->moov->mvhd)` (line 77), guards mvhd only. Instantiated trigger: file with moov[mvhd, trak[mdia[minf without stbl]]] opened in default (non-READ_DEBUG) mode reaches this loop and dereferences NULL, terminating the parsing process.

NULL pointer dereference (CWE-476). mov->moof was assigned at line 309 from `a`, the box parsed from attacker file content; mfhd is a child box of moof whose presence is attacker-controlled. `mov->moof->mfhd->sequence_number` is dereferenced with no NULL check anywhere in this function (the identifier mfhd appears only at this use). Instantiated trigger: a file containing a moof box with no mfhd child, opened in GF_ISOM_OPEN_KEEP_FRAGMENTS mode (the fragmented-file editing mode), reaches this statement and dereferences NULL, terminating the process.

assumptions: mov->openMode (GF_ISOM_OPEN_KEEP_FRAGMENTS) and mov->FragmentsFlags are set by the caller at file-open time, not by any statement in this code; finding 2's trigger additionally requires the caller to have selected KEEP_FRAGMENTS mode, which is the normal mode for editing fragmented files such as the attacker-supplied one.

The box-tree builders (gf_isom_parse_root_box and per-box parsers) are not shown; no quotable statement in this code documents or enforces that a moov always contains an stbl in each trak or that a moof always contains an mfhd, so those structural fields are treated as attacker-data per GUARD ANCHORING.
Whether gf_isom_box_del tolerates a NULL argument, and whether gf_bs_seek/gf_list_add can fail in ways affecting control flow here, is callee behavior not shown.
limitations: Lines 381-383: `if (mov->root_ssix) { gf_isom_box_del(mov->seg_ssix); mov->root_ssix = NULL; }` frees mov->seg_ssix but leaves the mov->seg_ssix pointer dangling (it NULLs root_ssix instead). A later SSIX at line 278 (`if (mov->seg_ssix) gf_isom_box_del(mov->seg_ssix);`) would double-free. However, mov->root_ssix is never assigned a non-NULL value anywhere in this code, so the triggering state must originate outside the given code; not counted as a vulnerability here.

OTYP case (lines 212-218): if an otyp box precedes any ftyp, `gf_isom_box_del((GF_Box *) mov->brand)` is called with mov->brand == NULL; whether this crashes depends on gf_isom_box_del's NULL handling, which is not shown.
Unchecked return values of gf_list_add (lines 328, 425) and gf_list_new (line 424) are allocation-failure robustness issues with no attacker-instantiable security impact in this code.
Potential non-terminating loop if gf_isom_parse_root_box returns GF_OK without consuming bytes; no such behavior is quotable from the given code.
u64 accumulations (`totSize += a->size`, `mov->main_sidx_end_pos = mov->current_top_box_start + a->size`) have no bounds/memory sink within this function.

verdict.summary: This function hashes operator-supplied certificate-validation settings into a session-ID digest. No attacker-data input exists in the given code (no file/socket/peer content is consumed), and every memory access is bounded by the exact byte span of the object it reads: hash_buffer is EVP_MAX_MD_SIZE (64 bytes) against a 32-byte SHA-256 output, asserted via RELEASE_ASSERT(hash_length == SHA256_DIGEST_LENGTH) before use; the pin-list loops read exactly hash.size() * sizeof(value_type) bytes from hash.data(), which is the container's own byte span (sizeof(char)/sizeof(uint8_t) == 1 for the string/byte-container types this usage implies); all other updates read sizeof() of their own objects. Every fallible crypto call is followed by a fatal RELEASE_ASSERT (fail-closed, not fail-open). Candidate over-read and session-ID-collision scenarios could not be triggered from this code's own data flow.

assumptions: Declarations of verify_certificate_hash_list_, verify_certificate_spki_list_, verify_trusted_ca_, ca_cert_, and config_ are not in the given code; their types are inferred from usage (hash.data()/hash.size() implying string or byte-container elements with 1-byte value_type).
X509_digest (BoringSSL) is assumed to write at most EVP_MD_size(EVP_sha256())=32 bytes into the 64-byte hash_buffer and to set *hash_length; callee source not shown.
RELEASE_ASSERT is assumed to be fatal (abort on failure), making all error paths fail-closed.
The digest context md and hash_buffer/hash_length parameters are assumed to be supplied by trusted internal callers within the same component; no caller is shown.
limitations: Candidate (a): heap over-read if the pin-list elements had a value_type wider than 1 byte. Dismissed as speculative: for any element width T, hash.size()*sizeof(T) is exactly the byte span of hash.data(), so the read stays inside the container's allocation; an over-read cannot be instantiated by this code's statements.

Candidate (b): session resumption across differently-configured listeners (validation bypass) if a validation-affecting setting were omitted from the digest. Dismissed: every setting this code consumes is hashed (ca_cert_ digest, both pin lists, verify_trusted_ca_, SAN matchers, CRL, allow_expired, trust_chain_verification, only_leaf_crl), and the session-ticket acceptance logic that would realize the impact lives outside the given code.

Candidate (d): a RELEASE_ASSERT abort on a crypto failure would crash the process, but no attacker-instantiated trigger exists in this function (all inputs are operator configuration or internal state), so this is not an attacker-reachable denial of service within the given code.

verdict.summary: In IsConstantFoldable, the loop over a caller-supplied shape_map entry iterates i up to shape_it->second.size() (the number of recorded shapes) and passes i directly to n->output_type(i), which is only valid for i < n->num_outputs(). No check in this code relates the vector length to the node's output count, so a shape_map entry longer than the node's output list drives an out-of-bounds read at n->output_type(i) (minimum trigger: i == num_outputs).

evidence.reason: Root cause: the loop bound `i < shape_it->second.size()` constrains i by the length of the caller-supplied vector of shapes, not by the node's output count, yet i is used as an output index at n->output_type(i). Instantiated trigger: a shape_map entry for n->name() with more elements than n->num_outputs() makes iteration i = num_outputs reach n->output_type(i) with an out-of-range index, causing an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125, index validation CWE-129).

Origin of the tainted length: the attacker-supplied shape_map parameter is looked up by node name and its entry's vector length (shape_it->second.size()) later becomes the loop bound that indexes node outputs, with no validation against the node's actual output count.
