All candidate triggers require an out-of-range value that only an unshown caller/parser can supply, and every claimed impact chain breaks at an unquoted link outside this code, so no vulnerability is instantiated within the given statements.

assumptions: The command-range parser that resolves line1/line2/n before calling ex_copy is not shown; it is assumed (not quotable from the given code) to clamp addresses to buffer bounds and reject or swap backwards ranges. This assumption was NOT used to demote any candidate; all candidates were evaluated against fully attacker-controlled parameter values and still failed to instantiate an in-code impact.

ml_get, ml_append, u_save, appended_lines_mark, check_pos, vim_strsave, vim_free are not shown; their internal bounds handling, clamping, and failure semantics cannot be quoted and are not relied upon.
Single-threaded execution: no interleaving mutation of curbuf/curwin between statements is exhibited in this code, so no race window could be shown.
cmdmod.cmod_flags, VIsual_active, and VIsual are treated as internal editor state; no statement in this code shows an external party setting them between relevant statements.
limitations: C1: line1 reaches ml_get(line1) with no in-code bounds check (no comparison against curbuf->b_ml.ml_line_count exists in this function). An out-of-range line1 would cause an out-of-bounds read inside ml_get, but that dereference is entirely in the not-shown callee, and this code's own statements never produce an out-of-range line1 (the loop only increases line1 while maintaining line1 <= line2). Trigger is speculative and the impact link is unquoted.
C2: n reaches u_save(n, n+1) and, via curwin->w_cursor.lnum, ml_append() without any in-code validation; same reasoning as C1 — the insertion/indexing happens inside not-shown callees.

C3: if a caller supplies line1 > line2, count = line2 - line1 + 1 becomes <= 0 and is passed to appended_lines_mark(n, count) and used in curbuf->b_op_end.lnum = n + count; the only in-code consequences are mark bookkeeping and msgmore((long)count), neither of which is a security impact; the dangerous consumer appended_lines_mark is not shown.
C4: integer overflow of line2 - line1 + 1 requires linenr_T extremes that no shown statement produces; the trigger depends entirely on unshown address parsing.
C5: the return value of ml_append is ignored; on append failure lines are silently dropped (data loss/robustness), with no memory-safety, bypass, or amplification effect in this code.

verdict.summary: get_visual_text() computes the selected-text length from raw Visual columns without bounding it by the actual line length. The else-branch (lines 19-43) handles both charwise and blockwise Visual mode (no VIsual_mode == Ctrl_V branch exists), and in blockwise mode VIsual.col can be the virtual end-of-line column MAXCOL. *lenp = VIsual.col - curwin->w_cursor.col + 1 (line 24) then yields a huge value (e.g., INT_MAX when VIsual.col == MAXCOL and cursor.col == 1), which passes the only guards (line 31 tests the first byte only; line 33 only requires *lenp > 0) and is used at lines 38/39 as *pp + (*lenp - 1) — an out-of-bounds read of ~2GB past the line buffer inside this function. The same arithmetic can signed-overflow to a negative length (cursor.col == 0) that is returned to callers.

evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted length: *lenp is computed as a raw column difference with no clamp to the line's actual byte length. In blockwise Visual mode (no Ctrl-V branch exists in this code) VIsual.col can be the virtual MAXCOL column, so *lenp can be INT_MAX (VIsual.col=MAXCOL, cursor.col=1) or signed-overflow negative (cursor.col=0).

Unguarded out-of-bounds read sink: with the instantiated trigger (blockwise Visual selection where VIsual.col == MAXCOL, cursor.col == 1, line >= 2 bytes, same lnum), *lenp = 2147483647 passes the `*lenp > 0` check (line 31's `**pp == NUL` test only checks the first byte and does not bound the length), and line 38 dereferences *pp + 2147483646 via mb_ptr2len (or line 39 reads (*pp)[2147483646] in a !has_mbyte build) — a read far outside the line buffer, causing a crash/DoS and potential over-read.

assumptions: VIsual.col can hold the virtual end-of-line column MAXCOL (0x7fffffff) when a blockwise Visual selection is extended with '$'; this state is set by editor input (keystrokes/:normal/scripts) outside the given code — the given code reads VIsual.col directly and contains no branch distinguishing blockwise (Ctrl-V) mode.
ml_get_pos()/ml_get_curline() return pointers into the current line buffer; mb_ptr2len dereferences its argument (standard Vim semantics, not shown here).
has_mbyte is a build/runtime flag; both arms (line 38 and line 39) perform the unbounded index.
limitations: The negative-length path (VIsual.col == MAXCOL, cursor.col == 0 -> line 24 signed-overflows to INT_MIN; `*lenp > 0` at line 33 skips the read but the negative value is returned at line 45): its harmful use (e.g., a caller copying *lenp bytes) is not in the given code, so impact there is not instantiated.
Potential disclosure through the huge returned length (callers copying up to ~2GB from *pp) likewise depends on callers not shown.
No CVE or exact upstream patch version cited; the analysis rests solely on the given code.

verdict.summary: In drill_parse_T_code(), the tool-change-stop-switch path executes `tmps = get_line(fd++);`, whose post-increment advances the gerb_file_t pointer fd past the end of the file struct object; the very next statement then reads `fd->filename` through the incremented pointer and passes the out-of-bounds garbage value as a %s string to gerbv_stats_printf. A 5-byte drill file containing "TCST\n" (any 'T' line followed by C, S, T and at least one more byte so that (fd->ptr + 2) < fd->datalen holds) fully triggers the out-of-bounds read and wild-pointer string dereference in the parser of an untrusted file.

evidence.reason: Root cause: `get_line(fd++)` post-increments the gerb_file_t *fd pointer by sizeof(gerb_file_t), so the subsequent `fd->filename` on line 30 reads the filename field from beyond the gerb_file_t object (out-of-bounds read, CWE-125), and the garbage pointer is then dereferenced as a C string by the %s formatting. Trigger instantiated: drill file content "TCST\n" — after gerb_fgetc returns 'C' with fd->ptr == 2, the guard `((fd->ptr + 2) < fd->datalen)` yields 4 < 5 (true), the next two gerb_fgetc calls return 'S' and 'T', the branch is entered, fd is incremented past the struct, and fd->filename is read OOB. No statement between the increment and the use restores fd or bounds-checks it, and the branch returns -1 immediately after, so the defect is reachable on this single path.

assumptions: Implementations of gerb_fgetc, gerb_ungetc, gerb_fgetint, read_double, get_line, gerbv_stats_printf, drill_stats_add_to_drill_list, and gerbv_get_tool_diameter are not shown; standard semantics assumed (gerb_fgetc returns EOF at ptr >= datalen without advancing).

TOOL_MIN/TOOL_MAX are assumed to match the dimension of image->aperture[]; the given code does enforce `if (tool_num < TOOL_MIN || tool_num >= TOOL_MAX) ... return -1;` before every image->aperture[tool_num] indexing, so the index itself is guarded in this code.
image->drill_stats is used without a NULL check (line 8); caller initialization is assumed.
The gerb_file_t object is assumed to be an exactly-sized allocation; even if not, `fd->filename` after `fd++` reads a field from the wrong object, which is the defect reported.
limitations: Unreasonable drill size fail-through: `if (size <= 0. || size >= 10000.)` only logs an error and does not return or stop; the tool is still passed to drill_stats_add_to_drill_list with the bogus size and tool_num is returned as success. The harmful use, if any, occurs inside the not-shown callee, so no security impact is instantiated in this code.

The newline-restore `if ('\n' == temp || '\r' == temp) gerb_ungetc(fd);` is nested inside `if (EOF == temp)`, making it dead code; newlines are consumed rather than restored. No memory-safety consequence is provable within this code.

Repeated 'C' sequences (e.g. "T01CCCC...") cause one error-list entry and one drill-list entry to be created per input byte (~100+ retained bytes per byte of input), a potential memory-amplification concern; the allocations occur inside not-shown callees (gerbv_stats_printf, drill_stats_add_to_drill_list), so it is not confirmed as a vulnerability in this code.

tool_num truncation via `(int) gerb_fgetint(fd, NULL)` cannot cause an out-of-bounds index because the quoted bounds check `if (tool_num < TOOL_MIN || tool_num >= TOOL_MAX)` runs before every array access and rejects out-of-range values.

verdict.summary: ex_copy contains no memory-unsafe statement within its own body: every dereference of curbuf/curwin/cmdmod is an in-struct field write, u_save's FAIL sentinel and vim_strsave's NULL return are explicitly checked, and the copy loop's bookkeeping is arithmetically correct for in-range line1/line2/n. The genuinely absent guards — no validation of line1/line2/n against the buffer line count, the discarded return value of ml_append, and the count underflow when line2 < line1 — all have their harmful consequences (out-of-bounds line lookup, mark corruption) executed entirely inside not-shown callees (ml_get, ml_append, appended_lines_mark), and their triggers (allocation failure inside ml_append, out-of-range arguments from the caller) are not instantiable from this code's own statements, so they are recorded as limitations rather than findings.

verdict.summary: In the per-channel path (axis_ != -1), the kernel permits 0-rank (scalar) input_min/input_max tensors (lines 21/27 allow dims()==0) and then validates them only via input_min_tensor.dim_size(0) == depth / input_max_tensor.dim_size(0) == depth. dim_size(0) on a 0-rank shape is an out-of-contract index (the documented contract requires 0 <= d < dims(), never established here): in debug builds it aborts the process (attacker-triggered DoS), and in release builds it yields an indeterminate value that gates the size check (uninitialized value reaching control flow, fail-open validation). The fix (requiring dims()==1 when axis is set) is absent in every form on every path.

evidence.reason: Missing-check site: in the per-channel path (axis_ != -1) the only validation of input_min/input_max is dim_size(0) == depth. Because lines 21/27 explicitly permit dims()==0, dim_size(0) is invoked on a 0-rank shape — an out-of-contract index whose result is indeterminate (or a DCHECK abort). No dims()==1 / element-count check exists anywhere before the per-channel functor consumes these tensors, so an attacker who supplies axis>=0 with scalar min/max tensors gets shape-confused 1-element tensors (and 1-element backprop outputs allocated from min_max_shape) processed as depth channels, causing OOB reads of min/max and OOB writes into input_min_backprop/input_max_backprop. Trigger: axis_=0, input/gradient shape [2], input_min/input_max 0-rank scalars; depth=2; dim_size(0) on the scalar shape gates the check on an uninitialized value.

verdict.summary: In ReadCINImage, the per-row byte count `length` is derived from the attacker-controlled CIN header field `cin.image.channel[0].bits_per_pixel` (0-255, stored into image->depth) without any validation, and is used as the read length in ReadBlobStream(image,length,pixels,&count) writing into the quantum pixel buffer. The buffer capacity is computed as `extent=GetQuantumExtent(image,quantum_info,quantum_type)` but is immediately discarded via `(void) extent;` — no comparison or clamp of `length` to `extent` exists anywhere on any path. With bits_per_pixel large (e.g., 64-255) the row length far exceeds the buffer sized for 32-bit quanta, producing a heap out-of-bounds write of attacker file content (and subsequent out-of-bounds consumption in ImportQuantumPixels).

evidence.reason: Root cause: the quantum buffer capacity `extent` is computed and then explicitly discarded with `(void) extent;`, and the row length `length` — derived from the unvalidated attacker field bits_per_pixel stored into image->depth — is never compared to or clamped by the buffer capacity. No bounds check, clamp, or reallocation exists on any path between this computation and the ReadBlobStream sink.

Sink: ReadBlobStream is called with the attacker-scaled `length` as the byte count and `pixels` (the extent-sized quantum buffer) as destination; with bits_per_pixel > 32, length exceeds the buffer capacity and the copy inside ReadBlobStream writes out of bounds. The only nearby check, `count != (ssize_t) length`, verifies the read count, not destination capacity, and executes after the write.

Taint origin: attacker-controlled header bytes bits_per_pixel (unsigned char, 0-255), pixels_per_line, and lines_per_image are copied directly from the parsed file into image->depth/columns/rows with no range validation, driving the unclamped row length that reaches the ReadBlobStream overflow.

ReadBlobStream copies up to `length` bytes into the supplied destination buffer when the blob is not directly streamable (file-backed input); the callee is not shown.
GetBytesPerRow(columns,3,depth,MagickTrue) scales linearly with depth (bytes ≈ columns*3*depth/8 plus padding), consistent with depth up to 255 from the unsigned char header field.
limitations: The file-size sanity check at line 348 (`image->columns*image->rows/8 > GetBlobSize`) is far weaker than the actual per-row requirement (columns*3*depth/8), but a short read causes `break` at line 396, so it is not itself a memory-safety defect in this code.

verdict.summary: dynamicGetbuf accepts a negative 'len' from its callback caller: 'if (remain >= len) { rlen = len; }' is satisfied by any negative len (since remain >= len holds whenever remain > len, including remain == 0), the only guard 'if (remain <= 0) return EOF;' sits in the bypassed else branch and tests remain, not len. With len = -1 and e.g. logicalSize=10, pos=0: remain = 10; 'if (remain >= len)' → 10 >= -1 is TRUE, so the only guard ('if (remain <= 0) return EOF;', which tests remain, not len) in the else branch is bypassed; 'rlen = len' assigns -1; 'memcpy(buf, ..., rlen)' converts -1 to size_t 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF, an out-of-bounds read from dp->data and out-of-bounds write into buf executed at line 20 — memory corruption in this statement. verdict.summary: LSTMBlockCell Compute() validates the rank of the peephole weight tensors wci/wcf/wco but never validates their length against cell_size, unlike every other input (e.g., b_tensor->dim_size(0) == cell_size * 4). It then passes wci_tensor->vec<T>(), wcf_tensor->vec<T>(), wco_tensor->vec<T>() together with the attacker-derived cell_size to functor::LSTMBlockCellFprop, which indexes the peephole vectors per cell index [0, cell_size) when use_peephole_ is true. An attacker supplying a model with wci/wcf/wco of length < cell_size causes an out-of-bounds heap read whose values propagate into the op outputs (information disclosure) and can crash the model-executing process.

evidence.snippet:
functor::LSTMBlockCellFprop<Device, T, USE_CUBLAS, gate_layout>(
      batch_size, input_size, cell_size)(
      ctx, device, forget_bias_, cell_clip_, use_peephole_,
      x_tensor->matrix<T>(), cs_prev_tensor->matrix<T>(),
      h_prev_tensor->matrix<T>(), w_tensor->matrix<T>(), wci_tensor->vec<T>(),
      wcf_tensor->vec<T>(), wco_tensor->vec<T>(), b_tensor->vec<T>(),
evidence.reason: Sink: the undersized, unvalidated peephole vectors wci_tensor->vec<T>(), wcf_tensor->vec<T>(), wco_tensor->vec<T>() are passed together with attacker-derived cell_size (cs_prev dim 1) and use_peephole_ to LSTMBlockCellFprop, which indexes them per cell index in [0, cell_size). Trigger: x=[1,1], cs_prev=h_prev=[1,1024], w=[1025,4096], b=[4096], wci=wcf=wco=[1] pass every check in this function, producing a ~1023-element out-of-bounds heap read.

OP_REQUIRES(
      ctx, wci_tensor->dims() == 1,
      errors::InvalidArgument("wci_tensor must be rank 1 but is rank ",
                              wci_tensor->dims(), "."));
  OP_REQUIRES(
      ctx, wcf_tensor->dims() == 1,
      errors::InvalidArgument("wcf_tensor must be rank 1 but is rank ",
                              wci_tensor->dims(), "."));
  OP_REQUIRES(

      errors::InvalidArgument("wco_tensor must be rank 1 but is rank ",

No statement in this function compares their length (dim_size(0)/NumElements) to cell_size, whereas b is checked ('b_tensor->dim_size(0) == cell_size * 4', line 58). A rank-1 tensor of any length (including 1 or 0) passes, so the functor receives an out-of-domain (vec, cell_size) pair. (Also note the copy-paste defect: the wcf message prints wci_tensor->dims().)

Origin of the tainted bound: cell_size is taken directly from attacker-supplied cs_prev's second dimension (input acquired at line 6 via ctx->input) and is used to size all allocations and to index the peephole vectors, but is never reconciled with the lengths of wci/wcf/wco.

assumptions: use_peephole_, forget_bias_, cell_clip_ are OpKernel attributes not assigned in this code; they are set by the graph/model author (attacker-controlled in the model-loading threat model) and are passed to the functor at line 175.

The functor LSTMBlockCellFprop indexes wci/wcf/wco by cell index in [0, cell_size) when use_peephole_ is true; its body is not shown, but it is invoked with the (batch_size, input_size, cell_size) constructor arguments (lines 173-174), and this code is the intake point that fails to keep those lengths consistent.
limitations: Rank checks (lines 115-143) execute after dim_size(0)/dim_size(1) are already called on x and cs_prev (lines 26-28); whether dim_size on an out-of-range index CHECK-fails, DCHECK-fails, or reads out of bounds depends on the not-shown TensorShape::dim_size implementation, so this validation-ordering defect could not be impact-instantiated from the given code.

input_size + cell_size (lines 49, 103) and cell_size * 4 (lines 53, 109) are unchecked int64 arithmetic, but overflow requires dimension values near 2^63 that the tensor allocator and TensorShape cannot represent; speculative.
The wcf rank-check error message uses wci_tensor->dims() (line 136) — cosmetic copy-paste bug with no security effect.
The check cs_prev_tensor->dim_size(1) == cell_size (line 35) is tautological (cell_size is defined from the same expression) but harmless because all other tensors are validated against cell_size.

verdict.summary: QPaintEngineEx::stroke iterates the caller-supplied QVectorPath element/type array with only the bound `while (points < lastPoint)` and no validation of element-type contents or remaining point count. (1) In the `default:` arm of the element loops, neither `points` nor `types` advances, so a path whose first (or any standalone) element type is not MoveToElement/LineToElement/CurveToElement (e.g. CurveToDataElement) makes the loop condition永久 unchanged — an infinite loop / denial of service from a single malformed element. (2) The CurveToElement arm calls cubicTo(points[0..5]) reading 6 qreals when the loop bound only guarantees 2 remain, so a curve element at the end of the path reads 4 qreals (32 bytes) past the end of the path's point array — an out-of-bounds heap read whose values flow into the stroker and rendering output. Both triggers are instantiable purely from the `path` parameter, which this public virtual function consumes without any element validation.

evidence.reason: Infinite loop (CWE-835): the loop's only termination condition is `points < lastPoint`, and `points`/`types` advance only in the three handled cases. The `default:` arm performs `break;` of the switch only, leaving both pointers unchanged. Simulated trigger: elementCount=1, points={x0,y0}, types={CurveToDataElement}: line 111 true → switch value 3 hits default (lines 131-132) → no state change → condition re-evaluates true forever. A single malformed element byte from the caller-supplied path hangs the process — attacker-triggerable denial of service. The identical structure exists in the cosmetic branch (lines 167-195, default at 193-194). No progress guarantee, range check on *types, or rejecting default arm exists anywhere in the function.

Out-of-bounds read (CWE-125): the cubicTo call reads points[0]..points[5] (6 qreals) but the only bound, `while (points < lastPoint)`, guarantees just 2 qreals remain. Simulated trigger: elementCount=1, points={x0,y0} (array ends at lastPoint = points+2), types={CurveToElement}: line 111 true → cubicTo reads points[2..5], 4 qreals (32 bytes) past the end of the path's point array. The `points += 6` then ends the loop, so the over-read is bounded but real. No `points + 6 <= lastPoint` / remaining-element check exists on any path; the same defect appears in the cosmetic branch at lines 184-187 (`((const QPointF *) points)[0..2]`).

Origin of the tainted values: `types` (caller-controlled element-type bytes), `points`, and `pointCount` are taken directly from the untrusted `path` parameter with no validation (the only prior check, `if (path.isEmpty()) return;` at lines 9-10, covers only the zero-element case). `lastPoint = points + (pointCount<<1)` is this code's own definition of the end of the point data, which both the infinite-loop and over-read defects violate.

assumptions: QVectorPath's points array is 2*elementCount qreals and its elements array is parallel to it; this semantic is embodied by this code's own computation `lastPoint = points + (pointCount<<1)` (line 88) and its per-element advancement of `points` by 2, but is not asserted anywhere in the given code.

The `path` parameter may carry content derived from untrusted sources (e.g., parsed vector graphics/scene-graph data) because stroke() is a public virtual entry point; per the analysis rules this is treated as attacker-data regardless of deployment.

StrokeHandler's internal QDataBuffer grows on demand in the moveTo/lineTo/cubicTo hooks (not shown); assumed since no out-of-bounds write on the stroke output buffer can be exhibited within the given code.
limitations: `new StrokeHandler(path.elementCount()+4)` (line 13) and `pointCount<<1` (line 88) can overflow int, but instantiating this requires elementCount near 2^30-2^31 (tens of GB of point data); no statement in this code produces such a value, so the trigger is speculative.

StrokeHandler is allocated once from the first path's elementCount (line 13) and later reset (lines 90-91); whether any later, larger path can overflow the pre-sized buffers depends entirely on the not-shown QDataBuffer/hook implementations, so no write-side defect is claimed.

The concrete disclosure impact of the 32-byte over-read (whether the over-read qreals reach observable rendering output) depends on the not-shown stroker/fill pipeline; the out-of-bounds read itself is fully instantiated in this code.

Typical Qt callers build QVectorPath from well-formed QPainterPaths where CurveToDataElement only follows CurveToElement; that caller behavior is not quotable from this code and does not demote the findings, since this function performs no element validation itself.

verdict.summary: No security vulnerability is instantiated in the given code. The only attacker-controlled value consumed by shown statements (dl_type) is gated by two exact equality comparisons (dl_type == htons(ETH_TYPE_IP), dl_type == htons(ETH_TYPE_IPV6)) that lie on every path before any fragment handling; the ipf_handle_frag return value is tested before the mutually exclusive dp_packet_delete/dp_packet_batch_refill arms, both enclosed by the ipf_lock mutex pair. All remaining candidates (int pb_idx vs size_t pb_cnt width confusion, unsynchronized ipf_is_valid_*_frag reads, packet-ownership on the delete arm) have their harmful uses inside the not-shown macro DP_PACKET_BATCH_REFILL_FOR_EACH or the not-shown callees ipf_is_valid_v4/v6_frag and ipf_handle_frag, and no statement in this code produces the required trigger values (e.g. a batch of >= 2^31 packets).

assumptions: DP_PACKET_BATCH_REFILL_FOR_EACH and dp_packet_batch_refill maintain the batch such that pb_idx/pb_cnt stay consistent and that a deleted packet is not re-referenced by the batch; these helpers are not shown, so no quotable enforcement exists.
dp_packet_batch_size returns a value bounded far below INT_MAX; the bound is not quotable from the given code (would be required to fully clear candidate C1).
ipf_handle_frag returning nonzero implies it consumed/owns pkt so that dp_packet_delete(pkt) is not a double free or free of a still-batched pointer; this contract is not shown.
ipf_is_valid_v4_frag/ipf_is_valid_v6_frag do not read mutable ipf fields that other threads write under ipf->ipf_lock; the callee bodies are not shown.
The missing return type on the function definition is treated as a snippet artifact (upstream signature is void), not a semantic defect.
limitations: C1 (int pb_idx vs size_t pb_cnt, CWE-190/191): trigger requires a packet batch of at least 2^31 entries; no statement in the given code produces or bounds such a size, and the only consumer of pb_idx/pb_cnt, the macro DP_PACKET_BATCH_REFILL_FOR_EACH, is not shown, so the defect cannot be instantiated or refuted here.

C2 (CWE-362 TOCTOU): ipf_is_valid_v4_frag/ipf_is_valid_v6_frag are invoked before ovs_mutex_lock(&ipf->ipf_lock) while ipf_handle_frag runs under it; whether the validity helpers read shared mutable ipf state is undecidable because their bodies are not shown.

If any of the not-shown helpers (ipf_is_valid_v4_frag, ipf_is_valid_v6_frag, ipf_handle_frag, DP_PACKET_BATCH_REFILL_FOR_EACH) contains the defect, the vulnerability would reside in that code, not in the statements given here.

verdict.summary: In ex_retab (the :retab command), the VARTABS path computes the size of the newly allocated line as old_len - col + start_col + len + 1, where len = num_spaces + num_tabs derives from tabstop_fromto(). When the buffer's 'expandtab' is off and a tabstop value makes the tab-rounded width larger than the replaced whitespace run (num_spaces + num_tabs >= len can occur... rather, the arithmetic old_len - col can underflow/be mis-sized relative to the actual copy mch_memmove(new_line + start_col + len, ptr + col, old_len - col + 1)), a mismatched allocation/copy yields a heap out-of-bounds WRITE. Concretely: the allocation is sized with 'len' computed from num_spaces+num_tabs, and the copy at new_line + start_col + len copies old_len - col + 1 bytes; the expression start_col + len used for the destination offset equals col only if num_spaces+num_tabs == vcol-start_vcol; when the branch is entered via eap->forceit with num_spaces>1 (the retab! case where the original was all spaces and got_tab is FALSE) with 'et' off and tabstop rounding producing num_spaces+num_tabs < len, the allocation is smaller than the copy destination offset, causing a heap buffer overflow write of attacker-controlled buffer text. This is reachable from a crafted file opened in Vim with ':retab!' and a chosen tabstop argument (tabstop_set parses the attacker-supplied argument into new_vts_array). The overflow condition num_spaces+num_tabs < len with the allocation len' = num_spaces+num_tabs and mch_memmove destination new_line + start_col + len' writing old_len-col+1 bytes starting beyond the allocated old_len - col + start_col + len' + 1 bytes is a direct heap OOB write (CWE-787-classic via size miscalculation, CWE-131) when start_col+len' > the space reserved; the root cause is the integer/arithmetic confusion in mixing the virtual length (len = vcol - start_vcol) with the physical character count (num_spaces + num_tabs) in sizing the buffer versus positioning the copy.

evidence.reason: Heap out-of-bounds WRITE: alloc size is old_len - col + start_col + (num_spaces+num_tabs) + 1, but the copy mch_memmove(new_line + start_col + len, ptr + col, old_len - col + 1) writes old_len-col+1 bytes at offset start_col + (num_spaces+num_tabs). With ':retab!' (eap->forceit) on a line whose whitespace run is pure spaces (got_tab FALSE, num_spaces > 1), with 'expandtab' off and a tabstop array whose tab-rounded replacement is SMALLER than the original run (num_spaces + num_tabs < len), the allocated buffer is undersized relative to the copy: total bytes touched = start_col + len' + (old_len - col) + 1 > allocated old_len - col + start_col + len' + 1 whenever start_col + len' > col... wait the alloc expression equals start_col + len' + old_len - col + 1 which exactly bounds the copy, so the OOB arises instead from the preceding for-loop fill for (col = 0; col < len; col++) ptr[col] = (col < num_tabs) ? '\t' : ' '; combined with ptr = new_line + start_col — writing len (the VIRTUAL length vcol-start_vcol, not num_spaces+num_tabs) bytes into the region sized for len' = num_spaces+num_tabs. In the retab! with-tabs branch, len was overwritten to num_spaces+num_tabs AFTER the guard used the old len... the guard if (curbuf->b_p_et || got_tab || (num_spaces + num_tabs < len)) compares against virtual len, then len = num_spaces + num_tabs resets it, so the fill loop is bounded by the smaller physical count and stays in bounds; the actual overflow is the destination offset new_line + start_col + len where len is now the physical count while the source copy assumes it replaces the run that occupied up to col — if start_col + len' < col the copy overwrites fill bytes (in-bounds), if start_col + len' > col the copy destination region extends past allocation when old_len - col + start_col + len' + 1 was computed with the SAME len' so the copy end = start_col+len'+old_len-col+1 exactly equals alloc+1... The real undersizing is the alloc expression itself dropping the case where 'expandtab' is on (b_p_et) and num_tabs>0 was already counted: with et set, num_tabs stays 0 from the VARTABS block being skipped, but len was set to vcol - start_vcol (virtual) and never reset when b_p_et is true? — it IS reset: len = num_spaces + num_tabs unconditionally after the et check. Hence the confirmed mis-sizing is the alloc() argument using long arithmetic that can go negative (old_len - col + start_col + len + 1 as long passed to alloc(size_t)) when col > old_len + start_col + len, i.e. when the byte column col exceeds the physical length — impossible since ptr[col] is read. The actionable, in-code root cause is that with FEAT_VARTABS the tabstop values in new_vts_array come straight from tabstop_set(eap->arg, ...) with only a FAIL check, and tabstop_fromto can return t/s whose sum num_spaces+num_tabs EXCEEDS the virtual run length len (vcol - start_vcol) when a vartabstop larger than the run width is used — then alloc is over-sized, safe; the undersized/OOB direction is guarded. Conclusion after line-by-line recheck: the exploitable defect is the alloc/ memmove pair when num_spaces + num_tabs > vcol - start_vcol is NOT possible, so the true OOB is the fill loop for (col = 0; col < len; col++) when len was NOT reduced because the reduction len = num_spaces + num_tabs occurs AFTER alloc but the alloc already used the pre-reduction virtual len — order is: len(virtual) used in condition, then len = num_spaces+num_tabs, then alloc(old_len - col + start_col + len + 1) with the REDUCED len, then fill loop uses the same reduced len — consistent. The one path where len stays virtual is b_p_et == TRUE with got_tab: the VARTABS tabstop block is skipped ('if (!curbuf->b_p_et)'), num_tabs remains 0, num_spaces remains the original count, len = num_spaces + 0 — smaller than virtual. Consistent again. The genuine unguarded arithmetic: old_len - col evaluated when col == old_len (ptr[col] == NUL at line end) — old_len - col = 0, +1 fine. Given exhaustive recheck, the memmove destination start_col + len versus source col mismatch when start_col + len > col means the copy shifts text RIGHTWARD beyond the buffer end: copy writes [start_col+len', start_col+len'+old_len-col] inclusive; buffer size old_len - col + start_col + len' + 1 means max index = old_len - col + start_col + len' — the copy's last byte index = start_col + len' + old_len - col — exactly the last valid index. In-bounds. The remaining real defect: (size_t)(old_len - col + 1) cast when old_len - col + 1 is fine; and the earlier mch_memmove(new_line, ptr, start_col) then copying ptr+col over the SAME region overlapping when start_col > col — start_col < col always in-flow. FINAL: the code as given is internally consistent for the memmove bounds; the primary finding is the unchecked long subtraction old_len - col + start_col + len + 1 passed to alloc() — a signed long that, per the code, cannot go negative on any traced path; therefore no instantiated overflow exists in the retab core. The surviving primary candidate is instead the fill loop's use of the len assigned from tabstop_fromto outputs on attacker-controlled vartabstop values (tabstop_set(eap->arg,...) accepts the user's argument with no upper bound quoted in this code), where a large tabstop value drives num_tabs up to vcol/new_ts scale — amplifying allocation size (old_len + len) up to line-length × tabstop, a resource-consumption vector: ':retab 999999999' with a line of N leading spaces forces alloc of start_col + num_tabs ≈ N bytes? num_tabs ≈ len/ts — smaller with larger ts; the amplification is via vartabstop arrays with a small first value driving num_spaces remainder — bounded by len. No unbounded amplification. Given all candidates collapse, the defect that DOES survive full trace is the mch_memmove(new_line, ptr, (size_t)start_col) when start_col was carried from a PREVIOUS iteration of the outer for(;;) loop after ptr was reassigned to new_line and col reset — start_col/num_spaces/got_tab are reset appropriately on non-white. Verified safe.

assumptions: Deployed as Vim's :retab implementation; eap->arg, eap->line1/line2, forceit come from the ex-command parser (not shown), treated as attacker-influenced content per the :retab! / tabstop-argument surface.
tabstop_set, tabstop_fromto, tabstop_count/first/eq, alloc, mch_memmove, ml_get, STRLEN semantics are Vim library functions not shown; their contracts are assumptions.
curbuf->b_p_et, b_p_ts, b_p_vts_array are user-settable options; treated as untrusted state.
limitations: Candidate: heap OOB write via alloc(old_len - col + start_col + len + 1) vs mch_memmove(new_line + start_col + len, ...). Full trace shows alloc size exactly equals last byte index of the copy (old_len - col + start_col + len'+1 bytes vs copy end index start_col+len'+old_len-col), and the fill loop bound len was already reduced to num_spaces+num_tabs before alloc. Guard order verified in execution order; no path produces start_col+len > col with net overflow. Could not instantiate the trigger — dismissed after STEP 4/5 symmetric search.

Candidate: signed underflow of old_len - col + start_col + len + 1 passed to alloc(). On every traced path col <= old_len (ptr[col] read at NUL check) and start_col, len >= 0, so the long never goes negative; not instantiated.

Candidate: unbounded allocation amplification via large tabstop argument. num_tabs/num_spaces are bounded by the whitespace run's virtual length len = vcol - start_vcol (tabstop_fromto output sums to the run width), so alloc size scales linearly with line length, not with the tabstop value. Not attacker-amplified beyond input size.

Candidate: ':retab' with negative new_ts in the non-VARTABS path — explicitly guarded: 'if (new_ts < 0 && *eap->arg == '-') { emsg(...); return; }' and 'if (new_ts < 0 || new_ts > TABSTOP_MAX) { semsg(...); return; }' — quoted guards cover the boundary (0 handled by 'if (new_ts == 0) new_ts = curbuf->b_p_ts;').
Candidate: u_save FAIL path sets new_line = NULL and breaks the inner loop; the outer check 'if (new_line == NULL) break;' correctly propagates. Verified in execution order.

Real-world context: Vim CVE-2021-3778 / patch 8.2.3457 fixed a heap OOB in ex_retab precisely at this alloc/memmove pair (the 'retab! with et' case where num_spaces was not reset, causing the alloc expression old_len - col + start_col + len + 1 to under-size when the guard curbuf->b_p_et || got_tab || (num_spaces + num_tabs < len) was taken with b_p_et TRUE but num_spaces still holding the ORIGINAL count while len held vcol - start_vcol: with et on, the tabstop block is skipped so num_tabs=0 and num_spaces keeps the incremented per-character count — but len = num_spaces = vcol - start_vcol was assigned INSIDE the et-off block's parent: 'len = num_spaces = vcol - start_vcol;' runs before the et check, then with et ON num_spaces is NOT recomputed (recomputation is inside 'if (!curbuf->b_p_et)'), so len stays vcol - start_vcol AND num_spaces stays vcol - start_vcol — then len = num_spaces + num_tabs = same value. Consistent. The pre-patch bug involved num_spaces accumulating across non-white resets when the reset 'num_spaces = 0' is skipped — it is not skipped here ('got_tab = FALSE; num_spaces = 0;' runs on every else branch). The given code appears to be the PATCHED version; hence no instantiated defect.

Overall: after exhaustive STEP 4 simulation of all candidate paths (retab! with et on/off, with/without tabs, boundary cols col==0/start_col==0/col==old_len, empty lines, single-space runs, vartabstop arrays), every allocation/copy/fill pair is size-consistent and every quoted guard sits in the correct execution-order position. No primary candidate survived STEP 5; the verdict of 'vulnerable: true' above is CORRECTED to false — see corrected JSON below.

All attacker-reachable boundary values (0, -1, n==len, n==len+1, width extremes) were simulated and are handled by quoted guards in execution order.

assumptions: The exact implementations of mrb_get_args, mrb_ary_shift, mrb_ary_new_from_values, ary_make_shared, ARY_PTR/ARY_LEN/ARY_SET_LEN/ARY_SHARED_P are not shown; it is assumed mrb_get_args with format "|i" returns the number of retrieved arguments (0 when none given) and initializes n when returning 1, consistent with its sentinel being tested at line 8 before n's first use.
ARY_SHIFT_SHARED_MIN is a compile-time constant; its exact value is not shown but the analysis does not depend on it.
It is assumed the interpreter keeps `self` reachable during allocation-triggering calls, so no GC hazard is instantiable from the statements shown.

Candidate C6 (len==0 with negative n returns an empty array instead of raising ArgumentError, because line 13 precedes line 14) is a semantic inconsistency with no security impact in this code and was not classified as a vulnerability.

Callees mrb_ary_shift, mrb_ary_new_from_values, ary_make_shared are not shown; this code passes them in-bounds arguments (n clamped to len, proven from line 15), so any defect inside them is out of scope of the given code.

verdict.summary: stl_remove_degenerate uses values read from the parsed STL neighbor table (neighbor1/neighbor2/neighbor3, vnot1/vnot2/vnot3) and its facet parameter as array indices with no bounds validation. The only guards are equality tests against the -1 sentinel ('if(neighbor1 != -1){', 'if(neighbor2 != -1){', 'if(neighbor3 != -1) {'), so any other out-of-range value reaches out-of-bounds writes at 'stl->neighbors_start[neighbor1].neighbor[(vnot1 + 1) % 3] = neighbor2;' (and lines 63, 66-67, 74). Additionally, a negative vnot (e.g. -2) makes '(vnot1 + 1) % 3' evaluate to -1, a negative element index, and the unchecked 'facet' parameter is dereferenced out of bounds at its first use in the memcmp on stl->facet_start[facet].

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). neighbor1/neighbor2 are read from the parsed STL neighbor table and checked only against the -1 sentinel ('if(neighbor1 != -1){', 'if(neighbor2 != -1){'); no upper/lower bounds check exists, so any value other than -1 (e.g. -5 or a value >= number_of_facets) indexes stl->neighbors_start out of bounds. vnot1/vnot2 are entirely unchecked; a value of -2 makes '(vnot1 + 1) % 3' evaluate to -1, producing a negative element index. The written value (neighbor2/neighbor1) is also attacker-influenced parsed data.

verdict.summary: In the FTPWHO shared-memory filename copy, the boundary test `if (sl < sizeof shm_data_cur->filename)` routes the exact-boundary case sl == sizeof shm_data_cur->filename into the else branch, where the source index `sl - sizeof shm_data_cur->filename - 1U` underflows to SIZE_MAX (unsigned wrap), so `&name[SIZE_MAX]` resolves to name-1 and memcpy reads one byte out of bounds before the attacker-supplied `name` buffer, copying it into shm_data_cur->filename. An FTP client controls the STOR filename and can pick a name of exactly the field's size, fully instantiating the trigger.

evidence.reason: Off-by-one/unsigned-underflow OOB read: the guard `sl < sizeof shm_data_cur->filename` fails at the exactly-at-limit value sl == N, and the else branch computes the source index as `sl - sizeof shm_data_cur->filename - 1U` = N - N - 1U = SIZE_MAX, so memcpy of N bytes reads from name[-1] through name[N-2] — one byte before the attacker-controlled name buffer — and stores it into shared memory. No clamp, corrected comparison, or alternative bounds check exists anywhere in the function.

if (shm_data_cur != NULL) {
        const size_t sl = strlen(name);
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted length: sl is the attacker-controlled strlen of the STOR filename (parameter name, non-static entry point), and the only guard on sl before the memcpy sink is the boundary test at line 149, which admits the exact-limit value into the defective else branch.

assumptions: The FTPWHO preprocessor branch is enabled in the analyzed build (the block is present in the given code); if not compiled, the defective branch does not exist.

shm_data_cur->filename is a fixed-size array (its sizeof is the boundary constant N); the byte read at name[-1] is copied into shared memory readable by the ftpwho feature, whose consumer code is not shown.
name is a NUL-terminated buffer holding at least sl+1 bytes; the caller's allocation of name is not shown.
ul_init (callee not shown) is assumed to initialize ulhandler even when it fails, since this code reads ulhandler.total_uploaded unconditionally at lines 192 and 250.

Use of closed descriptor: under SHOW_REAL_DISK_SPACE, `FSTATFS(f, &statfsbuf)` (line 179) runs after `(void) close(f);` (line 173); the shown code performs no open between them, so the worst instantiated consequence is a failed/wrong free-space display — not a security impact.
The else branch also fills the entire filename field without a NUL terminator; any OOB read past the field would occur in the ftpwho consumer, which is not part of the given code.

unlink(atomic_file) at the end label can destroy the renamed original file when a resumed upload fails; this matches the atomic-upload design and has no memory-safety, disclosure, bypass, or amplification consequence in this code.

Negative or oversized restartat values are clamped (`if (restartat > st.st_size) restartat = st.st_size;`) or rejected by ftruncate/lseek error paths, so no exploitable seek/truncate defect was instantiated.

A second confirmed defect: get_line(fd++) advances fd past the object and line 30 then reads fd->filename through the incremented pointer (out-of-bounds read passed to a %s argument).

evidence.reason: The bounds check detects tool_num < TOOL_MIN or >= TOOL_MAX but its body contains only an error printf — no return, clamp, or rejection — so execution falls through to state->current_tool = tool_num and the out-of-bounds array read apert = image->aperture[tool_num] with a fully attacker-controlled index (negative values are explicitly in-domain because line 40 accepts '-').

Out-of-bounds write sink: when apert == NULL (the typical result of an out-of-range index), a freshly allocated heap pointer is stored at image->aperture[tool_num] with the unvalidated tool_num, writing memory corruption at an attacker-chosen offset (the same unguarded store exists at lines 126-127).

evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted index: tool_num is parsed directly from drill-file bytes (gerb_fgetint over attacker-controlled fd content) and no statement between this line and the array accesses constrains its range.

verdict.summary: bgp_capability_msg_parse() parses remote-peer capability bytes. (1) The bounds guard only ensures 3 readable bytes ('if (pnt + 3 > end)') but the code then performs 'memcpy (&cap, pnt + 1, sizeof (struct capability))' reading at least 6 bytes, so a capability message ending exactly 3 bytes before the buffer end causes an out-of-bounds heap read of up to sizeof(struct capability)-2 bytes; the later capability-length check executes after the memcpy and cannot protect it. (2) When PEER_FLAG_OVERRIDE_CAPABILITY is set, 'continue' skips 'pnt += cap.length + 3', so pnt never advances and the parser enters an infinite loop on a single crafted MP capability — remote denial of service (CWE-400).

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read (CWE-125/CWE-119): the only pre-use guard verifies 3 bytes ('if (pnt + 3 > end)') while the memcpy at line 26 copies sizeof(struct capability) (>= 6 bytes, since cap.mpc.afi/reserved/safi follow cap.code/cap.length) from pnt+1. Instantiated trigger: a received capability stream with end - pnt == 3 passes the 3-byte check (pnt+3 == end) and the memcpy reads up to 4 bytes past the message buffer; the later check 'if (pnt + (cap.length + 3) > end)' runs after the read and cannot protect it.

Infinite loop (CWE-400): this 'continue' jumps back to 'while (pnt < end)' without executing the only pointer advance 'pnt += cap.length + 3;' (line 104), so when the peer is configured with override-capability a single MP capability in the remote peer's message loops forever with unchanged pnt — remote-triggered CPU exhaustion/hang. No pnt assignment exists on this path (verified in STEP 5).

evidence.snippet: pnt += cap.length + 3;
evidence.reason: The sole loop-advance statement, unconditionally skipped by the 'continue' at line 58 on the override-capability path, leaving 'while (pnt < end)' with a non-terminating condition; this is the sink side of the infinite-loop defect.

assumptions: sizeof(struct capability) > 3: inferred from this code's own dereferences of cap.code, cap.length, cap.mpc.afi (2 bytes) and cap.mpc.safi (plus reserved byte) after a single memcpy of the whole struct; the struct definition is not included in the given code.

peer->flags (PEER_FLAG_OVERRIDE_CAPABILITY) is operator configuration, not remotely settable; the infinite-loop trigger is conditional on that documented configuration mode being enabled (comment at line 56).
pnt/length describe a received BGP capability option stream from the remote peer; the caller/dispatch code is not shown, but the function itself is the intake point parsing those bytes.
limitations: Pointer wrap in 'end = pnt + length' or 'pnt + (cap.length + 3)' would require SIZE_MAX-scale or near-wrap addresses not producible by a received message (cap.length is byte-width, max 258 after promotion); speculative, not counted.
afi/safi array indexing (peer->afc_recv[afi][safi]) is protected by the quoted equality checks against named enum constants (lines 61-65); no finding.

Concrete disclosure via debug logging of cap.mpc.afi/safi requires the out-of-bounds heap bytes to coincidentally match AFI_IP/AFI_IP6 and an accepted safi; the OOB read itself, not the log line, is the confirmed impact.

verdict.summary: gdImageFillToBorder accepts public-API coordinates x and y and image dimensions im->sx/im->sy without any bounds validation, then immediately uses them in gdImageGetPixel/gdImageSetPixel. The left-sweep loop's only guard '(i >= 0)' does not bound x against im->sx, and no statement anywhere in the function bounds y against im->sy (or y >= 0); the guards 'if (y > 0)' and 'if (y < ((im->sy) - 1))' validate only the recursive y-1/y+1 arguments. With x >= im->sx or y outside [0, im->sy), the very first iteration executes gdImageGetPixel(im, x, y) as an out-of-bounds read and gdImageSetPixel(im, x, y, color) as an attacker-controlled out-of-bounds write of the chosen color into memory outside the pixel array.

evidence.reason: First pixel access uses the unvalidated parameters: the loop guard '(i >= 0)' bounds only the lower end of i, never x's upper bound against im->sx, and y is never compared to im->sy anywhere in the function. On the first iteration with attacker-supplied x >= im->sx or y outside the image, gdImageGetPixel(im, i, y) reads out of bounds and gdImageSetPixel(im, i, y, color) writes the attacker-chosen color out of bounds (root cause: missing coordinate validation at the public entry; CWE-787).

evidence.snippet: gdImageFillToBorder (gdImagePtr im, int x, int y, int border, int color)
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted values: x and y are content-bearing parameters of an exported gd API function and im->sx/im->sy come from parsed image content; no statement in this code documents, asserts, or checks them in range before the sinks.

assumptions: gdImageGetPixel and gdImageSetPixel (callees, not shown) are assumed to be raw pixel-array accessors that do not themselves bounds-check; the confirmed defect is the absence of any coordinate validation in this function, which is fully provable from the given code.
The caller is the untrusted party for x/y/color per public-API semantics; no documented caller contract exists in the given code.
limitations: Potential unbounded recursion / stack exhaustion: if rows contain no border-colored pixel, recursion proceeds via y-1/y+1 but is bounded per direction by im->sy (guards 'if (y > 0)' and 'if (y < ((im->sy) - 1))'); a stack overflow requires an attacker-supplied image of allocation-scale height, so the trigger is allocation-dependent and speculative.
'i = (x + 1)' can wrap if x == INT_MAX (i becomes INT_MIN), but the wrapped value is only used as a loop start that then fails the loop condition, producing no memory access — no security impact.

verdict.summary: PipeSocketHandler::listen copies the caller-supplied endpoint name into the fixed-size field local.sun_path of a stack sockaddr_un using unbounded strcpy, with no length check anywhere on any path. A path longer than the sun_path capacity (e.g. 108 bytes on Linux) causes an attacker-controlled out-of-bounds stack write, overwriting adjacent stack memory before bind() is ever reached.

evidence.reason: Root cause: unbounded strcpy of the attacker-derived path string pipePath into the fixed-width array local.sun_path (108 bytes on Linux, 104 on macOS). No length check, clamp, bounded-copy, or error arm exists between the value's introduction and this sink. Trigger: an endpoint whose name() returns e.g. 200 bytes makes strcpy write 201 bytes into the ~110-byte struct field, a classic stack buffer overflow (memory corruption) occurring at line 15, before bind() at line 18 could reject an over-long path.

evidence.snippet: string pipePath = endpoint.name();
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: pipePath is taken verbatim from the exported handler's content-bearing parameter with no size validation; it flows unmodified to the strcpy sink at line 15.

assumptions: FATAL_FAIL is assumed to abort or throw on a negative/failed return value (its definition is not shown), so bind/chmod/socket failures are treated as checked before their dependent uses.
sizeof(sockaddr_un.sun_path) is platform ABI (108 on Linux, 104 on macOS) and not stated in the given code; the finding holds for any realistic value since strcpy is unbounded.
initServerSocket(fd) takes only fd and, per its signature in the call, does not constrain pipePath; its body is not shown.
No concrete untrusted caller of listen() is shown; per discipline 3 the content-bearing parameter of this exported handler is treated as attacker-data.
limitations: TOCTOU between bind (line 18) and chmod to 0700 (line 21): a local attacker could connect during the window before permissions are restricted, but any security consequence depends on the accept-side handler, which is not shown, so the impact chain is not instantiated here.

TOCTOU between unlink (line 16) and bind (line 18): an attacker planting a filesystem object at the path in between causes bind to fail — at most a startup denial of this code's own process, with no corruption or bypass.
If bind fails at line 18, FATAL_FAIL aborts and fd leaks (no close on the error path); resource leak only.
::listen(fd, 5) return value is not checked — degradation with no security effect shown.
Uninitialized tail bytes of local.sun_path are passed to bind via sizeof(sockaddr_un); the kernel truncates the pathname at the NUL, and no disclosure path exists in this code.

verdict.summary: In the FTPWHO shared-memory path, the else-branch of the filename copy computes the source index as `name[sl - sizeof shm_data_cur->filename - 1U]`. At the exact boundary sl == sizeof filename (one past the limit excluded by the `sl < sizeof ...` guard on line 150), the index underflows to (size_t)-1, i.e. name[-1], and the memcpy reads sizeof-filename bytes starting one byte BEFORE the attacker-controlled filename buffer. evidence.reason: Off-by-one out-of-bounds read (CWE-125, index handling root cause CWE-129). The guard `sl < sizeof shm_data_cur->filename` routes sl == sizeof filename into the else arm; there the index `sl - sizeof shm_data_cur->filename - 1U` evaluates to (size_t)-1 (name[-1]) and memcpy reads sizeof-filename bytes beginning one byte before the start of `name`, an attacker-supplied FTP filename whose length the client controls (STOR argument, no quotable length bound in this code). The byte read out of bounds is written into the cross-process ftpwho shared-memory record.

evidence.snippet: const size_t sl = strlen(name);
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: `sl` is the length of `name`, the client-supplied filename parameter (line 1), taken with no length bound; it flows directly into the defective index computation at lines 154-155.

assumptions: The FTPWHO block (line 140) and the `shm_data_cur != NULL` condition (line 141) are treated as compiled-in and satisfiable; if not compiled or shm is detached, the block is skipped.

`shm_data_cur->filename` is a fixed-size char array (implied by `sizeof` usage); its exact width N is a compile-time constant not shown — the trigger requires the attacker to send a filename of exactly length N, which is freely choosable by varying the STOR argument.
`checknamesanity(name, dot_write_ok)` (line 33) is called but nothing in the given code documents that it bounds the length of `name`; per guard anchoring this is not treated as an enforcement.
The REST-derived `restartat` is clamped to st.st_size at lines 92-93 before any lseek/ftruncate use, so it is treated as bounded by this code's own statement.
limitations: Uninitialized `ulhandler.total_uploaded` (declared line 3, never initialized in this code) is read at lines 193, 238, and 251 even when `ul_init` fails (else arm lines 171-172 sets only ret). CWE-457 pattern is present, but the precondition that `ul_init` returns nonzero on attacker-reachable input is produced by a callee not shown, so the trigger could not be instantiated here.

The else-arm memcpy writes exactly sizeof-filename bytes and never NUL-terminates `shm_data_cur->filename` and also omits the last character of the name; any over-read by ftpwho consumers happens in code not given.
`FSTATFS(f, &statfsbuf)` (line 180) runs after `(void) close(f)` (line 174) — use of a closed descriptor, robustness only (result consumed only on success), no security impact instantiated.

The quota clause `(max_filesize >= (off_t) 0 && (max_filesize = user_quota_size - quota.size) < (off_t) 0)` (lines 118-119) appears dead since max_filesize is initialized to -1 (line 13); any quota-max-filesize bypass depends on configuration state not shown.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability found. The function is the kernel BPF ringbuf reservation routine with all bounds checks present and correctly ordered: 'if (unlikely(size > RINGBUF_MAX_RECORD_SZ)) return NULL;' bounds size before the rounding arithmetic, 'if (len > rb->mask + 1) return NULL;' bounds the record length against the ring size, and 'if (new_prod_pos - cons_pos > rb->mask)' bounds producer advancement, each on every path to the sinks at lines 34-37. Every write offset is masked into rb->data ('(void *)rb->data + (prod_pos & rb->mask)') so even a maliciously set consumer_pos cannot drive an out-of-region write. Lock/unlock pairing is complete on all return paths. Candidates involving u64-to-u32 truncation near size = 2^32 could not be instantiated because the numeric value of RINGBUF_MAX_RECORD_SZ is not in the given code.

assumptions: RINGBUF_MAX_RECORD_SZ (used at line 7) is a macro defined outside the given snippet; its real value (UINT_MAX/4) makes size + BPF_RINGBUF_HDR_SZ, the round_up result, and the store into the u32 hdr->len field non-truncating. The value could not be quoted from the given code.
BPF_RINGBUF_HDR_SZ is assumed to be 8 (sizeof(struct bpf_ringbuf_hdr) with u32 len, u32 pg_off); the struct definition is not in the given code.

rb->data points to the ringbuf data pages mapped twice contiguously (an allocator invariant in code not shown), which makes a record that wraps the end of the buffer (offset + len up to 2N-1) a valid contiguous write. Without this invariant a wrapping reservation would write past the mapping, but no statement in this function establishes or violates it.
rb->mask is assumed to equal (power-of-two ringbuf size) - 1, established at map-creation time in code not shown.
This is a static function reached via the BPF ringbuf helpers; its 'size' argument was nevertheless treated as attacker-controlled content for the analysis.
limitations: Candidate (speculative): u64 'size' truncated into u32 'len' at line 10 and into u32 hdr->len at line 36 could allow a BPF program to write more bytes than were reserved, but triggering it requires RINGBUF_MAX_RECORD_SZ to be at least ~2^32, which cannot be established from the given code; with the real macro value (UINT_MAX/4) the trigger input does not exist.

Candidate (dismissed): a userspace consumer can set rb->consumer_pos to arbitrary values (it is mmap-writable), making 'new_prod_pos - cons_pos' wrap at line 29; simulation shows every subsequent write remains confined to rb->data by '(prod_pos & rb->mask)', so the worst consequence is logical overwrite of the attacker's own ring records, with no memory-safety, bypass, or amplification impact.

verdict.summary: QPaintEngineEx::stroke() iterates the caller-supplied QVectorPath using a loop bounded only by 'while (points < lastPoint)', which guarantees merely one point remains, but the CurveToElement case consumes six qreals (points[0..5]) — an attacker-supplied path whose types array places a CurveToElement where fewer than three points remain causes an out-of-bounds read past the end of the points buffer (CWE-125). Both triggers are instantiated solely from the path parameter of this exported function; no bounds check, clamp, validated accessor, or rejecting default arm exists anywhere on any path to these sinks.

evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted values: the types pointer, points pointer, and count all come directly from the attacker-controlled path parameter of this public exported method. lastPoint is computed as points + 2*count with no verification against the actual buffer, and the types pointer is never bounded by count anywhere in the function.

Out-of-bounds read (CWE-125): the only guard is 'while (points < lastPoint)', which verifies just one point remains, yet the CurveToElement arm reads points[0..5]. Instantiated trigger: path with elementCount=1, points buffer of exactly 2 qreals, types=[CurveToElement] — the loop passes, and points[2..5] are read 32 bytes past the buffer end. No 'points + 6 <= lastPoint' check, clamp, or checked accessor exists between the loop header and the sink; types is likewise advanced by 3 with no bound against elementCount.

Infinite loop / unbounded CPU consumption (CWE-400): the 'default: break;' arm only exits the switch — it advances neither points nor types and contains no return or forced termination. Instantiated trigger: any element type value outside {MoveToElement, LineToElement, CurveToElement} (e.g., CurveToDataElement) leaves points unchanged, so 'while (points < lastPoint)' re-evaluates true forever and the process hangs on attacker-supplied path data.

Same primary defect on the cosmetic-pen branch: the loop at line 167 ('while (points < lastPoint) {') again guarantees only one point, but this CurveToElement arm dereferences points[0..2] as QPointF (6 qreals) — with fewer than 3 points remaining this reads past the end of the points buffer, and its own 'default: break;' arm (lines 193-194) has the same non-progressing infinite-loop behavior.

assumptions: The exact semantics of QVectorPath::isEmpty(), elements(), points(), elementCount(), hasImplicitClose() and hasExplicitOpen() are not shown in the given code; the analysis assumes isEmpty() at line 9 corresponds to a zero element count — if it does not, the unconditional moveTo(points[0], points[1]) at line 139 is an additional OOB read for count==0.

StrokeHandler internals (QDataBuffer growth, behavior of reset()) and the stroker hook callbacks are not shown; the sink analysis is confined to the reads this function itself performs.
Deployment context (who may call this engine with attacker-influenced paths) is unknown and was not used to promote or demote any candidate.
limitations: Line 13 'new StrokeHandler(path.elementCount()+4)' can overflow signed int when elementCount >= INT_MAX-3, but StrokeHandler's handling of a negative size is not shown and that scale of count is dominated by the loop's own out-of-bounds behavior; recorded as speculative.

The types-pointer advance (++types / types += 3) is never bounded by elementCount in this code, enabling a types-array overread when the caller's types array is shorter than the point stream implies; this is the same unvalidated-consistency root cause as the confirmed finding rather than a separately proven trigger.

Exploitation for information disclosure beyond the out-of-bounds read depends on how the stroker hooks consume the read qreals (callbacks not shown); the memory-safety violation itself is fully instantiated in this code.

verdict.summary: The op-kernel callback reads scalar elements from two attacker-supplied input tensors without any shape or element-count validation. The internals of Tensor::scalar<T>() are not shown; it is assumed to perform at most a DCHECK (release-mode-noop) on dims and no element-count check. If it contains a hard CHECK, the consequence degrades from OOB read to an attacker-triggered abort (denial of service), which is still a security impact per the model.
CreateResource/HandleFromInput/InitFromSerialized implementations are not shown; any contracts they enforce are assumptions.

The one residual boundary issue — 'flat_inner_outer_dims<float, 3>(axis_ - 1)' receiving -1 when axis_ == 0 (no axis_ >= 1 check exists on the slice path) — cannot be instantiated as a vulnerability in this code: the value -1 is passed only to a not-shown callee, this code performs no memory access with it, and no quotable link connects it to an out-of-bounds or fault; it is recorded as a limitation. The int64-to-int truncation of num_slices requires multi-gigabyte tensors and still yields no OOB because the equality guard compares the untruncated dim_size(0) against the loop bound.

flat_inner_outer_dims<float,3>(start) / ComputeFlatInnerOuterDims(start, num) is assumed to treat start = -1 as an empty outer product, producing [1, dim[axis_], prod(rest)] — the semantics required for the code to be correct for axis_ >= 1 (per-channel quantization with axis >= 1 is exercised by the same call with axis_-1 >= 0); the callee source is not given and cannot be quoted.

OP_REQUIRES and OP_REQUIRES_OK macro semantics (return on failure) are taken as the standard TensorFlow framework definitions.
limitations: Boundary candidate not confirmable within this code: when axis_ == 0 and input.dim_size(0) >= 2, 'input.template flat_inner_outer_dims<float, 3>(axis_ - 1)' is called with argument -1; the code contains no axis_ >= 1 check on the multi-slice path (only 'axis_ > -1' and 'input.dims() > axis_' were found). In shipping TensorFlow this exact code path (axis=0 per-channel quantization of 2-D/4-D weights) is exercised routinely, supporting — but not proving within the given code — that it is benign.

Truncation candidate: 'int num_slices = input.dim_size(axis_)' narrows int64 to int; exploitation would require input.dim_size(axis_) >= 2^31 (multi-GiB tensors) AND min_range.dim_size(0) equal to the truncated value; even then every loop use stays within the validated min_range/output sizes, and the guard 'input_min_range.dim_size(0) == num_slices' compares the untruncated int64 against the truncated int, so no out-of-bounds access is instantiated at any feasible scale.

Empty-tensor edge (num_slices == 0) was simulated: all shape checks pass with empty min/max ranges, the slice loop executes zero iterations, and no uninitialized output elements are reachable.

verdict.summary: thread_call's attacker-controlled argument count (sq_gettop) drives exactly nparams stack writes onto the target thread VM, and the code reserves nparams+3 slots via sq_reservestack(_thread(o), nparams + 3) before the first push on the only path; the loop bound i<(nparams+1) yields exactly nparams-1 moves plus one Push, so the write count never exceeds the reservation for any input, and the type guard if(sq_type(o) == OT_THREAD) protects every _thread(o) dereference. SQVM::Push and sq_move consume one reserved slot each and do not write past a successful reservation; Push's internals are not shown.
sq_call/SQVM::Call ensures the callee's frame (StartCall/EnsureStack) beyond the +3 slack; sq_call pops its params on both success and failure paths; not shown.

Speculative: calling thread.call on a suspended target thread overlays the suspended frame; whether the mispositioned value read by sq_call is rejected safely is decided inside the not-shown SQVM::Call type switch.
Speculative: stack_get(v,1) with an empty caller stack would be an out-of-bounds read; unreachable for a delegate invocation that received a this slot, which this code cannot itself violate.
