verdict.summary: In issuerAndThisUpdateCheck, the GSER quote-scanning loops for the issuer (lines 65-77) and thisUpdate (lines 107-111) values exit either at a terminating '"' or by exhausting x.bv_len with no terminator found. The code unconditionally advances x.bv_val by len+1 and subtracts len+1 from x.bv_len (lines 78-79, 112-113), so an input whose quoted value lacks a closing quote (while still ending in the required '}') makes x.bv_len underflow (ber_len_t unsigned, 0-1 = 0xFFFFFFFF) and leaves x.bv_val one byte past the end of the input buffer. The subsequent eat-spaces loop and ',' check (lines 122, 130) then read x.bv_val[0] out of bounds (the loop's x.bv_len term is huge and cannot stop it, and it keeps walking over further OOB bytes while they are spaces), giving an attacker-supplied input an out-of-bounds read / denial-of-service primitive in the parsing process.

evidence.reason: Root cause site 1 (issuer value): the scan loop can exit with is->bv_len == x.bv_len having never found a terminating '"' (e.g. input "{issuer rdnSequence:"AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA}" of exactly 38 bytes, which passes the line-19 minimum-length and line-21 brace checks). Line 78 then sets x.bv_val to one byte past the input buffer and line 79 computes x.bv_len = 16 - 17 = -1, an unsigned ber_len_t underflow to 0xFFFFFFFF. No check for a found terminator exists anywhere between the loop and these statements.

Root cause site 2 (thisUpdate value): identical defect. If the value opened at line 100-102 has no closing '"' before the region ends, tu->bv_len reaches x.bv_len, and line 113 subtracts (x.bv_len + 1) from x.bv_len, underflowing to -1 while line 112 moves x.bv_val past the buffer's final '}' byte. The line-100 check guards only the opening quote, not the terminator.

Impact sink: after the underflow, x.bv_val points one byte past the input buffer and x.bv_len is huge. The eat-spaces loop reads x.bv_val[0] BEFORE testing x.bv_len (which is nonzero anyway), performing an out-of-bounds read and walking further past the buffer while adjacent heap bytes are spaces; line 130 then reads the same out-of-bounds byte for the ',' comparison. The line-139 'if ( x.bv_len )' check executes only after these reads and cannot prevent them.

assumptions: ber_len_t (the type of bv_len) is unsigned, per the OpenLDAP ABI; the out-of-bounds read at lines 122/130 occurs regardless of signedness, since x.bv_val is already past the buffer and the reads are unconditional in that state.

The 'in' parameter carries externally supplied directory-string content (this function is the GSER intake parser; no precondition on 'in' is documented or asserted in the given code), so it is treated as attacker-data per the data-origin impact model.
STRLENOF is a compile-time constant equal to strlen of its literal (38 for the line-19 minimum-length literal).
limitations: Unchecked allocation results: ber_dupbv_x(&ni, is, ctx) at line 142 and slap_sl_malloc(ni.bv_len + 1, ctx) at line 148 are not tested for failure before *is = ni (line 158); on allocation failure the caller would receive a NULL bv_val. Trigger requires an allocation failure no attacker input can induce (ni.bv_len is bounded by the input length), so it is not counted as a vulnerability here.
The double-dquote probe is->bv_val[is->bv_len+1] (line 70) can read at most index x.bv_len, which is the in-buffer '}' byte; no out-of-bounds access from that probe itself.

No disclosure channel for the out-of-bounds bytes is shown in this code (the bytes are only compared, not returned); the instantiated impact is the out-of-bounds read itself and the resulting crash/DoS/unbounded walk in the process parsing attacker data.

verdict.summary: In parse_die, the loop bound `i < abbrev->count - 1` underflows when abbrev->count == 0 (size_t), wrapping to SIZE_MAX. An attacker-crafted DWARF binary with an abbreviation declaration containing zero attribute pairs drives the loop to write die->attr_values[i] (memset at the loop head and via parse_attr_value's output pointer) far past the zero-sized allocation, and read abbrev->defs[i] out of bounds — an attacker-scalable heap out-of-bounds write. No check anywhere in the function rejects count == 0 or bounds i before the first iteration's memset.

evidence.reason: Root cause: unsigned underflow in the loop bound. When abbrev->count == 0 (attacker-controlled abbreviation with zero attribute pairs from the parsed .debug_abbrev section), `abbrev->count - 1` wraps to SIZE_MAX, so `0 < SIZE_MAX` is true on the first iteration and the loop is effectively unbounded. The first statement executed, memset(&die->attr_values[0], ...), writes sizeof(RzBinDwarfAttrValue) bytes to an array sized for zero entries — an immediate out-of-bounds heap write — and parse_attr_value is then handed &abbrev->defs[0] (OOB read) and &die->attr_values[0] (OOB write target). Subsequent iterations continue writing sequentially past the allocation (i up to SIZE_MAX), giving attacker-scalable heap corruption. No guard of any form (count check, clamp, corrected bound, error arm, checked accessor) exists on any path before the sink.

assumptions: die->attr_values and abbrev->defs are allocated (in not-shown caller/callee code) proportionally to abbrev->count; no allocation or sizing statement is quotable in the given code, but the index-based access at lines 7, 9, 10, 12 makes attr_values[count]-proportional sizing the only coherent reading.

abbrev->count is derived by a not-shown abbreviation parser from file content; whether it can emit 0 is not quotable here — per guard-anchoring symmetry, no unquotable 'count >= 1' contract may dismiss the candidate.
debug_str_len/debug_str bounds enforcement and NUL-termination of DW_FORM_strp/string values are performed inside the not-shown parse_attr_value.
limitations: C2: the return of parse_attr_value (line 9) is never validated; if it returns NULL or a pointer past buf_end on malformed data, the next iteration's `buf_end - buf` wraps to a huge size_t and is passed back into parse_attr_value. The unguarded subtraction and missing failure-sentinel check are in this code, but the actual OOB dereference occurs inside the callee, whose behavior is not shown — impact chain not fully instantiated.
C3: strdup(comp_dir) at line 30 assumes comp_dir is NUL-terminated; termination depends on the not-shown parse_attr_value respecting debug_str_len — not provable here.

C4: for abbrev->count >= 1, the `- 1` silently skips the last attribute definition (e.g., a trailing DW_AT_comp_dir/DW_AT_stmt_list), a functional parsing defect with no demonstrated security consequence.
Whether a count==0 abbreviation declaration is emitted by the abbrev parser could not be quoted; the trigger rests on the attacker crafting the file content with no observable filter in this code.

verdict.summary: Two confirmed defects in bgp_capability_msg_parse: (1) infinite loop / unbounded CPU consumption (CWE-400) — the 'continue' taken when bgp_afi_safi_valid_indices rejects an attacker-supplied afi/safi (line 66, e.g. afi=0xFFFF) skips 'pnt += hdr->length + 3;' (line 102), the only statement advancing pnt, so 'while (pnt < end)' can never become false and the daemon spins forever on a 7-byte malformed MP capability (remote DoS of the whole bgpd process); (2) out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) — 'memcpy (&mpc, pnt + 3, sizeof (struct capability_mp_data))' (line 49) copies a fixed struct size although the preceding check (line 41) only validates hdr->length attacker-supplied bytes (which may be 0..3), so a capability ending the message with hdr->length < sizeof(struct capability_mp_data) reads up to 4 bytes past the message buffer.

evidence.reason: Root cause of the infinite loop: when the attacker-supplied afi/safi (ntohs(mpc.afi) at line 54, e.g. 0xFFFF) fails the validity lookup, this branch executes 'continue;', which jumps back to 'while (pnt < end)' without executing the loop's only pointer-advance statement (line 102). No statement in the taken path modifies pnt or end, so every guard passes identically on each iteration and the exit condition is unreachable — deterministic 100% CPU hang of the daemon from one malformed capability message (CWE-400).

evidence.snippet:
pnt += hdr->length + 3;
    }
evidence.reason: The sole statement that advances pnt sits at the bottom of the loop body and is bypassed by the 'continue;' statements at lines 59 and 66, leaving 'while (pnt < end)' (line 14) permanently true. STEP 5 verified no advance, break, return, or restructured loop bound exists on any continue path.

Out-of-bounds read: the only guard before the memcpy validates that hdr->length (an attacker byte) bytes remain in the message, but the memcpy copies a fixed sizeof(struct capability_mp_data) regardless. With hdr->length = 0 and a 3-byte message [SET, CAPABILITY_CODE_MP, 0], the check passes (pnt+3 == end) and memcpy reads the full struct starting exactly at end — past the message buffer. No minimum-length check, clamp, or length-bounded copy exists anywhere before line 49 (STEP 5 search).

assumptions: pnt/length arrive from the BGP dynamic-capability receive path (not shown); treated as attacker-data per the data-origin model since this is the exported parser for that message content.

sizeof(struct capability_mp_data) is defined outside the given code (standard BGP MP capability data: 2-byte afi, 1 reserved, 1 safi = 4 bytes); the OOB read at line 49 holds for any positive struct size whenever hdr->length is smaller and the capability ends the message.

bgp_afi_safi_valid_indices is defined outside the given code; the given code's own failure branch (lines 61-67) demonstrates its failure on message data is a designed-for state, and a 16-bit afi such as 0xFFFF is assumed outside the valid AFI index range.
Dimensions of peer->afc/afc_recv/afc_nego and the exact semantics of bgp_afi_safi_valid_indices, bgp_announce_route, bgp_clear_route, and peer_active_nego are not shown.
limitations: C3 (pointer overflow in 'pnt + hdr->length + 3', line 41) is speculative: hdr->length max 255 and pnt originates inside a heap message buffer, so address-space wrap is unreachable at that scale.

C4 (afi/safi array indexing, lines 79-89) is guarded by the quoted 'if (!bgp_afi_safi_valid_indices (afi, &safi)) ... continue;' on every path; correctness of the not-shown callee is an assumption, not a finding.
The zlog_debug at lines 64-65 passes more arguments than format specifiers; benign (extras ignored) and the format string is a literal, so no format injection.
OOB-read bytes only reach debug logs and, after the quoted validity check, bounded array indices; the read itself (CWE-125) is the violation — no larger disclosure sink exists within this code.

verdict.summary: display_dollar() uses the unvalidated parameter 'col' directly as a byte offset into the current line buffer: 'curwin->w_cursor.col -= (*mb_head_off)(p, p + col);' with p = ml_get_curline(). No statement in the function checks that col lies within the current line's length (0..STRLEN(p)), and no caller contract bounding col is quotable from this code. A col value greater than the line length (or negative) makes p + col point outside the allocated line buffer, and mb_head_off inspects bytes there, producing an out-of-bounds read at an attacker-influenced offset (crash/DoS, adjacent-memory exposure). The only later sanitizing call, curs_columns(FALSE), executes after the defective use and cannot protect it.

evidence.snippet:
p = ml_get_curline();
	curwin->w_cursor.col -= (*mb_head_off)(p, p + col);
evidence.reason: Sink: the parameter 'col' is used as a raw byte offset 'p + col' into the current-line buffer returned by ml_get_curline() (file-derived, attacker-influenced content). No bounds check on col against the line length exists anywhere in the function, and the recomputing call curs_columns(FALSE) on line 19 runs only after this use. Trigger instantiated: col = line length + 10 (or negative) makes p + col point past the end (or before the start) of the line buffer, and mb_head_off inspects bytes at that out-of-domain pointer — out-of-bounds read with attacker-influenced offset.

evidence.snippet: display_dollar(colnr_T col)
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: 'col' is a parameter of a non-static, exported function with no documented, asserted, or checked precondition in the given code; its content is controlled by the caller, so it is attacker-data at this code's entry point.

assumptions: colnr_T is assumed to be a signed integer type (as in the Vim codebase); negative col values would read before the buffer, but the primary trigger only needs col greater than the line length, which works for any integer width.
mb_head_off is assumed, per its name and two-pointer signature (base, candidate), to inspect bytes at and before its second argument; the dereference itself occurs in a callee not shown.

ml_get_curline() is assumed to return a NUL-terminated line buffer of length STRLEN(p); there is no quotable statement in this code establishing termination, but the defect only requires col to exceed whatever the actual buffer extent is.
Callers of display_dollar are not shown; no quotable contract bounds the col they pass, so col is treated as attacker-data per the trust-boundary rules.
limitations: C2 (integer underflow of w_cursor.col at line 17 if mb_head_off returned a value larger than col) is only reachable once p+col is already out of domain; it is subsumed by the confirmed out-of-bounds read and not counted separately.
C3 (signedness/width of the w_wcol < w_width comparison at line 20) has no memory or injection sink; the compared values only gate a cosmetic '$' putcall.
C4 (possible misbehavior of curs_columns(FALSE) with an invalid cursor column) concerns a callee not shown; no impact link inside this code.

The actual out-of-bounds byte dereference happens inside mb_head_off, which is not part of the given code; this code's confirmed defect is constructing and passing the out-of-domain pointer p + col without any bounds check.

verdict.summary: copy_page_to_iter_pipe publishes a pipe_buffer (buf->ops/page/offset/len set, then pipe->head advanced) without ever initializing buf->flags. A reused pipe ring slot retains stale flags from a previous buffer, including PIPE_BUF_FLAG_CAN_MERGE, so the published buffer advertises itself mergeable while pinning a read-only page-cache page (buf->page = page). A subsequent write() to the pipe appends directly into that page-cache page at buf->offset + buf->len, letting an unprivileged user splice a file and then overwrite its cached contents (the CVE-2022-0845 'Dirty Pipe' flaw). Fix is the missing one-line initialization buf->flags = 0; before publication.

evidence.reason: The pipe_buffer is constructed and published to the pipe (pipe->head = i_head + 1) while buf->flags is never assigned anywhere in the function. The slot's stale flags survive from prior pipe use, so the freshly published buffer can carry PIPE_BUF_FLAG_CAN_MERGE while its ->page is an attacker-selected page-cache page from splice(file) — triggering direct overwrite of file contents on later pipe writes. Trigger instantiated: attacker splices 1 byte of a target file into a pipe whose slot retains the merge flag; lines 35-41 publish the misrepresenting buffer.

evidence.snippet: buf = &pipe->bufs[i_head & p_mask];
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: the ring slot selected here (and again at line 30 after i_head++) retains flags from the previous buffer that occupied it; this code's own selection statement picks the stale slot that lines 35-41 then publish without clearing flags.

assumptions: The implementations of sanity(i) and pipe_full() are not shown; their behavior is assumed benign and cannot be quoted from the given code.

The consumer of buf->flags (the pipe write path that tests PIPE_BUF_FLAG_CAN_MERGE and appends into buf->page) resides in fs/pipe.c and is not part of the given code; however, the misrepresenting pipe_buffer value is produced and published entirely by lines 35-41 of this code.
PIPE_BUF_FLAG_CAN_MERGE being set on previously used anonymous pipe buffers reflects kernel behavior outside this snippet; this code neither clears nor checks flags on any path.
limitations: Candidate C3 (i->iov_offset = offset + bytes at line 42 possibly recording offset instead of the in-buffer offset) has no memory, index, or injection sink inside this code; it only feeds the line 23 merge comparison, so no security impact is instantiated within the given code.

The final overwrite of the page-cache page happens in the pipe write path outside this snippet; the finding rests on the misrepresentation created here (page-cache page published with stale merge-allowed flags), which is the defect fixed by adding buf->flags = 0; in this function.

verdict.summary: thread_call's argument marshalling is internally consistent: sq_gettop(v) yields the this+args count, the loop copies exactly the user arguments (edge-tested at u=0, u=1, exactly-at-limit), and the number of items pushed onto the target thread (1 roottable + nparams-1 args) exactly matches the nparams passed to sq_call. All given-code stack operations (Push, sq_move, sq_pop, stack_get) stay in bounds in every simulated thread state, and the only remaining concerns (missing target-thread state/reentrancy check before sq_call, missing 0-argument floor before stack_get(v,1)) have their harmful uses executed inside sq_call/SQVM internals that are not part of the given code, so no trigger with a fully quoted impact chain could be instantiated.

assumptions: thread_call is reached only through the thread default-delegate registration ('call', -1, 'v'), which enforces a minimum of one argument and that parameter 1 is a thread; this enforcement is NOT in the given code and cannot be quoted, so the 0-argument read of stack_get(v,1) (which would touch the slot at _top) is an assumption, not a verified guard.

Semantics of sq_gettop (returns _top-_stackbase, i.e., this+args for a native frame), stack_get(v,n) (slot _stackbase+n-1), sq_move, and sq_call (closure read at GetUp(-(params+1)) with stackbase _top-params) are upstream Squirrel facts not shown in the snippet; the internal consistency check (loop reads ending exactly at _top-1; pushes == nparams) corroborates them.
Squirrel threads are cooperative green threads on a single OS thread; no concurrent execution of two VMs, so no interleaving race is modeled.
limitations: No thread-state check exists in the code (verified: no sq_getvmstate/_suspended comparison anywhere on any path). Calling t.call() on a suspended or currently-running t (self-call is scriptable via a captured thread reference) makes sq_call read its closure slot from a non-entry stack position; the type-confused dispatch, frame handling, and any subsequent stack corruption occur inside sq_call/SQVM::Call/Execute, which is not given, so the impact chain could not be instantiated in this code. In the self-call simulation the slot resolves to the thread object itself; in the suspended-thread simulation it can resolve to an attacker-owned closure, which the script can already invoke via closure.call/acall, crossing no additional trust boundary.

On a sq_call failure or a callee-initiated suspend the given code does sq_move(v,_thread(o),-1)/sq_pop(_thread(o),1) or propagates _lasterror; whether sq_pop disturbs a suspended frame's live stack depends on the suspend protocol inside sq_suspendvm/sq_call (not shown) and could not be verified.
Integer wrap of nparams+1 would require roughly 2^63 call arguments, which the stack-allocation path cannot reach; trigger not instantiable.

If the caller is a raw host using sq_call directly with a misaligned stack (bypassing the delegate machinery), stack_get(v,1) could read an uninitialized slot; that path is not part of the given code's visible input surface.

verdict.summary: display_dollar() clamps its column argument only against negative values (col_arg < 0 ? 0 : col_arg) but never bounds it against the length of the current line obtained from ml_get_curline(). The unbounded col is then used to form the pointer p + col, which is passed to mb_head_off for dereference — an out-of-bounds read at an attacker-influenced offset past the end of the line buffer whenever col_arg exceeds the current line length.

evidence.snippet:
p = ml_get_curline();
	curwin->w_cursor.col -= (*mb_head_off)(p, p + col);
evidence.reason: Sink: p points to the current line buffer (contents of the edited file, arbitrarily short), while col comes from the unvalidated parameter col_arg. The expression p + col performs pointer arithmetic past the end of the line buffer when col exceeds the line length, and the resulting out-of-bounds pointer is passed to mb_head_off, which dereferences it (out-of-bounds read / invalid memory access). Trigger: a 2-byte current line with col_arg = 1000 reaches this line with p + 1000, ~997 bytes past the line's NUL terminator.

Origin of the faulty value: col_arg is a content-bearing parameter of this non-static (exported) function and is attacker-data. The only guard in the entire function, 'col_arg < 0 ? 0 : col_arg', clamps only the lower bound; there is no upper bound against the current line length anywhere on the path from here to the sink at line 18.

assumptions: has_mbyte (line 12) must be nonzero for the defective branch to execute; this holds under a multibyte 'encoding' such as the default utf-8 in standard builds, but the encoding flag itself is not set or checked in the given code.
redrawing() (line 6) must return nonzero for the function to proceed past the early return; normal redraw state assumed, not enforced by the given code.
mb_head_off dereferences its p_col argument (its implementation is not shown); the out-of-bounds pointer p + col is nevertheless constructed and handed off in this code at line 18.
colnr_T is treated as a signed int-width type, consistent with its use in 'col_arg < 0'.
limitations: Line 20, curs_columns(FALSE), also consumes curwin->w_cursor.col, which line 11 may have set beyond the current line length; however, the harmful use of that out-of-domain value occurs inside the callee curs_columns, which is not shown, so no finding is attached to it.

For small overshoots, p + col may land within adjacent bytes of the memory-line allocation (memline block layout not shown); the security-relevant case is the fully attacker-scaled offset, where col_arg up to the width of colnr_T places the read at an arbitrary distance from the line buffer, which can cross allocation/mapping boundaries.

How a caller of display_dollar derives col_arg from attacker input (keys/file content) is not shown; per the analysis rules the parameter of this non-static function is nonetheless treated as attacker-data with no quotable caller contract.

verdict.summary: This is the option-parsing and dispatch body of the mount utility. Every attacker-data value (option arguments, positional source/target paths) is passed by reference into libmount context accessors; no buffer arithmetic, indexing, copying, format-string assembly, or command execution occurs in this code itself. The non-root restriction gates were verified on every path: the option-loop gate (mnt_context_is_restricted(cxt) && !strchr("hlLUVvpris", c) && c != MOUNT_OPT_TARGET && c != MOUNT_OPT_SOURCE), the case-B gate (restricted && source && target), the case-C gate (restricted && source), and the case-D gate (restricted) all precede their respective uses in execution order, and the strchr NUL-match edge case is unreachable because no longopt in the shown table has val 0. Candidates concerning label/UUID quote injection and residual non-root mount authority have their defective sinks inside libmount code not given, so their impact chains break at unquoted links; they are recorded as limitations, not findings.

assumptions: getopt_long delivers NUL-terminated optarg strings and returns 0 only for long options with val==0 and NULL flag; since every entry in the shown longopts table has a non-zero val, c==0 is unreachable (libc interface behavior, not a statement in this code).
xasprintf is the checked allocation-and-format helper that terminates the process on allocation failure; its internal contract is not shown in this code.

sanitize_env, sanitize_paths, usage, print_all, append_fstab, exit_non_root, option_to_longopt, and table_parser_errcb are helpers whose bodies are not in the given code; their behavior (e.g., usage exiting, sanitize_paths re-canonicalizing already-set source/target paths) is assumed from the util-linux codebase, not quotable here.

mnt_context_mount and the mnt_context_* accessors enforce (or do not enforce) non-root mount policy, fstab user-entry matching, path canonicalization, and fstype-pattern safety inside libmount; none of that is quotable from this code.
Deployment privilege (setuid/daemon/CLI) cannot be determined from the given code; per the data-origin model this did not affect any judgment.
limitations: Label/UUID quote injection (C1): a non-root user may pass -L/-U with embedded double quotes; xasprintf(&srcbuf, "LABEL=\"%s\"", optarg) produces a source spec with unescaped quotes that is handed to mnt_context_set_source. Whether libmount's source resolution mis-parses such a spec is decided in code not given, so the impact chain is not instantiated in this code.

Non-root mount authority (C2): a restricted user with only --source or only --target and no positional argument passes all gates in this code and reaches mnt_context_mount(cxt). The actual authorization decision (fstab user-option matching) is inside libmount; if that layer were permissive, the vulnerability would live there, not in the statements given.

Unchecked append_fstab return (C3): case 'T' does not test the returned fstab pointer before mnt_table_set_cache(fstab, cache) and mnt_free_table(fstab). Only root can reach 'T' (restricted users hit exit_non_root first), and append_fstab's failure mode cannot be instantiated from shown statements, so no trigger with security impact was provable.

verdict.summary: No security vulnerability was confirmed in this code. The non-root restriction gate (strchr whitelist plus TARGET/SOURCE exception, executed before the option switch on every getopt iteration) and the case B/C/D exit_non_root checks deny every restricted-user path that could set both source and target, apply oper flags, or inject options; argv indexing is guarded by the argc==1/argc==2 branch conditions; all format strings are constant literals with attacker data only in %s argument position. The remaining concern — free(srcbuf) immediately after mnt_context_set_source(cxt, srcbuf) — depends on whether the not-shown libmount setter copies the string, and any use-after-free dereference would occur entirely in that callee; the impact chain cannot be instantiated from the given code.

assumptions: mnt_context_set_source/mnt_context_set_target duplicate the strings passed to them (srcbuf is freed immediately after mnt_context_set_source in the 'L'/'U' cases); this copy contract is not quotable from the given code.
exit_non_root(), err(), usage(), xasprintf(), and option_to_longopt() terminate the process / handle errors as their names and upstream semantics indicate; their bodies are not shown.
mnt_context_mount() (not shown) performs the actual fstab 'user' permission enforcement for restricted mounts; this code only performs the option-shape denials quoted in STEP 2/STEP 4.
append_fstab(), print_all(), mount_all(), and table_parser_errcb() are not shown; no defect could be evaluated inside them.
limitations: Candidate C2 (potential use-after-free of srcbuf): trigger fully instantiated up to free(srcbuf), but the harmful dereference requires mnt_context_set_source to store the pointer without copying — behavior existing only in code not given; per STEP 4 the impact is not instantiated.

Candidate C4 (non-root bypass): every simulated restricted-user path (e.g. 'mount -o ro /a /b', 'mount --make-shared /x', 'mount -L foo /t', 'mount --source a --target b') was denied by a quoted statement in this code; the only surviving shape (restricted user with --target plus one positional, or single positional) presents a single-operand mount whose permission decision is made inside mnt_context_mount, which is not shown.
Behavior of mnt_context_is_restricted (how non-root is determined) is not shown; judged as a trusted internal accessor per upstream libmount semantics.

verdict.summary: When the dyld-cache filter is enabled, file-controlled dependency data indexes the heap array 'deps' without any bounds check: 'ut16 dep_index = depArray[k] & 0x7fff; deps[dep_index]++;' uses an attacker-chosen index (0..32767) into an allocation sized only by cache->hdr->imagesCount, producing a heap out-of-bounds write (and OOB reads of depArray[k] and img[dep_index] since the scan loop k is bounded only by a file-controlled 0xffff sentinel, never by depListCount). Additionally, deps is allocated once with hdr[0].imagesCount while the j-loops use each cache->hdr[i].imagesCount, so multi-header caches also write deps[j] out of bounds. All malicious values originate from the parsed dyldcache file.

evidence.reason: Primary sink: unguarded heap out-of-bounds write. depArray is filled entirely from the cache file (r_buf_fread_at at line 46), so depArray[k] & 0x7fff is an attacker-chosen index 0..32767 with no comparison against imagesCount anywhere in the function; deps[dep_index]++ then writes 4 bytes far past the allocation made at line 19. The loop bound for k is only the file-controlled sentinel depArray[k] != 0xffff, never cache->accel->depListCount, so depArray[k] and img[dep_index] are also read out of bounds. Trigger fully simulated: accel present, depList entry 0x4cd8, extras[0].dependentsStartArrayIndex=0, imagesCount=1 → deps[3288]++ on a 4-byte heap allocation.

evidence.snippet: deps = R_NEWS0 (int, cache->hdr->imagesCount);
evidence.reason: Origin of the sink's bound: deps is allocated once, before the header loop, using only cache->hdr[0].imagesCount. This is the sole sizing statement for deps; no check, clamp, or reallocation ties dep_index (line 80) or the per-header j (hdr = &cache->hdr[i], line 29) to this allocation size.

Secondary confirmed out-of-bounds read/write of the same heap array: this inner loop is bounded by hdr->imagesCount where hdr = &cache->hdr[i] for each i < cache->n_hdr (file-controlled), but deps was sized at line 19 from cache->hdr[0].imagesCount only. verdict.summary: The buffer sizing for the generated TXT local-data record exactly matches the worst-case expansion: each of the sizeof(struct SignedCert) cert bytes is emitted as either one printable char or a 4-char \%03d escape (c is a uint8_t promoted to int, so %03d never exceeds 3 digits), the allocation quotes '4 * sizeof(struct SignedCert)' plus the exact prefix ('%s 86400 IN TXT "' == strlen(provider_name)+strlen(ttl_class_type)), trailing quote, and NUL, and every write into rr uses snprintf bounded by 'rrlen - 1' / 'rrlen - 1 - strlen(rr)' (which cannot underflow because snprintf always NUL-terminates within rrlen-1). The escaping loop routes '"' and '\\' (isprint(c) && c != '"' && c != '\\') and all non-printables to the 4-char escape, so cert bytes cannot break out of the TXT quoting. Remaining concerns are speculative: uint16_t truncation of rrlen would require a provider_name of ~64940+ characters whose origin is not attacker-reachable in this code, and at the exact all-non-printable worst case the trailing quote is silently truncated (malformed RR, no memory error).

assumptions: struct SignedCert's definition is not shown; both the allocation multiplier and the read loop bound use the same expression '4 * sizeof(struct SignedCert)' / 'j<sizeof(struct SignedCert)', so the worst-case sizing is self-consistent regardless of the actual struct size.

The origin and non-NULL guarantee of dnscenv->provider_name, dnscenv->signed_certs, signed_certs_count, rotated_certs, and rotated_certs_count are not shown in this code; no quotable contract exists for their validity.
Semantics of cfg_str2list_insert / cfg_strlist_insert (ownership, NULL handling) are not shown.
malloc(0) behavior is platform-dependent (glibc returns non-NULL).
limitations: uint16_t truncation of rrlen: if strlen(provider_name)+15+4*sizeof(struct SignedCert)+2 >= 65536, rrlen wraps; if it wraps exactly to 0, 'rrlen - 1' evaluates to (int)-1 and is converted to SIZE_MAX as snprintf's size after malloc(0), giving an unbounded write. Trigger requires a provider_name of roughly 64940+ characters; no statement in this code produces or accepts such a value from an attacker-reachable origin, so the trigger is speculative (STEP 4 branch c).

Exact-boundary truncation: when every cert byte expands to the 4-char \ddd escape, the final 'snprintf(rr + strlen(rr), rrlen - 1 - strlen(rr), "\"")' receives size 1 and drops the closing quote, yielding a malformed TXT record; no out-of-bounds access occurs (max index used is rrlen-2 inside a rrlen-byte buffer).

verdict.summary: Stack-based out-of-bounds write in the BMP v4/v5 header path: when the attacker-controlled header field biSize is 108 or 124, ReadOK(fd, buffer, Bitmap_File_Head.biSize - 4) reads 104 or 120 attacker-controlled file bytes into the 64-byte stack array `buffer`, overwriting 40-56 bytes past its end with fully attacker-chosen content (memory corruption, potential control-flow hijack). Secondary confirmed finding: on the fopen-failure path, `goto cleanup` reaches an unguarded `fclose(fd)` with fd == NULL, crashing the process for an attacker-supplied unopenable path (CWE-476, denial of service).

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write (root cause CWE-787): the branch condition admits biSize == 108 or 124, so the read length biSize - 4 is 104 or 120 bytes, but the destination is the 64-byte stack array `unsigned char buffer[64]` declared at function entry. Instantiated trigger: file with magic 'BM', 12-byte header, bfOffs=200, then 4-byte biSize=0x0000006C; the branch at line 188 is taken and line 193 reads 104 attacker-controlled bytes into buffer[64], writing 40 bytes past the end (56 for biSize=124). STEP 5 search found no bounds check, clamp, larger buffer, checked helper, or reject arm anywhere on this path; the analogous bound 'biSize >= 56 && biSize <= 64' that protects the 56-64 branch has no counterpart here.

evidence.snippet: unsigned char buffer[64];
evidence.reason: Origin of the undersized destination: the stack buffer that the ReadOK calls at lines 38, 53, 67, 79, 103, 131, 162, and 193 write into. All other reads are within 64 bytes; the read at line 193 (biSize-4 = 104 or 120) exceeds it.

Secondary confirmed finding (CWE-476 NULL dereference): the cleanup label unconditionally calls fclose(fd). When fopen fails (lines 15-18: 'if (!fd) { ... goto cleanup; }'), fd is NULL and control jumps here, so fclose(NULL) dereferences NULL and crashes the process. Instantiated trigger: attacker-supplied filename that cannot be opened. STEP 5 search found no 'if (fd)' guard or alternate handling on this path. Does not drive the verdict CWE.

Origin of the NULL value reaching fclose at line 351: fopen fails on the attacker-controlled filename parameter, fd becomes NULL, and this branch jumps directly to cleanup without setting or guarding fd.

assumptions: ReadOK(fd, buf, n) is assumed to be an fread-style wrapper that writes up to n bytes from the file into buf; its definition is not shown. The out-of-bounds write is executed inside ReadOK, but the destination object (buffer[64]) is declared in this code and the oversized length (biSize-4 = 104/120) is computed here from attacker data, so the defect is located at line 193.
ToL/ToS are assumed to be little-endian 4/2-byte readers from the buffer; definitions not shown.
fclose(NULL) is assumed to crash on common libc implementations (it is undefined behavior per ISO C).
limitations: ColormapSize (line 252, derived from attacker bfOffs via (bfOffs - biSize - 14)/Maps) is only upper-clamped ('if (ColormapSize > 256) ColormapSize = 256;') and can be negative (e.g., bfOffs=0, biSize=40 gives -13); additionally ColormapSize=256 with Maps=4 implies up to 1024 bytes for ColorMap[256][3] (768 bytes). The writes occur inside ReadColorMap, which is not shown and has no quotable contract, so the impact is not instantiated in this code.
ReadImage (line 340) consumes rowbytes, biClrUsed, ColorMap, and masks; any misuse of these values occurs in code not given.

Dimension truncation at line 349: (unsigned short)Bitmap_Head.biWidth silently narrows widths up to ~67 million (permitted by the check at line 301) to 16 bits before at_bitmap_init; the consequence of the mismatch is inside at_bitmap_init, which is not shown.
The return value of fseek(fd, Bitmap_File_Head.bfOffs, SEEK_SET) at line 337 is unchecked; the resulting mis-positioned reads affect only the not-shown ReadImage.

In the biSize==40/BI_BITFIELDS branch, ReadOK(fd, buffer, 3 * sizeof(unsigned long)) reads 24 bytes on LP64 where the format defines 12, desynchronizing subsequent reads; the write stays within buffer[64], so this is a correctness defect, not memory corruption.

verdict.summary: ReadCINImage computes the per-row read length 'length' from attacker-controlled, unvalidated header fields (image->depth = channel[0].bits_per_pixel, range 0-255, and image->columns) via GetBytesPerRow, and passes it as the copy size into the fixed-size quantum pixel buffer 'pixels' at ReadBlobStream(image,length,pixels,&count). The row extent corresponding to the buffer capacity is computed (extent=GetQuantumExtent(...)) but explicitly discarded via '(void) extent;', no statement ties length to the buffer capacity, the only data-sufficiency check uses the wrong unit (columns*rows/8 instead of 3*columns*ceil(depth/8)), and the count validation executes only after the copy has already occurred. A crafted CIN file with bits_per_pixel > 32 (e.g. 192) makes length up to 8x the quantum row buffer, producing an attacker-controlled heap buffer overflow write repeated for every image row.

evidence.reason: Taint origin: image->depth and geometry are taken directly from file header fields read at lines 136/140/142 (bits_per_pixel is an unsigned char, range 0-255, via ReadBlobByte) with no validation anywhere before their use in sizing the pixel read.

Root cause: the code computes the quantum row extent matching the pixel buffer capacity and explicitly discards it ('(void) extent;'), then computes 'length' by a different formula using the unvalidated attacker depth (0-255) and columns; no statement compares length to extent or clamps length.

Sink: ReadBlobStream copies up to 'length' attacker-derived bytes into 'pixels' (obtained unchecked from GetQuantumPixels at line 388), whose capacity is never bounded by 'length' on any path; the count check on line 398 executes only AFTER the copy, so it cannot prevent the out-of-bounds write (instantiated trigger: bits_per_pixel=192, columns=256, rows=2 yields length=18432 bytes per row copied into the quantum row buffer).

assumptions: The CINInfo struct layout and the exact return types/semantics of ReadBlobLong, ReadBlobByte, GetBytesPerRow, GetQuantumExtent, GetQuantumPixels, and ReadBlobStream are not defined in the given code; standard ImageMagick semantics were assumed (ReadBlobStream writes up to its length argument into the supplied buffer for file-backed blobs).

The capacity of the buffer returned by GetQuantumPixels (callee not shown) is assumed to correspond to the quantum row extent computed by GetQuantumExtent on the same quantum_info; no statement in this code bounds it by 'length' — this is the one unquoted link, and per guard anchoring it cannot serve as a guard.
limitations: The depth<32 path may leave the pixel buffer under-filled and ImportQuantumPixels (callee not shown, no length argument passed) may import beyond the bytes actually read; impact depends on not-shown callee behavior, so it is not asserted as a finding.
Line 172 assigns green_primary_chromaticity[0] to image->chromaticity.red_primary.x (copy-paste bug) — metadata mis-assignment with no security effect.
cin.film.count is read but never used (dead field).
Edge cases image->depth==0 or image->columns==0 yield length==0 and are expected to fail harmlessly (SetImageExtent/QueueAuthenticPixels error paths); not treated as findings.
The blob-size check at line 350 uses the wrong unit (columns*rows/8, ignoring depth and channel count) and would need replacement by a depth-aware bound as part of the fix for the primary finding.

ls->envn is the interned name '_ENV' assigned during parser initialization (luaY_parser), which is not part of the given code.
lua_assert is active only in debug builds and expands to a no-op in release builds; the given code contains no release-mode enforcement of `var->k != VVOID`.

str_checkname, singlevaraux, codestring, and luaK_indexed are implemented outside the given code; their internal contracts (e.g., str_checkname aborting the parse on a non-name token, luaK_indexed requiring VLOCAL/VUPVAL) are not quotable from the given code.
