Even if instantiated, the harmful use would occur inside luaK_indexed, which is not given, so the impact chain breaks at an unquoted link.

Candidate B (attacker-controlled identifier string varname from line 2 flowing to codestring at line 9 and luaK_indexed at line 10): this code performs no copy, length computation, indexing, or memory write on varname; the string is an already-interned TString allocated by the lexer (not shown). Any misuse would occur in non-shown callees, so the impact is not instantiated in this code.

verdict.summary: In issuerAndThisUpdateCheck, when the attacker-supplied GSER value's issuer or thisUpdate quoted string has no closing '"', the quote-scan loop exits by running out (is->bv_len/tu->bv_len == x.bv_len) and the unchecked subtraction 'x.bv_len -= is->bv_len + 1' (and its thisUpdate analog) underflows the unsigned ber_len_t to a huge value while x.bv_val is advanced one byte past the end of the input buffer. The subsequent 'x.bv_val[0]' dereferences at the space-eating loop and the ',' check read out of bounds past the heap buffer before any length check can reject, and can walk further through out-of-bounds heap memory if adjacent bytes are spaces or commas. Both trigger paths were fully simulated with concrete attacker inputs of valid length and brace form.

evidence.snippet: struct berval x = *in;
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted data: the attacker-controlled syntax value 'in' is copied into the working cursor 'x' that all subsequent parsing, length arithmetic, and dereferences consume; no validation beyond the minimum-length and brace checks on lines 19 and 21 is applied before the parse loop.

evidence.snippet:
x.bv_val += is->bv_len + 1;
			x.bv_len -= is->bv_len + 1;
evidence.reason: Issuer-path sink: the quote-scan loop at line 65 ('for ( ; is->bv_len < x.bv_len; )') can exit by loop-condition failure when the issuer string has no closing quote (is->bv_len == x.bv_len, also reachable via the pair-skip 'is->bv_len += 2' at line 73), and there is no check that a quote was found before this subtraction. With is->bv_len == x.bv_len the unsigned x.bv_len underflows to a huge value while x.bv_val is advanced one byte past the input buffer.

thisUpdate-path sink: when the timestamp string has no closing quote the scan loop exits with tu->bv_len == x.bv_len; the only post-loop check ('if ( tu->bv_len < STRLENOF("YYYYmmddHHmmssZ") )') is a minimum-length test and passes on the defect value (simulated with 40 characters). 'x.bv_len -= tu->bv_len + 1' then underflows the unsigned length and x.bv_val is moved one byte past the input buffer, e.g. for input '{issuer rdnSequence:"",thisUpdate "XXXX...}' of length 76, where x.bv_val becomes in->bv_val + 76 and x.bv_len wraps to (ber_len_t)-1.

evidence.snippet:
/* eat leading spaces */
		for ( ; (x.bv_val[0] == ' ') && x.bv_len; x.bv_val++, x.bv_len-- ) {
evidence.reason: First out-of-bounds read: executed immediately after the underflowing subtraction on every iteration, this dereference reads x.bv_val[0] one byte past the end of the attacker-supplied input buffer (and before testing x.bv_len, which is wrapped huge anyway, so the '&& x.bv_len' term cannot bound it). It runs before the final 'if ( x.bv_len ) return LDAP_INVALID_SYNTAX;' on line 141, so no later check prevents the OOB read; if the out-of-bounds bytes are spaces the loop continues walking past the buffer.

Second out-of-bounds read on the issuer-only underflow path (have != HAVE_ALL): the comma check dereferences the pointer that now lies one byte past the input buffer; if that out-of-bounds byte happens to be ',', lines 136-137 advance the cursor and the next iteration's strncasecmp and space-eating loops read further out-of-bounds heap memory with a wrapped near-SIZE_MAX length.

assumptions: ber_len_t (the type of x.bv_len) is unsigned, as in OpenLDAP's lber_types.h; the subtraction on lines 79/115 therefore wraps to a huge value instead of going negative. The wrap behavior of the code as written is what was simulated.
The berval buffer holds exactly bv_len bytes; no NUL terminator or slack is guaranteed by anything quotable in this code, so reading in->bv_val[in->bv_len] is out of bounds.

This function is a syntax validator for LDAP directory values (certificate issuer/thisUpdate matching), so 'in' carries content crossing a trust boundary; this is consistent with, but not relied upon for, the data-flow analysis — the defect is reachable from any caller passing an arbitrary berval.
limitations: slap_sl_malloc (line 150) and ber_dupbv_x (line 144) results are unchecked; a NULL ni.bv_val from allocation failure would be dereferenced at line 155 or returned via '*is = ni'. This requires memory exhaustion not inducible by an attacker through this code, so it is not counted as a vulnerability.

The extent of the out-of-bounds walk past the first byte depends on adjacent heap contents (spaces/commas), which the attacker does not directly control; the reliably instantiated impact is the out-of-bounds read of at least one byte past the buffer plus potential crash at a page boundary.

strncasecmp calls (lines 35, 52, 83) read at most to the in-bounds '}' guaranteed by line 21, which mismatches every keyword character, so they do not overread in normal flow; they can overread only after the confirmed underflow, which is already covered by the primary finding.

verdict.summary: SQClass::NewSlot is internally memory-safe as written: every indexed write (_defaultvalues[_member_idx(temp)], _methods[_member_idx(temp)], _metamethods[mmidx]) is either guarded by a quoted check evaluated in execution order (_isfield(temp), sq_type(temp)==OT_NULL else-arm, mmidx != -1) or is fed an index this code itself generates as the pre-push vector size and pairs with push_back. The reachable anomaly — a key that exists as a method being silently re-encoded as a field when a non-closure value is assigned (final branch) — leaves the member map, _defaultvalues and _methods mutually consistent within this function; the orphaned _methods entry keeps a valid index because the vectors only grow. No out-of-bounds write/read, overflow, injection, or fail-open path is instantiated by the given statements.

assumptions: Macros _isfield/_ismethod/_member_idx/_make_field_idx/_make_method_idx are not defined in the given code; the analysis assumes the standard Squirrel encoding (even integer = field index, odd = method index, _member_idx = value>>1), on which the guards' correctness at _defaultvalues[_member_idx(temp)] and _methods[_member_idx(temp)] depends.
SQObjectPtr temp; default-constructs to OT_NULL (needed so sq_type(temp)==OT_NULL reliably detects 'key not found' after a failed _members->Get); the constructor is not shown.
SQTable::Get does not write temp on failure and SQTable::NewSlot overwrites existing keys; SQTable semantics are not in the given code.
ss->GetMetaMethodIdxByName(key) returns either -1 or a valid _metamethods index; the range above -1 cannot be verified here.
SQVM::IsEqual always writes its bool& out-parameter before returning; isconstructor is otherwise used uninitialized.
SQClassMember/SQObjectPtr assignment releases the previous value, keeping _base refcounts balanced after __ObjAddRef(_base).
_constructoridx is initialized (e.g., to -1) elsewhere in the class; SQClass copy/derivation keeps _members indices consistent with copied _defaultvalues/_methods vectors.
limitations: C1 (mapping-level type confusion): when a key already exists as a method and NewSlot is called with a non-closure value and bstatic=false on an unlocked class, the final branch re-encodes the key as a field (fresh _make_field_idx(_defaultvalues.size())) while the old closure stays orphaned in _methods, and _constructoridx (if set) keeps pointing at the orphan. All indices remain in bounds in this code; any memory-safety consequence would occur in SQInstance construction / SQVM member dispatch, which is not given, so the impact is not instantiated here.
C3: 'bool isconstructor;' is used uninitialized unless SQVM::IsEqual writes it; the callee is not shown, so no trigger can be proven in this code (CWE-457-shaped only if the callee misbehaves).
C4: _make_field_idx/_make_method_idx left-shift of size overflows only at 2^(width-1) members; memory is exhausted by the paired push_back long before, so the wrap cannot be exercised as written.
C6: _metamethods[mmidx] upper-bound validity rests entirely on the not-shown GetMetaMethodIdxByName; only the -1 sentinel is tested here.

C5: closures and bstatic values may still modify a locked class (override field defaults, add methods) by explicit design of the quoted belongs_to_static_table branch; the non-static locked path is fail-closed (return false). Whether that lock design is a security boundary for a given embedding is a deployment question, not quotable from this code.

verdict.summary: Heap buffer overflow (out-of-bounds write) in _inplace_src_spans: span lengths derived from the rasterizer callback's span array (`len = spans[1].x - spans[0].x`) are written into the fixed-size mask buffer via `*m++` and `memset(m, spans[0].coverage, --len)` with no bound, clamp, or error check against the mask's size anywhere in the function. Any span with partial coverage (0x00 < coverage < 0xff, or 0xff with len < run_length) bypasses the only length-related test (`len >= run_length && coverage == 0xff`), so an attacker-influenced span whose extent exceeds the mask allocation overflows the heap with attacker-chosen byte values and length.

evidence.reason: Primary sink: the else branch handles every span that is neither a long full-coverage run nor an empty run, and writes `len` bytes (1 via *m++, len-1 via memset) into the mask at `m`, advancing m by len. `m` is only ever reset to `base` (lines 51-52, 80-81); nothing bounds m or len against the mask allocation. `if (len > 1)` tests only magnitude >= 2, never mask capacity. Trigger instantiated: spans[0]={x:0,cov:0x80}, spans[1]={x:0x10000} gives len=0x10000, fails the 0xff test at line 16, fails the 0x0 test at line 53, reaches `memset(m, 0x80, 0xFFFF)` at line 85 -> heap out-of-bounds write with attacker-controlled value and length.

Origin and routing of the tainted value: `len` is computed directly from the span coordinates passed into this callback (attacker-data parameter). The `if` at line 16 is the only length-related check in the function, and it only diverts long runs to direct composites when coverage == 0xff; for partial coverage (0x00 < coverage < 0xff) it is false for every len, including lengths exceeding the mask size, routing the unbounded value into the memset/pointer-advance sink at lines 83-86.

assumptions: The allocation size of r->mask, r->u.composite.run_length, and all of r->u.composite.* state are configured outside this function; none of their sizes or invariants are quoted/enforced in the given code.

This function corresponds to cairo's image-compositor in-place source span renderer, historically affected by a mask buffer overrun (CVE-2020-35492 family). This is corroboration only; the verdict rests solely on the given code's absent bound.
limitations: Secondary candidate (speculative): `spans[1].x` at line 15 executes on the first do-while iteration even when num_spans == 1 (the quoted guard `if (num_spans == 0) return CAIRO_STATUS_SUCCESS;` covers only 0), reading one element past the span array. Trigger requires the caller to pass exactly 1 span, which no statement in this code produces or forbids; recorded as a contract-dependent OOB read (CWE-125), not primary.
`int len = spans[1].x - spans[0].x` can overflow int (UB) for extreme span x values; no independent impact beyond the primary missing-validation defect was instantiated.

pixman_image_composite32 calls receive span-derived x/width values, but any clipping happens inside the not-shown callee; the concrete overflowing write (memset) is in this code and is the reported defect.

verdict.summary: This is Lua's standard singlevar() parser helper. All attacker-derived values (the identifier token from str_checkname) flow only into key lookups and constant-key construction with no memory, index, size, or injection sink in this code. The VVOID branch's envn lookup is validated only by lua_assert, but the failing precondition (the pre-declared _ENV variable missing from parser state) is established by parser-initialization code outside the given snippet and cannot be instantiated from these statements, and the potential misuse of a VVOID expdesc would occur inside luaK_exp2anyregup, a callee not shown. No defect is present in the given code.

assumptions: lua_assert is a debug-only macro that is compiled out in release builds; the given code does not show its definition, so 'lua_assert(var->k != VVOID)' cannot be treated as a runtime guard.

The invariant that ls->envn (_ENV) is always resolvable by singlevaraux is established by parser-initialization code (e.g., open_func/pre-declaration of _ENV) that is not part of the given snippet; no statement in the given code enforces or re-checks it at runtime.
The compiled source text (hence the identifier varname) is treated as untrusted input; the context (embedded Lua, untrusted scripts) is an assumption about deployment, not evidence.
Behavior of the not-shown callees str_checkname, singlevaraux, luaK_exp2anyregup, codestring, and luaK_indexed on out-of-domain arguments is not quotable from the given code.
limitations: Candidate C1 (luaK_exp2anyregup receiving a VVOID expdesc if the envn lookup fails and lua_assert is compiled out) is speculative: the failing state requires the pre-declared _ENV variable to be absent from parser state, which is prevented (or not) by parser-init code outside this snippet, and the actual harmful consumption would occur inside luaK_exp2anyregup, whose behavior on VVOID is not shown.
Candidate C2 (uninitialized expdesc key reaching luaK_indexed) was disproven: codestring(&key, varname) executes unconditionally, in execution order, before luaK_indexed on every path.
Candidate C3 (identifier token as attacker data) has no sink in this code: varname is used only as a lookup key and constant-string key, with no length arithmetic, indexing, or injection use.

verdict.summary: This internal JIT pass walks compiled-pattern bytecode between cc and ccend, advancing by operand-derived sizes with no runtime bounds checks and relying on debug-only SLJIT_ASSERTs. Candidate defects (operand-driven pointer overshoot to out-of-bounds reads, unchecked NULL sentinel from next_opcode, unchecked GET2 index into optimized_cbracket, unchecked *alternative read in OP_COND) all require bytecode whose operand sizes, indices, or opcodes are inconsistent with the buffer or with the compiler's opcode alphabet. Every such value is produced by the pattern compiler (not shown), and this code contains no statement that can itself generate a malformed or out-of-range operand; the invariants are documented and asserted in this code (SLJIT_ASSERT(cc == ccend), SLJIT_ASSERT(cc != NULL), SLJIT_ASSERT(PRIVATE_DATA(cc + 1) != 0)). No trigger precondition could be instantiated from this code's actual input surface, so no primary vulnerability is confirmed.

assumptions: The bytecode traversed by cc..ccend is produced by the pattern compiler (pcre2_compile, not shown) and its operand sizes, offsets, and indices are internally consistent with the buffer extent; this contract cannot be quoted from the given code.
SLJIT_ASSERT is a debug-only macro that compiles to a no-op in release builds (its definition is not in the given code); in debug builds the asserts do abort on violation.

Definitions of GET, GET2, PRIVATE_DATA, HAS_EXTRALEN, GET_EXTRALEN, IMM2_SIZE, LINK_SIZE, and the CASE_ITERATOR* macro families (which determine opcode lengths and hence whether each `cc += n` matches the real opcode size) are not included in the given code; correctness of the walk for type iterators (cc += 1) cannot be verified without them.
common->optimized_cbracket is allocated by the caller with at least top_bracket+1 entries and filled by earlier JIT passes; the GET2 group number is compiler-assigned within that range.
next_opcode returns non-NULL for every opcode the compiler can emit in this position; its NULL return is reachable only on opcodes outside that alphabet.
limitations: Out-of-bounds read via operand-driven skips (e.g. `cc += 1 + 2 + cc[1];` for OP_MARK, `cc += PRIVATE_DATA(cc + 1);` for OP_KET, `cc += size;` for OP_XCLASS) with no runtime check cc+size <= ccend: speculative — trigger requires the compiler to emit a length inconsistent with the stored operand; no statement in this code can produce it, and the invariant is asserted by `SLJIT_ASSERT(cc == ccend);`.

NULL-pointer dereference if `next_opcode(common, cc)` returns NULL: only `SLJIT_ASSERT(cc != NULL);` guards it (no runtime check), but the trigger requires an opcode in the bytecode that next_opcode rejects, which the not-shown compiler never emits.

Out-of-bounds read of `*alternative` after `alternative = cc + GET(cc, 1);` in the OP_COND case: no in-code bound check exists, but a compiler-emitted COND offset always points inside the pattern; trigger not instantiable here.

Out-of-bounds index into `common->optimized_cbracket[GET2(cc, 1 + LINK_SIZE)]`: no in-code range check exists, but the group number is compiler-assigned within the allocated range; trigger not instantiable here.
Signed overflow of the returned `int length` would require on the order of 2^31 per-opcode increments (multi-gigabyte pattern); not exercisable by the code as written.

A mis-walk producing an under-computed `length` would cause the caller (not shown) to allocate too few private-data words; even if instantiated, the harmful allocation/write occurs entirely in code not given, so the impact chain breaks at an unquoted link.

verdict.summary: In load_image, attacker-controlled 32-bit header fields bh.width/bh.height/bh.bytes are multiplied at line 122 (`size = bh.width * bh.height * bh.bytes;`) in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic, so the product wraps mod 2^32 and yields a small value even though the sanitize check at line 51 only bounds the mathematical product against G_MAXSIZE (2^64-1 on LP64). The wrapped size is passed to g_malloc, producing a heap buffer far smaller than bh.width*bh.height pixels; the bytes==2 conversion loop (lines 190-206) then reads `*buf` at 2-byte stride and writes `brush_buf[i]` for i up to bh.width*bh.height, causing heap out-of-bounds read and write with values derived from the attacker's brush file. The same 32-bit wrap at line 165 (`g_malloc (4 * bh.width * bh.height)`) in the .gpb pattern path similarly under-allocates before the loop at lines 167-177 writes `brush_buf[i*4+3]`. Confirmed trigger: width=65536, height=32769, bytes=2, version=2 with valid magic passes every guard and yields a 131072-byte buffer iterated 2147549184 times.

evidence.snippet:
size = bh.width * bh.height * bh.bytes;
  brush_buf = g_malloc (size);
evidence.reason: Root cause: the multiplication of the three guint32 header fields is evaluated in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic and wraps (e.g., 65536 * 32769 * 2 = 2^32 + 131072 -> 131072), so g_malloc receives a wrapped, undersized size. The only multiplicative guard (line 51, G_MAXSIZE / bh.width / bh.height / bh.bytes < 1) bounds the untruncated product against G_MAXSIZE and does not cover this wrap; no cast to gsize or product re-check exists between here and the loops.

Instantiated OOB sink: with width=65536, height=32769, bytes=2 (passes lines 47-51 on LP64 and the version-2 magic check at 85-86), size wraps to 131072 and brush_buf is a 131072-byte heap buffer, but the loop bound bh.width * bh.height = 2147549184. `*buf` reads past the buffer from iteration 65536 and `brush_buf[i] = ...` writes past it from iteration 131072, with attacker file bytes driving both the read and the written value — heap out-of-bounds read and write in this function.

Second sink of the same root cause: `4 * bh.width * bh.height` wraps in 32-bit arithmetic (e.g., width=65536, height=32769, bytes=1 -> 4*(2^30+65536) mod 2^32 = 262144), so the new RGBA buffer is under-allocated while the loop is bounded by ph.width * ph.height, which the checks at lines 156-157 force equal to bh.width * bh.height. `read (fd, brush_buf + i * 4, 3)` and `brush_buf[i * 4 + 3] = plain_brush[i]` (line 177) then write out of bounds for i >= 65536.

assumptions: BrushHeader/PatternHeader fields (header_size, version, width, height, bytes, magic_number, spacing) are guint32, as implied by the g_ntohl 32-bit network-order conversions at lines 38-44 and 145-150 and by the GIMP gbr plugin definition; the struct definitions are not shown in the given code. If the fields were 64-bit, the 32-bit wrap would not occur.
GIMP_MAX_IMAGE_SIZE is at least 65536 (it is 262144 in GIMP 2.x); its definition is not shown in the given code.

Target is an LP64-style platform where gsize is 64-bit, gint/gint32 is 32-bit, and unsigned int arithmetic wraps mod 2^32 (well-defined in C). On such platforms the line-51 check against G_MAXSIZE (2^64-1) does not bound the 32-bit intermediate product.
GBRUSH_MAGIC and GPATTERN_MAGIC are not secrets; any real brush/pattern file reveals them, so an attacker can satisfy the magic checks at lines 85 and 152.
limitations: On 32-bit platforms the G_MAXSIZE check at line 51 rejects the bytes==2 trigger (product 2^32+131072 > 2^32-1), though the bytes==1 pattern path (line 165) still wraps and triggers there because w*h*1 fits within G_MAXSIZE while 4*w*h wraps.

When `size` wraps on the bytes==4 path (no in-function loop touches the buffer), the undersized brush_buf is later passed to gimp_pixel_rgn_set_rect (line 262) together with bh.width/bh.height; the resulting out-of-bounds read occurs inside a callee not shown, so it is recorded as a consequence of the same root cause rather than a separate finding.
The sanitize-fail error path (line 58) returns without close(fd) — an fd leak with no security impact beyond resource exhaustion of the loader process.
g_new/g_malloc abort the process on allocation failure (GLib semantics); no attacker-inducible corruption arises from that alone.

verdict.summary: ReadTGAImage allocates a non-zeroed heap buffer for the attacker-controlled TGA image comment (id_length bytes, up to 255) and never validates the byte count returned by ReadBlob before NUL-terminating at id_length and storing the buffer via SetImageProperty. On a truncated file (or any file shorter than the declared id_length), the unread portion of the buffer remains uninitialized heap memory and is persisted as the image 'comment' property, disclosing process heap contents (e.g., data from previously processed images) into output metadata. The code's own short-read checks elsewhere (count != 1 for the header and runlength bytes, ReadBlob(...) != 2/3/4 for pixels) confirm short reads are an expected outcome, yet no such check guards the comment read.

evidence.reason: Sink and missing-check site: ReadBlob is asked for id_length bytes (up to 255) into a freshly AcquireQuantumMemory'd, non-zeroed buffer, but the returned count is never checked (no comparison, no memset, no reject arm between the read and the sink). On a truncated file ReadBlob returns fewer bytes, comment[id_length] only NUL-terminates the end, and SetImageProperty stores the uninitialized heap bytes [count, id_length) as the image comment — instantiated trigger: 18-byte header with id_length=255 and immediate EOF, leaking up to 255 bytes of uninitialized heap memory into image output metadata.

evidence.snippet: count=ReadBlob(image,1,&tga_info.id_length);
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: tga_info.id_length is an attacker-controlled header byte (0-255) read from the file; it later sizes the comment read at line 154 and the NUL terminator at line 155. Note the code validates count for this 1-byte read (line 69) but omits the equivalent validation for the id_length-byte comment read, demonstrating the missing check is not a code-wide invariant.

assumptions: ReadBlob returns fewer bytes than requested on truncated input and leaves the unread tail of the caller's buffer untouched; AcquireQuantumMemory does not zero memory. These callee semantics are not shown, but this code's own short-read checks (`count != 1` at line 69, `ReadBlob(image,2,pixels) != 2`, `!= 3`, `!= 4`, and the runlength `count != 1` check in the pixel loop) corroborate that short reads are an expected outcome in this code's model.

SetImageProperty persists the string as the image 'comment' property retrievable/writable by downstream consumers; the exact exfiltration channel (identify output, format writers) is outside the given code, while the property-store statement itself is the in-code sink.
ConstrainColormapIndex and AcquireImageColormap are unshown ImageMagick helpers; no bound they provide can be quoted from this code.
limitations: Colormap indexing (`pixel=image->colormap[(ssize_t) ConstrainColormapIndex(image,(ssize_t) index,exception)];` for 8bpp, and `index=(Quantum) ConstrainColormapIndex(image,((ssize_t) (k << 8))+j,exception);` for 15/16bpp) is not verifiable: this code can set image->colors as low as colormap_index (lines 188-189) or 1<<bits_per_pixel (line 129) while file pixel bytes supply indices up to 255/65535, and the only range enforcement lives inside the unshown ConstrainColormapIndex helper. If that helper fails to validate, this is an out-of-bounds read; the trigger could not be instantiated because the helper's semantics are not in the given code.

AcquireImageColormap(image,image->colors,...) can be called with image->colors==0 (colormap_type!=0, colormap_index==0, colormap_length==0, e.g. TGARGB 8bpp); behavior of the unshown allocation/lookup for a zero-color colormap could not be evaluated.

TGAMonochrome with bits_per_pixel 24 or 32 reaches image->colors=one<<24 / one<<32 (line 129); the overflow guard at line 130 passes on 64-bit, producing a huge allocation attempt, but the failure path at lines 132-133 is a quoted check, so no unhandled DoS/corruption was instantiated.

For 8-bit PseudoClass images with colormap_type==0 and bits_per_pixel<8, the per-pixel index stored via SetPixelIndex is not range-checked against image->colors in this function; any out-of-range use occurs in code not shown.

verdict.summary: No exploitable defect found in this code. The function consumes one untrusted-origin value (the MMIO-read hw_rev) and guards it with a quoted failure-sentinel check (`if (trans->hw_rev == 0xffffffff)` → -EIO path) before any use; hw_rev never reaches a memory, index, size, or injection sink (its only string use is a bounded snprintf with sizeof(trans->hw_id_str)). Every allocation and call failure sentinel consumed in this code — iwl_trans_alloc, alloc_percpu, pcim_iomap_table, pcim_enable_device, both DMA-mask attempts, pcim_iomap_regions_request_all, iwl_pcie_prepare_card_hw, iwl_finish_nic_init, iwl_pcie_alloc_ict, iwl_pcie_init_msix_handler, devm_request_threaded_irq — is checked with a quoted guard on the execution path before any use, and the error-path resource accounting (out_free_ict/out_no_pci) is balanced with no double-free or leak. The single unchecked result, alloc_workqueue into trans_pcie->rba.alloc_wq, has no dereference, dispatch, or free sink within this code (only INIT_WORK on an embedded struct follows), so its impact is not instantiated here.

assumptions: cfg_trans, pdev, and ent are supplied by the kernel PCI core and the driver's static config tables; their scalar fields consumed here (gen2, use_tfh, device_family, pdev->device, pdev->subsystem_device, pdev->irq) are treated as kernel-internal rather than attacker-content because no statement in this code derives them from file/socket/device content — under a strict data-origin model a hostile PCI device description could influence cfg selection, but the selected values are compile-time constants that reach no memory/index/size sink.

iwl_trans_alloc, IWL_TRANS_GET_PCIE_TRANS, iwl_read32, iwl_pcie_alloc_ict/free_ict, and the other callees are assumed to behave as their names/standard kernel semantics indicate; their internals are not shown.
CSR_HW_REV_STEP and IWL_PCIE_MAX_FRAGS macros are assumed to be pure value transforms as in the upstream driver.
limitations: The result of `trans_pcie->rba.alloc_wq = alloc_workqueue("rb_allocator", WQ_HIGHPRI | WQ_UNBOUND, 1);` is never checked (no NULL guard exists anywhere in this function — verified by searching for every fix form). This is a latent NULL-dereference risk, but the trigger requires kernel allocation failure (not attacker-determinable) and the dereference would occur only in later RX-allocator code not shown here (queue_work on rba.alloc_wq), so the impact is not instantiated in this code.

`iwl_pcie_set_interrupt_capa(pdev, trans, cfg_trans);` return value is not inspected; within this code its observable effect is only trans_pcie->msix_enabled, which is subsequently branched on (`if (trans_pcie->msix_enabled)`), so no fail-open path exists here, but callee-internal error handling is not shown.
Behavior of not-shown callees receiving trans (e.g., iwl_disable_interrupts, iwl_pcie_init_msix_handler internals) was not audited; this analysis covers only the statements in the given code.

verdict.summary: PipeSocketHandler::listen copies the attacker-controlled endpoint name into the fixed char sun_path[108] with strncpy(local.sun_path, pipePath.c_str(), sizeof(local.sun_path)) and no length check or manual NUL termination. A name of length >= sizeof(sun_path) (108 bytes on Linux) leaves sun_path unterminated; the subsequent unlink(local.sun_path) and chmod(local.sun_path, ...) consume it as a C string, reading past the end of the 110-byte stack sockaddr_un object (out-of-bounds read), and bind creates the socket at a silently truncated 108-byte path that no longer matches the recorded pipeServerSockets key — allowing a second listener whose name shares the 108-byte prefix to unlink and rebind over an existing socket.

evidence.reason: Root cause: unbounded copy of the caller-controlled name into the fixed 108-byte sun_path with strncpy using the full array size, so any source string of length >= 108 leaves sun_path with no NUL terminator. Instantiated trigger: endpoint.name() of 200 chars passes the only branch in the function (the duplicate-map check at line 5 tests map membership, not length), reaches line 15, and strncpy writes 108 non-NUL bytes. Direct impact links in this code: line 16 unlink(local.sun_path) and line 21 chmod(local.sun_path, ...) must strlen the buffer, reading past the end of the 110-byte sockaddr_un stack object (CWE-125), and line 18 bind creates the socket at the silently truncated 108-byte path while line 24 records the full untruncated name — so a second listen() with a different name sharing that 108-byte prefix passes the line-5 check, unlinks the first server's socket at line 16, and rebinds over it at line 18.

evidence.snippet:
string pipePath = endpoint.name();
  if (pipeServerSockets.find(pipePath) != pipeServerSockets.end()) {
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: pipePath is the content of the endpoint parameter of this non-static exported function (no length, charset, or canonicality precondition is documented, asserted, or checked in this code). The only guard on pipePath is this map-membership duplicate-listen check, which compares full strings and imposes no bound on the name's length before it reaches the strncpy at line 15.

assumptions: FATAL_FAIL is a macro not shown in this code; its behavior on failure (throw vs. abort) is assumed to be a fatal exit and is not part of any evidence chain.
initServerSocket(fd) is not shown; its effect on fd is not relied upon.

sizeof(local.sun_path) is 108 bytes on Linux (104 on some other Unixes); the defect boundary is any name length >= sizeof(sun_path), verified at exactly the limit (108) where strncpy writes no terminator.
Kernel behavior of bind() on an unterminated sun_path is outside this code; the primary finding rests on the in-code C-string consumers unlink() and chmod().
limitations: bind->chmod permission window (TOCTOU): the socket file is created at line 18 with umask-derived permissions and restricted to 0700 only at line 21; a local attacker could connect in between, but exploitability requires the default socket permissions to permit connect (depends on the process umask, which no statement in this code controls or quotes).

Empty endpoint.name(): sun_path becomes all NULs and, on Linux, bind() with a leading NUL byte may create an abstract-namespace socket that chmod cannot restrict; the chmod failure then reaches FATAL_FAIL whose semantics are not shown — impact chain partially outside this code.

unlink(local.sun_path) deletes any pre-existing file at the caller-chosen path (arbitrary file deletion at the process's own privilege), but the caller executes in this same process with equivalent capability and could call unlink itself, so no privilege boundary inside this code is crossed.

The truncated-path collision (second listener hijacking the first's socket path) is confirmed as a code-level consequence of the same missing bound; the downstream accept/authorization handling of hijacked connections is not shown in this code.

verdict.summary: In do_mouse(), the drag-in-tab-line paths index TabPageIdxs[mouse_col] without the mouse_col < Columns bounds check that guards the click path, allowing an out-of-bounds read when a mouse drag event reports a column at or beyond Columns.

evidence.reason: Drag event in the tab page line indexes TabPageIdxs with the attacker-supplied mouse_col without any bounds check; the only guard (mouse_col < Columns) exists solely on the is_click branch and is never executed on this path (the branch returns FALSE first). Trigger: a click in the tab line (sets in_tab_line via line 275, bounds-checked) followed by a drag event with mouse_col >= Columns.
Second unguarded indexing of TabPageIdxs[mouse_col] on the tab-line drag path taken when the drag leaves row 0; identical missing mouse_col < Columns check as line 261.

The click path demonstrates the required bounds contract: mouse_col < Columns is checked before the identical TabPageIdxs indexing, proving the array's valid index domain and the absence of any equivalent check on the drag paths.

assumptions: TabPageIdxs is a buffer sized for Columns entries (its allocation is outside this excerpt; the in-code guard 'mouse_col < Columns' at line 273 documents the valid index domain).

Mouse events originate from terminal escape sequences (row/col) that a malicious content source can emit with arbitrary coordinates; mouse_row/mouse_col are globals set from these reports upstream of this handler, which is the direct consumer.
mod_mask, State, VIsual_*, and clipboard globals are maintained by the framework outside this excerpt.
limitations: The downstream use of the out-of-bounds-derived value c1 in goto_tabpage(c1)/find_tabpage(-c1)/tabpage_move (lines 262, 290, 305, 320) occurs inside non-shown callees; their behavior with an out-of-domain index is not analyzed, so only the OOB read itself is claimed as impact in this code.
Sites 319-320 reach the same defect but require the drag to leave row 0; both are covered by the same missing guard as line 261.

verdict.summary: This iwlwifi PCIe transport allocation routine consumes only kernel-static configuration (cfg_trans), PCI-core-managed device fields, and internally-checked allocation/lookup results. Every sink is guarded in execution order: allocation results are NULL-checked before use (iwl_trans_alloc, alloc_workqueue, alloc_percpu, pcim_iomap_table), the MMIO base is validated before any register access, the device-read failure sentinel (hw_rev == 0xffffffff) is rejected before the hw_rev bit-manipulation, DMA mask setup has a fully-checked 32-bit fallback, snprintf is bounded by sizeof(trans->hw_id_str), and the hw_id arithmetic cannot overflow u32. All error paths (out_free_ict, out_no_pci, out_free_trans) free exactly the resources allocated prior to each goto, with no leak, double-free, or use-after-free. No attacker-controlled data value reaches a memory, injection, authz, or amplification sink in this code.

assumptions: iwl_trans_alloc (not shown) is assumed to allocate and zero-initialize the iwl_trans/iwl_trans_pcie memory; no statement in this code performs or verifies that initialization.

cfg_trans (including cfg_trans->base_params) is assumed to be a valid static entry from the driver's PCI ID table selected by the PCI core; this code contains no NULL check on cfg_trans or cfg_trans->base_params, so if any table entry had a NULL base_params the dereference at 'if (!cfg_trans->base_params->pcie_l1_allowed)' would fault — but no statement here can produce such an entry.
iwl_pcie_set_interrupt_capa (not shown) is assumed to set trans_pcie->msix_enabled before the 'if (trans_pcie->msix_enabled)' branch; the field is not initialized in this code.
IWL_PCIE_MAX_FRAGS, CSR_HW_REV_STEP, IWL_TRANS_GET_PCIE_TRANS and the ISR handlers are macros/callees not shown; their internal safety could not be verified here.

pdev->device, pdev->subsystem_device and pdev->irq are PCI-core-managed fields ultimately sourced from hardware config space; they are treated as kernel-trusted since this code performs no parsing of external content.
limitations: Potential NULL dereference of cfg_trans->base_params->pcie_l1_allowed: speculative — triggering requires a cfg_trans table entry with a NULL base_params, which no statement in this code can produce; the table is not shown.

Uninitialized trans_pcie fields (e.g., msix_enabled) if iwl_trans_alloc does not zero memory: speculative — depends entirely on the not-shown allocator; no attacker-influenced value reaches control flow from an uninitialized field in the statements given.
Behavior of not-shown callees (iwl_read32, iwl_pcie_alloc_ict, iwl_pcie_init_msix_handler, ISR handlers) on error paths could not be audited; their defects, if any, lie outside this code.

pdev->irq and config-space-derived fields could in principle be influenced by malicious hardware (an attacker-supplied PCIe device), but no statement in this code converts those values into an out-of-bounds, injection, or corruption primitive; impact would reside in not-shown handlers.

verdict.summary: NBD newstyle option negotiation handler. Every sink reachable with values this code's own statements produce is guarded by quotable checks: optlen is bounded by 'optlen > MAX_REQUEST_SIZE' before malloc and all reads; the OPT_INFO/GO arm enforces 'optlen < 6', 'exportnamelen > optlen-6' and the exact length equation 'optlen != 4 + exportnamelen + 2 + 2*nrinfos' before any index use, keeping all memcpy reads at or below data[optlen-1]; the meta-context arm enforces 'optlen < 8' and 'opt_index+4 > optlen' before each field read; TLS-required mode fails closed ('tls == 2 && !conn->using_tls' returns -1) and cross-TLS cached state is wiped. The residual edge — uint32 wrap in 'opt_index = 4 + exportnamelen' plus 'opt_index+4 > optlen' for exportnamelen in {0xFFFFFFF8..0xFFFFFFFF}, which would cause a wild out-of-bounds read at 'memcpy (&nr_queries, &data[opt_index], 4)' — can only be triggered if the unshown check_export_name accepts a ~4GiB export name against its explicit maxlen argument (optlen-8); that precondition is not instantiable from the given code and is recorded as a limitation, not a finding.

assumptions: check_export_name validates its namelen against its 4th (maxlen) argument before reading the name; this code passes optlen, optlen-6, and optlen-8 as maxlen — the enforcement statement itself is not in the given code.
check_string validates its len against its maxlen argument before the name is used by strncmp/debug '%.*s'; this code passes 'optlen - opt_index' as maxlen — enforcement not quotable here.

send_newstyle_option_reply_info_str treats length -1 (size_t SIZE_MAX, set by 'namelen = -1' and the literal 'desc, -1') as 'use strlen' — convention is shown by usage in this code, but the callee is not shown.
send_newstyle_option_reply_exportnames writes a sane reduced value into &nr_options (it receives the loop counter by address); its behavior is not shown.
MAX_REQUEST_SIZE is finite and below INT_MAX (so optlen fits an int for '%.*s' and 'optlen+1' cannot wrap size_t), and MAX_NR_OPTIONS is finite — constants not shown.

conn_recv_full reads exactly the requested byte count or returns -1; finish_newstyle_options/check_export_name/finish paths use (pointer, length) pairs rather than requiring NUL termination of 'data' (whose trailing byte data[optlen] is never initialized by this code).
limitations: Uninstantiated wrap trigger: with wire exportnamelen in {0xFFFFFFF8..0xFFFFFFFF}, 'opt_index = 4 + exportnamelen' wraps and the guard 'if (opt_index+4 > optlen)' also wraps, so 'memcpy (&nr_queries, &data[opt_index], 4)' would read at data + ~4GiB (wild out-of-bounds read). Trigger requires check_export_name to accept exportnamelen >> optlen-8; no statement in the given code instantiates that, so this is speculative in this code.

Uninstantiated querylen trigger: if check_string accepted querylen > optlen - opt_index, 'strncmp (&data[opt_index], "base:allocation", 15)' and 'opt_index += querylen' could read/write past the buffer, and 'debug ("... %.*s", (int) querylen, ...)' with querylen > INT_MAX yields a negative precision (unbounded strlen of a heap buffer with no guaranteed NUL). Blocked only by the unshown check_string maxlen validation.
Uninstantiated strndup trigger: 'strndup (&data[4], exportnamelen)' would over-read if exportnamelen exceeded optlen-4; depends on unshown check_export_name behavior.

NBD_INFO_NAME sets 'size_t namelen = -1' (SIZE_MAX) and passes it to an unshown callee; if that callee's length parameter were a narrower unsigned type, truncation could mis-size a subsequent copy — impact chain lies entirely in code not given.

Repeated NBD_OPT_SET_META_CONTEXT overwrites conn->exportname_from_set_meta_context without freeing the previous value (bounded memory leak, at most MAX_NR_OPTIONS rounds, each requiring the client to transmit the equivalent optlen bytes — no amplification, robustness only).

verdict.summary: gdImageFillToBorder recurses into itself (Above/Below) with no depth bound, visited-set, or iterative work-list anywhere in the function. The defect is aggravated by asymmetric coordinate validation: the quoted clamps 'if (x >= im->sx) { x = im->sx - 1; }' and 'if (y >= im->sy) { y = im->sy - 1; }' handle only the upper bounds; negative y is never rejected or clamped and is passed as an out-of-range row index to gdImageGetPixel/gdImageSetPixel on the first loop iteration (the memory access itself occurs in the not-shown accessors).

evidence.reason: Primary sink: unguarded recursive self-call. The guard on line 56 only bounds y from above; nothing in the function bounds recursion depth. For an attacker-supplied image whose row y+1 pixels differ from both 'border' and 'color' (e.g., a 1x300000 solid-color image with border absent), every frame recurses at the next row, producing a chain of ~im->sy stack frames — stack exhaustion / attacker-scalable resource consumption (CWE-674). A symmetric unguarded recursion exists at line 47 for the 'Above' direction.

Origin of the tainted coordinate and the missing check: y is clamped only against the upper bound ('if (y >= im->sy)'); there is no corresponding 'y < 0' rejection or clamp, so an attacker-supplied negative y reaches gdImageGetPixel(im, i, y) / gdImageSetPixel(im, i, y, color) on the very first loop iteration as an out-of-range row index, and also passes the Below-recursion guard, letting |y| set the recursion depth. The defective use is the absence of a lower-bound check here.

im->sx, im->sy, and the pixel values returned by gdImageGetPixel are assumed attacker-influenced, since im is a pointer parameter of this exported function and in normal use is an image decoded from untrusted content; no statement in this code revalidates them.

verdict.summary: sug_filltree walks the spell-file case-folded tree with a stack index `depth` that is incremented on every descent (tword[depth++] = c; arridx[depth] = idxs[n]; curi[depth] = 1; wordcount[depth] = 0;) without any upper-bound check against the MAXWLEN-sized stack arrays arridx/curi/tword/wordcount. The only bounds check in the function (n + 1 < slang->sl_fbyts_len) guards an unrelated read; the loop condition bounds depth only from below.

evidence.reason: Unguarded descent sink: depth is incremented and immediately used to index the MAXWLEN-sized stack arrays arridx, curi, tword, and wordcount with no check that depth < MAXWLEN anywhere on any path (the loop condition `depth >= 0` only bounds depth from below). Trigger: a word in the attacker-controlled case-folded tree (sl_fbyts from a parsed spell file) with more than MAXWLEN non-NUL bytes; once depth reaches MAXWLEN, `tword[depth++] = c` writes the attacker byte c out of bounds and `arridx[depth] = idxs[n]` writes an attacker-influenced tree value one element past arridx — an attacker-scalable stack out-of-bounds write (CWE-787).

verdict.summary: expand_case_fold_string computes the byte length of the current character with `len = enclen(reg->enc, p)` (line 32) without passing or clamping against the node's end pointer. When the pattern string node ends with an incomplete multibyte lead byte (attacker-controlled regex pattern content), enclen returns the full encoding length, so `fold_len` (line 67) exceeds `end - p`. The code then copies the range [p, p+len) via onig_node_new_str(foldp, foldp + fold_len) (line 79) or onig_node_str_cat(snode, foldp, foldp + fold_len) (line 87), reading past the end of the heap-allocated pattern buffer — an out-of-bounds heap over-read (crash/DoS, disclosure potential). No clamp of len to end - p exists anywhere on any path; upstream fixed this exact defect by changing the call to enclen(reg->enc, p, end).

evidence.snippet: len = enclen(reg->enc, p);
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted length: enclen is called with only p and no end bound, so for an incomplete multibyte character at the final position of the string node it returns a length greater than end - p. This value is never clamped against end anywhere in the function.

When the lookup returns n == 0 for a truncated final byte, the unclamped enclen value is assigned as the span length: foldp = p and fold_len = len, so foldp + fold_len points beyond end of the node's buffer.

Sinks: both onig_node_new_str(foldp, foldp + fold_len) and onig_node_str_cat(snode, foldp, foldp + fold_len) copy the attacker-derived span [p, p + len), which for a truncated final multibyte lead byte reads past the end of the pattern buffer. Simulated trigger: pattern node "a\xC3" in a 2-byte encoding gives iteration 2 p = &S[1], n = 0, len = 2, end - p = 1, is_ambig = 1 (set by NODE_STRING_SET_AMBIG on iteration 1), so line 79 executes with (foldp, foldp+2) reading S[2] out of bounds.

assumptions: enclen(reg->enc, p) returns the encoding's full character length for the byte at p without regard to any remaining-byte count; the function shown provides no end parameter to it, which is the defect.
String node contents (sn->s..sn->end) derive from the attacker-controlled regex pattern; no documented or asserted precondition on their encoding-validity is quotable in this code.

ONIGENC_MBC_CASE_FOLD (line 62) is assumed to respect the passed end pointer and the fixed-size buf[ONIGENC_MBC_CASE_FOLD_MAXLEN]; its implementation is not shown, so the n != 0 fold path (fold_len from the callee) is treated as a callee contract, not a finding here.

expand_case_fold_string_alt and expand_case_fold_make_rem_string are not shown; they receive end (lines 104, 137) and are assumed to bound their reads, but they also receive the unclamped len at line 104.
No deployment context (setuid, daemon, library) is assumed; the pattern bytes are untrusted input at this code's own entry point.
limitations: The exact parser statements that build a string node ending in an incomplete multibyte character are not in the given code; the trigger relies on such content being constructible from the attacker-controlled pattern, and no quotable parser-side rejection exists to dismiss it. Upstream Oniguruma history confirms this defect class was reachable (later fixed by enclen(reg->enc, p, end)).

verdict.summary: This static JIT-internal helper walks compiled pattern bytecode and computes private-data frame sizes. Several memory-safety sinks are unguarded in this code (NULL dereference if next_opcode returns its NULL sentinel in the default arm, since the only check is the debug-only SLJIT_ASSERT(cc != NULL); unvalidated GET2 group index into common->optimized_cbracket and OVECTOR(offset<<1); unvalidated *alternative read in OP_COND; cc[1] boundary read in OP_MARK; unchecked cc advancement past ccend caught only by SLJIT_ASSERT(cc == ccend)). However, every one of these triggers requires malformed compiled bytecode (unknown/truncated opcode, out-of-range group number, dangling link, truncated MARK argument), and no statement in this code produces or can produce such bytecode — the regex-to-bytecode transform lies entirely in a not-shown stage. Per STEP 4, no trigger precondition could be instantiated from this code's actual input surface or its own statements, so no candidate survives as a vulnerability here; they are recorded as speculative limitations.

assumptions: The compiled bytecode between cc and ccend is well-formed (opcodes known, operands complete, group numbers consistent with the compiled pattern). No statement in the given code documents, asserts at runtime, or enforces this; the producing stage (pattern compilation) is not shown.
SLJIT_ASSERT is a debug-only assertion (no-op in release builds); no #define or comment in the given code states this, but nothing else in the code gives it runtime effect.
next_opcode (callee, not shown) returns NULL for unknown opcodes or truncated code; its actual bounds logic cannot be quoted.
recurse_check_bit (macro/callee, not shown) indexes common->recurse_bitset within common->recurse_bitset_size and sets bits as a seen-set; its bounds behavior cannot be quoted.

common->optimized_cbracket is sized to at least (max group number + 1) and common->recurse_bitset is allocated with recurse_bitset_size covering all private-data offsets, by not-shown earlier JIT stages.
get_class_iterator_size (callee, not shown) does not itself read out of bounds for well-formed class opcodes.
limitations: C1 (CWE-476, speculative): default arm does 'cc = next_opcode(common, cc); SLJIT_ASSERT(cc != NULL);' with no runtime NULL test; if next_opcode returned NULL, 'while (cc < ccend)' with cc==NULL is true and 'switch(*cc)' would dereference NULL. Uninstantiable precondition: bytecode containing an opcode next_opcode rejects or truncated at the code end — not producible by any statement in this code.

C2 (CWE-125/CWE-129, speculative): 'offset = GET2(cc, 1 + LINK_SIZE);' then 'common->optimized_cbracket[offset]' and 'recurse_check_bit(common, OVECTOR(offset << 1))' with no bound on offset in this code. Uninstantiable precondition: compiled bytecode whose group number exceeds the capture-group array bound — not producible by any statement in this code.

C3 (CWE-125, speculative): OP_COND does 'alternative = cc + GET(cc, 1); ... *alternative == OP_KETRMAX' with no bound on the link value. Uninstantiable precondition: an OP_COND link pointing outside the compiled code.

C4 (CWE-125, speculative): 'cc += 1 + 2 + cc[1];' reads cc[1], which is one byte past ccend if OP_MARK sits at ccend-1. Uninstantiable precondition: an opcode stream ending mid-operand; also the increment can only skip forward past ccend, after which the loop guard 'while (cc < ccend)' safely terminates.

C5 (int overflow of 'int length', not a finding): each opcode contributes at most 3 to length and occupies at least one byte, so overflow requires multi-gigabyte compiled input with no amplification, and the wrong value is only returned to a not-shown caller — impact chain breaks outside this code.

If an application ever fed attacker-controlled raw bytecode (e.g., deserialized compiled patterns without validation) to this JIT stage, candidates C1-C4 would become reachable memory-safety defects; that deployment path is an assumption, not evidence from the given code.

verdict.summary: In the '@' (register) case of eval7, the two Vim9 error branches detect invalid attacker-controlled register references/syntax — `semsg(_(e_syntax_error_at_str), *arg)` for whitespace and `emsg_invreg(**arg)` for invalid registers — but never assign `ret = FAIL`. Control falls through with `ret == OK` and `rettv` still in its entry state: only `rettv->v_type = VAR_UNKNOWN;` was set (line 20) and `rettv->vval` was never initialized. The indeterminate typval is then passed to `handle_subscript(...)` (line 263), optionally to `eval7_leader(rettv, ...)` (line 269), and returned to the caller as a successfully evaluated expression (line 270). This is fail-open error handling: input the code itself identified as erroneous is accepted, and an uninitialized value reaches control flow and output of the expression evaluator. The correct pattern exists in the same function ('.' check: `semsg(...); ++*arg; return FAIL;` at lines 36-38), confirming the omission is a defect.

evidence.reason: Root cause / missing-check site: the branches at lines 129-130 and 131-132 detect invalid attacker-controlled register selectors (e.g. `@!` in a Vim9 script: valid_yank_reg('!', FALSE) fails → emsg_invreg executes) but contain no `ret = FAIL;` — only the message call. With ret still OK (set at line 13 and never modified), rettv keeps v_type == VAR_UNKNOWN and an uninitialized vval; the parser then continues at lines 140-142, advancing past the invalid character and breaking out with success. Instantiated trigger: vim9 script, evaluate = TRUE, expression text `@!` (or `@ `).

evidence.snippet: rettv->v_type = VAR_UNKNOWN;
evidence.reason: Origin of the uninitialized value: only v_type is initialized; rettv->vval is never assigned on the '@' error path (the assignments at lines 135-136 are in the else branch only), so the indeterminate typval is what the error path returns as a valid evaluation result.

Sinks receiving the unguarded error-path state in execution order: with ret == OK after the '@' error branches, the VAR_UNKNOWN/indeterminate rettv is handed to handle_subscript (method/subscript processing, e.g. `@!->fn()` passes it as a call argument), possibly to eval7_leader (which reads it via tv_get_bool), and finally returned to the caller as a successful evaluation — fail-open propagation of an uninitialized value into control flow and output.

assumptions: handle_subscript, eval7_leader, and upstream expression consumers are not shown; their exact treatment of a VAR_UNKNOWN typval is assumed only to the extent needed for severity, not for the verdict — the fail-open return of the indeterminate typval is fully instantiated by this code's own statements.
The expression buffer is assumed NUL-terminated within its allocation (unquotable), which bounds the `*(*arg + 1)` lookahead read at line 30.
limitations: Line 154 dereferences `rettv->vval.v_partial->pt_func` guarded only by `ret == OK && evaluate` (line 152); if get_lambda_tv could return OK without a VAR_PARTIAL rettv this would be an invalid dereference, but the callee is not shown and no producing statement can be quoted — speculative, not counted.

When a name comes from get_name_len's `alias` (lines 197-199) and evaluation succeeds, `name_start = s` (line 245) may point to the buffer freed by `vim_free(alias);` (line 257) before it is passed to `handle_subscript` (line 263) — potential dangling-pointer read inside the not-shown callee; the harmful use is not quotable here.

verdict.summary: In input_bmp_reader, ColormapSize is derived from attacker-controlled file bytes as (bfOffs - biSize - 14) / Maps (line 253). When bfOffs < biSize + 14 the subtraction underflows/wraps and, after division, is stored into int ColormapSize as a negative value. The only guard is one-sided: 'if (ColormapSize > 256) ColormapSize = 256;' bounds only the upper end, so a negative count passes every sanity check and is handed to ReadColorMap(fd, ColorMap, ColormapSize, Maps, ...) as the count for filling the fixed 256x3 stack array ColorMap declared in this function (line 334). Trigger fully instantiated with a crafted BMP (bfOffs=0, biSize=40, biClrUsed=1, biBitCnt=8 gives ColormapSize = -13); no lower-bound check, unsigned comparison, or bfOffs range check exists anywhere on any path (STEP 5 search over all fix forms). This code is the file-format intake point, so the missing validation is the defect here; the exact overwrite behavior of the negative count sits in the not-shown callee, limiting quoted impact to the out-of-domain value escaping all enforced bounds.

evidence.reason: Root cause: integer underflow. bfOffs and biSize are attacker-supplied file fields; when bfOffs < biSize + 14 the subtraction underflows/wraps and ColormapSize becomes negative. The reset at 'ColormapSize = Bitmap_Head.biClrUsed = 1 << biBitCnt' only runs when biClrUsed == 0, and the clamp 'if (ColormapSize > 256) ColormapSize = 256;' tests only the upper boundary, so a negative ColormapSize (e.g. -13 for bfOffs=0, biSize=40, Maps=4, biClrUsed=1) passes every check in this function and reaches ReadColorMap as the count for the fixed ColorMap[256][3] stack array.

evidence.snippet: Bitmap_File_Head.bfOffs = ToL(&buffer[0x08]);
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: bfOffs is read directly from attacker-controlled file bytes (bytes 8..11 of the 12-byte header read at line 54) with no range validation anywhere in this function before it is consumed in the ColormapSize computation at line 253.

Sink: the unvalidated, negative ColormapSize is passed as the entry count for ReadColorMap, which fills the 768-byte stack array 'unsigned char ColorMap[256][3]' declared at line 7 of this function. The count has escaped the intended [0,256] domain because the only clamp (lines 261-262) bounds the upper end only; the trigger (bfOffs=0, biSize=40, biClrUsed!=0, biBitCnt<=8) was fully simulated through every intervening sanity check.

assumptions: ToL/ToS parse little-endian values from the file and ToL returns an unsigned type, as is conventional for this BMP reader; Bitmap_File_Head.bfOffs/biSize are assumed unsigned per the struct's typical definition (not shown).
ReadOK(fd, buf, n) reads up to n bytes and reports success; ReadColorMap, ReadImage, at_bitmap_init, ReadChannelMasks, setMasksDefault implementations are not shown.

If ToL/struct types were signed, the same trigger still yields a negative ColormapSize via plain signed arithmetic (0 - 40 - 14 = -54, -54/4 = -13), so the finding does not depend on the width assumption.
limitations: The precise consequence of the negative count inside ReadColorMap is not shown: if it iterates 'i < number' with a signed int, the negative count is a no-op; if it treats the count as unsigned or uses it in size arithmetic, reads/writes would exceed the 768-byte stack ColorMap. This code is the intake point that derives and passes the out-of-domain count, so the missing validation is reported here rather than deferred, but the overwrite itself is not quotable from the given code.
biClrUsed == 256 passes the '> 256' check at exactly the boundary; it is in-domain as a count for the 256-entry map, and any index-256 misuse would be inside the not-shown ReadImage.

Line 350 casts biWidth/biHeight to unsigned short for at_bitmap_init; negative biHeight (explicitly permitted by this code) becomes 65436 and dimensions >= 65536 are truncated, misrepresenting the bitmap's metadata, but all consumers of at_bitmap fields are outside the given code.
Negative biHeight, RLE compression/bit-count combinations, and rowbytes are passed to ReadImage, whose handling is not shown; no in-code defect was provable for those flows.
The BA-loop iterates once per 14 file bytes and terminates at EOF via the ReadOK failure path; no attacker-scalable amplification was instantiated.

verdict.summary: squashfs_opendir reads attacker-supplied directory data from directory_table using an offset (bytes) that is bounded only by a size derived from the attacker-controlled inode field (*i)->data, never against the actual allocated size of directory_table; additionally the inner while(dir_count--) loop advances bytes without any bounds re-check, so memcpy calls at bytes can read far out of bounds, leaking/crashing when parsing a malicious squashfs image.

evidence.reason: size is computed solely from the attacker-controlled inode field (*i)->data plus bytes; no statement anywhere compares bytes (or bytes + sizeof(dirh)) to the allocated length of directory_table, so the loop guard while(bytes < size) permits indexing directory_table + bytes far past the end of the table, giving an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) when a crafted image supplies a large data value.

Inside the inner while(dir_count--) loop the only bounds check (while(bytes < size), line 50) is not re-evaluated: bytes advances by sizeof(*dire) and later by dire->size + 1 (attacker-chosen, up to 256) for up to SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT entries without any bounds check on any path, so the memcpy at directory_table + bytes reads out of bounds even if size were the true table length; the read data is subsequently stored into dir->dirs[].name via strcpy.

assumptions: The allocated size of directory_table is not shown in the given code; it is assumed (from typical unsquashfs) to be the table's on-disk length, which the code never references in any bounds check.
read_inode()'s failure behavior (whether it can return NULL before *i is dereferenced at line 25) is not shown.
Values of SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT, SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN, DIR_ENT_SIZE, and the layout of squashfs_dir_entry_2 come from headers not shown.
limitations: Potential NULL dereference of *i (line 25) if read_inode can fail and return NULL is speculative: the callee is not shown and no return-value check exists here, so it cannot be instantiated from the given code.
int overflow in size = (*i)->data + bytes could wrap to negative and terminate the loop early; this is subsumed by the primary out-of-bounds read finding and produces no separate impact beyond it.
