`php_stream_readdir` is assumed to fill `d.d_name` within its declared width and to return NULL only at end-of-directory; its implementation is not shown.

Behavior of `load_1`, `set_text_binary`, `coalesce_entries`, `magic_entry_free`, `cmpstr`, and `apprentice_sort` is not shown; no contract for their outputs (e.g., mset[j].me/mp non-NULL when count>0) can be quoted.
PHP allocator semantics for erealloc failure (whether it ever returns NULL) are not shown and were not relied upon.
limitations: Invalid free of a stack buffer: `efree(mfn);` inside the `erealloc(...) == NULL` branch frees `mfn`, declared as `char mfn[MAXPATHLEN]` (a stack array). If reached, this corrupts the heap allocator. Trigger requires erealloc to return NULL for `mlen = maxfiles * sizeof(*filearr)`; no statement in this code induces that allocation failure, so the trigger is speculative (environment-only). Not classified as a vulnerability per STEP 4.
Integer overflow of `mlen = maxfiles * sizeof(*filearr)` requires approximately 2^61 array entries, which the preceding readdir loop cannot produce; speculative.

Potential NULL dereference of `mset[j].me[i].mp->cont_level` if `load_1` (not shown) sets `mset[j].count > 0` with a NULL `mp`; no producing statement in this code, no quotable contract — speculative.

TOCTOU between `stat(mfn, &st)`/S_ISREG and the later `load_1(ms, action, filearr[i], ...)` reopening the same path; the impact of a swapped file materializes entirely inside the not-shown callee, so the impact chain is not instantiated here.
Memory leaks on error paths: entries `filearr[i..files-1]` and `filearr` itself leak when `goto out` is taken from within the load loop; bounded per invocation, no attacker-scalable retention shown.
`qsort(filearr, 0, ...)` / `qsort(NULL, 0, ...)` when a directory is empty is formally undefined behavior but performs no memory access; benign.

verdict.summary: copy_page_to_iter_pipe() is the post-Dirty-Pipe (CVE-2022-0847) fixed implementation. The stale-buffer merge-flag vulnerability is closed by the unconditional 'buf->flags = 0;' before the buffer is published via 'pipe->head = i_head + 1;'; ring overflow on the new-buffer path is prevented by the pipe_full() check placed on the only path that initializes a fresh slot; and count underflow is prevented by the bytes clamp. The remaining unguarded values (page-relative offset/bytes not checked against PAGE_SIZE in the merge path, ring_size validity, iterator slot liveness) cannot be driven out of range by any statement in this code — the out-of-range trigger values would have to be supplied by a caller or by iterator/pipe state not produced here, so no trigger was instantiated. sanity() is invoked but its implementation is not shown and was not relied upon.

assumptions: sanity(i) at line 17 is an external helper whose body is not in the given code; any invariant it enforces (e.g., iterator head/tail consistency, iov_offset within a page) is an assumption, not a quotable guard, and no surviving finding depends on it.
pipe_full(i_head, p_tail, pipe->max_usage) is assumed to compare ring occupancy against max_usage; its implementation is not shown.
pipe->ring_size being a nonzero power of two (so that p_mask = ring_size - 1 masks correctly) is not enforced or asserted in this code.
pipe->max_usage <= pipe->ring_size is not enforced in this code.
get_page(page) is assumed not to fail; it returns void and its effect is not shown.
limitations: Merge path (lines 22-27) lacks any check that offset and bytes stay within one page (no PAGE_SIZE bound, no check that buf->offset + buf->len == off). Repeated merges with offset == a monotonically grown iov_offset >= PAGE_SIZE would grow buf->len beyond the page and cause an out-of-bounds read when the pipe is drained. The out-of-page offset value can only originate from a caller (this code only consumes 'offset'; it produces iov_offset from caller-supplied values), so the trigger is not instantiable from the given code.

The merge path trusts that slot pipe->bufs[i_head & p_mask] holds the live partially-filled buffer; if the iterator were left with i->head == pipe->head while iov_offset != 0 (state no statement here creates), a stale buf->page could match and merge into a dead slot. Trigger requires external iterator mutation not shown.
p_mask = pipe->ring_size - 1 yields UINT_MAX if ring_size == 0, making the bufs[] index unmasked; ring_size is never validated here and no statement in this code sets it.
buf->len (32-bit) accumulates size_t bytes via 'buf->len += bytes;'; truncation requires a bytes/count value of ~2^32 scale that this code's own flow cannot produce given the merge preconditions.

The function is static; its in-file callers (iov_iter framework) are not shown, so caller-side guarantees on offset/bytes/page could not be quoted and were not used to dismiss any candidate whose trigger was instantiable.

verdict.summary: squashfs_opendir performs out-of-bounds reads of the decompressed directory table: the only positional guard, `while(bytes < size)` (line 50), is evaluated solely at the outer loop head and never bounds the read lengths (sizeof(dirh), sizeof(*dire), dire->size+1) against the end of the data region; the inner `while(dir_count--)` loop never re-checks `bytes` at all, and `size` itself is computed from the attacker-controlled inode field `(*i)->data` (line 48), so `bytes` can be driven arbitrarily far past the directory_table allocation. A malicious squashfs image sets a large `data` field and a maximal `dirh.count`, causing memcpy reads up to ~dir_count x (sizeof(entry)+256) bytes past the heap buffer — an attacker-scalable out-of-bounds read (heap disclosure potential / denial of service).

evidence.reason: Root cause: the inner `while(dir_count--)` loop never re-validates `bytes` against `size` or the table end; it advances `bytes` by `sizeof(*dire)` (line 78) and `dire->size + 1` (line 113) and reads `sizeof(*dire)` bytes at line 76 and up to `dire->size + 1` bytes at line 86-87 from `directory_table + bytes` with no bounds check. The only quoted guards inside this loop (line 81 `dire->size >= SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN`, and check_name) bound the name length, never the table offset. Instantiated trigger: attacker image supplies a large inode `data` field (making `size` exceed the real table length, line 48) and a `dirh.count` within SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT, so `bytes` walks past the end of the directory_table buffer for up to dir_count iterations — heap out-of-bounds read with attacker-scalable extent.

Origin of the faulty bound: `size = (*i)->data + bytes;` uses the attacker-controlled inode field `data` with no clamp to the actual directory_table length, so the only positional guard `while(bytes < size)` (line 50) can hold for bytes offsets far past the real table end. Additionally, this guard is only evaluated at the loop head: when `bytes == size - 1` the fixed-size `sizeof(dirh)` read at line 56 already crosses the end of the data region — no check of the read length against the remaining bytes exists anywhere on the path.

assumptions: The declaration and allocation size of the global `directory_table` (the decompressed directory table buffer) are not in the given code; its total length cannot be quoted. This does not demote the finding because `size` is itself attacker-authored via `(*i)->data` (line 48), allowing `bytes` to exceed any finite buffer length.

`struct dir_ent` (destination of `strcpy(dir->dirs[dir->dir_count].name, dire->name)` at line 107) is not in the given code, so the capacity of its `name` field cannot be quoted; the source is bounded to <= 256 chars + NUL by the quoted checks at lines 81 and 87.

`SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT`, `SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN`, `sizeof(squashfs_dir_header_2)` and `sizeof(squashfs_dir_entry_2)` are external constants whose values cannot be quoted from the given code; the analysis relies only on their existence as quoted at lines 63, 81 and the memcpy length expressions.
limitations: C3 (possible destination overflow in `strcpy(dir->dirs[dir->dir_count].name, dire->name)`, line 107) is speculative: the capacity of `struct dir_ent`'s `name` member is not in the given code, so the trigger precondition (destination smaller than 257 bytes) could not be instantiated. The source length is bounded at <= 256 + NUL by the quoted check at line 81 and the NUL write at line 87.

Whether OOB-read heap data is disclosed to the user (e.g., as extracted filenames) depends on consumers of `dir->dirs[].name` not shown in this code; the confirmed impact is the out-of-bounds read itself (crash/denial of service and potential heap disclosure).

`bytes += (*i)->offset` (line 47) and `size = (*i)->data + bytes` (line 48) can overflow int on extreme attacker values; these are subsumed by the primary finding (the unbounded `bytes` index) and not counted separately.

verdict.summary: The brush-file loader computes the allocation size at line 121 with `size = bh.width * bh.height * bh.bytes;` in the 32-bit type of the header fields (each a 32-bit unsigned int per g_ntohl byte-swapping), while the only overflow guard (line 51, `G_MAXSIZE / bh.width / bh.height / bh.bytes < 1`) validates the product in 64-bit gsize arithmetic and therefore passes any header whose 32-bit product wraps (e.g. width=65536, height=32770, bytes=2: 64-bit product 4,295,229,440 passes the guard; 32-bit product wraps to 262,144). brush_buf is then allocated undersized (256KB), and the case-2 conversion loop at line 189 is bounded by the raw `bh.width * bh.height` (2,147,614,720 iterations), reading `*buf` out of bounds from i=131,072 (line 199/201) and writing `brush_buf[i]` out of bounds from i=262,144 (line 205) — a linear heap buffer overflow of attacker-scale length driven purely by malicious .gbr file content. The same 32-bit wrap exists at line 164 (`g_malloc (4 * bh.width * bh.height)`) versus loop bound line 166, giving a second OOB-write path.

evidence.reason: Origin of the defect: the allocation size is computed as a 32-bit product of the attacker-controlled header fields (width, height, bytes read from the brush file and byte-swapped at lines 38-42), so it wraps modulo 2^32. The guard at line 51 (`G_MAXSIZE / bh.width / bh.height / bh.bytes < 1`) evaluates in 64-bit gsize arithmetic and passes for width=65536, height=32770, bytes=2, yet the 32-bit multiplication here yields 262,144 instead of 4,295,229,440, so brush_buf is undersized. The read check at line 124 compares against the same wrapped size and cannot detect the wrap.

evidence.snippet: for (i = 0; i < bh.width * bh.height; i++, buf++)
evidence.reason: The case-2 conversion loop is bounded by the raw 32-bit product `bh.width * bh.height` (2,147,614,720 for the simulated header) with no relation to the allocated size (262,144 bytes from the wrapped computation at line 121); no check, clamp, cast, or corrected loop bound exists on any path between the allocation and this loop.

evidence.snippet: brush_buf[i] = (guchar) (short_float.f * 255.0 + 0.5);
evidence.reason: Heap out-of-bounds WRITE: with brush_buf allocated only 262,144 bytes (line 122) while the loop at line 189 runs 2,147,614,720 iterations, this store writes past the end of the buffer from i = 262,144 onward; the read `GUINT16_FROM_BE (*buf)` at line 199/201 likewise reads out of bounds from i = 131,072. Trigger fully instantiated: a brush file with version=1, bytes=2, width=65536, height=32770, plus 256KB of brush data, passes every check in the function and reaches this write.

evidence.snippet:
brush_buf = g_malloc (4 * bh.width * bh.height);

                for (i = 0; i < ph.width * ph.height; i++)
evidence.reason: Second instantiation of the same 32-bit overflow: `4 * bh.width * bh.height` wraps when width*height >= 2^30 (e.g. width=height=32768 gives a wrapped allocation of 0 bytes; width*height = 2^30+100 gives 400 bytes) while the loop bound `ph.width * ph.height` (equal to bh.width*bh.height, verified at lines 155-156) runs width*height times, making the `read (fd, brush_buf + i * 4, 3)` at line 168 and `brush_buf[i * 4 + 3] = plain_brush[i];` at line 176 write out of bounds past the undersized heap buffer.

assumptions: BrushHeader fields are 32-bit unsigned integers; this is inferred from the code's own comment at line 37 ('rearrange the bytes in each unsigned int') and from each field being assigned a g_ntohl (32-bit) result at lines 38-44. If the fields were 64-bit, the multiplication at line 121 would not wrap; the struct declaration is not part of the given code.

GIMP_MAX_IMAGE_SIZE (referenced at lines 47-48 but not defined in the given code) is at least 65536 so that the simulated width=65536 passes `bh.width > GIMP_MAX_IMAGE_SIZE`; the real GIMP constant is 262144.
gsize/G_MAXSIZE is a 64-bit unsigned type (standard GLib), which is why the line 51 guard validates the 64-bit product while line 121 computes in 32-bit.
sizeof(BrushHeader) = 28 (7 x 32-bit fields); only relative comparisons (`bh.header_size > sizeof (BrushHeader)`, `bn_size > 0`) depend on it, and they hold for any plausible value.
limitations: gimp_any_to_utf8 (line 109) may return NULL for an unconvertible name string, which would later cause a NULL dereference at strlen(name)/gimp_layer_new; the callee is not shown, so this cannot be instantiated (CWE-476 candidate, unproven).

bn_size (line 95) can be up to ~2.1e9 from a ~40-byte header, making g_new attempt a multi-GB allocation (line 97) that glib aborts on failure; the abort-on-OOM behavior is not shown, so this is recorded as allocation amplification/possible DoS, not a primary finding.

For the bytes=1 and bytes=4 paths, the undersized brush_buf produced by the line 121 wrap is ultimately consumed by gimp_pixel_rgn_set_rect (not shown), whose out-of-bounds read occurs outside the given code; the in-code case-2 and case-1-pattern overflows already confirm the same defect.

The size-wraps-to-zero variant (e.g. width=65536, height=32768, bytes=2 gives size=0) relies on glib's g_malloc(0) returning NULL and read(fd, NULL, 0) returning 0, neither of which is quotable from the given code; it is a weaker variant of the confirmed overflow.

Minor non-security defects observed: fd is not closed on the sanitize-failure return (line 58) or the final 'Unsupported brush depth' return; brush_buf leaks on that same path; a version-2 file with bytes=18 is allocated then rejected, leaking brush_buf. No security impact demonstrated.

verdict.summary: win_redr_status appends a ' ' and status flags to the fixed-size global buffer NameBuff with no capacity or termination check. At the exactly-at-limit case (translated buffer name of MAXPATHL-1 bytes), line 54 overwrites the NUL terminator and sets len to MAXPATHL; the following vim_snprintf calls use size 'MAXPATHL - len' (0 or negative) with an out-of-bounds destination, and the unguarded STRLEN(p + len) / mb_string2cells(p, -1) read past the end of NameBuff. The oversized len then drives OOB writes ('*p = <' at p+i-1 / p += len - (this_ru_col-1), and vim_snprintf with a negative size widened to size_t), i.e. out-of-bounds read and write of a fixed global buffer triggered by a boundary-length buffer name.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the attacker-influenced buffer name is placed in the fixed MAXPATHL-byte global NameBuff and len = STRLEN(p) is never checked against MAXPATHL before '*(p + len++) = ' '' appends the space. When the translated name is exactly MAXPATHL-1 bytes (at-limit edge), the write lands on the last byte, destroying the NUL terminator and leaving len == MAXPATHL; the subsequent flag appends and string scans operate on an unterminated buffer past its end. No bounds, clamp, or re-termination statement exists anywhere in the function.

evidence.snippet:
vim_snprintf((char *)p + len, MAXPATHL - len, "%s", "[+]");
	    len += (int)STRLEN(p + len);
evidence.reason: Instantiated consequence: with len == MAXPATHL produced by the unchecked append at line 54, vim_snprintf receives a one-past-the-end destination and size MAXPATHL - len == 0 (no NUL is written), then the unconditional STRLEN(p + len) reads past the end of NameBuff (out-of-bounds read), inflating len beyond MAXPATHL. Later calls pass 'MAXPATHL - len' negative (widened to a huge size_t) with destination p + len out of bounds, and the non-mbyte/mbyte branches use the oversized len in 'p += len - (this_ru_col - 1); *p = '<'' / 'p = p + i - 1; *p = '<'' — out-of-bounds writes of the fixed global buffer.

assumptions: NameBuff is a global char_u array of MAXPATHL bytes; this is inferred from the code's own sizing expression 'MAXPATHL - len' in the vim_snprintf calls and get_keymap_str(wp, ..., NameBuff, MAXPATHL).

get_trans_bufname fills NameBuff with a NUL-terminated translated buffer name truncated to MAXPATHL, so len <= MAXPATHL-1 is reachable, including the exactly-full value len == MAXPATHL-1 used in the trigger.
vim_snprintf takes a size_t length; with size 0 it writes no bytes (leaving no NUL), and a negative int argument widens to a huge size_t. This callee behavior is not shown in the given code.

Buffer names (file paths) and the changed/ro/help/terminal flags are settable from files, the environment, and Vim script — treated as attacker-data per the data-origin model; Vim's process is the target of the corruption.
limitations: For a modified terminal buffer, the space is appended at line 54 but the '[+]' append is suppressed by '&& !bt_terminal(wp->w_buffer)', so the status line runs into stale NameBuff bytes from a previous redraw; this is in-bounds and only misrepresents already-user-visible editor UI content — not counted as a vulnerability.

this_ru_col = ru_col - (Columns - wp->w_width) has no upper clamp, so screen_fill/screen_puts can be given columns beyond the window; whether that is harmful depends on clipping inside the not-shown screen_fill/screen_puts — impact chain not instantiated here.

The distance of the out-of-bounds write (via the inflated len) depends on the position of the first NUL byte in the global memory adjacent to NameBuff, which is not shown; the out-of-bounds read itself (STRLEN/mb_string2cells past NameBuff) is unconditional once the terminator is destroyed.
The 'static int busy' recursion guard is not thread-safe; no two interleavable operations with an attacker window were exhibited (Vim is assumed single-threaded), so no race condition is claimed.

verdict.summary: gopherToHTML processes a raw gopher server response (untrusted network content) and, for a complete line whose accumulated length is exactly TEMP_BUF_SIZE - 1, writes the NUL terminator at line[llen + 1] — one element past the end of the TEMP_BUF_SIZE-byte local array `line`. The only bound, `if (gopherState->len + llen >= TEMP_BUF_SIZE)` clamping `llen = TEMP_BUF_SIZE - gopherState->len - 1`, permits llen == TEMP_BUF_SIZE - 1 (and the leftover path then raises llen to that value via `llen += gopherState->len`), so the terminator store at index llen+1 == TEMP_BUF_SIZE is an out-of-bounds stack write (memory corruption). The same misplaced terminator also leaves line[llen] stale, splicing residue of previous lines into parsed strings. Additionally, the gopher-server-controlled `host` field is interpolated unescaped into client-facing HTML at the standard-link and WWW-link sinks (CWE-79), unlike the telnet branches which escape it.

evidence.reason: Off-by-one out-of-bounds write (CWE-787, root cause CWE-119 boundary error): the terminator is stored at line[llen + 1] although llen bytes were just memcpy'd into the TEMP_BUF_SIZE array `line`, and llen can equal TEMP_BUF_SIZE - 1 (either directly from a server line of that length, or after `llen += gopherState->len` on the leftover path). Trigger instantiated: a gopher server (untrusted origin supplying inbuf/len) sends a DIR/CSO line of exactly TEMP_BUF_SIZE - 1 bytes; the clamp at lines 75-78 does not fire (gopherState->len + llen == TEMP_BUF_SIZE - 1 < TEMP_BUF_SIZE), so line[TEMP_BUF_SIZE] is written one past the buffer — memory corruption of adjacent stack storage. The same store also misplaces the NUL (should be line[llen]), leaving a stale byte spliced into the parsed line.

Origin of the faulty value: this is the only bound on llen, but it clamps to TEMP_BUF_SIZE - gopherState->len - 1 (maximum llen = TEMP_BUF_SIZE - 1) and is evaluated before `llen += gopherState->len` at line 91. It therefore bounds the memcpy length, not the index llen + 1 used at line 96 — at exactly-the-limit values (gopherState->len + llen == TEMP_BUF_SIZE - 1) the guard passes and the one-past-end write proceeds.

Secondary confirmed defect — HTML injection (CWE-79): `host` is carved directly from the attacker-controlled gopher server line (lines 122-127) and interpolated into the client-facing HREF attribute without html_quote/rfc1738 escaping, unlike the telnet branches (lines 220/224) which escape it. A server-supplied host containing "> and script markup breaks out of the attribute and is emitted to the client via entry->append(outbuf.rawContent(), ...) at line 327.

assumptions: LOCAL_ARRAY(char, line, TEMP_BUF_SIZE) is assumed to allocate exactly TEMP_BUF_SIZE bytes on the stack (macro definition not in given code); the off-by-one holds for any TEMP_BUF_SIZE >= 2.
TEMP_BUF_SIZE's numeric value (4096 in Squid) is not shown; the concrete simulation uses 4096 but the defect is size-independent.
gopherState->buf is assumed to be TEMP_BUF_SIZE bytes (declaration not shown); the code's own clamp keeps gopherState->len + llen <= TEMP_BUF_SIZE - 1 there.
Initial gopherState->len is assumed < TEMP_BUF_SIZE; every subsequent value is produced by this code under its own clamp (lines 77, 83-84, 92).

inbuf/len are assumed to carry the gopher server's response chunk (network origin) — no in-code statement validates or transforms them before the loop, so they are treated as attacker-data per discipline 3.
limitations: atoi(s_code)/atoi(s_recno) NULL dereference (lines 269/271) was not reachable: strtok is monotonic and the guard `if (!result) break;` at line 266 precedes the atoi calls, so s_code or s_recno NULL implies result NULL and the break fires first.

The read at line 149 (`port[2]`) and strchr(host, '\r') can index up to line[llen+2] when the stale byte at line[llen] is a TAB; this requires a prior longer line in the same buffer, is a consequence of the confirmed misplaced terminator, and was folded into the primary finding rather than reported separately.
Outbuf growth is bounded by input length (each iteration consumes at least one input byte via pos = lpos or breaks), so no attacker-scalable amplification was found.

verdict.summary: nft_flow_rule_create derives num_actions from the attacker-influenced rule expression list and uses it to size the offload structure. Within the given code, every sink is guarded: zero action count is rejected by a quoted check, allocation failures are checked, every error goto sets err before ERR_PTR(err), kfree(ctx) occurs once after its last use, and the counting loop and offload loop traverse the identical expression set under identical conditions, so count and consumption are internally consistent in the shown statements. The only security-relevant hypothesis — a heap overflow if a not-shown offload callback or nft_flow_rule_transfer_vlan adds more actions than num_actions — cannot be instantiated from this code, since no shown statement writes into the action array and the over-add precondition lives entirely in code not given.

assumptions: expr->ops points to kernel-registered expression ops with a valid positive size and consistent offload_flags; ops is populated by rule-construction code not shown and cannot be quoted here.

nft_flow_rule_alloc(num_actions) sizes the action array from num_actions and returns NULL on failure; its implementation is not shown, but its return value is checked with 'if (!flow) return ERR_PTR(-ENOMEM);'.
kfree(NULL) is a no-op (kernel contract), relied on for the kzalloc(ctx) failure path where err_out does 'kfree(ctx);' with ctx == NULL.
kzalloc zeroes the allocation, so ctx->dep.l3num is 0 unless a not-shown offload callback sets it; the given code never reads it before kzalloc completes.

The rule object is assumed reachable via the nftables configuration path (netlink); the privilege required to submit rules is a deployment fact that is not quotable from this code and was not used to demote any candidate.
limitations: Candidate (a) sizing mismatch: if any expression whose offload callback runs in 'err = expr->ops->offload(ctx, flow, expr);' adds more than one action, or if 'nft_flow_rule_transfer_vlan(ctx, flow);' or a non-ACTION-flagged expression adds entries to flow->rule->action.array, the array sized by 'flow = nft_flow_rule_alloc(num_actions);' would overflow (potential CWE-131/CWE-787). All action-array writes occur in code not given; the trigger precondition (an over-adding callee) is neither an input of this code's surface nor a state produced by statements in this code, so the impact is not instantiated.

Candidate (b) signed overflow of num_actions (CWE-190) requires a single rule containing at least 2^31 ACTION-flagged expressions (a multi-gigabyte rule object); no shown statement can construct or accept such an object, and even after wrap the value flows into nft_flow_rule_alloc where the quoted 'if (!flow) return ERR_PTR(-ENOMEM);' catches the allocation failure.

Candidate (e) non-termination of either walk loop requires an expr with ops->size == 0; ops content is set by not-shown rule-init code and cannot be produced by any statement in this code, so the trigger is speculative.

verdict.summary: squashfs_opendir reads directory entries from the global directory_table at an offset 'bytes' whose bound is computed solely from attacker-controlled inode fields. After the sentinel check on lookup_entry, 'bytes += (*i)->offset' and 'size = (*i)->data + bytes - 3' add unvalidated image values, and the loop 'while(bytes < size)' bounds 'bytes' only by that attacker-derived size, never by the extent of directory_table. A crafted filesystem with an inflated directory-size field drives 'directory_table + bytes' past the end of the table buffer in SQUASHFS_SWAP_DIR_HEADER, SQUASHFS_SWAP_DIR_ENTRY, and memcpy, yielding a scalable out-of-bounds heap read whose contents are copied into filenames (dire->name, then strcpy into dir->dirs[].name and printed), i.e. information disclosure and crash/DoS during listing/extraction.

evidence.snippet: *i = read_inode(block_start, offset);
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted values: read_inode parses the attacker-supplied filesystem image; the resulting inode fields (*i)->offset and (*i)->data (consumed at lines 48-49) are attacker-crafted content with no documented contract in this code.

Root cause and first sink: after the only check on bytes ('if(bytes == -1)', line 44, which tests only lookup_entry's failure sentinel), bytes is advanced by the unvalidated inode offset and the loop is bounded by size, itself computed from the attacker-controlled inode data field. No statement compares bytes to the size of directory_table, so SQUASHFS_SWAP_DIR_HEADER(directory_table + bytes, &dirh) reads out of bounds once bytes exceeds the table's finite extent.

Secondary OOB read sink on the same unbounded index: memcpy reads dire->size + 1 bytes from directory_table + bytes, which the loop (line 51) can drive past the end of the directory table; the out-of-bounds bytes are then surfaced as directory entry names (strcpy into dir->dirs[dir->dir_count].name at line 89 and TRACE output), giving information disclosure in addition to crash/DoS.

assumptions: The declarations of struct squashfs_dir_entry (type/width of the 'size' field), struct squashfs_dir_header, SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN, SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT, and DIR_ENT_SIZE are not in the given code; the analysis of the dire->size guard (line 71) assumes size is an unsigned field whose maximum value is below SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN, as in upstream squashfs_fs.h.

The allocation and extent of the global directory_table buffer are not shown; it is necessarily finite (loaded from the image), which is all the finding requires — no assumption about its exact size is used to dismiss or promote candidates.
read_inode's failure behavior (whether it can return NULL or exit) is not shown; (*i) is dereferenced unguarded at line 25, but the trigger depends on a not-shown callee.
limitations: Candidate C2 (signed dire->size passing the check 'dire->size >= SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN' with a negative value, producing a huge memcpy length) is speculative: the struct field's signedness/width is not declared in the given code, so the trigger precondition could not be instantiated from quoted statements.
Candidate C4 (NULL dereference of *i if read_inode can fail) is speculative: it requires callee behavior not shown in this code.

Candidate C5 (strcpy at line 89 overflowing dir_ent.name) is not confirmable: the destination struct's field size is not shown, and the source length is bounded to at most SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN characters plus NUL by the guards at lines 71 and 78.

verdict.summary: The EVT_TRANSACTION parser never bounds the attacker-controlled AID length before copying: skb->data[1] (0-255) is used directly as the memcpy length into an allocation sized only skb->len - 2 bytes, and the minimum-length guard uses '&&' instead of '||' so a 2-byte frame with tag 0x81 bypasses it entirely (skb->len - 2 = 0 allocation via devm_kzalloc(0)). The memcpy at the sink therefore writes up to 255 attacker-supplied bytes past a heap allocation of at most skb->len - 2 (as little as 0-5 bytes) and reads out of bounds from the skb; the same defect repeats for params_len. Heap buffer overflow in kernel context with attacker-controlled length and content.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the validation guard uses '&&' so a frame is rejected only when it is BOTH too short AND mis-tagged; a 2-byte frame starting with tag 0x81 (or a len==7 frame) passes, and no statement anywhere bounds aid_len against skb->len or against the allocation. The allocation is sized skb->len - 2 (0 bytes when skb->len == 2, and devm_kzalloc(0) returns non-NULL ZERO_SIZE_PTR so the !transaction check passes), then aid_len is loaded unvalidated from skb->data[1] (0-255) and used as the memcpy length into that undersized allocation: out-of-bounds heap write with attacker-controlled length and content, plus out-of-bounds read of the skb. Trigger fully instantiated: attacker-supplied frame {0x81, 0xFF} or len=7 frame {0x81, 0xFF, ...} reaches the memcpy with aid_len=255 vs a 0/5-byte allocation.

Second instance of the same unvalidated-length overflow: params_len is read from skb->data[aid_len + 3] (itself an unbounded OOB read index up to 258 into a possibly 2-byte skb) and used as the memcpy length into the same skb->len - 2 sized allocation, again with no bound check anywhere on any path.

assumptions: NFC_MIN_AID_LENGTH, NFC_EVT_TRANSACTION_AID_TAG (0x81), and NFC_EVT_TRANSACTION_PARAMS_TAG (0x82) are constants not defined in the given snippet; their values are taken from the kernel headers and the in-code spec comment (AID 5 to 16, PARAMETERS 0 to 255).

struct nfc_evt_transaction layout (aid_len/aid/params_len/params) is not shown in the given code; the OOB-write conclusion does not depend on it because the entire allocation is only skb->len - 2 bytes while the copy length is up to 255.

skb originates from the HCI/NFC device event pipeline (attacker-influenced secure-element frame per the quoted ETSI 102 622 comment); no caller-side validation of frame contents is quotable in this code, so this function is treated as the last line of defense.
limitations: skb->data[0] is read at line 23 before any check that skb->len >= 1; with a zero-length skb this is an OOB read, subsumed by the primary bounds defect.

transaction is devm_kzalloc'd per event and never freed on this path (only freed at device unbind), so repeated EVT_TRANSACTION events cause unbounded devm allocation accumulation (resource retention proportional to attacker event count); recorded as a secondary concern, not the primary finding.
The -EPROTO early returns at lines 24 and 37 skip kfree_skb(skb); whether skb ownership passes to the caller on error is not determinable from this code alone.
Real-kernel history: this exact code was later fixed by changing '&&' to '||' and adding aid_len/params_len bounds checks plus a sized allocation, consistent with the analysis above.

verdict.summary: All writes into the MAXPATHL-sized NameBuff are guarded by quotable bounds: the ' ' append is gated by 'len < MAXPATHL - 1', each vim_snprintf uses a constant format with size MAXPATHL - len (>= 1 by induction since len is re-derived via STRLEN after every append), the truncation writes '*p = <' only at in-bounds offsets (i > 0 / len - (this_ru_col - 1) with this_ru_col >= 2 enforced by the earlier 'if (this_ru_col <= 1)' branch), and len <= this_ru_col - 1 holds in every arm before screen_fill. No instantiated memory-safety, injection, or fail-open defect exists in this function.

assumptions: get_trans_bufname() and get_keymap_str() leave NameBuff NUL-terminated within MAXPATHL bytes — the producing statements are in callees not shown; STRLEN(p) at entry and every 'len += (int)STRLEN(p + len)' depend on this contract.

(*mb_ptr2len) returns at least 1 per call, so the mbyte scan loop 'for (i = 0; p[i] != NUL && clen >= this_ru_col - 1; i += (*mb_ptr2len)(p + i))' advances and terminates within the string; the advancing expression is callee code.
screen_puts, screen_fill, and screen_putchar clip row/column arguments to the physical screen dimensions — clipping happens inside callees not shown.

ru_col, Columns, and window geometry fields (w_width, w_wincol, w_status_height, w_vsep_width) are internal redraw/config state not shown to be attacker-settable at arbitrary scale; the int arithmetic 'ru_col - (Columns - wp->w_width)' cannot be shown to reach overflow scale from statements in this code.
limitations: Speculative: STRLEN overread if get_trans_bufname ever produced a non-NUL-terminated NameBuff; no statement in this code can produce that value, and the callee is not shown.

Speculative: the mbyte truncation 'p = p + i - 1; *p = '<';' replaces the last byte of a multibyte character, yielding an invalid byte sequence; this is in-bounds and only flows to display (screen_puts), with no memory-safety or security-state consequence in this code.

Speculative: a 1-byte overread inside (*mb_ptr2len)(p + i) if a multi-byte lead byte sat at index MAXPATHL-2 with the string NUL at MAXPATHL-1; per UTF-8/DBCS ptr2len semantics (callee code) a NUL is not a trail byte, so the trigger cannot be instantiated here.

Screen-column arithmetic assumes screen_fill tolerates start >= end (this_ru_col <= 1 arm yields endcol = this_ru_col + w_wincol <= 1 + w_wincol <= start); the loop is inside the callee and no write occurs in this code on that path.

verdict.summary: parseDragons allocates b = malloc(size) and takes ownership of file_name, but both `if (available != size) { ... return NULL; }` error paths (after the initial read and after the off-8 retry read) return without freeing them; the only `free (b)` is on the fall-through path. The retry read is invoked at `off - 8` with no check that off >= 8 (the only offset guard, `if (off >= size)`, does not reject off < 0 or off < 8), so an attacker-controlled offset below 8 makes the retry read fail and instantiates the leak of an attacker-sized allocation (size = buffer size - off, only bounded below by the `size < 32` check).

evidence.reason: Memory leak (CWE-401): after `ut8 *b = malloc (size);` the error branch `if (available != size) { eprintf (...); return NULL; }` returns without freeing b (or the R_OWN file_name). No free, cleanup label, or deallocation exists on this path; the only `free (b)` (line 71) is bypassed by this early return. Instantiated trigger: off < 0 passes the sole guard `if (off >= size)` (negative never >= size), inflates size via `size -= off`, malloc succeeds, and the read at the invalid address returns short, reaching this leaking return with attacker-controlled magnitude (size derived from file size).

Second leak path: when the attacker-controlled file content makes magicCombo != 2, the code re-reads at `off - 8` with no check that off >= 8. Simulated trigger: off = 0, 64-byte file without the magic at b[0..3] or b[8..11]: first read succeeds (available == 64), magicCombo stays 0, retry reads at 0 - 8 = -8, the read returns != size, and `return NULL` leaks b (malloc'd at line 14) and file_name. Neither `free` nor any cleanup exists inside this branch.

Origin of the unvalidated value enabling the trigger: the only bound on `off` is `off >= size`, which tests only the upper boundary. Edge values off = 0..7 and off < 0 all pass, allowing `size -= off` to enlarge size past the buffer (negative off) and allowing the later `off - 8` retry (line 55) to go negative. No statement in this code checks off >= 0 or off >= 8.

assumptions: The behavior of r_buf_read_at and r_coresym_cache_element_new (both outside the given code) is unknown; this analysis assumes only what the given statements enforce, i.e., that a failed/short read yields available != size and the shown error branches run.

`off` is a parameter of a static helper whose caller is not shown; since no statement in the given code bounds off to >= 8 or >= 0, it is treated as attacker-data (file-derived offset) rather than a contract value.

The process is assumed to be capable of parsing more than one attacker-supplied file over its lifetime for the leak to accumulate; per-invocation the leak is bounded by the attacker-controlled file size.
limitations: Negative offset passed to callee: `r_buf_read_at (buf, off - 8, b, size)` with off < 8 (or the initial read with off < 0) passes a sign-wrapped address and an int-truncated length into r_buf_read_at; the harmful dereference, if any, occurs entirely inside the not-shown callee, so its impact chain is not instantiated here (recorded, not counted).

st64 size -> int length truncation for buffers > INT_MAX: the `available != size` comparison (available <= INT_MAX < size) always rejects before b's contents are used, so no in-function out-of-bounds use results; requires a >2GB buffer.

Fail-open parsing: the `else { eprintf ("... invalid magic retry ..."); }` branch continues to r_coresym_cache_element_new despite failed magic validation; the consequence depends on the not-shown callee and is not a security-state presentation in this code.
The leak of the R_OWN file_name on every early return is the same CWE-401 class as the primary finding and is covered by it.

verdict.summary: nft_flow_rule_create consumes an attacker-influenced nftables rule, but every sink inside this function is guarded in execution order: num_actions == 0 is rejected before allocation, flow and ctx allocation failures are checked, all goto err_out paths assign err before ERR_PTR(err), and err_out is reachable only after flow is known non-NULL, so there is no uninitialized read, NULL deref, double free, or use-after-free in the given code. The remaining theoretical defect — an overflow of the action array sized by num_actions if an offload callback appends more actions than the counting loop counted, or a traversal of a malformed rule blob — cannot be instantiated or its impact located within the given code: the array writes happen inside expr->ops->offload callbacks and the blob consistency is enforced by ruleset validation code, neither of which is shown. Those are recorded as limitations, not findings.

assumptions: expr->ops points to a valid registered nft_expr_ops and the rule blob is internally consistent; this is enforced by nftables ruleset validation at rule insertion, which is not shown and cannot be quoted from the given code.
nft_expr_first/nft_expr_more/nft_expr_next iterate the rule blob safely; their bodies are not shown.
nft_flow_rule_alloc(num_actions) allocates an action array sized by num_actions, and nft_flow_rule_destroy/nft_flow_rule_transfer_vlan behave consistently with it; their bodies are not shown.
expr->ops->offload and expr->ops->offload_action callbacks append at most one action per expression counted by the first loop; this contract is not quotable from the given code.
The rule is not concurrently freed while this function runs (ruleset locking held by the caller); the caller is not shown.
limitations: Action-array sizing mismatch (CWE-131/CWE-787 candidate): the array is sized by num_actions from the first loop, while writes occur inside expr->ops->offload callbacks and nft_flow_rule_transfer_vlan in the second loop. If any callback appended an action for an expression whose offload_action returned false (or appended more than one action), an out-of-bounds write would occur — but both the capacity semantics of nft_flow_rule_alloc and the write itself are in code not given, so the impact chain could not be instantiated here.
num_actions integer overflow (CWE-190 candidate): would require a rule blob with more than INT_MAX expressions; no shown statement can produce such a blob, so the trigger is speculative.
Malformed rule blob traversal (expr->ops deref candidate): triggering requires bypassing the not-shown rule validation/parse path; speculative.
Race on the rule's lifetime during the two traversal loops: no two ordered interleavable operations are exhibitible in the given code; speculative.

verdict.summary: expand_case_fold_string computes len = enclen(reg->enc, p) from the current byte of the pattern-derived string node without ever checking p + len <= end, then calls onig_node_str_cat(snode, p, p + len). For a multibyte encoding, a truncated lead byte as the final byte of the node's string makes enclen return 2-6 while fewer bytes remain, so the copy reads past sn->end (heap out-of-bounds read; OOB bytes are also copied into the compiled AST, and the same unchecked len is passed to expand_case_fold_string_alt). No bounds check, clamp, or error arm exists anywhere on the path, so an attacker who supplies a regex pattern ending in an incomplete multibyte sequence to a case-insensitive compile can read beyond the string-node buffer and crash/corrupt the compiling process.

evidence.reason: len is derived solely from the byte at p via enclen(reg->enc, p) and is never bounded against end. When p is at end-1 holding a multibyte lead byte (e.g. 0xF0 in UTF-8 gives len=4), onig_node_str_cat(snode, p, p + len) copies bytes past sn->end, reading out of bounds from the heap-allocated string node buffer. Trigger: attacker-supplied regex pattern whose string node ends with a truncated multibyte sequence, compiled with case folding under a multibyte encoding. The only loop guard, while (p < end), admits p = end-1 and no check, clamp, or error arm between line 29 and the sink exists (the same unchecked len is also passed to expand_case_fold_string_alt at line 66).

Origin of the tainted data: the byte range [sn->s, sn->end) is the pattern text carried in the parsed string node, and end is the buffer limit. The code only checks start >= end and p < end; it never establishes that end falls on a character boundary of reg->enc, so a node whose last character is truncated by end leaves enclen's result unbounded for the final iteration.

assumptions: The string node passed via node is assumed to be non-NULL and to contain pattern bytes; the function quotes no NULL or content contract, and STR_(node) dereferences it immediately.

Construction of the string node from the raw pattern is performed by the parser, which is not shown; whether the parser can place a truncated multibyte sequence at a node's end is not provable from the given code. Per guard anchoring this unquotable contract was not used to dismiss the candidate, but it lowers confidence.

expand_case_fold_string_alt, onig_node_str_cat, enclen, and ONIGENC_GET_CASE_FOLD_CODES_BY_STR are external to the given code; their internal behavior (e.g., enclen table values per encoding) is assumed from standard multibyte encoding semantics.

The deployment context (regex library embedded in a process compiling user-supplied patterns) is an assumption; the verdict rests on the fact that the node's byte content and encoding selection are attacker-influenced inputs consumed at this code's own sinks.
limitations: NULL dereference of node or reg (lines 9, 22) could not be instantiated: no attacker-data path in this code produces NULL and the caller is the internal compiler; treated as a contract question, not a finding.

Potential UAF/double-free around the ending swap_node(node, top_root) / onig_node_free(top_root) and the root = NODE_CAR(prev_node) reassignment could not be instantiated without the semantics of expand_case_fold_string_alt and NODE_CAR, which are not given.
alt_num int overflow is bounded by the THRESHOLD_CASE_FOLD_ALT_FOR_EXPANSION break and is not reachable.
Error paths (mem_err/err) leak prev_node/snode when top_root is NULL; memory leak with no attacker-scalable security effect.

If the unshown parser strictly rejects truncated multibyte sequences for every encoding, C1 would not be triggerable; no statement in the given code enforces this, so it is recorded as an assumption rather than a dismissal.

verdict.summary: The ST21NFCA_EVT_TRANSACTION handler allocates only skb->len - 2 bytes for a struct nfc_evt_transaction but then writes the full struct and a flexible params array through that pointer. The entry guard uses && instead of ||, admitting short frames; the params_len bound at line 47 unsigned-underflows when skb->len - 2 < sizeof(struct nfc_evt_transaction), so the check passes for any params_len. memcpy(transaction->params, skb->data + aid_len + 4, params_len) then writes up to 255 attacker-controlled bytes past the undersized heap allocation (and reads out of bounds from the skb), a heap buffer overflow.

evidence.reason: Sink: memcpy of attacker-controlled params_len (up to 255) into transaction->params of an allocation of only skb->len - 2 bytes. The bound at line 47 unsigned-underflows to ~0xFFFFFFE8 whenever skb->len - 2 < sizeof(struct nfc_evt_transaction), so the check passes and the memcpy overflows the heap allocation. Trigger: skb->len=10, data={0x81,0x00,0x82,0xFF,...} passes the line-22 guard, allocates 8 bytes, aid_len=0 passes line 33, tag 0x82 passes line 40, params_len=255 passes the underflowed line-47 check, and line 50 writes 255 bytes into the 8-byte allocation.

Origin of the faulty value: the entry-length guard joins its conditions with && instead of ||, so any frame whose first byte is the AID tag (0x81) bypasses the minimum-length check regardless of skb->len. The subsequent allocation is sized skb->len - 2 with no check that it is at least sizeof(struct nfc_evt_transaction), so the struct writes (aid_len at line 30, aid at line 36, params_len at line 44) and the params memcpy at line 50 all operate on an undersized heap buffer.

assumptions: struct nfc_evt_transaction and NFC_MIN_AID_LENGTH are not defined in the given code; the analysis assumes the struct's fixed members (aid_len, aid[], params_len, params[] flexible array) exceed skb->len - 2 for small skb->len. The trigger is robust to any plausible layout because the allocation is exactly skb->len - 2 bytes while the code writes struct fields and a params_len-sized tail into it.

skb content arrives from the NFC controller/secure element over HCI and is treated as attacker-data per the data-origin model; no caller validation of skb exists in the given code (nothing asserts skb->len or contents).
devm_kzalloc with size 0 (skb->len == 2) returns a non-NULL ZERO_SIZE_PTR, so the !transaction check at line 27 would not reject it; this path also permits writes past a zero-sized allocation.
limitations: skb->data[1], skb->data[aid_len+2], skb->data[aid_len+3] and the memcpy sources can read past skb->len (CWE-125); these OOB reads are part of the same malformed-frame trigger and are not listed as separate CWEs.

The NULL dereference of hdev->ndev (lines 5, 53) and the devm-managed lifetime of transaction relative to nfc_se_transaction's later use were not analyzed further because the callee is not shown and the primary heap-overflow finding is fully instantiated.

verdict.summary: The function consumes only a driver-internal handle (priv) and its registration-time state. Every numeric sink is guarded in execution order (gpio_is_valid before gpio_free, rejecting negative and out-of-range values including the one-past-limit edge), the ndev snapshot at entry prevents a visible use-after-free ordering defect, and the free sequence unregister->free_device->kfree is standard. The remaining candidates — NULL priv/ndev/nfc_dev dereference, a pending firmware-download worker surviving nfcmrvl_fw_dnld_deinit and touching freed priv, GPIO ownership mismatch on reset_n_io, and TOCTOU on fw_download_in_progress — all require either a caller contract violation or defects inside callees (nfcmrvl_fw_dnld_abort/deinit, nci_unregister_device) or registration code not given, whose statements cannot be quoted; none can be triggered by attacker-controlled data reaching any statement in this code.

assumptions: priv is the handle returned by this driver's registration path and is not attacker-writable; no statement in the given code produces or mutates it.
priv->ndev and ndev->nfc_dev are set at registration time by code not shown; no runtime mutation path is exhibited.
priv->config.reset_n_io is copied from device-tree/module configuration at registration and no lower-privileged runtime write path appears in the given code.
gpio_is_valid is assumed to be the kernel's standard range check (rejects negative and >= ARCH_NR_GPIOS); its implementation is not shown.
limitations: NULL dereference candidates: priv, priv->ndev and priv->ndev->nfc_dev are dereferenced at lines 3 and 5 with no NULL guard in this code; a trigger requires the caller to pass a NULL/invalid handle, which no statement in this code makes attacker-controllable — speculative.

Use-after-free candidate: if nfcmrvl_fw_dnld_deinit (line 8) does not flush a pending firmware-download worker, that worker could touch priv after kfree(priv) (line 15) — the defect and impact would be entirely inside the not-shown callee/worker; not instantiable from the given statements.

GPIO edge: reset_n_io == 0 passes gpio_is_valid; if the registration path (not shown) treats 0 as 'unset' or never requests GPIO 0, gpio_free(0) would free an unrequested GPIO — the producing registration code is not given, so this remains unprovable here.
TOCTOU on fw_download_in_progress between the line-5 check and later frees requires a concurrent mutation path not exhibited as two ordered operations in this code.
Ordering of gpio_free (line 11) before nci_unregister_device (line 13) could matter if unregister-time callbacks use the reset GPIO; no such callback is shown.

verdict.summary: FindEmptyObjectSlot only consumes internally produced values: a loop counter bounded by the quoted loop guard 'for(i = 0; i < MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS; i++)' and an optional OUT pointer guarded by the quoted 'if(handle)' before the sole write. No attacker-controlled data reaches any memory, index, size, or injection sink in this function. Remaining concerns (handle arithmetic wrap at MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS >= 2^31, concurrent double-allocation of a slot, and stale non-attribute fields in a recycled OBJECT) are speculative or have impact chains that break in caller code not given.

assumptions: The global array s_objects is declared with exactly MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS elements; its declaration is not in the given code, so the loop bound's correspondence to the array size cannot be quoted from the given snippet (it is a compile-time internal declaration, not attacker-influenced).
MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS is a small compile-time constant (far below 2^31), so 'i + TRANSIENT_FIRST' cannot wrap; neither constant's definition is shown in the given code.

Execution is single-threaded; the code contains no locking or reentrancy points, so the slot-allocation TOCTOU (occupied flag checked here but set by the caller after return) cannot be triggered within this code.
limitations: Integer wrap of 'i + TRANSIENT_FIRST' would require MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS near 2^31; no statement in this code can drive i there and no external input touches i, so the trigger is not instantiable here.

In a concurrent environment, two callers could both pass 'occupied == CLEAR' and receive the same slot before either caller marks it occupied; the interleaving window cannot be exhibited as two ordered operations in the given code.

The function zeroes only OBJECT_ATTRIBUTES, not the whole OBJECT, so a recycled slot retains stale non-attribute content (potentially prior sensitive material); any disclosure would occur only if caller code (not given) reads those fields before initializing them.

verdict.summary: The attacker-data paths in this code (directory-entry names combined into a fixed MAXPATHLEN buffer, and the dynamic filearr growth) are correctly guarded: snprintf's negative sentinel is checked before any use of mflen, and the ternary clamp '(mflen > sizeof(mfn) - 1)? sizeof(mfn) - 1: mflen' bounds the estrndup copy length for every boundary value (0, exactly-at-limit, one-past, fully truncated), preventing the historical out-of-bounds read of the unclamped would-be length. The 'if (files >= maxfiles)' growth check runs immediately before 'filearr[files++]' on every iteration with no bypassing branch. Remaining candidates (uint32_t i wrap against size_t files requiring 2^32 directory entries and multi-hundred-GiB allocations; NULL mset[j].me[i].mp produced by the not-shown load_1; set_text_binary non-advance) could not be instantiated as triggers in this code and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: PHP allocator semantics: ecalloc/erealloc/estrndup — erealloc failure in PHP bails the process rather than returning NULL; estrndup(s, len) allocates len+1 and copies at most len bytes. These are runtime-library behaviors not quotable from the given code.
php_stream_dirent.d.d_name is a NUL-terminated string of at most MAXPATHLEN-1 characters filled by php_stream_readdir; its struct definition is not shown.

Callees load_1, set_text_binary, set_last_default, coalesce_entries, magic_entry_free, cmpstrp, and file_oomem are not shown; their internal behavior is assumed benign for the values this code passes.
Whether an attacker can populate the magic-file directory (fn) is a deployment question not decidable from the code; the analysis treated d.d_name as attacker-data regardless.
limitations: Width confusion: 'for (i = 0; i < files; i++)' compares uint32_t i against size_t files; if files reached UINT32_MAX+1 the loop restarts and efree(filearr[i]) runs twice (double-free/UAF). Trigger not instantiated: it requires 2^32 regular files in the magic directory, ~32 GiB of pointer-array allocation and >=2^32 estrndup strings (hundreds of GiB) to succeed first — a scale this code's own erealloc calls cannot reach and no shown statement can produce.

NULL dereference risk: 'mset[j].me[i].mp->cont_level' dereferences mp without any quotable validation; mp is populated solely by the not-shown load_1. If load_1 could record an entry with mp == NULL within count, this line would crash. The precondition ('load_1 never leaves me[i].mp NULL within count') cannot be verified or instantiated from the given code.

Potential non-termination: in 'i = set_text_binary(ms, mset[j].me, mset[j].count, i);' the loop only advances i when cont_level != 0; if set_text_binary (not shown) returns its index argument unchanged, the loop spins forever. The callee body is not given, so the trigger is speculative.
size_t overflow in 'maxfiles = (maxfiles + 1) * 2' wraps only at ~2^62 entries — unreachable scale, speculative.

TOCTOU between php_sys_stat(fn)/php_stream_opendir/stat(mfn) and load_1: a party able to modify the magic directory between calls could swap entries, but such a party already controls the magic files' contents, so no privilege boundary is crossed.

Truncation side effect: when snprintf truncates, the clamped mfn is stat'ed and loaded as a shorter path, potentially a different file than the full entry name — no memory-safety or authorization impact beyond what the directory-writer already controls.

Memory leaks on the 'goto out' error paths inside the readdir loop (already-stored filearr entries and the snprintf-failure path's prior filearr are not freed) — availability-neutral resource leak with no attacker-scalable security impact shown.

verdict.summary: In mobi_parse_index_entry, the control_bytes pointer is advanced once per TAGX tag with control_byte == 1 with no bound against tagx->control_byte_count or the buffer end, and is then dereferenced (control_bytes[0]). Because tagx->tags_count and each tag's control_byte flag are attacker-controlled file content, a crafted MOBI file can walk control_bytes past the end of the record buffer and perform an out-of-bounds heap read whose value feeds parsing control flow.

evidence.reason: Root cause / sink: the loop increments control_bytes once for every tag with control_byte == 1 (bounded only by attacker-controlled tagx->tags_count, independent of tagx->control_byte_count and of the bytes remaining in the buffer) and then dereferences control_bytes[0]. With a TAGX record containing more control_byte tags than control bytes available past buf->offset near the end of the record buffer, control_bytes[0] reads past the end of the buffer allocation (heap out-of-bounds read), and the value read flows into value/value_count and downstream parsing decisions.

evidence.snippet:
control_bytes = buf->data + buf->offset;
    mobi_buffer_seek(buf, (int) tagx->control_byte_count);
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted pointer: control_bytes is derived from the buffer position after the label; the only related statement, the seek of control_byte_count bytes, moves the buffer cursor (return unchecked) and never bounds the control_bytes pointer, which is subsequently advanced unboundedly inside the tag loop.

assumptions: idxt.offsets, tagx->tags[], ordt, and buf contents originate from parsing an untrusted MOBI file; the parsing code itself is not shown.

The element type of idxt.offsets, the value of INDX_LABEL_SIZEMAX, the value of MOBI_NOTSET, and the allocation semantics of buf->data are not defined in the given code; analysis assumes the conventional libmobi definitions (uint32_t offsets, INDX_LABEL_SIZEMAX >= 256, buf->data a heap buffer of at least buf->maxlen bytes).

Behavior of mobi_buffer_setpos, mobi_buffer_seek, mobi_buffer_get8, mobi_buffer_get_varlen, mobi_getstring_ordt, and mobi_indx_get_label (bounds enforcement, error flags, return ranges, NUL-termination of text) is not shown and is treated as unknown, not as guaranteed.
limitations: idxt.offsets[curr_number + 1] (line 7) is indexed without any in-function bound on curr_number; the calling loop is not given, so the off-by-one/OOB-read trigger on the offsets array could not be instantiated.
