verdict.summary: In the IRC 352 (WHO reply) handler, arg_start is set to 9 when argv[8] equals "*", but argv[arg_start][0] is dereferenced without verifying that argc exceeds arg_start. With argc exactly 9 (satisfying the only guards, argc > 8), argv[9] is read one past the last valid argument and dereferenced, causing a NULL/out-of-bounds read and process crash from a single attacker-controlled IRC message (remote denial of service). The argc > arg_start checks that do exist appear only after the dereference and never guard it.

evidence.reason: Root cause and sink: arg_start becomes 9 whenever argv[8] is "*" (line 20), but the only size guards in effect are `if (argc > 8)` (line 18), which permits argc == 9. Line 21 then reads and dereferences argv[9] — one past the last valid argument index (argc-1 = 8) — with no `argc > arg_start` check on any path. Trigger: a 352 message with argc == 9 and argv[8] == "*" passes MIN_ARGS(5) (9>=5), passes `if (argc < 8)` (9<8 false), enters the `argc > 8` branch, sets arg_start = 9, and crashes at `argv[arg_start][0]`. This is an out-of-bounds read / NULL-pointer dereference remotely triggerable by the IRC server.

evidence.snippet:
pos_hopcount = (argc > arg_start) ? argv[arg_start] + 1 : NULL;
            pos_realname = (argc > arg_start + 1) ? argv_eol[arg_start + 1] : NULL;
evidence.reason: Execution-order proof that the needed bound check exists only AFTER the defective use: these `argc > arg_start` checks are the fix form that should protect line 21, but they are inside the branch taken only after `argv[arg_start][0]` has already been dereferenced, so they arrive too late and never guard the first use. With argc == 9 and arg_start == 9, the process never survives to reach them.

assumptions: argv/argv_eol are constructed outside the given code (message splitting). If the splitter NULL-terminates the array, argv[9] is NULL and line 21 is a NULL dereference (CWE-476); if not, argv[9] is an out-of-bounds pointer read then dereference (CWE-125). Both behaviors crash the process at the same statement; the code's own argc accounting proves index 9 is past the valid argument range either way.
server, command, date, and server->cap_list are framework-supplied state; cap_list content is not treated as attacker-data for any sink in this analysis.
limitations: Integer overflow of `length = strlen (argv[4]) + 1 + strlen (argv[5]) + 1;` (line 45) requires more than INT_MAX total bytes across two message parameters; no statement in this code instantiates such input, so the trigger is speculative. malloc failure is handled by `if (str_host)` (line 46).
`argv[arg_start + 1] + 1` (line 30) can yield a one-past-NUL pointer if the argument is an empty string, but space-split arguments being empty is not demonstrable from this code — speculative.
Unchecked `strdup` result at line 66 can only set ptr_nick->realname to NULL, which is an accepted state elsewhere in the function — no security consequence.

verdict.summary: EC_GROUP_new_from_ecparameters, the intake point for attacker-supplied explicit EC domain parameters, validates every memory-safety-relevant value it consumes with checks that are quoted, positioned in execution order before the corresponding use, and correct at boundary values: fieldID/fieldType/union pointer NULL checks; a/b data NULL checks; GF2m field size check (field_bits > OPENSSL_ECC_MAX_FIELD_BITS); strict trinomial (m > tmp_long > 0) and pentanomial (m > k3 > k2 > k1 > 0) basis chains that also reject negative or zero m on every branch; prime-field negativity/zero and size checks; order negativity/zero and Hasse-bound checks; base-point data-NULL and zero-length checks before the data[0] read and oct2point; and exact-size checked allocation before the seed memcpy (with the assignment-before-check pattern preventing any dangling seed pointer on failure). Remaining candidates fail trigger instantiation or have impact chains that leave the given code: a missing seed->data NULL check is not triggerable by any value this code's own statements can produce (the DER decoder that could produce it is not given and no statement here constructs the structure); params==NULL requires an unquoted caller contract; an invalid point-conversion form (data[0]==0x00) can only manifest in serialization code not shown; unvalidated tiny fields/cofactors affect downstream cryptographic consumers not shown; and all allocations are linear in the attacker's own input with no amplification.

assumptions: The ASN.1 decoder that produces the ECPARAMETERS structure (not shown) is assumed to never deliver an ASN1_STRING with data == NULL and length > 0; this code checks data != NULL for curve->a, curve->b, and base, but NOT for curve->seed, so the memcpy seed sink lacks a quotable data-NULL guard in this code.
No NULL check on the params pointer itself exists in this code; it is assumed the (not-shown) internal caller never passes NULL, and no quotable contract in the given code documents this.

params->base->data[0] & ~0x01 can yield an invalid point_conversion_form_t (e.g., 0x00 for an identity-point encoding); it is assumed EC_POINT_oct2point and later serialization code (not given) reject or safely handle such forms.

Cofactor (params->cofactor) is not range-checked (may be negative, zero, or oversized) and no minimum field size is enforced; safe handling is assumed to occur in EC_GROUP_set_generator and downstream consumers, none of which are given.
OPENSSL_ECC_MAX_FIELD_BITS is assumed to be the small constant (661) it is defined as upstream; it is not defined in the given code.
limitations: Missing seed->data NULL check (memcpy(ret->seed, params->curve->seed->data, params->curve->seed->length)): the trigger precondition (data == NULL with length > 0) cannot be instantiated by any statement in this code, and the producing DER parser is not given, so it cannot be raised to a finding here; if the decoder or a programmatic caller can produce such a structure, this would be a NULL-dereference (CWE-476) crash.
params == NULL dereference at the first if-statement: trigger requires an unquoted caller contract; worst case a crash; not attacker-instantiable within the shown input surface.

Acceptance of tiny prime fields (e.g., 2-bit p) and unvalidated cofactors permits creation of cryptographically weak or mathematically invalid groups; the exploitation occurs in key-agreement/signature code not given, so the impact chain is not instantiated in this code.
An invalid conversion form 0x00 can be stored on the group when base encodes the identity point; any resulting mis-serialization occurs in code not shown.

Large (up to ~2 GB) attacker-chosen string lengths cause correspondingly large allocations, but they are linear in the attacker's own input size and freed on every path, so no amplification vulnerability is instantiated.

verdict.summary: This do_put() implementation contains verbatim, correctly positioned guards for every memory sink: the block-mode multiplication overflow check (count > (INT_MAX - (bd.startspaces + bd.endspaces)) / (yanklen + spaces)) and the single-line check (count > INT_MAX / yanklen) prevent integer overflow into alloc sizes; write totals were arithmetically verified to equal or fit the allocated buffers in every branch; y_size/y_array NULL-and-empty checks, the VIsual col > oldlen skip (which also catches the MAXCOL sentinel from getvpos failure), the y_current_used anti-UAF consistency check, the early u_save against autocommand invalidation, the len > 0 guard before mb_head_off, and refetching oldp after ml_append all close the historically exploitable paths in this function. No trigger for any candidate (overflow, truncation, OOB read/write, UAF, underflow) could be instantiated from this code's own data flow.

assumptions: alloc()/ALLOC_MULT return NULL on failure and allocate at least the requested size; ml_get/ml_get_curline return NUL-terminated lines and y_current->y_array entries are NUL-terminated (external contracts, not quotable here).

curwin->w_cursor.col/lnum lie within the current line/buffer and curbuf->b_visual endpooints lie within the buffer — a Vim-core maintained invariant; this code's own adjustments (col += bytelen under gchar_cursor() != NUL, the col > len clamp, adjust_cursor_eol()) preserve it for values derived here.

count is >= 1 from real callers; this is not quotable in the given code, but a negative count was separately shown to produce no out-of-bounds write (write totals still bounded by the same arithmetic).
getvcol/getvpos/mb_ptr2len/mb_head_off/lbr_chartabsize return values in range for their inputs (external callee contracts).
limitations: C3 (speculative): 'totlen + oldlen + 1' is int arithmetic that is theoretically UB when totlen is near INT_MAX and the line is large; the wrapped negative converts to a huge size_t so alloc fails and no write executes, and reaching it needs ~2GB line/register content — no undersized allocation is producible, so it is not a finding.
C4 (speculative): 'spaces = y_width + 1' truncates long to int; would need y_width > INT_MAX which no statement here can produce (virtual-column block widths are far below that scale).
C8/C5 (speculative): '--bd.textcol' underflow and negative tail-memmove size require vcol > col without the scan loop having advanced, which the loop conditions preclude.

Non-memory oddities (changed_lines() argument ranges, b_op_end.col = bd.textcol + totlen - 1 potential int overflow at extreme totlen) affect mark/redraw values only, with adjust_cursor_eol() and the col > len clamp correcting cursor state; no memory, injection, or authorization sink is involved.

The op's shape function enforces that epsilon and num_streams inputs are scalar tensors; enforcement is in op registration not shown, so scalar<float>()()/scalar<int64>()() CHECK behavior on non-scalar inputs is assumed unreachable.

verdict.summary: gen_assignment (mruby codegen) was analyzed for memory-safety, integer, stack-accounting, and injection defects. The node type from parsed AST data is handled by total switch statements with explicit error arms ("default: codegen_error(s, \"unknown lhs\");", "case NODE_NVAR: codegen_error(...)"). The argument counter n reaching bytecode operands is bounded to at most 15 on every path by quotable statements: "if (n < 0) { n = 15; push(); }", "n = 15;" (packing), and "if (n < 15) { n++; if (n == 15) {". Every pop_n/pop is matched on all simulated paths by the values produced by gen_values/gen_hash/codegen(rhs), including the boundary cases n=13/14 with and without keyword arguments (the limit "(tree->cdr->car)?13:14" ensures pop_n(14) is only reachable with 14 pushed positional values). No candidate's trigger and impact chain could be fully instantiated within the given code; remaining concerns depend on unshown callees (lv_idx, gen_values, gen_hash, genop_*) whose contracts cannot be quoted and are recorded as assumptions/limitations.

assumptions: codegen_error(s, ...) aborts compilation and does not return; if it returned, the second switch's default arm would re-error, so no unsafe use occurs either way, but non-return is not quotable from this code.
push()/pop()/pop_n(n)/cursp() are compile-time stack-pointer bookkeeping macros over s->sp; their exact definitions are not shown.

gen_values(s, tree->car, VAL, limit) returns the number of pushed values, never exceeding the passed limit (13 or 14), and a negative sentinel for variable length; contract not quotable here but its sentinel IS tested in this code ("if (n < 0)").
gen_hash(s, tree->cdr->car->cdr, VAL, 0) leaves a hash occupying one stack slot with the following push() accounting for it; semantics not shown.
lv_idx(s, sym) returns a valid stack slot index for a local variable or <=0 for an upvar; only the "> 0" half is checked in this code ("if (idx > 0)").

The AST nodes for the switched node types (NODE_CALL, NODE_SCALL, NODE_COLON2, NODE_MASGN, etc.) are well-formed cons cells produced by the parser; structural dereferences such as "tree = tree->cdr->cdr->car;" rely on this.
genop_2/genop_3 encode their operands (including n in the range 1..15) without truncation; the instruction encoding is not shown.
sp and val parameters arrive within valid compiler stack-pointer ranges; no precondition about them is documented in this code.
limitations: Candidate: idx from lv_idx used in gen_move(s, idx, sp, val) without an upper-bound check in this code. Speculative: an out-of-range idx can only be produced by lv_idx (not shown) violating an unquotable contract, and the harmful slot access would occur inside gen_move (not shown). This code quotes only "if (idx > 0)".

Candidate: structural AST dereferences (tree->cdr, tree->cdr->cdr->car, tree->cdr->car) could read out of bounds on a malformed tree. Speculative: producing a malformed tree requires the parser (not shown) to emit one for the specific node types already filtered by the switch arms; no statement in this code constructs such a tree.

Candidate: n exceeding the bytecode operand field at genop_3. Dismissed after full path enumeration: every arithmetic path in this code caps n at exactly 15 ("n = 15;", "if (n < 15) { n++; if (n == 15) {"); no path produces 16 or a negative n at a sink.

Candidate: stack underflow at pop_n(2)/pop_n(14)/pop(). Dismissed after simulating all boundary paths (n=13/14/15 with and without keyword arguments); each pop is matched by quoted producers on the stack.
Impact of any bytecode mis-accounting would materialize in the VM interpreter or codegen helpers, which are not part of the given code; no impact link inside this code could be quoted.

verdict.summary: All in-code sinks are guarded: the field reads are protected by the explicit size check 'if (p + 4 > max) return PJLIB_UTIL_EDNSINSIZE;' and both callee failures are checked. Potential defects (buffer sizing consistency between get_name_len and get_name, negative name_part_len) depend entirely on the unshown callees get_name_len/get_name and cannot be instantiated from the given code.

assumptions: get_name_len returns a nonnegative name_part_len and a name_len consistent with the string get_name later writes into the name_len+4 allocation — enforced only in the not-shown callee bodies.
pj_pool_alloc returns non-NULL (pjlib convention, not shown/asserted here); no dereference of the allocation occurs in this code.
pkt/start/max are well-ordered pointers (start <= max) as arranged by the caller.
limitations: Potential heap overflow if get_name writes more than name_len+4 bytes into q->name — the write occurs inside get_name, which is not given; the impact chain is unverifiable.

Potential OOB read if name_part_len could be negative, letting p fall before start and pass the 'p + 4 > max' check — requires get_name_len's success path to return a negative value; callee body not shown, trigger speculative.
Caller behavior and deployment context (e.g., pj_dns_parse_packet) not shown; reachability assumed typical.

verdict.summary: TfLiteIntArrayGetSizeInBytes computes an allocation byte size from an unvalidated signed int parameter: in 'size_t computed_size = sizeof(dummy) + sizeof(dummy.data[0]) * size;' the negative or oversized int is converted to size_t and multiplies, wrapping around. A caller-supplied size of -1 yields a return value of 0 on both the flexible-array and _MSC_VER paths (4 + 4*(SIZE_MAX) ≡ 0, resp. 8 + 4*(SIZE_MAX) - 4 ≡ 0), so the exported sizing API reports zero bytes for a count the caller will subsequently use to write elements, producing an undersized allocation and downstream heap out-of-bounds writes. No sign check, range check, clamp, or overflow-checked arithmetic exists anywhere in the function.

evidence.reason: The int parameter 'size' (line 1) enters with no documented precondition or validation. At line 4 it is implicitly converted from signed int to unsigned size_t inside 'sizeof(dummy.data[0]) * size'; for size = -1 the product is 2^N-4, and adding sizeof(dummy) (4, or 8 with the _MSC_VER data[1] layout minus the line-7 subtraction of 4) wraps to exactly 0. The function therefore returns 0 bytes for a negative element count, corrupting the allocation size it exists to compute (root cause: integer overflow / signedness confusion in a buffer size calculation). STEP 5 confirmed no bounds check, clamp, corrected comparison, checked arithmetic, or error arm exists on any of the function's single straight-line paths to 'return computed_size;'.

assumptions: The definition of TfLiteIntArray is not given; sizeof(dummy) is assumed to be 4 (int 'size' plus flexible array member 'data[]') on the non-MSVC path and 8 (int 'size' plus data[1]) on the MSVC path, based on the structure of the arithmetic and the _MSC_VER correction comment.

Callers of this exported helper are assumed to use the returned value as a malloc/allocation size and then store 'size' elements, the universal TFLite pattern (e.g., TfLiteIntArrayCreate/Copy); that malloc-and-write site is not shown in the given code, so the final heap-overflow write is an unquoted link.

Attacker reachability of a negative or oversized 'size' (e.g., a count parsed from an untrusted .tflite model file) is assumed from the function's role as the public sizing API; the parse site is not shown.
limitations: The positive-overflow variant (large positive size wrapping size_t) only wraps on 32-bit size_t targets (size >= ~2^29); on 64-bit size_t, INT_MAX*4 does not wrap. The negative-size trigger (size = -1 returning 0) was verified on both widths and both preprocessor paths and is the primary basis for the finding.

The concrete out-of-bounds write (malloc(0) followed by element stores) occurs in caller code not included in the snippet; the instantiated in-code impact is the wrapped/zero allocation size returned by this function.

verdict.summary: parse_query reads the 2-byte type and 2-byte class from p = start + name_part_len without any bounds check against max; when the QNAME ends at (or within 3 bytes of) the end of the packet buffer, the pj_memcpy calls read out of bounds past max, leaking adjacent heap memory into q->type/q->dnsclass. Trigger fully instantiated by an attacker-crafted DNS packet.

evidence.reason: After the parsed name, p is advanced by name_part_len with no check that at least 4 bytes remain before max. If the attacker's QNAME consumes all bytes up to max (name_part_len == max - start), p == max and the two pj_memcpy calls read 2 and 2 bytes past the end of the packet buffer (up to 4 bytes OOB). No bounds check, clamp, or error arm exists on any path to these memcpys; max is never compared with p in this function.

assumptions: get_name_len/get_name (callees, not shown) are assumed to validate the name itself against max; even granting that, the worst in-bounds case name_part_len == max - start still triggers the OOB read here, so this assumption does not demote the finding.
The packet buffer is heap-allocated with size exactly matching max - pkt; read past max is past the allocation.
limitations: name_len+4 allocation arithmetic (line 17) could overflow only if the unshown get_name_len returned an extreme value; no producing statement is visible in this code, so not confirmed.
Actual historical pjproject fix (PJ_EMODIFIEDSIZE check) is external context, not used as evidence.

verdict.summary: In SingleComponentLSScan::ParseMCU, the run-length fill loop 'while(run) { ... *lp++ = a << preshift; ... run--,length--; }' is bounded only by 'run', the attacker-controlled return value of DecodeRun(length,m_lRunIndex[0]) read from the entropy-coded JPEG-LS bitstream. No statement in this code compares 'run' against the remaining line length 'length' (initialized to m_ulWidth[0]) or clamps 'lp' to the line buffer. If run > length, the loop writes past the end of line->m_pData (heap out-of-bounds write), drives 'length' negative, and the subsequent 'if (length)' test (true for negative values) plus 'while(++lp,--length)' continue performing out-of-bounds writes on every further iteration until the signed counter wraps, giving an attacker-controlled, attacker-scalable heap buffer overflow.

evidence.reason: Root cause and sink: 'run' is decoded from the attacker-controlled bitstream by DecodeRun and its first use is as the loop bound 'while(run)'. No check anywhere bounds run by 'length' or clamps lp to the line buffer; 'length' is only decremented in lockstep ('run--,length--'). With a crafted scan (e.g. m_ulWidth[0]=4, run=100), iterations 5..100 execute '*lp++ = a << preshift' past the end of line->m_pData, and the resulting negative 'length' passes the later 'if (length)' and 'while(++lp,--length)' tests, continuing out-of-bounds writes on every subsequent iteration — a heap buffer overflow (CWE-787/CWE-119) with attacker-controlled extent.

evidence.snippet:
LONG length = m_ulWidth[0];
    LONG *lp    = line->m_pData;

Gap-fill loop `for (int64_t b = 0; b < N; ++b)` runs up to N iterations, but N is bounded by the prior `TensorShape({N})` allocation of N*8 bytes, so the work is proportional to attacker-allocated input, not amplified.

verdict.summary: xQueueGenericCreate computes the queue storage size as (size_t)(uxQueueLength * uxItemSize) where the multiplication is performed in UBaseType_t width before the cast, so a large attacker-supplied length/item-size pair wraps and yields a small xQueueSizeInBytes. With asserts disabled, pvPortMalloc(sizeof(Queue_t) + wrapped_size) allocates a block holding only the queue header, while the unmodified uxQueueLength/uxItemSize are recorded via prvInitialiseNewQueue — the returned queue claims capacity it cannot hold, so the first queue write operation performs a heap out-of-bounds write.

evidence.reason: The size is computed by multiplying uxQueueLength * uxItemSize in UBaseType_t width BEFORE the cast to size_t, so the product wraps (e.g., 0x10000 * 0x10000 = 0 on a 32-bit UBaseType_t). verdict.summary: gf_text_get_utf8_line reads attacker-controlled file bytes into szLine (capacity lineSize, per memset/gf_fgets) and, for unicode_type==0, expands each non-UTF8 high-bit byte into two output bytes with no bound on the write index j against the 2048-byte stack buffer szLineConv or against lineSize; the result is a stack OOB write during the conversion loop (when lineSize>1025) and, for any lineSize>=2, an OOB write past szLine via strcpy(szLine, szLineConv) copying up to 2*len+1 bytes into a lineSize-byte buffer. Separately, for unicode_type==2 (LE), the byte-swap loop while(1){...} has no i+1<lineSize bound: an attacker UTF-16-LE line that fills the buffer without an even-aligned 00 00 pair drives reads and writes past szLine until a double zero is found in adjacent memory. Both triggers are instantiated solely by file content at this function's entry points.

evidence.reason: Origin of the size miscalculation: for unicode_type==0, every attacker byte >=0xC0 followed by a non-continuation byte (e.g. a file line of 0xC1) takes this branch and writes one byte here plus one more via the fall-through at line 53, so the output index j grows to 2*len while the loop is bounded only by i<len (line 14) and len can be lineSize-1 (line 13). No statement anywhere bounds j against sizeof(szLineConv)=2048 (line 5) or against lineSize, so szLineConv[2048] overflows in the loop when lineSize>=1026.

evidence.snippet:
szLineConv[j] = 0;
		strcpy(szLine, szLineConv);
evidence.reason: Sink of the OOB write: after the doubling conversion j=2*(lineSize-1), so line 56 writes the terminator out of bounds for lineSize>=1026, and line 57 strcpy copies 2*(lineSize-1)+1 attacker-derived bytes into the lineSize-byte buffer szLine (capacity defined by the code itself at lines 8-9), overflowing it by lineSize-1 bytes for any lineSize>=2. Simulated trigger: attacker file line of 0xC1 bytes longer than the buffer, unicode_type==0; no length check, clamp, strncpy, or bound on j exists on any path.

The UTF-16 byte-swap loop is bounded only by the double-zero test at line 70; there is no i+1<lineSize bound. With an attacker UTF-16-LE line (e.g. 'A',0x00 repeated) longer than the buffer, gf_fgets fills szLine with lineSize-1 bytes whose zeros sit at odd offsets only, so no even-aligned 00 00 pair exists; at i=lineSize-2 the loop swaps and advances to i=lineSize, then line 70 reads szLine[lineSize] and szLine[lineSize+1] past the buffer (guaranteed OOB read), and lines 71-73 write those out-of-bounds locations if either byte is nonzero, continuing unbounded until adjacent memory happens to contain 00 00. Trigger is file content alone with unicode_type==2.

assumptions: gf_fgets reads at most lineSize-1 bytes, NUL-terminates, stops at newline/EOF, and retains embedded NUL bytes for UTF-16 lines; the code's own comment at line 81 ('many chances the gf_fgets never reads the \0 after a \n') and its use of lineSize as capacity at lines 8-9 are the only quotable evidence for these semantics.
signed char promotion does not change the triggers: szLine[i] & 0x80 is nonzero for all bytes >= 0xC0 regardless of sign.
limitations: Line 79 'szLineConv[i] = 0;' uses the return of gf_utf8_wcstombs (line 78) with no failure-sentinel or i<2048 check; if that callee can return (u32)-1 or exactly 2048 on attacker UTF-16 input, this is a one-byte/before-buffer OOB write, but the callee is not shown and its failure sentinel cannot be quoted, so the trigger is not instantiated here.

The 3/4-byte UTF-8 branches never read past the string: at the last byte the first sub-branch always wins because the NUL satisfies (szLine[len] & 0xc0) != 0x80; the maximum index touched is len <= lineSize-1, in bounds.

A caller passing a lineSize larger than the real szLine buffer would violate the capacity contract embodied by lines 8-9; that contract question is separate from the overflow proven here, which holds even when the buffer is exactly lineSize bytes.

The one internal defect found — freeing s->session->tlsext_tick without nulling the pointer before a malloc-failure 'goto err' path — could leave a dangling pointer, but its trigger requires OPENSSL_malloc to return NULL (OOM, or ticklen==0 with implementation-defined malloc(0) behavior, wrapper not shown) and the double-free itself would occur in SSL_SESSION_free outside this code, so it is speculative under the trigger/impact-instantiation rules and is recorded in notes.limitations.

s->session->session_id is at least 32 bytes (SSL_MAX_SSL_SESSION_ID_LENGTH) so the SHA256 (32-byte) or SHA1 (20-byte) EVP_Digest output fits; the SSL_SESSION struct width is not shown.
ssl_session_dup(s->session, 0) returns a valid duplicate or NULL; its internal semantics are not shown.
OPENSSL_malloc is a wrapper whose behavior for size 0 (NULL vs unique pointer) is not shown; on glibc targets malloc(0) returns non-NULL.
SSL_SESSION_free / connection teardown (which would free s->session->tlsext_tick a second time in the dangling-pointer scenario) is not part of the given code.

A later SSL_SESSION_free (outside this code) would double-free it. Trigger not instantiated: ticklen>0 requires OOM (not attacker-inducible), and ticklen==0 requires OPENSSL_malloc(0) to return NULL (callee behavior not shown; glibc returns non-NULL); impact link (second free) is also outside the given code. Speculative, not classified as a vulnerability in this code.

Session-cache state mutation (removal of the old session via SSL_CTX_remove_session / remove_session_cb, its replacement via ssl_session_dup/SSL_SESSION_free, and freeing of tlsext_tick) occurs before the ticket message is validated by 'if (ticklen + 6 != n)', so a malformed ticket discards the previously cached session and connection aborts with s->state = SSL_ST_ERR. No memory-safety, disclosure, or bypass consequence is instantiated within this code.

The memcpy bound relative to the underlying s->init_msg buffer rests on the unquoted ssl_get_message contract (init_msg holds >= n bytes); within this code, ticklen is consistently pinned to n-6, and this code's own data flow cannot produce an n exceeding the buffer.

The handshake layer is assumed to derive the 1-RTT read cipher only after the client Finished (CFIN), per the comment 'Clear limit because CFIN is received at this point' — the enforcing logic is in the TLS layer, not shown.

The handshake-layer getters (unique_ptr returns) are assumed to hand each cipher over at most once per handshake epoch unless regenerated internally by the callee; the write-cipher duplicate throw suggests duplicates were considered possible, but regeneration behavior is not shown.

No NumElements/shape check, clamp, checked accessor, or rejecting error arm exists anywhere on the path.

evidence.reason: Root cause: out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). Line 14 error-checks only the TensorHandle lookup, not the tensor's shape; line 15 indexes flat element 0 with no element-count guard, so a LOCAL DT_RESOURCE handle carrying a zero-element tensor reads past the end of the tensor buffer; line 16 then reads handle.device() (a std::string) from the out-of-bounds object, amplifying the read and potentially dereferencing garbage. Trigger fully instantiated in STEP 4 (dtype==DT_RESOURCE, NumElements==0); STEP 5 verified no NumElements/shape check, clamp, checked accessor, or rejecting error arm exists on any path.

Origin of the attacker-data path: this branch selects the DT_RESOURCE handling path for an attacker-supplied local TensorHandle and routes its unvalidated tensor contents into the unchecked flat indexing at lines 14-16; no shape or size validation is performed between this branch and the sink.

assumptions: Eigen's flat() accessor and operator() perform bounds checks only in debug builds; in release builds tensor->flat<ResourceHandle>()(0) is an unchecked pointer computation plus dereference (standard library semantics, not quotable from the given code).
ResourceHandle::device() returns a std::string member read from the referenced object (standard TF type semantics).
TensorHandle::Tensor(&tensor) sets the out-parameter on success (standard TF status contract).

This trigger's reachability (custom-device op reaching GetDeviceForInput with a local non-resource, non-host-memory tensor on a non-CPU device) and the trust boundary of the aborting process cannot be instantiated from the given code, so this DoS candidate is recorded as speculative and does not affect the verdict.

Whether the surrounding framework can actually produce zero-element DT_RESOURCE tensors (e.g., via specific ops) is not shown; per the analysis rules this unquotable framework fact was NOT used to dismiss the candidate — the missing NumElements validation at the point of use in this code is itself the defect.

Unlike the sibling input 'epsilon', which is range-checked by 'OP_REQUIRES(context, epsilon > 0, ...)' before use, num_streams has no positivity, non-zero, or bounds check anywhere between its read and its use — the gap contains only a blank line. A one-line guard mirroring the epsilon check is absent in every form (no range check, clamp, corrected comparison, or checked accessor exists on any path).

evidence.reason: Root cause: missing input validation of the attacker-controlled 64-bit scalar num_streams. It is read directly from the op's input tensor (line 15) and used to construct QuantileStreamResource (line 18) with no positivity/non-zero/range check — in contrast to epsilon, which is validated by 'OP_REQUIRES(context, epsilon > 0, errors::InvalidArgument("An epsilon value of zero is not allowed."))' before the same constructor call. Instantiated trigger: a caller supplying num_streams = 0, -1, or INT64_MAX passes through unmodified (nothing between line 15 and line 18 checks it), the resource is built with the out-of-domain stream count, and CreateResource (line 19) persists it under an attacker-chosen handle for consumption by later ops.

assumptions: OpKernel Compute is a public op entry point whose tensor inputs can carry untrusted content (untrusted-model threat model); no in-code statement enforces or documents caller-side validation of tensor contents.

The behavior of the not-shown QuantileStreamResource constructor and consumer ops (e.g., use of num_streams for sharding modulo, allocation sizing, or max_elements_*num_streams arithmetic) is unknown from the given code; the specific downstream memory/division defect cannot be quoted.

verdict.summary: TfLiteIntArrayGetSizeInBytes computes the allocation byte count as sizeof(dummy) + sizeof(dummy.data[0]) * size and narrows the size_t result into a 32-bit int with no validation of the attacker-reachable parameter size. Attacker reachability of size is established by the exported non-static signature per the data-origin impact model; the concrete transport (e.g., a count parsed from a model file by callers) is not shown in this code.
limitations: The physical heap-buffer-overflow consequence (malloc of the returned undersized count followed by copying/writing size elements) occurs in callers such as the TfLiteIntArray allocation/copy helpers, which are not part of the given code; within this snippet no memory is allocated or written. The finding rests on the allocation-sizing sink being this function itself and on it being the last line of defense for the unvalidated size value.

The MSVC-only subtraction arm (line 7) was edge-tested (size = 0 returns 4 bytes, correct) and is not a defect; negative-size behavior (returns 0) additionally depends on how callers treat the size field, also not shown.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the given code. The only in-function memory sinks are bounds-enforced (snprintf with sizeof(cl.lockfile)-1 cannot overflow and always NUL-terminates) and pointer-dereference guards are correctly ordered (find_site_by_name failure returns -EINVAL before local->local = 1). All call-result failure sentinels (read_config, read_authkey, gcry_check_version, check_config) are tested before first use. Candidates involving config-derived booth_conf->name (potential path escape into the pid-file path) and ignored find_myself errors (potentially unset 'local' for later consumers) have their harmful uses in code not shown, so their impact links are not instantiated here; recorded as limitations.

assumptions: read_config returning >= 0 implies booth_conf is set and non-NULL; no statement in this code asserts or checks booth_conf before booth_conf->name is read at the snprintf call — this callee contract could not be quoted from the given code.
is_auth_req() returns a definitive boolean and read_authkey()/check_config() use negative errno sentinels; their implementations are not shown.

cl (cl.configfile, cl.site, cl.type, cl.lockfile) is populated by not-shown initialization/command-line parsing; cl.lockfile[0] empty at entry was edge-tested by this code's own check 'if (!cl.lockfile[0])'.
The actual pid-file creation/opening of cl.lockfile occurs in code not given; this function only assembles the path string.
limitations: Path-injection candidate (CWE-22-like): booth_conf->name originates from the parsed configuration file and is interpolated into '%s/%s.pid' under BOOTH_RUN_DIR with no canonicalization or '..'/'/' rejection anywhere in this code. Trigger simulated concretely (read_config=0, empty cl.lockfile, name='../../x') and the escaped string is built, but the open/write of cl.lockfile does not occur in this code, so the security impact is not instantiated here.

Ignored-error candidate: the code explicitly ignores find_myself errors ('/* Set "local" pointer, ignoring errors. */' and 'find_myself(NULL, type == CLIENT || type == GEOSTORE);'), so 'local' may remain unset on the else-branch; however no statement in this function dereferences local on that path — any NULL dereference would occur in check_config or later code not given.

NULL-dereference candidate for booth_conf->name would require read_config to return >= 0 while leaving booth_conf unset — a callee behavior not shown and not producible by this code's own statements; speculative.
Truncation of a long booth_conf->name by the bounded snprintf yields a truncated pid-file path — no memory-safety effect in this code; consequence, if any, lies in the not-shown pidfile consumer.

verdict.summary: gopherToHTML contains an off-by-one out-of-bounds write: the overflow clamp (line 77-79) bounds gopherState->len + llen to TEMP_BUF_SIZE - 1, but the terminator is written at line[llen + 1], so a gopher-server-controlled line of exactly the limit length writes a NUL byte at line[TEMP_BUF_SIZE], one past the TEMP_BUF_SIZE-byte 'line' buffer (line 6). Additionally, the host field parsed from the gopher reply is interpolated into the generated HTML without escaping in the standard-link and http-link branches (lines 241-242, 248-249), allowing HTML/attribute injection (XSS) into the proxied client's page, whereas the telnet branches escape it (rfc1738_escape_part(host)).

evidence.reason: The only bound on the line length. It clamps gopherState->len + llen to exactly TEMP_BUF_SIZE - 1, leaving no room for the terminator subsequently written at index llen + 1 (line 99). The boundary value llen = TEMP_BUF_SIZE - 1 passes this guard (TEMP_BUF_SIZE - 1 >= TEMP_BUF_SIZE is false), producing the out-of-bounds index TEMP_BUF_SIZE at the sink.

Sink of the off-by-one out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). With a gopher-server-controlled line of exactly TEMP_BUF_SIZE - 1 bytes (or a leftover gopherState->len of TEMP_BUF_SIZE - 1 followed by any line, which the line-77 clamp reduces to total TEMP_BUF_SIZE - 1), final llen == TEMP_BUF_SIZE - 1 and line[llen + 1] writes line[TEMP_BUF_SIZE] — one byte past the buffer declared LOCAL_ARRAY(char, line, TEMP_BUF_SIZE) at line 6. Trigger fully simulated; no second bound, corrected comparison, or clamp to TEMP_BUF_SIZE - 2 exists anywhere on the path.

Origin of the untrusted host value: it is a raw, attacker (gopher server) controlled field delimited only by TAB / CR / LF. Nothing on this path escapes it, and only the selector is escaped (line 157: escaped_selector = xstrdup(rfc1738_escape_part(selector))).

XSS sink (CWE-79): host and gtype are interpolated into the generated HTML without any escaping, unlike name (html_quote) and selector (escaped_selector). A gopher reply line such as 'iN\tS\t\">\t70\n' makes host = '">' which breaks out of the HREF attribute; the result is appended to the client response via outbuf.append(tmpbuf) (line 254) and entry->append(...)/entry->flush(). The same unescaped host appears in the http-link branch (lines 241-242) and port is unescaped in the telnet branches (lines 230/234), while only lines 229/233 escape host there — no escaping exists on the standard/http paths.

assumptions: The declaration of gopherState->buf and its size are not present in the given code; the memcpy at line 86 cannot be bounds-verified and is assumed (not proven) to have capacity TEMP_BUF_SIZE.
LOCAL_ARRAY is a macro; its storage class (static vs stack) is not shown, but the declared size TEMP_BUF_SIZE is quotable from line 6 and is the bound used in the analysis.
gopherState->len persists across calls, as documented by the in-code comment '/* there is something left from last tx. */' (line 91).
Behavior of html_quote / rfc1738_escape_part / rfc1738_escape_unescaped / mimeGetIconURL is not shown; they are treated as opaque helpers.
limitations: CSO branch atoi(s_code)/atoi(s_recno) NULL-dereference candidate was dismissed: the quoted 'if (!result) break;' precedes both atoi calls, and by strtok semantics an earlier NULL token implies all subsequent strtok(NULL, ...) calls return NULL, so the break fires first.
Potential overflow of gopherState->buf at line 86 could not be evaluated because the buffer's declaration/size is not in the given code.

The byte at line[llen] is never written for the current line, so parsing/strtok may read stale bytes from a previous line of the same response; this is same-origin data with no cross-trust-boundary disclosure and was not counted as a finding.
The off-by-one write is a single fixed NUL byte at a deterministic location just past the buffer; exploitability depends on the surrounding memory layout, which is not visible in the given code.

verdict.summary: gf_text_get_utf8_line writes attacker-controlled line data into a fixed 1024-byte stack buffer szLineConv with an unbounded output index j (up to 2x the caller-supplied line length in the non-UTF8 branch, and via strcpy at lines 57/80), causing stack-based out-of-bounds writes; additionally the UTF-16 byte-swap loop indexes szLine past lineSize with only a zero-pair termination check (OOB read/write), and the return value of gf_utf8_wcstombs is used as an index into szLineConv without testing the (u32)-1 failure sentinel or the 1024 limit.

evidence.snippet: char szLineConv[1024];
evidence.reason: Origin of the faulty bound: the conversion buffer is fixed at 1024 bytes while the input line length is bounded only by the uncontracted parameter lineSize, so nothing relates the two sizes.

Out-of-bounds write sink: j is never compared to 1024 anywhere; in this arm one input byte produces two output bytes (this write plus the fall-through write at line 53), so j reaches 2*len. Trigger: unicode_type=0, lineSize=1024, file line of 700 bytes of 0xC2 -> at i=512, j=1024 and szLineConv[1024] is written, continuing to j=1400; stack memory past szLineConv is corrupted with attacker-derived bytes.

Second unbounded write (fall-through copy and terminator at j up to 2*len) plus classic strcpy overflow: szLineConv can hold up to 2*len bytes while the destination szLine has capacity lineSize, so strcpy writes past szLine (e.g., 1400-byte string into a 1024-byte buffer).

The byte-swap loop's only exit is a zero-byte pair; i is never bounded against lineSize. Trigger: unicode_type=2, lineSize=1024, a UTF-16 line of 1023 nonzero bytes fills the buffer so the NUL sits at odd index 1023; the last in-bounds pair (1022,1023) is (data,0), the swap proceeds, i becomes 1024, and szLine[1024]/szLine[1025] are read out of bounds (and written out of bounds if adjacent stack bytes are nonzero).

The parse result i is used as an index with no test for the (u32)-1 failure sentinel and no check i<1024 before szLineConv[i]=0: an invalid UTF-16 sequence (e.g., unpaired surrogate 0xD800) in the attacker-supplied line makes the converter return its failure value, and szLineConv[0xFFFFFFFF]=0 is a wild out-of-bounds write; additionally strcpy copies up to 1024 bytes into szLine whose capacity lineSize may be smaller (e.g., lineSize=512, 250 CJK chars -> 751-byte copy into 512-byte buffer).

assumptions: The internal behavior of gf_fgets and gf_utf8_wcstombs (NUL-termination; failure sentinel (u32)-1 on invalid UTF-16; honoring the 1024 output limit) is not shown; only their call sites are quoted. The defects at lines 79-80 rest on the parse call in this code returning a failure sentinel or a length up to 1024 on attacker data, with the sentinel test missing here.

szLine is assumed to be a buffer of exactly lineSize bytes, as this code itself models via memset(szLine, 0, sizeof(char)*lineSize); no statement in this code bounds lineSize against szLineConv's fixed 1024 bytes, so no contract can be quoted to dismiss the overflows.
Build endianness determines which of unicode_type 2/3 selects the swap loop; the trigger is stated for the little-endian (#else) arm; the big-endian arm is symmetric.
limitations: The OOB write in the swap loop (lines 71-73) beyond index lineSize occurs only when the out-of-bounds bytes read at line 70 are nonzero (adjacent stack content), which the attacker does not directly control; the out-of-bounds READ at line 70 is unconditional for the instantiated trigger.

Reads at line 17 (szLine[i+1] with i=len-1) touch only gf_fgets' in-buffer NUL and the multi-byte UTF-8 arms only advance past verified continuation bytes, so those reads stay within [0,len]; no candidate was generated from them.

verdict.summary: SparseCountSparseOutputShapeFn calls c->Dim(c->input(0), 1) without verifying that the attacker-supplied shape of input(0) has rank >= 2 (or any rank at all). Graph/model content crossing the trust boundary can supply a rank-0, rank-1, or unknown-rank shape for input(0), making the dimension index 1 out of range; the function also unconditionally returns Status::OK() without testing the Dim result's failure sentinel, so shape inference fails open on the error path. Direct consequence: out-of-range dimension access / process abort during shape inference (denial of service for the process consuming the untrusted model), matching the known CHECK-failure class of TensorFlow shape-function vulnerabilities.

evidence.reason: Line 2 is the very first use of the untrusted input shape c->input(0) and accesses dimension index 1 with no preceding (or following) rank check anywhere in the function. Trigger instantiated by simulation: attacker-supplied graph content sets input(0) to a rank-1 shape [5] (or rank 0 / unknown rank); c->Dim(c->input(0), 1) is then called with idx=1 >= rank -> out-of-range dimension access at the shape-inference trust boundary, terminating the process (DoS). The returned rank is then consumed at line 4 by c->Matrix(nvals, rank) with no failure-sentinel test, and line 7 returns Status::OK() unconditionally (fail-open on the error path).

assumptions: The behavior of InferenceContext::Dim/Matrix/Vector (bounds check vs CHECK abort vs returning an invalid DimensionHandle for out-of-range indices) is not shown in the given code; per TensorFlow's documented InferenceContext contract, Dim REQUIRES 0 <= idx < rank and aborts otherwise, which is the assumed mechanism of the crash.

The op registration (number of inputs, declared shapes, SetShapeFn wiring) is not shown; it is assumed SparseCountSparseOutput has at least one input and that this function is the registered shape-inference handler invoked on graph shapes.
Shape inference is assumed reachable with attacker-controlled shapes at graph-construction / tf.function-tracing time via untrusted serialized model content (saved models, loaded graphs).
limitations: If the linked InferenceContext::Dim implementation bounds-checks the index and gracefully returns an unknown dimension, the direct abort harm disappears and the residual defect is only incorrect/incomplete shape inference (unknown output shapes) with no memory-safety effect; this could not be verified because the callee is not part of the given code.

No memory-corruption primitive is claimed inside this code itself; the out-of-bounds access or CHECK abort occurs inside the not-shown callee, which this code feeds an out-of-domain index against an unvalidated attacker-supplied shape.

verdict.summary: DoCompute passes fully attacker-controlled index values (indices tensor, c->input(1)) into the scatter functor (ScatterScalarFunctor / ScatterFunctor) that writes into the resource variable's buffer at those row offsets, BEFORE any bounds validation exists. The only index-value check, OP_REQUIRES(c, bad_i < 0, ...), executes after the functor has already run, so it is a check-after-use: out-of-range indices (negative, or >= params->dim_size(0)) reach the write sink unvalidated, giving an attacker-controlled out-of-bounds write into process memory.

evidence.reason: Scalar-update sink: indices_flat (raw, unvalidated attacker index values) is handed to the scatter functor, which consumes them as row offsets into params_flat. The only bounds check on index values (OP_REQUIRES(c, bad_i < 0, ...)) is positioned after the functor call, so the write occurs before validation — check-after-use out-of-bounds write.

Vector-update sink: same defect. No statement before this call validates any indices_flat(i) against params->dim_size(0); the checks at lines 21-26 and 28-33 bound only element counts, and the bad_i check runs only after the scatter has executed with the attacker-controlled index.

evidence.snippet: const Tensor& indices = c->input(1);
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted data: the indices tensor whose element values (used as row indices into the variable buffer) are fully attacker-controlled at this op's input surface; no contract in this code constrains them.

assumptions: The scatter functor implementation (ScatterFunctor/ScatterScalarFunctor) is not shown; per guard-anchoring, its internal behavior cannot be cited as a guard. The defect attributed to this code is the passing of unvalidated attacker index values to the sink and the post-hoc ordering of the bad_i check.

OpKernelContext inputs (c->input(1), c->input(2), HandleFromInput(c, 0)) are treated as attacker-controlled, as DoCompute is the trust-boundary intake point for the op request; framework-level validation of index values is not quotable from this code.
limitations: The physical out-of-bounds write statement resides inside the not-shown functor; every statement this code contributes (unvalidated indices_flat reaching the functor call, check ordered after the call) is quoted, but the write primitive itself could not be quoted verbatim.
C2 (indices_flat(bad_i) reading with a functor-returned bad_i >= N) is speculative: no statement in this code produces an out-of-range bad_i, and the producing callee is not shown.

C3: the divide-by-zero guard for the DIV update op is skipped on non-CPU devices (line 36 restricts it to isCPUDevice<Device>()), but the worst consequence is inf/NaN result values, not corruption, bypass, or amplification — not promoted to a finding.
num_updates / N division and shaped({N, num_updates / N}) are safe: N > 0 is guarded by line 41 and divisibility follows from the StartsWith shape check at lines 57-58.

verdict.summary: In ReadOneMNGImage, the DEFI chunk handler derives object_id from attacker-controlled chunk bytes and validates it with 'if (object_id > MNG_MAX_OBJECTS)', an off-by-one check that permits object_id == MNG_MAX_OBJECTS and explicitly clamps oversized ids to MNG_MAX_OBJECTS — one past the last valid index of the mng_info arrays (sized MNG_MAX_OBJECTS, per the init loop and the correct 'i >= MNG_MAX_OBJECTS' guard used in the CLIP handler). object_id then indexes mng_info->exists[], frozen[], invisible[], x_off[], y_off[] and object_clip[] for out-of-bounds reads and attacker-influenced out-of-bounds writes ( MagickTrue, p[2], and full 32-bit offsets / MngBox structs ), a memory-corruption primitive triggered directly by an attacker-supplied MNG file.

evidence.reason: Off-by-one bounds check on attacker-derived object_id: '>' instead of '>=' allows object_id == MNG_MAX_OBJECTS, and the clamp itself sets object_id to the one-past-limit value MNG_MAX_OBJECTS; mng_info->exists[object_id] and the subsequent writes (exists, invisible, x_off, y_off, object_clip) are then out of bounds for arrays of MNG_MAX_OBJECTS elements (size confirmed by 'for (i=0; i < MNG_MAX_OBJECTS; i++) mng_info->object_clip[i].right=...').

evidence.snippet: object_id=(p[0] << 8) | p[1];
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted index: object_id is composed from attacker-supplied DEFI chunk bytes (p[0]<<8|p[1], range 0..65535), fully under attacker control from the MNG file content, and flows unvalidated at the boundary into the mng_info array indices above.

Out-of-bounds writes reached with object_id == MNG_MAX_OBJECTS: MagickTrue is written past the end of mng_info->exists[] and the attacker byte p[2] past mng_info->invisible[], a concrete memory-corruption sink on the DEFI path.

assumptions: ThrowMagickException is a non-aborting exception reporter: execution continues after it, as evidenced by the JHDR pattern where 'mng_info->jhdr_warning++;' and further parsing follow the identical call, and by this DEFI block where 'object_id=MNG_MAX_OBJECTS;' is meant to execute after it.

MNG_MAX_OBJECTS is the declared element count of the mng_info exists/frozen/invisible/x_off/y_off/object_clip arrays, as indicated by the initialization loops bounded 'i < MNG_MAX_OBJECTS' and the correct CLIP guard 'i >= MNG_MAX_OBJECTS'.
limitations: LOOP chunk: 'loop_level=chunk[0];' (attacker byte 0..255) indexes mng_info->loop_active/loop_jump/loop_count/loop_iteration with no check in this code; the declared size of those arrays is not shown, so out-of-bounds behavior cannot be proven from the given code.
DISC/SEEK: 'i=p[j-1] << 8 | p[j]; MngInfoDiscardObject(mng_info,i);' passes indices up to 65535 into a not-shown callee; the harmful use is inside that callee with no quotable bounds contract.

TERM chunk: when repeat==3 and length < 10, 'mng_get_long(&p[2])' and 'mng_get_long(&p[6])' read uninitialized heap within the length+MagickPathExtent allocation (AcquireQuantumMemory does not zero); no out-of-bounds, values only reach delay/iteration fields.
Line numbers in evidence are approximate counts from the top of the given code; the quoted snippets are verbatim.

verdict.summary: In this quantization-calibration OpKernel, the loop bound `depth` is taken from `input_max.NumElements()` (line 6), but the only guards check `input_min.dim_size(0)` and `input_max.dim_size(0)` (lines 7-14) — never the flat element counts of the min/max tensors and never the input tensor's inner dimension. An attacker who supplies input tensors whose shapes violate these unvalidated relations makes the loop read `transposed_input.chip<0>(i)` (lines 44/46) past the end of the input tensor whenever input's inner dim < depth, and read `input_min_data[i]`/`input_max_data[i]` (line 52) past the end of the min/max buffers whenever their dim_size(0) equals depth but their NumElements is smaller (e.g. shape [depth, 0]). The out-of-bounds values flow through ranges[i] and out_min_max into the outputs (line 73), giving a heap out-of-bounds read with partial information disclosure, plus a crash surface.

evidence.reason: Sink of the out-of-bounds read. The loop runs i to depth-1 where depth = input_max.NumElements(), but transposed_input's first dimension is input's inner dimension (from input.flat_inner_dims<qint32>() and shuffle) and input_min_data/input_max_data point into buffers whose flat element counts were never checked against depth — only dim_size(0) was. Trigger: input shaped [2,3] with input_max/input_min shaped [10] makes chip<0>(i) read past the 6-element buffer for i=3..9; or input_min shaped [10,0] passes the dim_size(0) check with 0 elements, making input_min_data[i] read out of bounds for every i. Eigen chip has no bound enforcement in release builds.

Origin of the faulty bound and the defective guards. depth is attacker-controlled via input_max's element count; the guards validate only the first-axis length (dim_size(0)) of input_min/input_max — the wrong unit relative to the flat indexing at line 52 — and no statement anywhere validates input's inner dimension against depth, so the OOB reads at lines 44/46/52 are unguarded.

assumptions: OpKernel::Compute is a framework-dispatched handler whose input tensor shapes and contents are attacker-influenced (graph/runtime input); no shape contract for `input` is documented or asserted anywhere in the given code, so all shape relations are attacker-data.

TF release builds disable Eigen's eigen_assert (NDEBUG), so chip<0>(i) performs no runtime bound check; even if asserted, an attacker-triggered CHECK failure across the trust boundary is a denial of service.
`input.flat<float>()` enforces dtype float on min/max (framework-internal CHECK); this constrains the attacker to float-typed tensors but does not limit the shape mismatch exploited here.
limitations: Data race on `is_non_negative` (line 55, written inside the OpenMP parallel loop with no reduction clause) and on `out_min_max` under the MSVC path (line 36 has no reduction clause) could mis-state the sign of the calibration output; requires the ENABLE_ONEDNN_OPENMP build and a specific thread interleaving not exhibitable as two ordered statements in this code — speculative, not counted.
`static_cast<float>(1L << 31)` would be signed-overflow UB only on an ILP32 long target; the code declares 64-bit index types, so this behavior is not exercised as written — speculative.

verdict.summary: This is libpq's PQconnectPoll connection state machine. The untrusted data it consumes (server-supplied protocol framing: message type byte, 4-byte length word, negotiation response bytes) is validated with in-order, quoted guards before every use: 'R' lengths are bounded to 8..2000 and 'E' lengths to 8..30000 (with the pre-3.0 fallback consuming and failing closed), negative and oversized lengths are rejected before any subtraction or buffer-space arithmetic, message types are allowlisted, SSL/GSS negotiation bytes are allowlisted with fail-closed downgrade rejection for sslmode require/verify, the port is range-checked 1..65535 before formatting, the Unix socket path length is checked with >= against the buffer bound, the connhost index is guarded on every path, and error-message indexing short-circuits on zero length. No trigger for memory corruption, OOB access, injection, or verification bypass could be instantiated within this code; candidates whose impact depends on not-shown callees (PQgetvalue field indexing, getaddrinfo addrlen contract) are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: pqReadData, pqGetc, pqGetInt, pqGets_append, pqCheckInBufferSpace, and pqPacketSend manage conn's input/output buffers with their own internal bounds; their implementations are not shown, so their safety is a callee contract, not a fact quotable from this code.
pg_getaddrinfo_all returns addrinfo whose ai_addrlen fits within conn->raddr.addr (struct sockaddr_storage); the memcpy of ai_addrlen bytes relies on this getaddrinfo contract not shown here.
PQgetvalue returns an empty string for out-of-range tuple/field indices per libpq's documented contract; that behavior is not shown in the given code.

conn->sslmode, conn->gssencmode, conn->requirepeer, conn->connhost[] and conn->whichhost are initialized as non-NULL NUL-terminated strings / valid indices by libpq connection-parameter parsing code not shown; this code only reads them.
Macro behavior of UNIXSOCK_PATH, IS_AF_UNIX, DEF_PGPORT, and the pg_hton32/NEGOTIATE_* constants is taken as standard.

The application that owns the PGconn supplies the connection parameters (host, port, sslmode, requirepeer); a malicious or man-in-the-middle SERVER supplies the protocol bytes, which were treated as attacker-data throughout.
limitations: PQgetvalue(res, 0, 0) in CONNECTION_CHECK_WRITABLE and CONNECTION_CHECK_STANDBY is guarded by PQresultStatus(res) == PGRES_TUPLES_OK && PQntuples(res) == 1 but the field count (PQnfields) is not checked in this code; a server replying with a zero-field single-tuple result would make field index 0 out of range. The harmful indexing occurs entirely inside PQgetvalue, which is not given, and libpq's documented PQgetvalue contract returns an empty string for out-of-range indices, so the impact chain breaks at an unquoted link and this is recorded as a limitation rather than a finding in this code.

The memcpy(&conn->raddr.addr, addr_cur->ai_addr, addr_cur->ai_addrlen) could overflow only if getaddrinfo produced ai_addrlen > sizeof(sockaddr_storage); no statement in this code can produce such a value, and the producing callee is not shown, so the trigger is speculative.

Deep protocol handling of authentication requests (pg_fe_sendauth), error notices (pqGetErrorNotice3), and results (PQgetResult/PQconsumeInput) occurs in callees not given; msgLength is bounded to [0,1992] at the pg_fe_sendauth call site by the quoted checks, but the callees' internal use of message contents was not auditable here.

verdict.summary: unix_expandpath() copies directory entry names returned by readdir() into a heap buffer allocated as STRLEN(path) + BASENAMELEN + 5 using unchecked STRCPY (STRCPY(s, dp->d_name) and the subsequent STRCPY(buf + len, ...) appends) with no statement anywhere in the function measuring or bounding STRLEN(dp->d_name) against the remaining space in buf. A directory entry name longer than the fixed BASENAMELEN slack writes past the end of the allocation, a heap out-of-bounds write (memory corruption) whose only mitigation is the unquoted external assumption that the platform limits file-name length below BASENAMELEN.

evidence.snippet:
STRCPY(s, dp->d_name);
		len = STRLEN(buf);
evidence.reason: Unchecked copy of the untrusted readdir() result dp->d_name into buf. The buffer was sized at line 32 as STRLEN(path) + BASENAMELEN + 5; the wildcard component previously occupying s..e may be as short as one byte, so the copy is safe only if strlen(dp->d_name) fits the BASENAMELEN slack. No statement between readdir (line 138) and this STRCPY (the dot-filter at 141-144 and the regexec match at 145-148) bounds the name length; a name of BASENAMELEN+6 bytes writes one past the allocation, and longer names write further past it. len = STRLEN(buf) then propagates the oversized length to the appends at 157-158. Root cause: missing length validation of attacker-controlled directory content at a strcpy sink.

evidence.snippet:
STRCPY(buf + len, "/**");
		    STRCPY(buf + len + 3, path_end);
evidence.reason: Second-stage unguarded writes: after the unchecked d_name copy, len = STRLEN(buf) already includes the unbounded name, and these STRCPYs append "/**" plus the remaining path at buf+len with no check that len + 3 + STRLEN(path_end) + 1 stays within the allocation made at line 32 — the same missing bound, extending the out-of-bounds write when the entry name exceeds the fixed slack.

evidence.snippet: buf = alloc(STRLEN(path) + BASENAMELEN + 5);
evidence.reason: The single sizing statement of the destination buffer. It reserves only a fixed BASENAMELEN + 5 bytes of slack beyond the original pattern, which must simultaneously absorb the replaced directory-entry name (up to the unbounded strlen(dp->d_name) copied at line 150) and the "/**" suffix and remaining path appended at lines 157-158; no later statement re-checks, clamps, or reallocates, so the slack is the only — unchecked — bound.

Origin of the tainted data: dp->d_name is content read from the filesystem (directory entries an attacker can create), the only untrusted datum consumed by this function beyond the pattern itself. The only sentinel test performed on it is the end-of-directory NULL check; the length of the returned name is never validated before it reaches the strcpy sinks at lines 150 and 157-158.

assumptions: The value of BASENAMELEN (defined in vim.h, not in the given code) is unknown from this code; in the real Vim source it is 1000, which in practice exceeds the 255-byte NAME_MAX of mainstream filesystems — this external relation is an assumption recorded here, not a quotable guard, and was not used to demote the finding.
wildoff is assumed non-negative and <= STRLEN(path) by callers not shown; this code's own recursive calls pass (int)(s - buf) and len + 1, which are in-range by construction.
alloc() is assumed to return a properly sized block or NULL (NULL is checked at lines 33-34); vim_regfree is assumed to tolerate a NULL regprog.

verdict.summary: send_control_msg copies a control message of length `len` into a receive element popped from the guest-controlled c_ivq without ever checking that the guest-supplied buffer (elem.in_sg capacity, attacker-chosen at any time) is large enough. The copy at line 15 silently truncates, and `virtqueue_push(vq, &elem, len)` at line 17 reports the full requested length as the used length — so the guest driver is told `len` bytes were written into a buffer that holds fewer, presenting a truncated control message (with stale guest memory where the remainder should be) as complete. The code itself acknowledges the missing guard with the comment "TODO: detect a buffer that's too short, set NEEDS_RESET".

evidence.reason: Root cause: the guest-controlled capacity of the popped element (elem.in_sg/elem.in_num, supplied by the malicious guest via the c_ivq vring) is never compared to `len`. Trigger: guest posts a 1-byte writable descriptor to c_ivq; when the host sends a 12-byte control message, iov_from_buf writes only 1 byte (silent truncation) and virtqueue_push records used-length = 12 for the 1-byte buffer, presenting a truncated control message as complete. The TODO comment is the code's own admission that the check is missing, and no clamp, capacity test, use of iov_from_buf's return value, or reject/NEEDS_RESET arm exists anywhere on the path.

Origin of the attacker-data: elem.in_sg/in_num (the receive-buffer capacities) come from descriptors the guest places in the control queue at any time; only the success/failure of the pop is checked here, never the popped capacity, and that unvalidated capacity flows directly to the copy and push sinks at lines 15 and 17.

assumptions: iov_from_buf's implementation is not shown; standard QEMU semantics bound the copy per iovec (it truncates and returns the copied count). Under those semantics no host OOB write occurs; if it were unbounded for short iovec chains, this would additionally be an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787).
Callers of send_control_msg construct `buf` with exactly `len` valid bytes (host-generated control messages); this contract is not quotable in the given code.
virtqueue_push's internal unmapping is assumed bounded by the element's in_sg lengths; its implementation is not shown.
limitations: Exploitation of the false used-length by the guest kernel virtio-console driver (over-read of its short buffer / parsing of stale bytes) occurs in code not given; in the QEMU threat model the guest is the attacker, so no host-side memory corruption is demonstrable from this code alone. The misstated used-length itself, however, is produced directly by line 17 in this code.
The OOB-write candidate (iov_from_buf writing `len` bytes into a shorter chain) could not be instantiated because the callee's implementation is not quoted in the given code.
