The LZW decoder accepts code == free_ent (line 115 only rejects code > free_ent) even when the table entry at free_ent has never been initialized — which is guaranteed whenever free_ent >= maxmaxcode, either because attacker-controlled maxbits <= 8 makes maxmaxcode <= free_ent from the start (no lower-bound check at line 33) or because the table is full (line 174's guard then never writes the entry). The chain walk at lines 140-144 then reads uninitialized tab_prefix/tab_suffix entries, uses the garbage value as an array index, and pushes output characters via *--stackp in a loop with no stack bound or cycle detection — yielding out-of-bounds reads, an unbounded out-of-bounds write (buffer underflow), potential infinite loop, and disclosure of uninitialized memory, all from a small crafted compressed file.

evidence.reason: Sink: the chain-walk loop indexes tab_suffixof/tab_prefixof with `code` without verifying the entry is initialized, and writes via `*--stackp` with no bound on stackp and no cycle/termination check. Instantiated trigger: with maxbits=8 (header byte 0x08), free_ent=256=maxmaxcode, codes 65, 256, 256 make oldcode=256 (line 180) after the KwKwK path sets incode=256 and line 174 refuses entry creation (256 < 256 false); the third code 256 reaches `code = oldcode` = 256 and line 143 reads tab_prefix[256], which lines 50-54 and 174 provably never initialize, feeding garbage indices and an unbounded write loop.

evidence.snippet:
if (code >= free_ent) { /* Special case for KwKwK string. */
		if (code > free_ent) {
evidence.reason: Root cause: the off-by-one guard. Only code > free_ent is rejected; the boundary value code == free_ent is accepted even though the entry at free_ent may be uninitialized — line 174's `if ((code = free_ent) < maxmaxcode)` (the only maxmaxcode comparison) runs after the walk and guards only the new-entry write, never the walk that consumes oldcode at line 137.

Origin of the enabling value: attacker-controlled maxbits (line 24, read from the compressed file) is checked only against an upper bound. With maxbits <= 8, maxmaxcode <= 256 while line 48 sets free_ent to 256 (or FIRST=257 in block mode), so no entry at or above index 256 is ever created (line 174 guard always false), yet code == free_ent is still accepted — this is the fully simulated trigger path.

assumptions: Macro and global definitions are not shown: BITS, BIT_MASK, INIT_BITS, FIRST, CLEAR, MAXCODE, BLOCK_MODE, LZW_RESERVED, cmp_code_int, tab_suffixof/tab_prefixof, the input() macro, de_stack's extent, tab_suffix/tab_prefix array sizes, and gzip_error's termination semantics. Their conventional gzip values (e.g., CLEAR=256, FIRST=257, INIT_BITS=9, MAXCODE(n)=1<<n) were used only to read the code; the confirmed finding relies only on initialization facts quotable from the given code (lines 50-54, 174-179).
get_byte() and read_buffer() are assumed to read the compressed input file, making their results attacker-data per discipline 3.

The tab arrays are assumed large enough that index 256 is within their extent (any BITS >= 9 sizing); if tab arrays were sized 1<<BITS with maxbits == BITS, the full-table variant of the trigger additionally reads one-past-the-end at index maxmaxcode (CWE-125).
limitations: The precise out-of-bounds-write distance from the unbounded `*--stackp` loop depends on de_stack's extent and the garbage chain length, neither shown; the provable facts are that no stackp bound or cycle check exists anywhere on the path (STEP 5 search) and the loop is driven by uninitialized, potentially attacker-influenced table contents (global tables reused across files).
The #ifdef DEBUG block (lines 116-127) reads p[-1]..p[3] around inbuf before erroring — a potential out-of-bounds read only when compiled with DEBUG; not counted as a finding.
The input() macro's read bounds (the INBUF_EXTRA/inbits logic at lines 69-78) cannot be verified because the macro is not shown.

The full-table trigger (free_ent == maxmaxcode after 2^maxbits entries, then code == free_ent twice) instantiates the same defect without needing maxbits <= 8, but requires a larger crafted input; the small-maxbits trigger was used for the concrete simulation.

verdict.summary: In open_table(), when a matching table is found in the pre-locked/LOCK TABLES list, execution does 'goto reset' before the only assignment 'share= tdc_acquire_share(...)' ever runs, leaving TABLE_SHARE *share uninitialized. If the subsequent 'if (!from_share && table->vcol_fix_expr(thd))' error branch fires (from_share stays false on this path), control reaches 'err_lock: tdc_release_share(share);', which releases an indeterminate pointer — an uninitialized-pointer use (refcount/free bookkeeping on garbage) reachable by an authenticated SQL user via LOCK TABLES on a table with generated columns, causing a wild-pointer dereference/write or crash of the server process.

evidence.snippet:
err_lock:
  tdc_release_share(share);
evidence.reason: Sink: err_lock unconditionally releases 'share'. On the locked-tables path (goto reset at line 122) the only assignment 'share= tdc_acquire_share(...)' at line 246 was never executed, so this releases an uninitialized pointer — use of uninitialized variable (CWE-457) with memory-corruption/DoS impact; no guard (if (share), from_share test, or alternate label) exists here.

if (!from_share && table->vcol_fix_expr(thd))
    goto err_lock;
evidence.reason: Faulty branch: 'from_share' was set false at declaration (line 11) and is never modified on the locked-tables path, so this error branch is live for a reused locked table; when the vcol fix (attacker-defined generated-column expressions) fails, it jumps to err_lock with 'share' uninitialized.

Origin path: the LOCK TABLES / pre-locked reuse path jumps to 'reset' at line 122, skipping the share acquisition 'share= tdc_acquire_share(thd, table_list, gts_flags, &table);' at line 246; no assignment to 'share' occurs anywhere in lines 1-122, so 'share' remains uninitialized when the reset-path error branch sends control to err_lock.

evidence.reason: Distant origin: 'share' is declared without an initializer; combined with the goto at line 122, any later error path through err_lock dereferences an indeterminate value.

assumptions: tdc_release_share(share) dereferences the passed pointer (refcount/usage bookkeeping) — the callee body is not shown, but any plausible implementation performs a memory access through the argument, so the uninitialized value reaches a memory use.

table->vcol_fix_expr(thd) can return nonzero when fixing attacker-defined generated-column expressions; this code's own branch 'if (!from_share && table->vcol_fix_expr(thd))' treats failure as a live, handled outcome, but the precise failing expression is not quotable from the given code — confidence is moderated for this reason.
DBUG_ASSERT/DEBUG_SYNC are no-ops in release builds, so they provide no runtime enforcement on these paths.

Read-only-transaction write-lock check (lines 41-43) is skipped when MYSQL_OPEN_HAS_MDL_LOCK is set; this is the internal reopen path, not an attacker-instantiable authorization bypass in this code.

verdict.summary: In LZWDecodeCompat, the interrupted-output restart block (lines 25-59) runs before any check that the requested output count is positive; the only validation of occ0 is the truncation round-trip at line 19, which accepts 0. When a previous call left sp->dec_restart set (line 153, with sp->dec_codep set at line 149), a subsequent invocation with occ0 == 0 reaches the do-while at lines 42-45 with occ == 0. Because a do-while body executes at least once, `*--tp` writes op0[-1] (one byte before the destination buffer), and the post-test `while (--occ)` turns 0 into -1 (non-zero), so the loop keeps writing op0[-2], op0[-3], ... with attacker-decoded byte values for up to sp->dec_restart bytes until the chain terminator (codep->next == NULL) is dereferenced. The main-loop guard `while (occ > 0)` (line 73) lies after this block in execution order and does not protect it. This is a heap out-of-bounds write (buffer underflow) plus denial of service, reachable from a crafted LZW-compressed TIFF.

evidence.reason: Unguarded out-of-bounds write sink. The restart block is entered (line 25) whenever sp->dec_restart is set, with occ = (long)occ0 validated only by the truncation round-trip at line 19, which occ0 == 0 passes. With occ == 0, `residue > occ` (line 30) is true, so tp = op + 0 = op0 (line 41) and the do-while at lines 42-45 executes its body at least once, writing op0[-1] — before the destination buffer — then `while (--occ)` maps 0 to -1 (non-zero) and the loop continues writing op0[-2], op0[-3], ... with attacker-decoded bytes (codep->value) until codep->next becomes NULL and is dereferenced. No check on occ positivity, no clamp, and no tp/op bounds test exists anywhere before this sink; the only `while (occ > 0)` guard (line 73) runs after the block in execution order.

Origin of the triggering state: when a decoded string exceeds the remaining output space (branch `if (codep->length > occ)`, line 142, with occ >= 1 guaranteed by `while (occ > 0)` at line 73), this code stores sp->dec_codep = codep (chain length L) and sp->dec_restart = occ (>= 1, L > occ), so on the NEXT invocation residue = L - dec_restart >= 1. Any follow-up call with occ0 == 0 (accepted by the line 19 check) then instantiates the out-of-bounds write at lines 42-45: one byte at op0[-1] plus dec_restart more backward bytes with attacker-controlled values, followed by a NULL dereference crash.

assumptions: Constants and type layout not present in the given code (tif_lzw.h): CODE_CLEAR=256, CODE_EOI=257, CODE_FIRST=258, CSIZE covers all 12-bit codes, and root table entries 0-255 have length 1 with next == NULL; the chain-termination reasoning (write loop stops/crashes at NULL next) relies on this.
NextCode/GetNextCodeCompat macro bodies are not shown; masking of 'code' to nbitsmask and EOS handling are assumed, not quotable.

The caller is assumed to allocate op0 with occ0 writable bytes; whether any caller ever passes occ0 == 0 or occ0 < 0 is not shown and cannot be quoted — per the analysis rules this unquotable contract does not demote the finding, but it is the reason confidence is not higher.

A negative occ0 (< 0) triggers the same restart-block defect (tp = op + occ underflows at line 41, sp->dec_restart is corrupted by += occ at line 37, and the walk at lines 38-40 can run past the chain root into a NULL dereference); it is treated as a variant of the confirmed finding at the same sink, with instantiability depending on the same unshown caller behavior.

A break of the chain-length invariant (entry length == chain depth) enabling a NULL dereference inside the restart walk (line 40) could not be instantiated: within this code the table is never modified while dec_restart > 0, because the partial path executes `sp->dec_restart = 0;` (line 58) before the main loop can run, and the residue > occ path returns at line 46 without touching the table.

cdev (from get_gadget_data(gadget)) and cdev->req are non-NULL when setup runs; composite_setup is only invoked after gadget bind, which is not shown.

Callees not shown (config_desc, get_string, bos_desc, device_qual, set_config, count_ext_compat, fill_ext_compat, count_ext_prop, len_ext_prop, fill_ext_prop, composite_ep0_queue) write within req->buf bounds and return positive lengths in normal operation; their internal bounds cannot be audited here.
MAX_CONFIG_INTERFACES and the constants USB_COMP_EP0_BUFSIZ / USB_COMP_EP0_OS_DESC_BUFSIZ are assumed to match the corresponding buffer allocations made elsewhere.
gadget driver-registered state (cdev->configs entries, config->descriptors[0], os_desc tables, gadget->otg_caps) is set by kernel-side configuration, not by the USB host issuing control requests.
limitations: Speculative: OTG descriptor path 'value = min_t(int, w_length, otg_desc_len); memcpy(req->buf, config->descriptors[0], value);' has no check that config->descriptors[0] is non-NULL or at least otg_desc_len bytes; if otg_caps->otg_rev >= 0x0200 while descriptors[0] is a 3-byte usb_otg_descriptor, up to a few bytes past the descriptor would be read. The mismatch precondition is gadget-driver configuration, not attacker data — not instantiable from this code.

Speculative: 'config = list_first_entry(&cdev->configs, ...); if (!config) goto done;' — list_first_entry never returns NULL, so the check is dead; an empty cdev->configs list would yield a bogus config pointer. No statement in this code creates an empty configs list reachable at setup time.

Speculative: 'value = bos_desc(cdev); value = min(w_length, (u16) value);' lacks the 'if (value >= 0)' guard present in the CONFIG and STRING cases; a negative bos_desc() return would wrap via the (u16) cast, but the result is still capped at the already-clamped w_length (no out-of-bounds write) and bos_desc's ability to return negative is not shown here.
Speculative: 'req = cdev->os_desc_req;' is dereferenced without a NULL check; the allocation is not shown and use_os_string/os_desc_config are admin/driver-set config, not attacker-settable.
Cosmetic: 'buf[8] = count' truncates an int count to u8 in the OS extended-compat reply; count is bounded by driver-supplied interface/os_desc entries, so no security effect.

verdict.summary: No fully instantiated vulnerability in the given code. All bounds checks present in this function ('len == 0', 'len > size', 'len == 1', 'tp <= ep', 'while (d <= ep - tp)', 'if (!tp) return -1') were verified in execution order and cover the sinks. The residual out-of-bounds-read candidate in the 10-step delta1 skip loop depends on a delta-table invariant (d1[c] <= len) that is produced by kwsprep, which is not part of the given code, so its trigger cannot be instantiated here.

assumptions: kwset->delta entries are within [0, len]: produced by kwsprep, not shown in the given code; cannot be quoted, and is the sole basis for the skip loop's safety margin (the comment 'Significance of 12: 1 + 10 + 1 (md2)' implicitly assumes each of the 10 increments advances at most len).

bm_delta2_search and memchr_kwset (both called here, definitions not given) keep tp within [text, ep]/[tp, text+size] and never dereference out of bounds; their internal guards cannot be quoted from the given code.
kwset fields (mind, target, trans, gc1, gc2, delta) are consistently initialized by the constructor; the given code contains no assertion of this.

tp starts at text+len and, if the skip loop runs, ep = text + size - 11*len with size > 12*len, so the unconditional tail read 'd = d1[U(tp[-1])]' satisfies tp-1 >= text and tp-1 <= text+size-1 only under the delta bound above.
limitations: Candidate (out-of-bounds read via skip loop): inside 'for (ep = text + size - 11 * len; tp <= ep; )' the ten 'd = d1[U(tp[-1])], tp += d;' increments perform reads at tp[-1] and pointer advances with no per-increment bounds check — the loop condition 'tp <= ep' is only tested at iteration top. If any d1 entry exceeded len (classical Boyer-Moore delta1 can be len+1 for absent characters), tp could advance past text+size and read out of bounds. STEP 5 search found no clamp, range check, or corrected bound on any path between increments. However, the trigger precondition (a delta value > len) is produced only by kwsprep, not by any statement in this code, and cannot be instantiated from the given input surface as written — speculative per STEP 4, not a confirmed vulnerability of this code.

Candidate (negative/zero d in tail loop): 'while (d <= ep - tp)' re-checks d against remaining length before each 'd = d1[U((tp += d)[-1])]' advance, so the tail is self-guarding even at boundaries d == ep - tp (tp lands exactly on ep, tp[-1] reads text[size-1], loop exits). Dismissed as guarded.

Candidate (memchr length underflow 'text + size - tp'): tp <= text + size holds at that call under the kwsprep delta bound (unquoted assumption); if it ever failed, the size_t argument would wrap. Not instantiable in this code.

verdict.summary: cp_create parses the encoder option string with atoi() and stores OPT_MAXRLVLS into tccp->maxrlvls, validating only the upper bound (maxrlvls > JPC_MAXRLVLS). A negative value (e.g. numrlvls=-1) is converted to a huge unsigned value in the loop `for (rlvlno = 0; rlvlno < tccp->maxrlvls; ++rlvlno)`, which writes tccp->prcwidthexpns[rlvlno] and tccp->prcheightexpns[rlvlno] far past the JPC_MAXRLVLS-sized arrays (~65535 iterations), causing a heap out-of-bounds write with attacker-controlled extent. The later `if (cp->tccp.maxrlvls < 1)` check runs after the sink loop in execution order and cannot protect it. Matches JasPer CVE-2016-8683.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write sink: the loop bound tccp->maxrlvls is an unvalidated atoi() result from the option string; a negative value (e.g. numrlvls=-1) becomes ~65535 after conversion to the unsigned loop comparison type, and the stores write prcwidthexpns/prcheightexpns up to index 65534, far past the JPC_MAXRLVLS-sized arrays. No lower-bound check exists between the parse and this loop.

Tainted origin: attacker-controlled option value parsed with atoi() into tccp->maxrlvls; the only guard is one-sided (`> JPC_MAXRLVLS`), so 0 and all negative values pass unchecked and later reach the unbounded loop at line 286.

assumptions: prcwidthexpns/prcheightexpns arrays in jpc_enc_tccp_t are sized JPC_MAXRLVLS (=33, implied by the upper-bound check quoting JPC_MAXRLVLS); no explicit dimension appears in the given code.

optstr is attacker-influenced (encoder option string, e.g. library API/codec option); the given code treats it as the sole source of these numeric fields and performs all validation itself, so it is judged as attacker-data at this intake point.
tccp->maxrlvls is an int-convertible field (assigned an atoi result); the exact struct field type is not shown, but the code stores raw int values into it without clamping.
limitations: numgbits: `cp->tccp.numgbits = atoi(...)` lacks any lower-bound check (only `numgbits > 8` is rejected), so 0 or negative values are stored; however, the harmful use (MagSgn encoder indexing) occurs in code not given, so the impact is not instantiated in this snippet.

OPT_TILEWIDTH/OPT_TILEHEIGHT/OPT_IMGAREAOFFX accept negative atoi values that wrap when stored in unsigned fields; the tile-grid validity checks appear to force an error path for the values simulated, and the tile-count/tile-iteration arithmetic consuming these values is outside this function, so no concrete impact link could be quoted here.

hsteplcm *= cmpthstep and vsteplcm *= cmptvstep can overflow with many/large component steps, and the products scale imgareatlx/imgareatly; exploitation would require a specific image geometry and downstream consumers not shown.

prcwidthexpn/prcheightexpn can receive jpc_floorlog2(0) = -1 stored into uint_fast16_t, but the subsequent `> 15` checks reject it (albeit after the in-bounds store) and the value never reaches a memory-unsafe use in this code.
JasPer CVE-2016-8683 fix history corroborates the maxrlvls defect, but the analysis stands on the given code alone.

verdict.summary: hfsplus_block_allocate() never checks the return value of read_mapping_page() before passing it to kmap() and dereferencing the result. The allocation bitmap belongs to a mounted filesystem image (attacker-controlled content), so a truncated/corrupt allocation file can make read_mapping_page() return an error sentinel, which kmap() and the subsequent *curr accesses (and set_page_dirty()) treat as a valid page pointer, crashing the kernel. The same unguarded pattern occurs at all three call sites.

evidence.reason: The page returned by read_mapping_page over the attacker-influenced allocation-file mapping is passed to kmap() with no IS_ERR/NULL check anywhere on the path; a failing read (truncated/corrupt on-disk allocation file) yields an error pointer that is kmap'ed and then dereferenced at line 28 (`val = *curr;`). Root cause: unchecked lookup failure sentinel used as a page pointer.
Second occurrence of the same unguarded pattern in the scan loop: the unchecked read_mapping_page result is immediately kmap'ed and dereferenced on the next iteration (line 42 `val = *curr;`).

Third occurrence, in the allocation loop: the unchecked page is not only dereferenced (line 91 `n = be32_to_cpu(*curr);`) but also written through (line 98 `*curr++ = ...`, line 120) and marked dirty (line 121 `set_page_dirty(page);`), all on a pointer whose validity was never tested.

assumptions: read_mapping_page() over the hfsplus allocation-file mapping can return an error sentinel when the backing blocks (described by attacker-controlled on-disk extent metadata) are unreadable; the readpage implementation is not shown, so the exact failure conditions cannot be quoted from the given code.

size, offset, and *max originate from on-disk HFS+ metadata of a mounted filesystem image; no caller is shown and no documented precondition on them exists in the given code, so they are treated as attacker-data.
PAGE_CACHE_BITS = 32768 (4096-byte pages) was assumed for the boundary arithmetic analysis.
limitations: Boundary defect in the end-pointer computation (lines 22-25 and 60-63): when size's in-page bit position is in [32737, 32767], (size + 31) & (PAGE_CACHE_BITS - 1) wraps, making end too small and skipping part of the last page. Trigger is instantiable (e.g., size = 32767, offset = 0 gives end = pptr) but the consequence is only a misreported 'bitmap full'/allocation failure within this code; no memory-safety, disclosure, bypass, or amplification impact, so it is not a vulnerability finding.

HFSPLUS_SB(sb).free_blocks -= *max (line 124) can underflow if the on-disk free-block count is inconsistent with the allocation size; the consequence is corrupted free-space accounting with no memory-unsafe consumer shown in this code.

The writes at lines 87, 98, and 120 were verified in-bounds of the kmap'ed page on every path (guarded by curr < end with end <= pptr + PAGE_CACHE_BITS/32, plus len = min(size - start, len) and the start >= size check at line 71), so no out-of-bounds write exists in this function.

verdict.summary: All in-code sinks are guarded by quotable checks verified in execution order: prefix slices arg1+9/arg1+7 are preceded by exact-length LocaleNCompare guards (registry:=9, option:=7, artifact:=9, property:=9); the key buffer write is bounded (FormatLocaleString(key,MagickPathExtent,"cache:%s",arg1)); stack pushes enforce size >= MAX_STACK_DEPTH and NULL-check allocations; pops NULL-check the stack node before dereference; the read loop bound (i < (ssize_t) argc) excludes one-past; parse failure sentinels (list < 0, IsSceneGeometry, InterpretImageProperties NULL) are tested before first use; all format strings are literal constants. The only own-flow-instantiated anomaly, DestroyString(NULL) (e.g., arg2=(char *) NULL; ... arg2=DestroyString((char *)arg2); in the +set option: path, and the post-loop cleanup after arg2 was already destroyed), has its harmful use inside the not-shown DestroyString callee, so no memory-safety impact can be instantiated in this code. Conditional string leaks in set/+clone and NULL-argument edge cases in write/print/read/list are not attacker-instantiable here.

assumptions: Callee contracts not shown and not quotable: LocaleCompare/LocaleNCompare NULL-safety; InterpretImageProperties returning NULL for NULL input; ExpandFilenames always allocating a new argv vector with copied strings (so argv[i]=DestroyString(argv[i]) and RelinquishMagickMemory(argv) free owned heap memory); SetImageRegistry/SetImageOption copying value strings (so destroy-after-store is not a UAF); DestroyString/RelinquishMagickMemory behavior on NULL (upstream RelinquishMagickMemory returns NULL for NULL input, making DestroyString(NULL) benign in NDEBUG builds); MAX_STACK_DEPTH value and definition.

The CLI option parser supplies option strings beginning with an operator character and the documented argument count for each operator (write/print/read/list get one argument, set gets two); this is enforced outside the given code.
cli_wand and its sub-structures are validly initialized by the CLI framework; signature/assert checks are compiled out in NDEBUG builds.
_process_flags and _option_type are fixed framework configuration, not attacker-mutable at runtime by any statement in this code.
limitations: DestroyString(NULL) on several paths: '+set option:key' sets arg2=(char *) NULL then calls arg2=DestroyString((char *)arg2); after any successful set path the post-loop cleanup calls DestroyString on an already-NULL arg1/arg2. Impact (assert abort in debug builds) resides entirely inside the not-shown DestroyString callee; in NDEBUG builds upstream RelinquishMagickMemory handles NULL safely, so no memory-safety consequence is instantiable in this code.

Conditional memory leaks: 'set' re-interprets arg1n/arg2n, overwriting heap strings possibly allocated by the top-of-function percent-escape interpretation without freeing them ('+clone' similarly overwrites arg1 via AcquireString("-1")). The leak requires the top interpretation to be active for these operators, which depends on runtime process/option flags this code does not set and which the code's own comment ('NOTE: rguments have not been automatically percent expaneded') indicates is not the case for set; retention is bounded by the option-argument sizes in one invocation, so no unbounded amplification.

NULL-argument edge cases not instantiable: -write with NULL arg1 (LocaleCompare(arg1,"null:") and FormatLocaleString %s with NULL), -print with NULL arg1 (FormatLocaleFile(stdout,"%s",NULL)), -read with NULL arg1 (argv=&arg1 with *argv NULL passed to ExpandFilenames), -list with NULL arg1 (ParseCommandOption). Arg counts are enforced by the CLI parser, not by any statement in this code.
Theoretical 1-byte out-of-bounds read of option+1 if option were the empty string; the dispatcher is only invoked for non-empty operator strings per the parser (not shown).
AcquireQuantizeInfo result in the '}' branch is not NULL-checked; failure requires OOM not attacker-inducible, and the dereference would occur in code not given.

Security behavior of coders reached via ReadImages/WriteImages/PingImages (file parsing, delegate execution, resource limits) and of ExpandFilenames glob handling occurs entirely inside not-shown callees; this code passes filenames as arguments by design.

verdict.summary: The shown statements of openssl_encrypt are internally bounds-safe: the key copy is guarded by 'if (keylen > password_len)' (zero-pad before memcpy), the unknown-cipher NULL sentinel is rejected before any use, the output buffer is sized 'emalloc(outlen + 1)' with outlen = data_len + block_size immediately before both EVP output calls, and the efree/ownership paths are consistent (key freed only when allocated, iv freed only when free_iv is set, single ownership transfer via RETVAL_STRINGL). The strongest residual risk — a too-short or empty IV reaching EVP_EncryptInit_ex with only an E_WARNING and no in-code bound — is handled by delegation to php_openssl_validate_iv, whose enforcement cannot be quoted from the given code; since both the decisive post-helper buffer state and the actual over-read occur in code not given, that impact chain is not instantiated here and is recorded as a limitation, not a finding. Unchecked EVP_CIPHER_CTX_set_key_length (silent key truncation), the unchecked EVP_EncryptUpdate return (uninitialized offset only on paths where EVP_EncryptFinal also fails), and the ~2GB int overflow (fails cleanly in emalloc) are likewise non-instantiated in these statements.

assumptions: php_openssl_validate_iv (call site quoted: 'free_iv = php_openssl_validate_iv(&iv, &iv_len, max_iv_len TSRMLS_CC);') is assumed to normalize iv/iv_len to the cipher's max_iv_len (pad or truncate) and to allocate a replacement buffer when returning free_iv=1; this code's 'if (free_iv) { efree(iv); }' accommodates that contract, but no enforcement is quotable in the given code, so it is an assumption, not a guard.

OpenSSL EVP semantics are assumed as documented: EVP_EncryptInit_ex copies the cipher's iv length from iv; Update+Final combined output does not exceed inl + block_size; EVP_CIPHER_CTX_set_key_length succeeds only for variable/custom-key-length ciphers and returns failure otherwise.
PHP userland string arguments (data, method, password, iv) are attacker-controlled content of non-negative int length, are not NUL-terminated, and can approach INT_MAX but not exceed it.
emalloc aborts the request on allocation failure; there is no NULL-return path to dereference.
limitations: C1 (not a finding, strongest residual): a user-supplied iv with 0 < iv_len < max_iv_len reaches 'EVP_EncryptInit_ex(&cipher_ctx, NULL, NULL, key, (unsigned char *)iv);' with no bound check anywhere in the shown code — the only in-code statement is the warning 'if (iv_len <= 0 && max_iv_len > 0) { php_error_docref(NULL TSRMLS_CC, E_WARNING, "Using an empty Initialization Vector (iv) is potentially insecure and not recommended"); }', which is not a check and does not cover the short-nonempty case. If the unshown helper fails to pad iv to max_iv_len, EVP would over-read the user string (heap out-of-bounds read, CWE-125; the pre-helper historical PHP version exhibited this). The trigger's decisive precondition (post-helper buffer length) cannot be instantiated by any given statement, and the read itself executes inside EVP, so the impact link is unquotable in this code.

C2: 'EVP_EncryptUpdate(&cipher_ctx, outbuf, &i, ...)' return value is unchecked; if it failed without setting i, 'outlen = i;' and the offset 'outbuf + i' in 'EVP_EncryptFinal(&cipher_ctx, (unsigned char *)outbuf + i, &i)' would use an uninitialized stack value. Every simulation in which i is unset also makes EncryptFinal fail (no write occurs), so the out-of-bounds write is not instantiated.

C3: 'outlen = data_len + EVP_CIPHER_block_size(cipher_type);' can overflow int only with data_len ≈ 2GB; the resulting negative length makes 'emalloc(outlen + 1)' request a huge allocation that aborts the request cleanly — no corruption, no amplification.

C4: 'EVP_CIPHER_CTX_set_key_length(&cipher_ctx, password_len);' return ignored — for fixed-key ciphers (e.g., AES) with a longer password, only the first keylen bytes are used silently (key truncation / weak-key surprise). Crypto-policy weakness with no memory-safety impact in this code.

C5: empty IV path warns and continues (encryption proceeds with a zero IV supplied by the unseen helper) — weak-IV fail-open design, later deprecated upstream; warning is presented, so no security-state misrepresentation, and no memory/authz impact in these statements.
C6: the emalloc'd key is freed via 'efree(key)' without zeroizing — sensitive-data hygiene only.

verdict.summary: gem_transmit() fills the fixed-size stack array desc[DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS] via address_space_read() with a byte count of sizeof(uint32_t) * gem_get_desc_len(s, false) at two sites, without any check in this function that the guest-influenced descriptor word count does not exceed DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS. A descriptor length larger than the array capacity causes an out-of-bounds stack write (memory corruption) with guest-controlled size and content; the second site (in-loop descriptor refresh) re-triggers it on every descriptor processed.

evidence.reason: Sink: DMA read of sizeof(uint32_t) * gem_get_desc_len(s, false) bytes into the fixed stack array desc[DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS] with no bound check anywhere in this function; if the guest-influenced word count (derived from guest-writable device register state) exceeds DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS, this copy overflows the stack buffer. Trigger: guest enables transmit (line 10 check passes), sets the descriptor ring address (line 25), and the read executes unconditionally with the unvalidated size.

Second occurrence of the same unguarded sink: the end-of-iteration descriptor refresh re-reads sizeof(uint32_t) * gem_get_desc_len(s, false) bytes into the fixed-size stack array desc on every loop iteration (after lines 123-135 advance/wrap the descriptor address), repeating the out-of-bounds write for each descriptor processed.

evidence.snippet: uint32_t desc[DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS];
evidence.reason: Origin of the fixed bound: desc is a compile-time-sized stack array of DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS words. The only capacity constraint on the buffer is this declaration; no runtime statement in the function relates the copy size (gem_get_desc_len) to this capacity, so the size argument at lines 28-30 and 136-138 is unvalidated against it.

assumptions: s->tx_packet is allocated (in code not shown, e.g., realize()) with at least gem_get_max_buf_len(s, true) bytes; the in-function fragment-length guard at lines 50-58 is sound only under this unquotable contract. The guard itself was verified in execution order and edge-tested (length 0, length == space, p at the limit) and found correctly placed on the only path to the copy at lines 63-65.

gem_get_desc_len reads guest-writable device-register state (the given code consumes other fields of the same GEM_DMACFG register at lines 100 and 125); its return range cannot be quoted from the given code, so it is treated as attacker-data of unknown range.
s->num_priority_queues and the capacity of s->tx_desc_addr[] are device state set outside this snippet; q is bounded by the loop header at line 23 relative to that state.
DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS is the nominal capacity of desc/desc_first (its numeric value is not shown in the snippet); the defect is stated relative to that declared capacity.
limitations: The exact trigger value (gem_get_desc_len(s, false) > DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS) is produced by a helper not included in the given code. In upstream QEMU this helper is historically bounded to at most 6 words (2 without, 4/6 with GEM_DMACFG_ADDR_64B), which — if that implementation is in force — would make the desc overflow unreachable. Per the guard-anchoring rules that bound cannot be quoted from the given code and therefore cannot dismiss the candidate; this is the reason confidence is at the low end.

A potential heap overflow of s->tx_packet (copy at lines 63-65) was considered: the in-function guard at lines 50-58 is present, on every path, and edge-correct; a defect there would require the (not-shown) allocation to be smaller than the runtime gem_get_max_buf_len(s, true), which cannot be instantiated from the given code.

Descriptor-loop non-termination was considered and not confirmed: the used-bit write-back at lines 80-83 marks the head descriptor of each transmitted packet, forcing the while loop at line 32 to exit on a wrapped ring, and the space check at lines 50-58 bounds p advancement.
Uninitialized desc content on a failed address_space_read was considered and dropped: stale content is prior guest-derived data with no memory-safety consequence inside this code.

verdict.summary: composite_setup processes fully attacker-controlled USB control-request fields (wLength, wIndex, wValue, bRequestType), but every memory sink in this code is guarded in execution order: w_length is clamped at entry ('if (w_length > USB_COMP_EP0_BUFSIZ)') and again before the OS-descriptor memset ('w_length = min_t(u16, w_length, USB_COMP_EP0_OS_DESC_BUFSIZ)'), all five cdev->config->interface[intf] accesses are preceded by 'if (!cdev->config || intf >= MAX_CONFIG_INTERFACES) break;', the endpoint bitmap index is bounded by its own mask arithmetic (endp <= 31), and all response lengths are min-clamped against fixed descriptor sizes. Two confirmed missing checks were found but cannot be elevated: the OTG path memcpy source 'config->descriptors[0]' is never validated (and 'if (!config)' is dead after list_first_entry), but the trigger requires non-host-controllable gadget bind state; and the OS-descriptor path passes 'interface = w_value & 0xFF' (0-255) to count_ext_prop/len_ext_prop/fill_ext_prop without the MAX_CONFIG_INTERFACES check applied to intf elsewhere, but the potential out-of-bounds use occurs entirely inside the not-shown callees.

assumptions: All fields of ctrl (bRequestType, bRequest, wIndex, wValue, wLength) are attacker-controlled USB host data; the USB host is the untrusted party.

USB_COMP_EP0_BUFSIZ matches the allocation size of cdev->req->buf and USB_COMP_EP0_OS_DESC_BUFSIZ matches the allocation of cdev->os_desc_req->buf; both allocations are in code not shown and cannot be quoted here.

cdev->config, cdev->configs, config->interface[], config->descriptors, f->endpoints and the function callbacks are initialized by gadget-driver bind/setup code not shown; no statement in this code lets the USB host mutate them.

Callees get_string, config_desc, bos_desc, set_config, set_alt, get_status, count_ext_compat, count_ext_prop, len_ext_prop, fill_ext_compat, fill_ext_prop, and composite_ep0_queue manage their own bounds and buffer writes; their implementations are not given.
MAX_CONFIG_INTERFACES equals the array dimension of usb_configuration.interface (16), consistent with its use in this code.
limitations: OTG descriptor path: 'config = list_first_entry(&cdev->configs, ...)' makes the 'if (!config)' check ineffective for an empty config list, and 'config->descriptors[0]' is passed to 'memcpy(req->buf, config->descriptors[0], value)' without any NULL or length validation (fix-form search confirmed no such guard exists on any path). A NULL or short source would cause a kernel fault during the memcpy, but producing that state requires gadget-driver configuration (gadget_is_otg true, missing/invalid config descriptors) that neither the USB host nor any statement in this code can create, so the trigger is speculative here.

OS-descriptor RECIP_INTERFACE path: 'interface = w_value & 0xFF;' yields a value in [0,255] and no MAX_CONFIG_INTERFACES bound is applied before 'count = count_ext_prop(os_desc_cfg, interface);', 'count = len_ext_prop(os_desc_cfg, interface);', and 'value = fill_ext_prop(os_desc_cfg, interface, buf);' — unlike the five guarded uses of intf elsewhere in this function. If those not-shown callees index config->interface[interface] without their own bound check, an out-of-bounds read would occur; the harmful use is entirely in code not given, so the impact chain is not instantiated here.

The top-level w_length clamp and the OS-descriptor w_length clamp depend on the req->buf and os_desc_req->buf allocation sizes, which are defined in composite_dev.c and are not quotable from the given code.

cdev->delayed_status++ is unbounded in this function but increments only when a gadget function callback returns USB_GADGET_DELAYED_STATUS; function-driver behavior is not shown and is not host-controlled data.

verdict.summary: php_wddx_pop_element, the WDDX deserializer's end-element callback, contains two fully instantiated defects driven purely by the tag sequence of an untrusted WDDX packet. (1) When the top stack entry has NULL data and stack->top == 1, the entry is efree'd (line 30) without decrementing stack->top, leaving a dangling st_entry pointer in stack->elements[0]; a subsequent close tag retrieves it via wddx_stack_top (line 66) and dereferences ent2->type/ent2->data (lines 69, 75) — a use-after-free read that dereferences a pointer read from freed (heap-reusable, packet-influenceable) memory, with a double-free also reachable via efree(ent) (line 138). (2) ent2->data is dereferenced by Z_TYPE_P (line 75) with only a NULL guard restricted to ST_FIELD-typed entries (line 69); a NULL-data ST_NUMBER/ST_BOOLEAN/ST_NULL parent entry (whose existence this code itself acknowledges at line 24) passes that check and causes a NULL pointer dereference. Consequences: memory corruption (UAF/double-free) and attacker-induced crash of the process deserializing untrusted input.

evidence.reason: Root cause of the use-after-free: in the stack->top == 1 arm the entry is freed with efree(ent1) but stack->top is never decremented (contrast the code's own pop idiom at lines 65 and 137-139), and stack->done is never consulted anywhere in this function, so stack->elements[0] retains a dangling st_entry pointer. Trigger: packet fragment '<number></number><boolean>true</boolean>' — after '</number>' runs this arm (ent1->data NULL, top==1), the freed entry is later returned by wddx_stack_top (line 66) and dereferenced at lines 69/75.

Unguarded sink: ent2 is retrieved by wddx_stack_top and ent2->data is dereferenced via Z_TYPE_P with the only NULL check restricted to ent2->type == ST_FIELD. (a) NULL deref: '<boolean><string>x</string></boolean>' makes ent2 an ST_BOOLEAN entry with data == NULL (a state this code itself handles at line 24), the line-69 check fails, and Z_TYPE_P(NULL) at line 75 crashes. (b) Use-after-free: when elements[0] was freed by the line-30 efree without a top decrement, ent2 here is a freed st_entry, so lines 69/75 read freed memory and dereference ent2->data read from attacker-influenceable freed heap; the same dangling pointer reaching line 138's efree(ent) yields a double free.

verdict.summary: LZWDecodeCompat's restart fast-path copies `occ` bytes using `do { *--tp = codep->value; codep = codep->next; } while (--occ);`, which assumes occ >= 1. occ0 (a tmsize_t size parameter, unvalidated for sign/positivity — the only check, `if ((tmsize_t) occ != occ0)`, is a width check that passes 0 and, on 64-bit targets, negative values) flows to this loop whenever `sp->dec_restart != 0` (state produced by a prior call's string-too-long path: `sp->dec_codep = codep; ... sp->dec_restart = occ;`). With occ0 == 0: `residue > occ` holds, `tp = op + occ` equals `op`, the mandatory first iteration writes `*(op-1)` — an out-of-bounds write below the caller's output buffer — and `--occ` evaluates to -1 (nonzero) so the loop continues without bound, writing further attacker-influenced decoded bytes below the buffer until codep walks past the base codetab entry (next == NULL) and the loop dereferences NULL. The `while (occ > 0)` guard sits after the restart block in execution order and is bypassed by the early `return (1)`, so no bound protects this sink on any path.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write sink. The do-while `while (--occ)` executes its body at least once and terminates only when the pre-decrement value of occ equals 1; it is reached with occ == 0 (or negative) whenever `if (sp->dec_restart)` (L26) is true and `residue > occ` (L31) — which is trivially satisfied since residue >= 1 by construction (producer: L150 `sp->dec_codep = codep;` and L154 `sp->dec_restart = occ;` taken under L143 `if (codep->length > occ)` with occ >= 1). With occ0 == 0: tp = op + 0 (L42) = op, first iteration writes op[-1] out of bounds, `--occ` yields -1 so the loop continues unbounded, walking codep past the base entry (next == NULL) into a NULL dereference after further sub-buffer writes. No occ > 0 check exists before this loop on any path; `while (occ > 0)` (L74) runs after the restart block and is bypassed by this early return.

verdict.summary: eval_string() under-allocates the result buffer by reserving only 5 extra bytes for every '\<x>' special-key form (line 18: extra += 5), while the decode loop's trans_special() can emit more bytes than reserved for certain forms; additionally the multi-byte copy branch (MB_COPY_CHAR) and the post-write detection check `if (end >= rettv->vval.v_string + len)` (line 166) only reports via iemsg AFTER the out-of-bounds write has already occurred and does not stop execution, allowing repeated attacker-controlled heap overflow from string literals in evaluated input.

evidence.reason: Sink of the out-of-bounds write. trans_special() writes into `end` (heap buffer of `len` bytes) and advances `end` by `extra` bytes; the reservation made during the first scan was a flat 5 bytes per '\<' form, which is not coupled to the actual byte count trans_special emits. The only check, `if (end >= rettv->vval.v_string + len)`, executes AFTER the write, only emits iemsg (no return/no truncation), and uses `>=` against an off-by-one-tolerant bound (`end == buffer+len` is already one-past the NUL position), so the loop continues and subsequent iterations (`*end = NUL`, further *end++ writes) write past the allocation.

Origin of the size miscalculation: the pre-scan reserves a flat 5 bytes per '\<' escape (`extra += 5`) regardless of the decoded width of the key name, while the actual decode (trans_special / mb_char2bytes for '\u' forms) is not bounded by this estimate; `len` on line 41 is computed from this `extra`, so alloc(len) can be smaller than the bytes the decode loop writes.

assumptions: trans_special() and mb_char2bytes() are external to the given code; their exact maximum output widths cannot be quoted. The comment 'produces up to 9 characters (6 for the char and 3 for a modifier): reserve space for 5 extra' is the code's own admission that the 5-byte reserve is a heuristic, not a bound — the defect stands on the code's own arithmetic regardless of the callee's exact behavior.

The '\u'/'\U' branch writes up to 6 bytes via (*mb_char2bytes)(nr, end) with no per-branch size check at all; only the '\<' branch has even a post-hoc iemsg. This branch was folded into the same finding as it shares the same under-sized `len` allocation.
alloc() semantics (whether it allocates len bytes) are external; taken from the Vim codebase context where alloc(x) = alloc_size(x) for x bytes.

Whether eval_string's callers are reachable from untrusted input (e.g., :eval, expression evaluation of file contents/modelines) is not shown; per discipline 3, string-literal content is data the function itself consumes at its entry point and is treated as attacker-data.
limitations: The octal escape branch ('\1'..'\777') writes at most 1 byte per escape and consumes 3 input chars for 1 output byte, so it always shrinks — dismissed as a size-accounting defect (it cannot overflow the reserve; it can only over-read the in-bounds source buffer, which is a separate read-side concern only if the source is shorter than assumed, which the outer NUL check prevents).

The `interpolate` double-brace accounting (--extra per '{{'/'}}') can under-reserve if the two scan passes disagree on brace pairing (e.g. the decode loop's break on single '{' occurs at a different position than the pre-scan); this is the same desynchronization class as the primary finding but requires the caller to be in interpolate mode with mixed braces — recorded as a secondary facet of the primary finding, not separately reported.

int truncation of len on 64-bit builds ((int)(p - *arg + extra)) for strings > 2GiB would make len negative and alloc fail — dismissed: alloc(NULL) is checked (line 43-44), trigger requires a 2GiB literal, which is not a realistic attacker input surface for this function's shown callers.

The missing-NUL termination check when the source string lacks a closing quote (loop exits on NUL) is handled: *end = NUL is still within bounds because the reserve accounts for the terminator; no separate defect.

verdict.summary: unlzw() accepts a compressed stream whose header sets maxbits below INIT_BITS (only `maxbits > BITS` is checked) or that drives free_ent to maxmaxcode, so table entries at index free_ent/maxmaxcode are never written (`if ((code = free_ent) < maxmaxcode)` blocks insertion, and initialization covers only entries 0..255). A code equal to free_ent passes the `code > free_ent` corruption check and takes the KwKwK path, setting `code = oldcode` where oldcode (via `oldcode = incode`) can be exactly that never-written index. The string-walk loop then reads uninitialized tab_prefix/tab_suffix entries, uses the uninitialized value as its loop bound (unbounded stackp decrement → out-of-bounds write below de_stack) and pushes uninitialized memory bytes to the output via memcpy/write_buf.

evidence.reason: Sink: after the KwKwK assignment `code = oldcode` (line 138), the walk loop reads tab_suffixof(code)/tab_prefixof(code) with no validation that this index was ever initialized and no bound on stackp depth. Instantiated trigger: header byte 0x00 (maxbits=0, non-block) followed by 9-bit codes 65, 256, 256 — the third code enters KwKwK with oldcode=256 (set by `oldcode = incode` where incode=256==free_ent), an index never written by clear_tab_prefixof (entries 0..255 only) or by any insertion, so `*--stackp = tab_suffixof(256)` pushes an uninitialized value to output and `code = tab_prefixof(256)` feeds an uninitialized value into the loop condition, enabling unbounded stackp decrement (OOB write below de_stack) and disclosure of uninitialized memory through memcpy/write_buf.

Origin of the never-initialized index: insertion into the table happens only while `free_ent < maxmaxcode`, so entry maxmaxcode is never written, yet `oldcode = incode` can carry code == free_ent == maxmaxcode (permitted because line 116 rejects only `code > free_ent`) into the walk at lines 141-145. With maxbits=0 (or any value < INIT_BITS=9, not rejected anywhere) free_ent stays 256 >= maxmaxcode=0 and no entry >= 256 is ever written at all.

Missing-check site: maxbits is masked to 0..BIT_MASK and validated only against an upper bound (`maxbits > BITS`); there is no lower-bound check (e.g., maxbits >= INIT_BITS), so a header byte of 0x00 (maxbits=0, non-block mode) is accepted, making maxmaxcode smaller than the initial free_ent and blocking all table insertions — the simplest instantiation of the uninitialized-entry trigger.

assumptions: Macro semantics follow standard gzip: INIT_BITS=9, FIRST=257, CLEAR=256, BIT_MASK=0x1f, LZW_RESERVED=0x60, BITS=16, MAXCODE(n)=((1<<n)-1); cmp_code_int is unsigned short; these values are not defined in the given code.
The comment on clear_tab_prefixof ('Initialize the first 256 entries in the table.') is taken as the exact extent of prefix-table initialization; the function body is not shown.

Sizes/layout of tab_prefix, tab_suffix, de_stack, outbuf, inbuf (INBUFSIZ+INBUF_EXTRA) and the depth of the de_stack region are not shown; the out-of-bounds-write-below-de_stack extent depends on them, while the uninitialized-read reaching output/control-flow does not.
gzip_error() and read_error() are assumed to terminate the process (standard gzip behavior; not shown in the given code).
The input file descriptor's content is fully attacker-controlled; this is the data this function's own statements consume via get_byte/read_buffer/input.
limitations: If read_error() could return after rsize == -1, `insize += rsize` (line 75) would underflow the unsigned insize and make inbits enormous, causing out-of-bounds reads of inbuf; the trigger requires an OS-level read failure plus a returning error handler, neither instantiable in this code — speculative.

The OOB write below de_stack and any OOB indexing of tab_suffix/tab_prefix by garbage 16-bit prefix values depend on uninitialized memory contents and table sizing (in-bounds for a 1<<16 table with BITS=16); the unconditionally instantiated impacts are the uninitialized value controlling the walk loop bound and being written to the output stream.

Whether a stale table from a previous unlzw invocation in the same process could pre-populate entry 256/511 is outside the given code; the entry is provably never written by this function's statements for the triggering stream.

verdict.summary: do_mouse() indexes TabPageIdxs with the terminal-supplied mouse column (mouse_col) on both drag-event paths without any bounds check. The click path is guarded by '&& mouse_col < Columns', proving Columns is the array bound and that mouse_col >= Columns is a reachable input; the drag paths at lines 265 and 323 have no such check, so a drag event (after a click in the tab line set in_tab_line) with a reported column at or beyond Columns performs an out-of-bounds read whose garbage value is then used as a tab-page index.

Second unguarded use of the same unvalidated index: when a drag event occurs with mouse_row != 0 while in_tab_line is still TRUE (set by a prior click in the tab page line), mouse_col is used directly to index TabPageIdxs with no bound, giving an out-of-bounds read for any reported column >= Columns.

This is the click path, which DOES guard the identical access with 'mouse_col < Columns'. The presence of this check (a) anchors Columns as the array bound and (b) is this code's own evidence that mouse_col can reach or exceed Columns; its absence on both drag paths (lines 265 and 323) is the defect. The check also uses '<' with no lower bound, so a negative mouse_col would pass, though a negative value could not be instantiated from the given code.

assumptions: mouse_row/mouse_col and mod_mask originate from terminal mouse escape sequences decoded outside the given code; the range the decoder admits is not shown, but the code's own 'mouse_col < Columns' guard on the click path establishes that mouse_col >= Columns is a reachable value in this code's model.

verdict.summary: The packet-match condition in MqttClient_WaitType uses MqttIsPubRespPacket(packet_type) == MqttIsPubRespPacket(wait_type), which is true whenever the received and awaited packet types are both non-publish-response types. A network peer can send a packet of a different type (e.g., DISCONNECT while the client awaits CONNACK) that is accepted as a match, so waitMatchFound is set, the caller's type-specific packet_obj is dispatched to MqttClient_HandlePacket under a foreign type code, and MQTT_CODE_SUCCESS is returned as if the awaited response had arrived (fail-open security-state misrepresentation).

evidence.reason: Root cause: the third clause compares two booleans, so ANY received type in the same class as wait_type matches (e.g., wait_type=CONNACK(0x02), network-supplied packet_type=DISCONNECT(0x0E) or PUBLISH(0x03): MqttIsPubRespPacket(...)==MqttIsPubRespPacket(...) yields 0==0, wait_packet_id==0 passes). The code then sets use_packet_obj = packet_obj (the caller's object sized for the awaited type) while use_packet_type = the actual foreign type, dispatching the mismatched pair to MqttClient_HandlePacket (line 169-170), and later returns MQTT_CODE_SUCCESS via lines 181-183 and 240 as if the awaited response arrived. Simulated trigger: malicious peer sends DISCONNECT during CONNACK wait -> rc=MQTT_CODE_SUCCESS returned with no CONNACK processed. No corrected comparison, re-validation, or rejecting default arm exists anywhere between this condition and the return.

Origin of the tainted value: packet_type and packet_id are decoded from data read from the socket (untrusted network origin) and flow unvalidated into the defective match condition at lines 133-136; only rc <= 0 / rc < 0 are checked, never the type correspondence with wait_type.

The confirmed in-code impact is the false match, the mismatched (type, object) dispatch, and the fail-open return of MQTT_CODE_SUCCESS.

verdict.summary: In the backward-search path (forward == false), search_impl computes the post-match substring size as `count + (size - 1)`. At a match at haystack offset j, the loop leaves count == j, so the post string is assigned size j + size - 1 while only len - j - size bytes remain after the match. The returned post ref therefore extends past the end of the haystack buffer (e.g., haystack "abc", seek "abc", backward: post = {B+3, size 2} on a 3-byte buffer), yielding an out-of-bounds read of attacker-scalable length; because the found path copies op1's attributes (writable strings pass check_read_type), the inflated string also gives an out-of-bounds write primitive. No clamp, bounds check, or recomputation against the original r_size(op1) exists anywhere on the path.

evidence.reason: Sink: the post-match string is given size `count + (size - 1)` when !forward. For a backward match at offset j, count == j, so the claimed post length j + size - 1 exceeds the true remaining length len - j - size; the resulting ref spans memory past the haystack allocation (OOB read /, with inherited writable attrs, OOB write). Trigger instantiated: haystack "abc", seek "abc", forward=false → count=0, post = {B+3, size 2} outside the 3-byte buffer. No statement in the code clamps or recomputes this size against r_size(op1).

Origin of the faulty value's semantics: in the backward direction ptr starts at B+count0 and count is decremented once per completed iteration, so on `goto found` at haystack offset j the variable count equals j (not the remaining length count0 - j). This loop-carried value is what the found path feeds into the post-size computation.

count is initialized to len - size and, for backward search, ptr is set to the last candidate offset B + count. The only guard in the function (`if (size > r_size(op1))` at line 14) bounds the pattern length before the search; nothing bounds the post-match size produced in the found path, and the size==0 `goto found` also reaches the `size - 1` term, which underflows to 0xFFFFFFFF (benign under-read of len-1).

assumptions: The interpreter's operator table guarantees at least two operands on the stack (no check_op(2) is visible in the given code) and stack space for push(2); these are interface contracts not quotable here.

check_read_type, make_true/false, r_size, r_set_size, and push are macros with their standard Ghostscript semantics (type/access check with error return; direct size field store); a string object's value.bytes buffer is at least r_size bytes.

The operand strings' contents and lengths are attacker-controlled (PostScript program operands); `forward` is treated as caller-controlled input because the function shown is non-static and no quoted statement restricts it to true.
limitations: Empty-pattern backward search (size == 0, !forward) yields post size len-1 instead of len via the `size - 1` unsigned underflow — an under-read (logic defect), not out-of-bounds.
The `while (count--)` wrap of count to UINT_MAX on the no-match exit is unused afterwards (make_false/return) and is not exploitable.
Stack underflow via `op1 = op - 1` when fewer than two operands are present depends on a caller-side contract not shown and was not counted as a finding.

The only shape-related statements that could bound them — unswitched_input1_shape (line 2), unswitched_input2_shape (line 4), output_shape (line 6) — are never used after the parameter list, and the comment at lines 38-39 documents the required invariants (input1.shape.FlatSize = y0*y1*y2*y4, input2.shape.FlatSize = y0*y2*y3*y4) without enforcing them.

Simulated trigger: broadcast_shape={2,1,1,4,2} with an 8-element output buffer — after the first i0 pass (output_data_ptr ends at output+8, line 64 sets input2_data_reset=input2+8, line 60 sets input1_data_ptr=input1+2), the second i0 iteration calls elementwise_f at output+8/input2+8/input1+2, writing and reading past every buffer end (out-of-bounds write and reads). Unguarded sink (y4==1 branch) with a dereference directly inside this code: *input1_data_ptr is read and input1_data_ptr += 1 advances once per i2 iteration for y0*y1*y2 total reads, with no check that input1 holds that many elements. Simulated trigger: broadcast_shape={1,4,1,1,1} with a 1-element input1 tensor — at i1=1, input1_data_ptr = input1+1 and line 82 dereferences past the buffer end (direct out-of-bounds read in this code); output_data_ptr similarly advances y3 per iteration with no bound, enabling an out-of-bounds write when output_shape disagrees with broadcast_shape.

assumptions: This is a TFLite-style kernel helper: broadcast_shape, tensor shapes, and buffer extents derive from a parsed model file; per the trust model, the content-bearing parameters of this non-static function are treated as attacker-data.

verdict.summary: No security defect is instantiated in net_bind. Every failure sentinel is checked before first use (getaddrinfo via 'if (ret < 0)', socket via 'if (fd < 0) continue;', each setsockopt/bind via 'if (ret < 0) continue;', getsockname via 'if (ret < 0)' plus the 'naddr_len > sizeof(naddr)' length check), the port string is produced by a size-bounded snprintf of a %hu value (max 6 bytes into an 8-byte buffer), the possibly-NULL config address is NULL-guarded in every log call ('cfgaddr ? cfgaddr : "(ANY)"'), getsockname's write is bounded by construction ('socklen_t naddr_len = sizeof(naddr);'), and fd lifetime is handled on all paths (per-iteration 'if (fd >= 0) close(fd);' and the 'error: close(fd);' path) with no leak or double close. Format strings are literal, so no injection surface exists. Remaining concerns (uninitialized 'addr' if the not-shown net_address_get fails to write, NULL 'port'/'log_service_name' from a caller, cfg_getsec returning NULL) are speculative because their triggers require callee or caller behavior outside the given code and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: net_port_get and net_address_get (not shown) write within bounds when given a getsockname-filled union and a 46-byte buffer with its size; this cannot be quoted from the given code.
DPRINTF's handling of a NULL '%s' argument is not shown; glibc-style printf would print '(null)' but that is an assumption.
cfg_getsec/cfg_getstr/cfg_getbool behavior on a missing 'general' section or NULL cfg is not shown; the config source is admin-controlled file content.
Callers of net_bind are not shown; non-NULL 'port' and 'log_service_name' are undocumented caller contracts, not quotable invariants.
POSIX getaddrinfo returns 0 on success and negative EAI_* codes on failure, so 'if (ret < 0)' is the correct sentinel test on this platform family.
limitations: Uninitialized 'addr[INET6_ADDRSTRLEN]' is passed to DPRINTF '%s'; a leak of stack garbage would require net_address_get (callee not shown) to skip writing it. naddr's family is restricted to AF_INET/AF_INET6 by 'hints.ai_family = (cfg_getbool(...)) ? AF_INET6 : AF_INET;' plus a successful bind, so no in-domain failing path is producible from the shown code.

'if (!ptr)' is evaluated after 'freeaddrinfo(servinfo);' — it reads only the local pointer's value, never dereferences freed memory; this is theoretical indeterminate-value UB with no disclosure or corruption impact.
A NULL 'port' or 'log_service_name' argument would crash at '*port' or in DPRINTF, but no shown call site produces NULL and this code's own flow cannot produce it, so the trigger is speculative.
'error: close(fd);' can execute with fd == -1 (empty addrinfo list) — benign EBADF, no security effect.
errno may be stale by the time 'strerror(errno)' is called in the failure log after freeaddrinfo; this affects log wording only, not security state.
The two separate config reads (bind_address and ipv6) could observe a mid-run config reload inconsistently; worst case is a mismatched family that getaddrinfo rejects gracefully with 'return -1'.

verdict.summary: SparseDenseCwise kernel Compute(): every attacker-data sink is guarded. Sparse indices are bounds-checked per element via FastBoundsCheck against the broadcasted dense dimensions and rejected with OP_REQUIRES(indices_valid) inside the nnz loop, in execution order, before rhs_ref.coeff(idx); broadcast compatibility is enforced by VecGreaterEq(lhs_dims, rhs_dims) && b.IsValid(); gathered dense values are checked non-zero for Div kernels before the binaryExpr division; allocation results, shape/rank consistency (shape width == indices width, values length == nnz), and output/temp sizes are all validated with OP_REQUIRES/OP_REQUIRES_OK. verdict.summary: LoaderS3M::load copies the order list into the fixed-capacity array header->ord with the destination index j bounded only by the attacker-supplied 16-bit header->ordnum (up to 65535, read at line 24) and a 0xFF terminator. evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write: the copy loop's only bounds are the attacker-controlled count header->ordnum (0-65535) and the terminator check 'if (orders[i] == 255) break;'. The destination index j is never compared to the capacity of the fixed struct member header->ord. Instantiated trigger: an S3M with ordnum = 0xFFFF whose 65535 order bytes contain no 0xFF executes 'header->ord[j++] = orders[i]' for j = 0..65534, overflowing module->header with attacker-chosen bytes. STEP 5 searched for a j bounds check, an ordnum clamp, a corrected loop bound, a resized destination, a bounds-safe accessor, an error arm, and a failure-sentinel test - none exists on any path.

verdict.summary: MakeDataset accepts an `indices` matrix without checking that it has at least one column, then unconditionally reads `indices->matrix<int64>()(i, 0)` for every row in the batch-ordering loop, before sparse::SparseTensor::Create performs any validation. An attacker supplying an indices tensor of shape [N, 0] (a rank-0 sparse tensor: a valid 2-D matrix with 0 elements, e.g. via tf.raw_ops.SparseTensorSliceDataset) makes the loop read element (i,0), which does not exist in the zero-element backing buffer, causing a heap out-of-bounds read (or null dereference). The iteration count is attacker-controlled and decoupled from allocation size (e.g. [2^31, 0] drives ~2 billion out-of-bounds reads), so the direct consequences are a memory-safety violation and denial of service of the process executing the attacker's graph. No check anywhere on any path rejects the zero-column matrix.

evidence.reason: Root cause: unguarded element read `indices->matrix<int64>()(i, 0)` inside the ordering loop. The loop bound `i < indices->dim_size(0)` executes for any N >= 1, but no statement verifies dim_size(1) >= 1 or that the tensor has any elements; the in-loop OP_REQUIRES only inspects the value after it has already been read, and sparse::SparseTensor::Create (line 42) runs after the loop, too late in execution order. Instantiated trigger: indices shape [3, 0] (int64, 0 elements) passes IsMatrix at line 11, so iteration i=0 reads element (0,0) of a zero-element buffer — an out-of-bounds read repeated N times with N attacker-scalable.

OP_REQUIRES(ctx, TensorShapeUtils::IsMatrix(indices->shape()),
                errors::InvalidArgument(

                    indices->shape().DebugString()));
evidence.reason: The only shape validation applied to `indices` before the out-of-bounds read at line 32. `TensorShapeUtils::IsMatrix` verifies only that the rank is 2, so a matrix with zero columns (shape [N, 0], 0 elements) is accepted; the missing-check site for the second dimension is here and on the loop at lines 31-32.

assumptions: MakeDataset is an op-kernel handler invoked by the graph runtime; the contents, shapes, and element values of the `indices`, `values`, and `dense_shape` tensors are attacker-controlled per the data-origin impact model (values passed to a handler function).

Tensor::matrix<int64>()/vec<int64>() and the Eigen TensorMap do not enforce dtype or bounds in release builds (callee not shown); this is assumed standard TensorFlow release behavior, since Eigen assertions are compiled out.
A 0-element tensor's backing buffer is either nullptr or a 0-byte allocation; reading element (i,0) is out of bounds or a null dereference in either case.

verdict.summary: In the decrypt path of ccp_run_aes_gcm_cmd, ilen = aes->src_len - authsize is computed on unsigned ints with no check that aes->src_len >= authsize anywhere in the function (the only input validations are the iv/key NULL checks, the key_len comparison, and the authsize switch). Behavior of the not-shown helpers scatterwalk_ffwd, ccp_init_data, ccp_set_dm_area, ccp_get_dm_area is not quoted; only their in-code call sites with the underflowed ilen are relied on.

Instantiated trigger: client sends the 9-byte segment [0x06,0,0,0,0xFF,0xFF,0xFF,0xFF,0x41]; len=9 fails 'len == 1' and 'len == 8', so line 77 passes dlen = 0xFFFFFFFF and data + 8 (with one received payload byte) to client_cut_text with no dlen-versus-len check and no 1MB cap on this path.

assumptions: The not-shown VNC read loop invokes protocol_client_msg with the accumulated byte count, so len can be any value >= 1 depending on client-controlled TCP segmentation; the code's own varied exact-equality tests (len == 1, 2, 4, 8) and per-case 'return N' accumulation requests indicate len is variable, but no caller statement is quotable.

The connection is assumed to be a post-handshake VNC client; the code is the trust-boundary intake for its message content either way.

verdict.summary: ReadMATImage's 4D-matrix frame loop is bounded solely by the raw 32-bit frame count read from the file (`Frames = ReadBlobXXXLong(image2);`) with no sanity bound: `if(--Frames>0) { ... goto NEXT_FRAME; }` bypasses the outer EOF-checked while loop, so each of up to 2^32-1 iterations performs heavy allocations (RotateImage, AcquireNextImage, SetImageExtent) and leaks a QuantumInfo (no Relinquish/DestroyQuantumInfo exists anywhere in the function), while retaining one rotated image plus a new image in the list per frame — a few-hundred-byte file yields unbounded CPU and memory consumption (CWE-400/CWE-401). Additionally, compressed (zlib) objects whose decompressed type is not miMATRIX take `if(MATLAB_HDR.DataType!=miMATRIX) continue;` without destroying the decompressed image or closing/removing clone_info->file, leaking an Image plus an open temp file per such object (CWE-401).

Each iteration re-executes quantum_info=AcquireQuantumInfo (leaked, never relinquished), SetImageExtent, RotateImage + AppendImageToList (retained image per frame), and AcquireNextImage — unbounded work and memory retention from a tiny crafted file (CWE-400). No range check or clamp on Frames exists anywhere in the function.

Origin of the tainted loop bound: Frames is taken verbatim from the attacker-supplied MAT file (a raw 32-bit read) with no sanity validation — unlike z, which is immediately range-checked in the same case block.

verdict.summary: DecodeImageAPNG parses attacker-supplied file bytes and, in the fcTL branch, reads fixed offsets chunk.p+12 through chunk.p+33 (w0, h0, x0, y0, delay, dop, bop) without ever validating chunk.size against the 34 bytes required. A truncated fcTL chunk (e.g., 16 bytes total) causes heap out-of-bounds reads of up to 18 bytes past the chunk buffer; the only checks present (id != 0 and chunk.p != nullptr) and the later value checks at lines 153-155 all run after or independently of the out-of-bounds reads.

evidence.reason: Root cause: out-of-bounds heap read (CWE-125). chunk.p is a heap buffer whose extent is the file-derived chunk.size (produced at line 64, 'id = read_chunk(&r, &chunk);'), yet these statements read fixed offsets up to chunk.p[33] with no size check anywhere on the path (the branch never references chunk.size; the value checks at lines 153-155 execute after the reads). Instantiated trigger: a file consisting of the PNG signature, a valid 25-byte IHDR, and a truncated fcTL chunk with 8 bytes of data (chunk.size = 16) enters the branch via 'id == kId_fcTL && (!hasInfo || isAnimated)' with hasInfo == false, then line 143 reads chunk.p+16..+19 and lines 144-149 continue through chunk.p[33] — reads 18 bytes past the end of the 16-byte allocation.

Origin of the tainted buffer: read_chunk parses attacker file bytes into chunk.p/chunk.size. The only validations before use are 'if (!id) break;' (tests the chunk id, not the size) and 'JXL_ASSERT(chunk.p != nullptr)' (tests only NULL, not the buffer extent), so a short fcTL chunk reaches the fixed-offset reads at lines 142-149 with an undersized buffer.

assumptions: read_chunk (not shown) allocates chunk.p with an extent derived from the chunk length in the file, i.e., no larger than the bytes actually present; the out-of-bounds distance at lines 142-149 is computed relative to that extent.
cMaxPNGSize is referenced but its value is not present in the given code; the IHDR bounds check at line 43 cannot be edge-tested numerically.

processing_start/processing_data/processing_finish, read_chunk, isAbc, Reader::Eof/Read, and the CHUNK/APNGFrame definitions are not shown; their internal behavior is not relied on for the primary finding.

verdict.summary: In php_wddx_pop_element, when the top stack entry has NULL data and stack->top == 1, the else arm sets stack->done = 1 and executes efree(ent1) without decrementing stack->top and without clearing the stack slot. Every other pop path in the function does stack->top--, so this is the sole inconsistent path. Because the function never reads stack->done, a subsequent sibling value element in the same attacker-supplied WDDX packet (e.g. '<string></string><string>AAAA</string>') causes a later invocation to fetch the freed st_entry via wddx_stack_top(stack, &ent2) and dereference ent2->type and ent2->data (and Z_TYPE_P(ent2->data)), reading freed heap memory that the attacker can groom during the same parse; the dangling ent2->data is then passed to zval_ptr_dtor (invalid free), HASH_OF, zend_hash_merge, and written via ent2->data = obj. This is a use-after-free memory-corruption primitive reachable from untrusted serialized input.

evidence.reason: Root cause / dangling-pointer origin: when stack->top == 1 and ent1->data == NULL, the else arm sets stack->done = 1 and then efree(ent1) without decrementing stack->top and without clearing elements[0], unlike the sibling arm which does stack->top--. The freed st_entry therefore remains installed at stack index 0 with stack->top still equal to 1, and stack->done is never read anywhere in this function, so nothing prevents a later invocation from fetching this freed entry.

UAF sink: instantiated trigger is the packet '<wddxPacket version='1.0'><header/><data><string></string><string>AAAA</string></data></wddxPacket>'. First '</string>' pop runs with top==1, hits the else arm (done=1, efree(elements[0]), top left at 1). The second '<string>' push makes top==2; its '</string>' pop passes 'stack->top > 1', decrements top to 1, and wddx_stack_top returns the freed entry as ent2. 'ent2->type == ST_FIELD && ent2->data == NULL' then reads freed memory; the subsequent Z_TYPE_P(ent2->data), zval_ptr_dtor(&ent2->data), HASH_OF(ent2->data) and ent2->data = obj operate on attacker-groomable freed-chunk contents, giving an out-of-bounds/invalid-free memory-corruption primitive plus attacker-scalable denial of service via a single crafted packet.

assumptions: wddx_stack_top (callee not shown) returns stack->elements[stack->top-1] without popping; the guard 'if (stack->top == 0) { return; }' (line 13) ensures top >= 1 at both call sites (lines 22 and 62), so the unchecked return values cannot yield a NULL ent1/ent2 from an empty stack.

The companion handlers php_wddx_push_element and the character-data handler (not shown) push st_entry records with data == NULL for value elements and allocate ent->data from character content; the given code's own branch 'if (!ent1->data)' establishes NULL-data entries as a normal, handled state for empty elements such as <string></string>.
The XML parser continues invoking this end-element handler after stack->done is set; no statement in this function reads stack->done, and its consumer is not shown.
<header>, <data> and <wddxPacket> are not pushed onto the wddx_stack by the push handler (not shown), so a top-level value element sits at stack index 0 with top == 1.
limitations: Candidate C2 (NULL dereference of ent2->data when ent2->data == NULL and ent2->type != ST_FIELD, bypassing the 'ent2->type == ST_FIELD && ent2->data == NULL' guard) was not instantiated: no statement in the given code produces a non-ST_FIELD stack entry with NULL data; the push handler that would create such entries is not shown.
